title: When Agent Governance Helps
comment: 35 pages, 14 figures. Companion empirical study to a Purdue D.Tech dissertation. Introduces the GAMPO framework from a 321-source qualitative evidence synthesis and probes a prompt-layer instantiation on the CHI-Bench healthcare benchmark across open and frontier models
summary: No specification says how a governed autotelic AI agent organization, where agents pursue self-generated goals inside guardrails, should be designed and evaluated. We answer in two parts. First, we synthesize the Governed Autotelic Multi-Agent Product Organization (GAMPO) framework from a document-based qualitative evidence synthesis of 321 sources, integrating agency, agile, platform, and governance theory into a runnable specification. Second, we probe a prompt-layer instantiation of GAMPO on CHI-Bench, a long-horizon healthcare benchmark, across open and frontier models. The result is a boundary condition: governance benefit is gated by a model's spare capacity and is domain- and model-specific. On capacity-constrained open models the full procedure yields no reliable benefit, whereas a single "verify your writes" sentence doubles task success (pass@1 2/20 to 4/20). At the frontier the same scaffold lifts prior-authorization 24% to 40% but nets zero on another model, a gap traced to a stable recommendation-override disposition. A second result refines the first: replacing the generic procedure with an answer-blind, per-task definition-of-done, keyed only to the case's own policy and published standards, never the hidden key, raises prior-authorization to 84% under best-of-five self-consistency (68% single-attempt, confirmed by a held-out board) and utilization-management to 44%, while care-management meets a subjective content-quality wall. The contribution is a named, auditable framework and capability-gated evidence that governance should be sized to spare capacity, and that at the frontier a case-grounded specification beats a uniform procedure. Findings are exploratory: partial instantiation, small per-cell samples (n = 5-25), and single trials.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and probes a framework (GAMPO) for governing self-directed multi-agent AI systems, showing that governance benefits depend on model capacity and are highly domain- and model-specific.
AI.motivation: There is no existing specification for how to design and evaluate governed autotelic (self-goal-generating) AI agent organizations that operate within guardrails. As multi-agent, tool-using systems become more powerful and autonomous, we lack principled, auditable frameworks for structuring governance and understanding when it actually helps or harms performance, especially on complex, long-horizon domains such as healthcare.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a document-based qualitative evidence synthesis of 321 sources spanning agency theory, agile methods, platform design, and governance theory. From this, they synthesize the Governed Autotelic Multi-Agent Product Organization (GAMPO) framework as a concrete, runnable specification for multi-agent governance. They then implement a prompt-layer instantiation of GAMPO and evaluate it on CHI-Bench, a long-horizon healthcare benchmark, using both open and frontier language models. They systematically vary governance scaffolds (full procedure, minimal hints like “verify your writes,” and case-specific definitions-of-done) and measure performance across tasks (e.g., prior authorization, utilization management, care management), including best-of-five self-consistency and external board confirmation for some results.
AI.result: 1) Governance benefits are gated by a model’s spare capacity and vary by model and domain. On capacity-constrained open models, the full GAMPO-style governance procedure provides no reliable benefit, but a minimal scaffold (“verify your writes”) modestly improves pass@1 from 2/20 to 4/20. On frontier models, the same scaffold raises prior-authorization performance from 24% to 40% on one model, but yields no net gain on another, whose behavior reflects a stable tendency to override recommendations. 2) A refined governance design—replacing a generic procedure with an answer-blind, per-task definition-of-done, keyed solely to each case’s policy and published standards (never the hidden ground-truth key)—substantially boosts performance: prior-authorization to 84% under best-of-five self-consistency (68% single-shot, validated by a held-out expert board) and utilization management to 44%. However, for care-management tasks, performance appears limited by a qualitative content-quality ceiling rather than procedural governance alone. These findings are based on partial framework instantiation, small per-condition sample sizes (n = 5–25), and single experimental runs, so they are exploratory.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces GAMPO, a named and auditable framework for governing autotelic multi-agent AI organizations, and provides capability-gated evidence about how governance should be applied. Governance mechanisms should be scaled to a model’s spare capacity: heavy governance can fail to help capacity-constrained models, which may instead benefit from very lightweight prompts, while high-capacity frontier models can gain substantially from structured, case-grounded specifications. Moreover, at the frontier, a case-specific, policy-grounded definition-of-done outperforms a one-size-fits-all generic procedure. The results are preliminary but suggest design principles for aligning and evaluating complex, self-directed multi-agent AI systems, especially in high-stakes, long-horizon domains like healthcare.

title: TamilEOT: A Dataset and Model for Semantic End-of-Turn Detection in Tamil Telephone Speech
comment: 13 pages, 7 tables. Code, data and models: https://github.com/santhosh-005/tamil-eot
summary: A voice agent has to decide, at every pause, whether the user has finished speaking. Without a model of the language that decision falls back to a fixed silence timeout: set it short and the agent interrupts, set it long and every turn pays the full wait. Open semantic end-of-turn detectors exist, but to our knowledge none covers a South Indian language. We release TamilEOT: 18,485 labelled turn boundaries cut from 116 real Tamil telephone conversations, and two audio-only detectors fine-tuned from Smart Turn v3. On a held-out split of 4,168 clips from 30 unseen calls, accuracy rises from 70.30% zero-shot to 83.71% (8.7 MB) and 86.13% (21 MB); ROC-AUC rises from 0.751 to 0.921. Both models run in under 150 ms single-threaded on a laptop CPU. We also report what building it cost. Rule-derived labels, checked against a blind human listening pass, were right 95.9% of the time on the positive class and 44.4% on the negative class, which is below chance, because the rule answered a different question than the model is asked. Replacing them with an audio-LLM labeller measured at 97.5% human agreement cost US$5.69. Of every training lever we measured, only encoder capacity moved the result; three runs at identical config and seed span 0.87 accuracy points, which is the floor below which none of our other deltas mean anything. Replaying the same labelled boundaries through the production VAD and streaming adapter costs a further 2.60 points, and 7.8% of boundaries are never surfaced to the model at all. Data, weights, code and every negative result are public.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TamilEOT, a dataset and models for detecting end-of-turn points in Tamil telephone conversations, achieving strong accuracy and latency while fully releasing data, code, and negative results.
AI.motivation: Voice agents must decide in real time when a user has finished speaking. Without language-aware end-of-turn (EOT) detection, systems rely on fixed silence timeouts, which either cause interruptions (if too short) or unnecessary delays (if too long). Existing semantic EOT detectors have not covered South Indian languages like Tamil, leaving a gap in resources and benchmarks for these languages in conversational AI.
AI.method: The authors compile TamilEOT, a dataset of 18,485 labeled turn boundaries extracted from 116 real Tamil telephone calls. They fine-tune two audio-only EOT detectors from a base model (Smart Turn v3) and evaluate them on a held-out split of 4,168 clips from 30 unseen calls. Initial labels are derived using rules, then quality-checked via blind human listening, revealing asymmetrical precision (high for positives, low for negatives) because the rules target a different decision task than the model’s. They then replace the rule-based labels with annotations from an audio-LLM labeller that shows 97.5% agreement with humans at a cost of US$5.69. Multiple training levers (hyperparameters, etc.) are probed, with encoder capacity emerging as the only factor that consistently impacts performance, and they quantify run-to-run variance as a noise floor for interpreting gains. They also evaluate deployment effects by feeding the same boundaries through the production VAD and streaming pipeline to measure real-world degradation and dropped boundaries.
AI.result: On the held-out test set, accuracy improves from 70.30% for a zero-shot baseline to 83.71% for the 8.7 MB model and 86.13% for the 21 MB model, with ROC-AUC increasing from 0.751 to 0.921. Both models run in under 150 ms on a single laptop CPU thread, meeting real-time constraints. Rule-derived labels are 95.9% correct on positive-class examples but only 44.4% on negatives; the audio-LLM labeller reaches 97.5% agreement with humans at a very low total monetary cost. Encoder capacity is found to be the only training lever with a clear impact, and three identical-config runs vary by up to 0.87 accuracy points, defining a practical variance floor. When integrated with production VAD and streaming, performance drops by an additional 2.60 accuracy points, and 7.8% of boundaries never reach the model.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first open Tamil end-of-turn dataset and strong audio-only EOT models that run in real time on commodity hardware, significantly improving over zero-shot performance. Label quality and model capacity are key determinants of success, while other training tweaks often fall below the noise introduced by run-to-run variability. Real-world deployment via existing VAD and streaming infrastructure incurs non-trivial performance loss and missing boundaries, underlining the importance of end-to-end evaluation. By releasing data, models, code, and negative findings, the authors aim to catalyze further research on EOT detection for low-resource and South Indian languages and to foster more transparent evaluation of conversational agents in practical settings.

title: Better Together: Complementary Query Rewriting Under a Strong RAG Baseline
summary: A popular way to improve Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is to rewrite the user's question into several variants and search with all of them. We test whether this actually helps once the underlying search is already strong. Under one fixed, competitive pipeline (BGE dense retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and MMR diversification), we compare four query-rewriting strategies (S1-S4) against two strong LLM baselines (HyDE, Query2Doc) on three datasets (HotpotQA, AmbigNQ, and the 512K-document EnterpriseRAG-Bench) over three seeds with paired-bootstrap significance tests. Our headline result is that rewriting alone is at best competitive with a strong baseline, but combining methods yields outsized gains because different strategies fail on different questions. A post-hoc union of four methods (S1+S3+S4+HyDE) improves HIT@10 over the baseline by +12.5 points on enterprise data (51.70 vs 39.22), and a five-method union reaches 52.98 (+13.8). Budget-matched controls capture only ~40% of this gain, confirming that complementarity, not retrieval budget, is the primary driver. On HotpotQA the union adds +1.6 to +1.8 points (p<0.001), saturating the all-method oracle; on AmbigNQ the same fusion hurts (-2.4 below the best solo, p<0.001), and we analyze when and why. Because rewriting is expensive, we evaluate in simulation a confidence-gated router that runs rewriting only when the baseline's own top-1 score is low. It captures about half of the enterprise full-merge gain (+4.3 HIT@10) while paying rewriting cost on <40% of queries, and automatically declines to rewrite on AmbigNQ. A downstream answer-quality evaluation confirms the router improves F1 by +1.92 (p<0.01) at roughly 40% of the expansion cost. In short: treat query rewriting as a complementary coverage source, applied through cost-aware routing, not as a standalone replacement for a strong baseline.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether query rewriting still helps Retrieval-Augmented Generation when the underlying retrieval stack is already strong, and finds that rewriting alone is only competitive, but diverse methods combined via unions and cost-aware routing provide substantial complementary gains.
AI.motivation: Many RAG systems improve retrieval by generating multiple reformulations of the user query, but much prior work assumes relatively weak retrieval backends. It is unclear if query rewriting adds value beyond a strong modern pipeline (dense retrieval, reranking, diversification), and how to best exploit it given its computational cost. The paper aims to rigorously test the real benefit of rewriting in such strong settings and to understand when, why, and how to use it effectively.
AI.method: The authors fix a strong retrieval pipeline using BGE dense retrieval, cross-encoder reranking, and MMR diversification, then plug in four query rewriting strategies (S1–S4) and two strong LLM-based expansion baselines (HyDE and Query2Doc). They evaluate on three datasets—HotpotQA, AmbigNQ, and EnterpriseRAG-Bench (512K docs)—over three random seeds and use paired-bootstrap significance tests. They compare standalone methods, method unions (e.g., S1+S3+S4+HyDE, five-method union), and budget-matched controls to separate complementarity from pure retrieval-budget effects. They also simulate a confidence-gated router that triggers rewriting only when the baseline top-1 score is low, and evaluate both retrieval metrics (HIT@10) and downstream answer quality (F1).
AI.result: Standalone query rewriting strategies are at best competitive with the strong baseline retrieval stack, not clearly superior. However, unions of multiple complementary methods deliver substantial gains: on EnterpriseRAG, a union of four methods boosts HIT@10 by +12.5 points (51.70 vs 39.22), and a five-method union reaches 52.98 (+13.8). Budget-matched controls explain only about 40% of this improvement, showing that complementarity across methods—each succeeding on different questions—is the main driver. On HotpotQA, the union adds +1.6 to +1.8 HIT@10 points (p<0.001) and essentially saturates an oracle; on AmbigNQ, the same fusion actually hurts performance (-2.4 vs the best solo, p<0.001), and the paper analyzes those failure modes. A simulated confidence-gated router recovers about half the full-merge gain on EnterpriseRAG (+4.3 HIT@10) while invoking rewriting for under 40% of queries, and naturally avoids rewriting on AmbigNQ. Downstream, the router increases answer F1 by +1.92 (p<0.01) at roughly 40% of the expansion cost.
AI.conclusion: Query rewriting should not be viewed as a replacement for a well-designed retrieval baseline, since alone it only matches strong systems. Its real value is as a complementary coverage mechanism: diverse rewriting/expansion strategies succeed on different queries, and combining them via unions yields large improvements that cannot be explained by budget alone. Because rewriting is costly and not universally beneficial (e.g., AmbigNQ), a cost-aware, confidence-gated routing policy is recommended: only apply rewriting when the baseline appears uncertain. Properly routed, rewriting delivers substantial retrieval and answer-quality gains at a fraction of the full expansion cost.

title: Who Maintains Agent Skills? A Longitudinal Study of Human-Governed, AI-Assisted Skill Maintenance
summary: Lifelong LLM agents increasingly rely on external skill artifacts as one element for preserving and reusing capabilities over time. These skills (usually portable Markdown files such as SKILL.md) describe when and how to apply a capability and must be corrected, expanded, and consolidated as tools and usage patterns shift over deployment. Recent work seeks to automate skill curation, but it largely evaluates against automated baselines and treats human maintenance as an unmeasured bottleneck. We study that missing process directly. We mine the full commit histories of five public AI-skill repositories, a purposive sample of AI-tooling organizations, covering 873 commits, 143 skill files, and 254 substantive post-creation edits from October 2025 to June 2026. We code each edit with pre-registered governance, operation, and trigger-evidence codebooks. Three findings emerge. First, every substantive edit is authored or merged through a named human account, while 62% carry an AI co-author trailer, with large repository-level variation. Second, these edits are genuine curation: an audited sample shows that most change skill content, and the coded operations are dominated by additions and corrections. Third, a pre-registered rule-likeness axis fails its reliability gate; reliably coding rule-likeness from commit artifacts remains an open measurement problem. We release the corpus, codebooks, mining scripts, and a replay protocol for automated skill curators. For self-evolving agents, public skill maintenance currently looks less like an autonomous pipeline than a human-governed, AI-assisted loop that future curators must measure against and operate within.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically studies how human developers actually maintain and curate external skill files (e.g., SKILL.md) used by lifelong LLM agents, using commit histories from public repositories, and finds that skill maintenance is a human-governed, AI-assisted process rather than a fully autonomous pipeline.
AI.motivation: Lifelong LLM agents depend on external skill artifacts to preserve and reuse capabilities as tools and usage patterns change over time. While recent research aims to automate the curation of these skills, it typically compares against automated baselines and implicitly treats human maintenance as an unexamined bottleneck. There is little empirical understanding of how skill files are actually edited and governed in practice, who performs these edits, and what kinds of changes are made. This gap makes it hard to design realistic automated skill curators or evaluate them against real-world human workflows.
AI.method: The authors select a purposive sample of five public AI-skill repositories from AI-tooling organizations and mine their full git commit histories between October 2025 and June 2026. The dataset includes 873 commits, 143 distinct skill files, and 254 substantive post-creation edits. They pre-register codebooks for annotating each substantive edit along three dimensions: governance (who is involved, how decisions are made), operation (what kind of change is made, such as addition, correction, or refactor), and trigger-evidence (what evidence or events led to the change). They then manually code the edits according to these codebooks and analyze patterns such as human vs AI authorship, the nature of changes, and the degree of rule-likeness of the skills. They also attempt to validate a pre-registered quantitative axis for measuring how rule-like each skill edit is, testing inter-rater reliability.
AI.result: (1) Authorship: Every substantive edit is either authored or merged through a named human account, showing that humans remain in the loop for all important skill changes. However, 62% of substantive edits include an AI co-author trailer, indicating that AI tools are widely used to assist with editing; this proportion varies substantially between repositories. (2) Nature of edits: Manual audit confirms that the majority of substantive commits actually change the content of the skills rather than being purely cosmetic. The coded operations are mainly additions and corrections, demonstrating that these edits are genuine curation and iterative improvement rather than simple reformatting or bulk generation. (3) Measurement challenge: The pre-registered "rule-likeness" axis, intended to quantify how rule-like or prescriptive a skill is, fails its reliability gate—annotators cannot consistently code this dimension from commit artifacts. This reveals that reliably measuring rule-likeness from version control history alone is currently not feasible. The authors also release the mined corpus, codebooks, scripts, and a replay protocol designed to support benchmarking of automated skill curation systems.
AI.conclusion: Public skill maintenance for self-evolving LLM agents currently functions as a human-governed, AI-assisted loop rather than an autonomous end-to-end pipeline. Humans remain responsible for authoring, reviewing, and merging substantive changes to skill files, with AI tools playing a supportive co-authoring role. Skill curation work primarily consists of meaningful additions and corrections to existing skills. Attempts to automatically and reliably code higher-level properties like rule-likeness from commit traces remain problematic, highlighting an open measurement challenge. The released datasets and tools provide a real-world benchmark environment for future automated skill curators, which should be evaluated against and designed to fit into this human-centered maintenance ecosystem.

title: Beyond Right and Wrong: Evaluating Second-order Social Reasoning in Large Language Models
summary: Previous AI alignment efforts have focused primarily on first-order social norms -- teaching models what is socially acceptable or unacceptable (e.g., `do not steal'). However, social intelligence depends not only on norm recognition, but also on anticipating who will enforce it and how (e.g., public shame or even imprisonment). These second-order expectations, known as metanorms, govern how people respond when social rules are broken. We introduce a novel framework for evaluating metanorm reasoning in Large Language Models (LLMs) along two dimensions: emotional appraisal and behavioral response, and propose new classification tasks, namely, predicting self-regulation in violators, and other-regulation in observers. We release a multi-perspective dataset, NormReact, of 450 norm violation scenarios, hand-annotated for emotions and behavioral responses across norm violators' gender and observers' social closeness. Current LLMs portray a harsher social world: across six models, they overpredict negative sanctions where humans would expect inaction, and alignment with human judgments deteriorates as social distance increases. These findings suggest that AI systems in norm-sensitive domains from conflict mediation to policy simulation, may risk producing a distorted picture of social regulation: one that over-represents punishment and under-represents the tolerance, restraint, and relational calibration that characterize actual norm enforcement in real world.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework and dataset to test whether LLMs understand not just social norms but also how people react when norms are broken (metanorms), finding that models systematically over-predict punishment compared to humans, especially as social distance grows.
AI.motivation: Most AI alignment work focuses on teaching models which actions violate social norms, but real social intelligence also requires understanding how people enforce norms and react emotionally to violations. Without modeling these metanorms, AI systems used in sensitive social contexts (e.g., conflict mediation, policy simulation) may misrepresent how social regulation actually works, exaggerating punishment and missing tolerance and nuance. The authors aim to fill this gap by formalizing and empirically evaluating metanorm reasoning in LLMs.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that decomposes metanorm reasoning into two dimensions: (1) emotional appraisal (how agents feel about a norm violation) and (2) behavioral response (how they act in response). They instantiate this via two classification tasks: predicting self-regulation (how violators will regulate themselves) and other-regulation (how observers will react). They construct NormReact, a dataset of 450 norm-violation scenarios, each annotated by humans for emotions and behavioral responses while varying the violator’s gender and the observer’s social closeness. Multiple LLMs (six models) are then evaluated on these tasks, and their predictions are compared with human annotations as a function of social distance and other factors.
AI.result: Across six LLMs, the models tend to predict a ‘harsher’ social world than humans report. They systematically overestimate the likelihood of negative sanctions or punitive responses in cases where humans would typically expect no action or mild reactions. Furthermore, the alignment between LLM predictions and human judgments worsens as the social distance between observer and violator increases; the models do not capture the nuanced calibration of responses based on relationship closeness. This pattern holds across emotional and behavioral dimensions in the proposed tasks.
AI.conclusion: LLMs, even when aligned on first-order social norms, exhibit systematic biases in metanorm reasoning: they over-represent punishment and under-represent tolerance and contextual restraint, particularly in distant social relationships. This miscalibration implies that AI systems deployed in norm-sensitive applications (e.g., conflict resolution, forecasting social responses to policy) may generate distorted depictions of social life, potentially amplifying perceptions of conflict and sanction. The work highlights the need for alignment efforts that explicitly target metanorm understanding and encourages further dataset and method development to bring model predictions closer to real-world patterns of social regulation.

title: A Rubric-Guided Large Language Model Solution for Opioid Use Disorder Computable Phenotyping
summary: Opioid use disorder (OUD) remains a public health crisis in the United States, yet it is difficult to identify from electronic health records (EHRs) because missing diagnosis codes and supporting evidence are buried in clinical narratives. Accurate OUD identification is critical to support interventions and improve health outcomes. This study developed a rubric-guided large language model (LLM) that incorporated Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) for OUD computable phenotyping (CP). The framework used an 18-item, expert-identified rubric to instruct LLMs to automatically extract critical text with supporting evidence to determine OUD flags. Two UF Health physicians (GMR and WMG) chart-reviewed 253 patients, including 68 OUD-positive cases. Our LLM-based computable phenotype (CP) achieved the best F1 score of 0.774 and an AUROC of 0.934, outperforming the machine learning-based CP using EHR and natural language processing-extracted variables, and zero-shot LLMs by relative F1 improvements of 12.8% and 44.4%, respectively. The proposed LLM-based CP could link LLM-extracted evidence to OUD phenotyping for better explainability.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a rubric-guided, prompt-optimized large language model to identify opioid use disorder from EHR clinical notes, achieving higher accuracy than prior machine learning and zero-shot LLM approaches.
AI.motivation: Opioid use disorder is under-diagnosed in structured EHR data because key evidence is missing or hidden in unstructured clinical notes, making accurate identification for interventions difficult. Existing machine learning phenotypes rely on coded data and limited NLP features and may miss nuanced clinical patterns, so there is a need for a more accurate and explainable automated phenotyping method.
AI.method: The authors design a computable phenotype framework that uses an expert-created 18-item rubric to guide a large language model. They integrate Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) to iteratively refine prompts so the LLM can systematically extract relevant textual evidence from clinical narratives and assign OUD flags. The approach is evaluated on 253 chart-reviewed patients (68 OUD-positive) from UF Health and compared against a traditional ML-based phenotype built from structured EHR data and NLP-derived variables, as well as zero-shot LLM baselines.
AI.result: The rubric-guided, OPRO-optimized LLM-based computable phenotype achieves an F1 score of 0.774 and AUROC of 0.934 for OUD identification. This performance exceeds that of the existing machine learning-based phenotype and zero-shot LLMs, with relative F1 gains of 12.8% over the ML model and 44.4% over zero-shot LLMs.
AI.conclusion: A rubric-guided, prompt-optimized LLM can more accurately and explainably identify opioid use disorder from EHR clinical notes than prior ML and zero-shot LLM approaches. By linking extracted text evidence to phenotype decisions, the method improves transparency and has potential to enhance OUD surveillance and support targeted clinical interventions.

title: CriticGen: Generation-Aware Evaluation as Actionable Feedback
summary: Current evaluation methods for large language models are coarse-grained and decoupled from generation, producing generic explanations that fail to provide actionable feedback for model improvement. We propose CriticGen, a fine-grained, generation-aware evaluation framework that turns evaluation into actionable control for answer improvement. CriticGen first generates sample-specific evaluation dimensions and scoring criteria under high-level categories such as subjective, objective, and self-derived constraints. These criteria then serve as a dynamic rubric for jointly producing a score, a reason, an executable refinement suggestion, and a refined answer. This rubric-conditioned refinement process enables models to diagnose flaws and perform targeted answer improvement. Experimental results show that fine-grained evaluation should be both instance-specific and actionable. CriticGen induces higher-quality rubrics, improving relevance/coverage from 3.33/4.03 to 3.97/4.24. CriticGen also achieves the best score correlations, with 0.9556 Pearson and 0.9560 Spearman, and raises the F1 of criterion-grounded reasons and executable suggestions from 0.6369/0.5994 to 0.7554/0.7900. Crucially, its feedback translates into reliable answer improvement, improving 73.17% of answers with a 93.28% non-degradation rate.

AI.tldr: CriticGen is a framework that makes LLM evaluation fine-grained, instance-specific, and directly tied to generating better answers rather than just scores.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluation is coarse and detached from the generation process, yielding generic feedback that does not help improve specific answers. The authors want an evaluation method that produces detailed, per-instance guidance that can actually refine model outputs.
AI.method: CriticGen first generates sample-specific evaluation dimensions and criteria under broad categories (subjective, objective, self-derived constraints). These criteria form a dynamic rubric that conditions the model to output, in one shot, a score, an explanation, an executable refinement suggestion, and a revised answer. The process couples evaluation and generation through rubric-conditioned refinement.
AI.result: Compared with baselines, CriticGen produces higher-quality, more relevant and comprehensive rubrics (relevance/coverage from 3.33/4.03 to 3.97/4.24), achieves the best correlation with gold scores (Pearson 0.9556, Spearman 0.9560), and substantially improves the F1 of criterion-grounded reasons and executable suggestions (from 0.6369/0.5994 to 0.7554/0.7900). Its feedback leads to improved answers in 73.17% of cases, with 93.28% of refinements not degrading quality.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained LLM evaluation should be instance-specific and actionable. By generating dynamic rubrics and using them to jointly evaluate and refine answers, CriticGen not only measures quality more faithfully but also reliably improves model outputs in practice.

title: Intra-Prompt Parallel Decoding for Common-Context Question Answering
summary: In common-context question answering (CCQA) tasks, multiple input questions share a common context to base their answers from. However, Large Language Models typically generate each answer using an independent prompt. While existing batching and caching techniques help improve parallelism and reduce repeated computations, the separation of questions across prompts limits the achievable speedup, as modern GPUs are underutilized due to a memory bottleneck during attention. We present Intra-Prompt Parallel Decoding (IPPD), a novel inference method that answers multiple common-context questions in parallel within a single prompt. IPPD directly addresses the bottleneck by efficiently sharing both memory and computation during the attention process, as the next token for every question is decoded in a single inference step. IPPD uses virtual position IDs and attention mask manipulation to generate the same output as standard prompting without requiring fine-tuning or any changes to the LLM architecture. Since all parallelism occurs within a prompt, IPPD is fully compatible with batched inference, even when each prompt features a different context. Our experiments show that IPPD delivers up to 7X the effective throughput as standard decoding without quality degradation, and outperforms prefix caching with PagedAttention in most settings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Intra-Prompt Parallel Decoding (IPPD), a method to answer many questions sharing a common context in parallel within a single prompt to greatly increase LLM inference throughput without changing model architecture or quality.
AI.motivation: Common-context QA workloads ask many questions over the same long passage. Current LLM inference answers each question with a separate prompt, so even with batching and prefix caching, attention remains memory-bound and GPUs are underutilized. The authors want to remove redundant attention work across questions and overcome the memory bottleneck to significantly speed up such workloads while preserving answer quality and avoiding model retraining or architectural changes.
AI.method: The authors design IPPD, an inference-time technique that packs multiple questions that share a context into a single prompt and decodes all of their next tokens in one forward pass. They introduce virtual position IDs and customized attention masks so that each question attends correctly to the shared context and its own history, but not to other questions’ tokens, reproducing standard prompting behavior. This design allows shared key-value memory and fused computation during attention. IPPD is implemented as a drop-in decoding modification, compatible with existing LLMs and with conventional batching across different contexts.
AI.result: Experiments on common-context QA benchmarks show that IPPD can increase effective throughput by up to 7× compared to standard decoding, with no measurable degradation in answer quality. It also outperforms prefix caching combined with PagedAttention in most evaluated configurations, demonstrating both better utilization of GPU resources and lower memory overhead.
AI.conclusion: IPPD is an effective, model-agnostic inference method for accelerating common-context QA by parallelizing decoding within a single prompt. By using virtual positions and attention-mask manipulation to safely share attention computation across questions, it breaks the memory bottleneck that limits existing batching and caching approaches, significantly boosting throughput while maintaining output equivalence to standard prompting and retaining compatibility with current deployment stacks.

title: When Does Memory Help? A Cost-Aware Evaluation of Long-Term Memory in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Long-term memory for LLM agents is evaluated today by conversational recall benchmarks (LoCoMo, LongMemEval), which measure question answering over dialogue history, not whether remembered facts change what a tool-using agent does. We present MERIT (Memory Evaluation for Realistic Instrumented Tasks), a benchmark and harness that measures the marginal utility of memory for task-executing agents under explicit cost accounting. MERIT provides episodic tool-use tasks in three domains whose dependence on earlier-episode facts is verified by an automated leak check; a difficulty ladder ending in updated-fact recall; controlled memory corruption; and full token and dollar metering of every memory operation. Across 23,440 scored episodes ($42.57), a two-generation pilot on gpt-4.1-mini and a preregistered 3-model x 3-seed grid (GPT-4.1, Claude Haiku 4.5; memory side held fixed), memory lifts dependent-task success from a leak-verified floor of 0.00 to 0.55-1.00. On updated facts, embedding retrieval collapses unpredictably (0.30-0.95 across models; max seed gap 0.45), and agents act on a correctly retrieved value only 55% of the time, while update-on-write stores (a structured fact store and, notably, LLM summarization) remain at 0.70-1.00; the hybrid is worse than the fact store alone. A latest-generation spot-check (Claude Sonnet 5, gated on a clean full-replay control) reproduces the pattern. Swapping a memory's implementation moves task success by up to 60 points, and full replay is never economical: the best condition per domain delivers 2.7-3.9x its marginal utility per dollar. We release the benchmark, harness, and all traces.

AI.tldr: MERIT is a new benchmark and evaluation harness that measures how much long-term memory actually helps LLM agents perform realistic, tool-using tasks under explicit cost accounting.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term memory benchmarks for LLMs mostly test conversational recall—whether a model can answer questions about prior dialogue. They do not directly measure whether remembered information changes an agent’s behavior in realistic tool-use settings, nor how this interacts with economic costs. There is also limited understanding of how different memory implementations (e.g., embeddings vs structured stores vs summaries) affect downstream task performance, especially for updated or changing facts.
AI.method: The authors design MERIT, a benchmark consisting of episodic tool-use tasks in three domains, where later tasks depend on facts introduced in earlier episodes. They automatically verify that tasks truly depend on past information by running a leak check. The benchmark includes: (1) a difficulty ladder ending in tasks requiring recall of updated facts; (2) controlled corruption of memory to estimate a leak-verified performance floor; and (3) full token and dollar metering for each memory operation. They run large-scale experiments (23,440 scored episodes) with multiple LLMs (gpt-4.1-mini in a pilot; GPT-4.1 and Claude Haiku 4.5 in a preregistered grid; plus a spot-check with Claude Sonnet 5), systematically varying the memory implementation: embedding-based retrieval, update-on-write structured fact stores, LLM-based summarization, and hybrids.
AI.result: With memory disabled or corrupted to the leak-verified floor, dependent-task success is near 0.00. Adding memory raises success to 0.55–1.00 depending on model and condition, demonstrating strong marginal utility of memory. For tasks involving updated facts, embedding-based retrieval is unstable: success ranges from 0.30–0.95 across models, with a seed-dependent gap of up to 0.45, and agents only act correctly on retrieved values about 55% of the time. In contrast, update-on-write memories—both a structured fact store and LLM summarization—achieve more stable and higher performance (0.70–1.00). Surprisingly, a hybrid of embeddings plus fact store underperforms the fact store alone. A replication with Claude Sonnet 5, under stricter controls, reproduces these qualitative patterns. Changing only the memory implementation can change task success rates by up to 60 percentage points. Full transcript replay is always less cost-effective than more selective memory mechanisms, with the best condition in each domain yielding 2.7–3.9 times higher marginal utility per dollar.
AI.conclusion: MERIT shows that memory can dramatically improve LLM agents’ performance on realistic tool-use tasks, but that the choice of memory implementation is crucial. Embedding retrieval is unreliable for updated facts, while update-on-write approaches—structured fact stores and LLM-based summaries—provide more robust gains. Hybrids are not automatically better, and naïve full replay is never economically optimal. The benchmark and released traces provide a principled way to measure both behavioral impact and cost-efficiency of memory systems, enabling more rigorous design and evaluation of long-term memory for LLM agents.

title: MedWER: A Reproducible, Model-Free Evaluation Protocol for Medical Speech Recognition
comment: 10 pages, 3 tables. Code, term list, and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/Nordis-Tech/medwer. Package: pip install medwer. Source archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22103865
summary: Overall word error rate hides clinically critical errors: a transcript can be 95% correct and still swap one drug for another. The usual fix weights errors on medical entities, and almost always depends on an evaluation-time named-entity recognition (NER) model or cloud API, which makes the metric's denominator a versioned black box. We present MedWER, an evaluation protocol and open-source tool for medical ASR whose denominator is a fixed, license-clean term list: 19,373 drug, diagnosis, symptom, and injury-mechanism entries projected from public sources. The protocol couples a pinned text normalizer with a phrase-aware term-restricted WER, the MedWER, so the only versioned component is a normalizer dependency held at an exact release and checked against committed golden fixtures. Coverage is validated against an independent provincial drug-benefit file the list was not built from; the matching heuristic is calibrated against ground-truth entity spans. Baselines for Moonshine~base, Whisper~base.en, and MedASR on two open benchmarks are scored with the released tool and reported with 95% confidence intervals from resampled per-utterance scores.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MedWER, a clinically-aware word error rate metric for medical ASR that avoids black-box NER dependencies by using a fixed, license-clean medical term list and stable normalization, and validates its coverage and scoring on public benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard word error rate (WER) can look good while masking clinically dangerous errors, such as confusing one drug with another. Existing clinically weighted metrics typically rely on external NER models or APIs at evaluation time, turning the metric into a moving target tied to opaque, versioned components. The authors want a reliable, reproducible, and transparent way to evaluate medical ASR systems that is sensitive to clinically important terms without depending on black-box services.
AI.method: They build a fixed, license-clean term list of 19,373 medical entries (drugs, diagnoses, symptoms, injury mechanisms) from public sources. They define an evaluation protocol that combines: (1) a pinned text normalizer, whose version is fixed and tested against golden fixtures; and (2) a phrase-aware, term-restricted word error rate (MedWER) that focuses on errors involving items from the term list. They validate coverage using an independent provincial drug-benefit file not used in list construction and calibrate their matching heuristic with ground-truth entity span annotations. They implement and release MedWER as an open-source tool.
AI.result: They compute MedWER baselines for multiple ASR systems—Moonshine base, Whisper base.en, and MedASR—on two open benchmarks. Scores are produced with the released tool and accompanied by 95% confidence intervals using resampled per-utterance scores, demonstrating both the practicality of the tool and its ability to characterize system performance on clinically relevant terms.
AI.conclusion: MedWER offers a transparent, reproducible, and clinically sensitive evaluation method for medical ASR by eliminating dependence on black-box NER services and using a fixed, public term list plus a version-locked normalizer. The protocol and open-source tool provide stable, auditable benchmarks for comparing medical ASR systems on errors that matter clinically.

title: AutoFyn Technical Report: Non-Parametric Expert Iteration for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: We introduce AutoFyn, an agent harness inspired by the Expert Iteration algorithm, adapting a frozen model across many rounds by updating persistent state from verified reward signals rather than model weights. Each round begins from a fresh model session, and durable information is reintroduced only through explicit interfaces such as persistent memory files, reports, and repository state. Within a round, an orchestrator explores, plans and builds many alternative approaches with specialized agents, while a task-grounded verifier verifies the work and supplies an objective reward for measuring progress. This reward is distilled back into the persistent state, which updates the effective policy for the next round. In this technical report, we formalize this loop and describe its persistent state and verification interfaces. We then demonstrate its use in three domains, namely olympiad mathematics, data science, and cybersecurity. On the six fresh problems of the 2026 International Mathematical Olympiad, every model with room to improve scores higher under AutoFyn than in its provider's own coding agent. AutoFyn also built the top-ranked agent on the Spider 2.0 dbt benchmark, and has produced $16$ maintainer-confirmed vulnerability advisories in Next.js, MetaMask, pnpm, Warp, LiteLLM, Langflow, and Open WebUI.

AI.tldr: AutoFyn is an agent framework that improves frozen models over multiple rounds using persistent state and verified rewards instead of updating model weights, achieving strong results in math, data science, and cybersecurity tasks.
AI.motivation: Large models are powerful but hard to continually fine-tune and adapt reliably to new tasks, especially when needing safety, verifiability and repeatable improvements across domains such as math problem solving, data science workflows, and security auditing. The authors want a way to iteratively improve performance without changing model weights, relying instead on structured interaction, verification, and memory.
AI.method: They design AutoFyn, an Expert Iteration–inspired agent harness where each round starts a fresh model session and only a persistent external state carries information forward. Within each round, an orchestrator coordinates specialized agents that explore solution strategies, plan, and build candidate outputs. A task-grounded verifier checks these outputs and produces an objective reward signal. This reward and related artifacts are distilled into the persistent memory (files, reports, repo state), effectively updating the policy for the next round without weight changes. They formalize this loop and specify the persistent-state and verification interfaces, then instantiate the framework in several domains.
AI.result: In olympiad-level mathematics (including the six fresh problems of the 2026 IMO), models that still had headroom all scored higher with AutoFyn than with their providers’ built-in coding agents. In data science, AutoFyn produced the top-ranked agent on the Spider 2.0 dbt benchmark. In cybersecurity, it discovered and led to 16 maintainer-confirmed vulnerabilities across several major projects (Next.js, MetaMask, pnpm, Warp, LiteLLM, Langflow, Open WebUI).
AI.conclusion: Persistently updating external state from verified rewards, instead of fine-tuning model weights, can reliably improve performance of frozen models across diverse domains. AutoFyn’s formalized loop of orchestration, verification, and state distillation is a practical and effective framework for iterative capability gains in complex tasks like olympiad math, data science pipelines, and vulnerability discovery.

title: Some Tokens Behave like Magnets: Revealing Linguistic Organization in the Layers of Language Models
summary:
We identify a special group of token vectors inside large language models (LLMs), which we term magnetic vectors, that organize the surrounding tokens by either attracting or repelling them. Particularly, tokens pointing the same way as an attracting magnet are elongated; tokens pointing the same way as a repelling magnet are compressed. Just as physical magnets pull or push away the iron filings around them, these vectors organize their surroundings through two opposing polarities. Moreover, we identify a statistically significant pattern in linguistic category where function words consistently act as repelling magnets in early layers, and we also find magnets consistently reorganize their polarities in unique ways deeper in the model. In a further case study we find this observation may unveil a deliberate, layer-wise organization in how LLMs process language.
  This pattern is consistent across different LLM architectures, sizes, and layer configurations. It is also causally relevant. When the LLM is fine-tuned for a downstream task, the task-functional tokens emerge as magnets. E.g., in question answering, the answer-span tokens become uniquely repelling magnets in the final layer, geometrically carving the answer out of the surrounding context. Furthermore, removing early-layer repelling magnets devastates syntactic tasks (POS tagging accuracy drops from 91% to below 10%) while sparing semantic ones, and removing late-layer attracting magnets does the reverse. We believe this phenomenon warrants further investigation, as it opens the first probe-free path to understanding how language models geometrically organize linguistic computation across their layers.

AI.tldr: The paper discovers “magnetic vectors” in LLMs—special token directions that attract or repel nearby token representations, shaping how information is geometrically organized across layers and tasks.
AI.motivation: To move beyond traditional probe-based interpretability and instead understand how LLMs natively and geometrically organize linguistic computation inside their embedding and hidden spaces across layers, in a way that is consistent, causal, and task-relevant.
AI.method: Analyze token representations inside various LLMs to detect token directions whose presence systematically lengthens (attraction) or shortens (repulsion) nearby token vectors. Examine which tokens instantiate these magnets across layers and models, test cross-architecture consistency, and conduct causal interventions by: (1) fine-tuning on downstream tasks and observing which tokens become magnets; (2) ablating or removing identified magnets in early vs. late layers and measuring performance changes on syntactic vs. semantic benchmarks such as POS tagging.
AI.result: They find a special class of token vectors—magnetic vectors—that either attract or repel neighboring token representations, analogously to physical magnets. Function words reliably act as repelling magnets in early layers, and magnet polarities reorganize in characteristic ways deeper in the network. Across different LLMs and configurations, this pattern is robust and becomes aligned with task-critical tokens under fine-tuning (e.g., answer-span tokens become repelling magnets in the final layer for QA). Causal ablations show that removing early repelling magnets cripples syntactic performance while leaving semantics relatively intact, whereas removing late attracting magnets preferentially harms semantic tasks.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic vectors provide a probe-free, geometrically grounded handle on how LLMs structure linguistic information across layers. They appear to form a layer-wise, linguistically meaningful organization that differentiates syntax and semantics and adapts to downstream task demands, suggesting a new, promising direction for mechanistic interpretability and for understanding how LLMs implement linguistic computation.

title: Damage-Aware Bandit Pruning for Vision and Language Transformers
summary: Structured post-training pruning of transformers requires selecting complete functional units whose suppression causes limited degradation. We formulate structured-unit selection for language and vision transformers as a damage-aware multi-armed bandit problem under a fixed candidate-evaluation budget. Attention heads and MLP channel groups are temporarily masked on calibration batches. Paired damage is the masked loss minus the base loss on the same batch, reducing batch-to-batch variation. A smooth bounded reward drives either a UCB-style policy or fractional-Beta Thompson Sampling, and the final mask is constructed sequentially by adding one unit at each step. The selected units are functionally zeroed in the original dense checkpoint; therefore, the reported parameter effects represent effective structural suppression rather than physical compression or measured speedup. Experiments on WikiText-2, LAMBADA, and Imagenette cover GPT-2, OPT, Pythia, Qwen2.5, SmolLM2, ViT-B/16, DeiT-Tiny, and Swin-Tiny, with comparisons against random, magnitude, static-saliency, and budgeted-greedy selection. Across five seeds, the bandit methods usually reduce degradation relative to budgeted greedy in the paired language-model comparisons. Of 28 comparisons highlighted in the paper, 23 bootstrap confidence intervals exclude zero and 11 paired tests have p < 0.05; six have q < 0.05 after Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the full family of 116 dataset-wise tests. Matched-evaluation results for ViT-B/16 and Swin-Tiny indicate that their gains are not explained solely by a larger candidate-evaluation budget.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a bandit-based method to choose which attention heads and MLP channel groups to prune in transformers, aiming to minimize performance damage under a fixed evaluation budget.
AI.motivation: Structured pruning of transformers needs to remove whole functional units (like heads or channel groups) but naively choosing them can overly hurt model performance, and exhaustive evaluation of all candidates is too expensive. The authors want a statistically principled, budget-aware way to pick units whose removal causes minimal loss increase, applicable across language and vision models.
AI.method: They cast unit selection as a damage-aware multi-armed bandit problem. Each unit (attention head or MLP channel group) is an arm. Temporarily masking a unit on calibration batches yields a paired damage signal: the increase in loss versus the unmasked baseline on the same batch, reducing variance. Using this signal, they define a smooth bounded reward and run either a UCB-style bandit policy or a fractional-Beta Thompson Sampling policy. Pruning is done sequentially: at each step one unit is selected by the bandit and added to the mask. In the final pruned model, these units are functionally zeroed in the original dense checkpoint (no physical weight removal or speed benchmarking).
AI.result: On language modeling tasks (WikiText-2, LAMBADA) for several transformer families (GPT-2, OPT, Pythia, Qwen2.5, SmolLM2) and on Imagenette for ViT-B/16, DeiT-Tiny, and Swin-Tiny, the bandit-based selection generally outperforms random, magnitude-based, static saliency, and budgeted-greedy selection, especially in language models. Over five random seeds in paired comparisons, bandit methods usually yield smaller performance degradation than budgeted greedy. In 28 highlighted comparisons, 23 bootstrap CIs exclude zero effect; 11 paired tests reach p < 0.05, and 6 remain significant (q < 0.05) after Benjamini–Hochberg correction across 116 tests. For ViT-B/16 and Swin-Tiny, additional experiments with matched evaluation budgets show that performance gains are not just due to more candidate evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Model-unit selection for structured transformer pruning can be effectively framed as a bandit problem using paired-damage signals, leading to more robust pruning decisions under limited evaluation budgets. The approach statistically improves over common baselines in many settings, especially for language models, and its benefits persist even when controlling for evaluation budget in vision models, though the work focuses on functional suppression rather than hardware-level compression or speed gains.

title: CrisisKD: Five-Stage Knowledge Distillation for Aspect-Level Sentiment and Emotion Analysis in Crisis Discourse
comment: Accepted to the 11th Workshop on Natural User-generated Text (W-NUT 2026), co-located with EMNLP 2026
summary: Identifying the target of emotional words or phrases in crisis situations, especially health-related ones, is important for understanding public concerns across cultural and linguistic contexts. We propose CrisisKD, a five-stage teacher--student knowledge distillation framework for aspect-level sentiment and emotion analysis on unannotated social media data. A teacher LLM generates aspect-level labels and reasoning traces that supervise a smaller student model across aspect extraction, syntactic parsing, opinion extraction, sentiment classification, and emotion classification. Using this framework, we construct and release a dataset containing 50,615 aspect-level labels, together with the annotation and fine-tuning scripts as open-source resources. The resulting student supports end-to-end ABSA and emotion detection at substantially lower inference cost than the teacher. On a manually annotated 500-tweet gold set, the 5-task Qwen2.5-7B student improves over the untuned model by 7.9 F1 points on aspect extraction, 17.0 points on emotion accuracy, and 6.5 points on sentiment accuracy. On the external ABEA benchmark, CrisisKD improves the same-model Qwen2.5-7B ICL baseline by 2.8 F1 points on ATE and 3.8 F1 points on joint ATE+AEC.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CrisisKD, a teacher–student knowledge distillation framework that uses a large language model to generate aspect-level sentiment and emotion labels for crisis-related social media, training a smaller, cheaper model that performs multi-task aspect-based sentiment and emotion analysis with strong performance gains.
AI.motivation: In crisis and health emergencies, it is crucial to understand what people are reacting to (the targets or aspects) and how they feel about them, across different cultures and languages. However, high-quality aspect-level sentiment and emotion annotations on social media are expensive and scarce. Existing models are often either large and costly to run, or limited in their ability to jointly handle aspect extraction, opinions, sentiment, and emotions in crisis contexts. The paper seeks a scalable way to leverage powerful LLMs to build efficient, domain-specialized models without requiring extensive manual labeling.
AI.method: The authors propose CrisisKD, a five-stage teacher–student knowledge distillation framework. A teacher LLM is prompted to perform detailed aspect-based sentiment and emotion analysis on unannotated crisis-related social media posts. It outputs aspect-level labels and reasoning traces across five tasks: aspect extraction, syntactic parsing, opinion extraction, sentiment classification, and emotion classification. These rich teacher outputs supervise a smaller student model (e.g., Qwen2.5-7B), which is fine-tuned end-to-end on these pseudo-labeled examples. The student thus learns multi-task aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) and emotion detection with significantly reduced inference cost compared to the teacher. The authors also package the pipeline, dataset, and scripts as open-source resources.
AI.result: Using CrisisKD, the authors construct a dataset with 50,615 aspect-level labels from crisis-related social media. The distilled Qwen2.5-7B student, trained on the teacher’s labels and rationales, achieves notable gains over its untuned counterpart on a manually annotated 500-tweet gold set: +7.9 F1 on aspect extraction, +17.0 accuracy on emotion classification, and +6.5 accuracy on sentiment classification. On the external ABEA benchmark, their CrisisKD-trained model improves over the same-model in-context learning baseline by 2.8 F1 on aspect term extraction (ATE) and 3.8 F1 on joint ATE+aspect–emotion co-occurrence (AEC), confirming that the framework generalizes beyond their own dataset.
AI.conclusion: CrisisKD demonstrates that a structured, multi-stage knowledge distillation pipeline from a teacher LLM can produce a smaller student model capable of end-to-end aspect-based sentiment analysis and emotion detection in crisis-related social media, at much lower inference cost. The approach yields a sizable, reusable dataset and reproducible scripts, and it improves both in-domain and external benchmark performance over untuned or ICL-only baselines. This suggests that reasoning-rich teacher supervision is an effective way to build efficient, domain-specific ABSA and emotion models for crisis informatics without extensive manual annotation.

title: Compiling VGDL into Causal Models
comment: To be published at IEEE Conference on Games 2026
summary: Reinforcement learning and large language models often struggle to accurately capture the causal mechanics of game environments. Standard reinforcement learning agents tend to rely on spurious correlations, while large language models are prone to hallucinating game rules. Although causal reinforcement learning improves interpretability, there is currently no formal methodology to map complex game mechanics directly into causal models. To address this, we propose a deterministic framework that compiles games specified in the Video Game Description Language into Dynamic Structural Causal Models. Rather than inferring causal structures from gameplay traces or noisy large language models' outputs, our methodology directly translates game components, including sprite dynamics, interaction rules, and termination conditions, into explicit structural equations. Each game tick represents a causal transition from state variables at time $t$ to $t+1$. By establishing this grounded mapping, the approach guarantees absolute causal fidelity to the ground-truth game mechanics. The resulting models offer transparent causal pathways that support counterfactual reasoning, causal reinforcement learning agent training, and procedural content validation. This framework provides a principled bridge between symbolic game descriptions and causally grounded game AI.

AI.tldr: They turn symbolic game descriptions (VGDL) into exact causal models, enabling perfectly faithful, interpretable game dynamics for AI agents.
AI.motivation: RL agents often exploit spurious correlations and struggle to understand the true causal rules of games, while LLMs may hallucinate or mis-specify game mechanics. Even causal RL lacks a systematic way to derive causal models from complex, formally specified games. There is a need for a principled, automatic way to obtain ground-truth causal models that exactly match game mechanics, so that agents and reasoning tools can operate on faithful causal structures.
AI.method: They define a deterministic compilation procedure that converts games written in the Video Game Description Language (VGDL) into Dynamic Structural Causal Models. The compiler maps each game element—sprites, their dynamics, interaction rules, and termination conditions—into explicit structural equations that describe how the game state at time t causally determines the state at time t+1. Each game tick is represented as a causal transition in the DSCM, avoiding any need to learn or infer causal structure from data or from LLM outputs.
AI.result: The output is a set of Dynamic Structural Causal Models that are provably aligned with the original VGDL specifications. These models expose explicit causal pathways, supporting applications such as counterfactual queries, training causal RL agents, and verifying or validating procedurally generated game content. The authors demonstrate that the mapping preserves the exact game mechanics (“absolute causal fidelity”), making the causal models trustworthy ground-truth representations of the games.
AI.conclusion: A deterministic framework can systematically translate symbolic game descriptions into dynamic structural causal models, eliminating reliance on data-driven or LLM-based causal discovery. This bridge between VGDL and causal models yields fully faithful, interpretable representations of game dynamics that can improve causal reasoning, RL training, and content validation in game AI, and more broadly shows how formal domain descriptions can be converted into grounded causal structures.

title: Recall Is Not Protection: Evaluating Safety Monitors Against Model Compliance
comment: Submitted to the NeurIPS 2026 JUDGe Workshop
summary: Safety monitors screen prompts sent to deployed language models, flagging harmful requests so they are never answered. They are evaluated by recall against harmfulness labels, but a catch only prevents harm if the model would otherwise have complied. We measure the difference directly: we sample repeated responses from the target model, call a harmful prompt \emph{elicitable} if the model complies at least once, and report monitor recall separately on elicitable and non-elicitable prompts. Across six monitor configurations and three model families, spanning activation probes, fine-tuned text guards, and a 120B policy-conditioned reasoning classifier, recall on elicitable prompts falls 0.22 to 0.38 below recall on non-elicitable prompts at a fixed false positive rate. The prompts a monitor misses are 2.8 to 5.6 times more likely to be complied with than the prompts it catches. The gap replicates across three model families and appears also in text-only monitors entirely independent of the target model. This suggests that standard recall may overstate the protection monitors provide in practice, and that monitors should be evaluated against what their models will actually answer.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that standard ways of evaluating safety monitors for language models overestimate real protection, because they don’t account for whether the base model would actually comply with harmful prompts. When you look only at harmful prompts the model is willing to answer, monitor performance is much worse.
AI.motivation: Current safety monitors for language models are usually evaluated by recall on a labeled dataset of harmful vs. harmless prompts. However, this assumes that blocking any harmful-labeled prompt is equally important, ignoring that some harmful prompts would not elicit harmful outputs from the base model anyway. The authors want to measure how much protection monitors truly provide in practice, by focusing on harmful prompts that the underlying model is actually willing to answer (elicitable prompts). This addresses a mismatch between offline evaluation metrics and real-world safety value.
AI.method: The authors define a harmful prompt as "elicitable" if, when sampling multiple responses from the target model, the model produces a harmful (complying) answer at least once. They then evaluate multiple safety monitor designs—activation probes, fine-tuned text guards, and a large policy-conditioned reasoning classifier—on a collection of harmful prompts. Crucially, they compute and compare recall separately on (1) elicitable harmful prompts and (2) non-elicitable harmful prompts, while controlling for a fixed false positive rate. They also test this across three different model families and even with text-only monitors that do not inspect the target model’s internal activations, to see whether the effect generalizes and is not an artifact of a particular model-monitor coupling.
AI.result: Across six different monitor configurations and three model families, the authors find that recall on elicitable harmful prompts is substantially lower—by 0.22 to 0.38—than recall on non-elicitable harmful prompts, when compared at the same false positive rate. Moreover, harmful prompts that the monitor fails to flag are 2.8 to 5.6 times more likely to elicit a harmful answer from the model than those it does catch. This pattern appears robust across the tested architectures and persists even with text-only monitors that are independent of the target model.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that standard recall metrics on labeled harmful prompts systematically overstate the real-world protection provided by safety monitors, because they do not condition on whether the underlying model would actually produce harmful content. Monitors are particularly weak on the subset of harmful prompts where their protection matters most—those that can successfully elicit harmful outputs. Therefore, evaluation protocols for safety monitoring should explicitly condition on model elicitation behavior and report metrics such as recall on elicitable prompts, to more accurately capture practical safety performance.

title: ARC-Bench: Closed-Loop Replanning Masks Broken Action Ranking in Frozen JEPA World Models
summary: Reward-free latent world models plan by scoring candidate actions with distances in a frozen latent space: an action is preferred if its predicted future embedding lands closer to the goal embedding. This silently assumes that latent closeness is action-rankable, i.e., that ordering candidates by latent distance agrees with ordering them by true cost. We audit this assumption directly. We introduce ARC-Bench, a no-leak, fixed-candidate protocol that measures whether frozen JEPA-style objectives rank candidate actions correctly, and apply it to official released JEPA-WM checkpoints across navigation and manipulation-style control. The assumption fails, severely and structurally: on the official manipulation audits the top-scored candidate is almost always suboptimal, and the same inversion appears in the maze domains. A controlled visual-backbone extension shows that the defect persists when DINOv2 is replaced by video-pretrained V-JEPA 1 and V-JEPA 2 encoders at ViT-L/ViT-G scale. Provenance, undertraining, matched-budget backbone controls, and metric-circularity controls rule out trivial explanations. We then explain why this defect has stayed invisible: closed-loop replanning masks it. When we reduce the planner's replanning frequency, success collapses in both a navigation and a manipulation domain, and the episodes rescued by frequent replanning are enriched for severe first-plan ranking failures in the PointMaze first-plan diagnostic. Closed-loop success rates therefore systematically overstate the rankability of frozen latent representations. ARC-Bench supplies the measurement, and the masking mechanism the explanation, for methods that adapt, amortize, or replan around latent-space planners without directly auditing released JEPA-WM action rankability.

AI.tldr: The paper audits whether frozen latent world models can reliably rank actions by latent distance to a goal and finds they systematically fail, even when performance appears good under frequent replanning.
AI.motivation: Many recent reward-free, JEPA-style latent world models plan by minimizing distance in a frozen latent space without explicitly checking whether that distance actually correlates with true task cost. The community often assumes that "closer in latent space" implies "better action" and trusts closed-loop planning success as evidence. The authors want to directly test this assumption, understand whether it holds across domains and backbones, and explain why current benchmarks may be overestimating representation quality.
AI.method: They build ARC-Bench, a benchmark that uses a fixed set of candidate actions and a no-information-leak protocol to test whether frozen JEPA-world-model-style objectives correctly rank actions according to true cost. They apply ARC-Bench to officially released JEPA-WM checkpoints in both navigation and manipulation settings. They also run controlled experiments replacing DINOv2 with larger, video-pretrained V-JEPA 1 and V-JEPA 2 encoders (ViT-L / ViT-G) and add controls for training budget, backbone capacity, provenance, and metric circularity. Finally, they study closed-loop planners with different replanning frequencies to see how often bad first-plan rankings get corrected by frequent replanning.
AI.result: ARC-Bench reveals that the latent distance objective often produces severely mis-ordered action rankings: in manipulation tasks, the top-ranked action according to the frozen latent objective is almost always suboptimal, and similar inversions are observed in maze navigation. These ranking defects persist even with stronger, video-pretrained V-JEPA backbones and under multiple controls, excluding simple explanations like undertraining or metric circularity. When replanning frequency is reduced in closed-loop control, success rates drop dramatically, and the episodes where frequent replanning helps are precisely those where initial action rankings are worst, as demonstrated in a PointMaze first-plan diagnostic.
AI.conclusion: Frozen JEPA-style latent spaces are not reliably action-rankable: latent closeness to a goal does not systematically correspond to lower true cost, even though these representations are often used as if they were suitable for planning. Closed-loop replanning can hide this structural defect, creating the illusion of good latent planning when, in fact, frequent corrections compensate for poor initial rankings. ARC-Bench offers a direct way to audit action rankability and shows that current success metrics can substantially overstate the planning value of frozen latent representations, especially for methods that adapt or replan around them without such audits.

title: Dynamic Lagging for Simultaneous Translation
summary: In cascaded simultaneous speech translation, the machine translation (MT) system cannot control the read--write schedule of the upstream recognizer: it must decide, from a growing source prefix, how much target text to commit. We make a sentence-trained, decoder-only LLM prefix-aware by fine-tuning it on stable prefixes---the longest prefix that any translation up to the current partial source has shared with the model's own full-source output---mixed with full-sentence pairs, and prompt it through a single force-decode turn that carries the committed target forward as more source arrives, making the system flicker-free by construction. We fine-tune Qwen3-8B for EN to DE, JA, ZH, simulating the source stream with reference-transcript prefixes. Prefix finetuning preserves full-sentence quality while improving worst-position chunk quality, and it improves calibration of token-level commit confidence, reducing expected calibration error (ECE) on early source prefixes against a stable-prefix oracle. A single training-free threshold on that confidence is the most effective of the three latency controls we compare: it traces a continuous quality--latency frontier that outperforms the discrete wait-$k$ and target-suffix-deletion quality-latency tradeoff mechanisms. The effect holds well on FLEURS, WMT24++, and CoVoST~2 test sets, under both COMET and MetricX.

AI.tldr: They adapt a decoder-only large language model for cascaded simultaneous speech translation by making it prefix-aware, enabling flicker-free, low-latency translation with better calibration and quality–latency tradeoffs than common baselines.
AI.motivation: In cascaded simultaneous speech translation, the MT system receives an incrementally growing source transcript from an upstream ASR system but cannot control when new input arrives. It must continuously decide how much of the target translation to commit based on partial, evolving source prefixes. Existing approaches can cause flicker (revisions of committed text), suffer from poor calibration of commit confidence, and rely on rigid latency strategies like fixed wait-k policies or heuristic target-suffix deletion, which do not optimally balance quality and latency. The authors want a method that preserves full-sentence MT quality, avoids flicker by construction, and provides a better, more controllable quality–latency tradeoff using a modern decoder-only LLM.
AI.method: They make a sentence-trained, decoder-only LLM (Qwen3-8B) prefix-aware through fine-tuning. Training data includes (1) stable prefixes: for each partial source prefix, they find the longest target prefix that matches the model’s own full-source translation and use these as supervision; and (2) full-sentence translation pairs, mixed together. At inference, they use a single force-decode style generation turn: the model is repeatedly prompted with the growing source prefix plus the already committed target text, and it continues generation while preserving previous commitments, which ensures flicker-free behavior. They simulate streaming input with reference transcript prefixes and evaluate on EN→DE, JA, ZH. They also compute token-level commit confidence, compare different latency-control mechanisms (single confidence threshold vs wait-k vs target-suffix deletion), and assess calibration (ECE) and quality–latency tradeoffs across datasets and metrics.
AI.result: Prefix fine-tuning maintains overall full-sentence translation quality while improving the quality of translations at difficult intermediate positions (worst-position chunk quality). It also yields better calibration of token-level commit confidence, significantly reducing expected calibration error for early source prefixes when compared to a stable-prefix oracle. Among the latency control strategies tested, applying a single, training-free threshold to the model’s commit confidence performs best: it forms a smooth quality–latency frontier that surpasses the discrete, hand-crafted baselines of wait-k and target-suffix deletion. These gains are consistent across multiple benchmarks (FLEURS, WMT24++, CoVoST 2) and quality metrics (COMET, MetricX).
AI.conclusion: A decoder-only LLM can be effectively adapted for cascaded simultaneous speech translation by making it prefix-aware through stable-prefix fine-tuning and using a force-decode mechanism that carries forward committed target text. This approach yields flicker-free translation, preserves full-sentence performance, improves mid-stream chunk quality, and delivers better-calibrated commit decisions. A simple confidence-threshold-based latency controller provides a superior and more flexible quality–latency tradeoff compared to traditional mechanisms like wait-k and target-suffix deletion, with improvements validated across languages, datasets, and metrics.

title: RAPID: Reliability-Aware Pair Importance Distillation
summary: Inter example relational distillation transfers a teacher's representation geometry by matching relations among examples within a mini batch. Computing all pairs has quadratic complexity in the batch size, whereas uniform subsampling may use a limited relation budget inefficiently. We introduce Reliability Aware Pair Importance Distillation, or RAPID, which separates a reliability gated relational target from a full support adaptive pair proposal.
