Reliability determines which teacher relations are emphasized, while calibrated teacher entropy and detached student-teacher residuals determine which relations are evaluated. Exact inverse proposal correction makes the loss and gradient estimators conditionally unbiased with respect to the gated mini batch target. We evaluate RAPID in two text classification settings: AG News with BERT-to-DistilBERT distillation using three paired seeds and a relation budget of 256, and SST-2 with DistilBERT to DistilBERT distillation using three paired seeds and a relation budget of 64. Reliability gated relational distillation achieves the highest observed mean student accuracy on both datasets: 94.285 plus or minus 0.054 percent on AG News and 88.800 plus or minus 0.532 percent on SST-2. RAPID ranks second, achieving 94.241 plus or minus 0.025 percent and 88.685 plus or minus 0.462 percent, respectively, compared with 94.154 plus or minus 0.124 percent and 87.271 plus or minus 0.162 percent for the cross entropy baseline. Pilot evaluations are counted toward the same total budget as the main relation evaluations. Across both settings, the gated target yields the highest mean accuracy, while the adaptive proposal remains within seed-level variation. These results support the modular view that target reliability and evaluation priority are separable design dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RAPID, a more efficient and reliable relational knowledge distillation method that selectively samples and weights example pairs while keeping the estimator unbiased, achieving better or near-best accuracy under tight pair (relation) budgets.
AI.motivation: Inter-example relational distillation can transfer a teacher model's geometry by matching relations between sample representations, but computing all pairwise relations in a batch is quadratically expensive. Naive uniform subsampling wastes a limited relation budget on uninformative or unreliable pairs. The authors aim to use a fixed, small budget of relation evaluations more effectively, while retaining theoretical soundness (unbiasedness) and improving student performance.
AI.method: They introduce Reliability Aware Pair Importance Distillation (RAPID). First, they define a reliability-gated relational target: only certain teacher relations (pairs) are emphasized based on a reliability notion that uses calibrated teacher entropy and student–teacher residuals (with gradients detached) to decide which relations are worth evaluating. Second, they construct an adaptive proposal distribution over all possible pairs within a batch to select which pairwise relations to compute, giving full support so every pair can be sampled. They then apply exact inverse-proposal importance weighting so that, conditioned on the gated mini-batch target, the loss and gradient estimates remain unbiased even though only a subset of relations is evaluated. They test the method on text classification distillation tasks with constrained relation budgets (64 or 256 pairs) and multiple random seeds.
AI.result: On AG News with BERT→DistilBERT distillation and a relation budget of 256, reliability-gated relational distillation achieves the best mean student accuracy: 94.285±0.054%. RAPID is a close second at 94.241±0.025%, both outperforming a cross-entropy baseline at 94.154±0.124%. On SST-2 with DistilBERT→DistilBERT and a budget of 64 relations, gated relational distillation again performs best at 88.800±0.532%, RAPID ranks second at 88.685±0.462%, while the cross-entropy baseline reaches 87.271±0.162%. Pilot evaluations are accounted for within the same total relation budget as main evaluations. The adaptive proposal component performs within seed-level variance relative to the best results, while the gated target consistently improves mean accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Reliability-aware relational distillation can more effectively use a limited relation (pair) budget than uniform subsampling, improving student accuracy while keeping estimators unbiased by correcting for the adaptive proposal distribution. The experiments suggest that (1) gating the relational target by reliability is the primary driver of performance gains, and (2) adaptive pair proposals mainly affect efficiency within the noise of seed-level variation. This supports a modular view where target reliability (which relations to care about) and evaluation priority (which relations to evaluate) are separable, tunable design dimensions in relational knowledge distillation.

title: AtomCite: Verification and Correction of Supplied Page-Level Citations in Multi-Page Documents
summary: Large language models answering questions over multi-page documents are expected to cite the supporting pages, yet supplied citations are sometimes inaccurate, and current evaluations score citations at generation time or against text passages: no existing benchmark evaluates whether a system can verify and correct a page-level citation already attached to an answer. We propose AtomCite, an agentic framework that parses an answer into claims, checks each claim against the image of its cited page, and applies a deterministic repair policy. To evaluate it, we introduce DocCite, to our knowledge the first benchmark for systems that verify and correct page-level citations in document images. Built on MP-DocVQA and DUDE, it combines 928 validated injected instances with 2,468 candidate natural errors harvested from frontier- and efficiency-tier models, of which a two-annotator audit confirms 1,909 as genuine errors. Primary labels are assigned deterministically, not by LLM judges, with the human audit as a separate validation layer. Across three model families (Gemini, Claude, and GPT), AtomCite reaches around 93% binary verification accuracy on the injected benchmark, significantly outperforming every OCR-only condition, including a compute-matched control, and exceeding every prior text-based baseline given the same OCR text. Its repair policy lifts citation precision on the injected mix from a constructed 34% to 87-90% while retaining over 90% of correct claims. AtomCite also transfers: with frozen prompts and zero training, it raises the hallucination-detection scores of two open 7-8B models on five public benchmarks above the same models prompted as direct judges. Finally, the audit shows that noise in automatic labels biases measured verifier accuracy and can reverse system rankings, so evaluations relying only on synthetic or automatic labels risk mismeasuring verification capability.

AI.tldr: AtomCite is an agent framework that verifies and repairs page-level citations for answers over multi-page document images, and DocCite is a new benchmark to evaluate such systems.
AI.motivation: Existing large language models often provide incorrect page-level citations when answering questions over multi-page documents. Current evaluations either check citations only at generation time or compare them to text spans, and there is no benchmark to test whether a system can verify and correct already-attached page-level citations, especially over document images. This creates a gap between real-world needs for reliable citation verification and current evaluation practices.
AI.method: The authors introduce AtomCite, an agentic system that decomposes an answer into atomic claims, checks each claim against the image of its cited page, and then applies a deterministic repair policy to confirm, fix, or remove citations. For evaluation, they build DocCite, a benchmark derived from MP-DocVQA and DUDE that includes both injected synthetic citation errors and naturally occurring citation errors collected from multiple LLMs. Primary labels for correctness are generated deterministically (not via LLM judges), and a two-annotator human audit validates and quantifies label noise. They test AtomCite and multiple baselines, including OCR-only and text-based verifiers, across several model families (Gemini, Claude, GPT). They also assess transfer by applying AtomCite-style verification prompts, without additional training, to open 7–8B models on existing hallucination benchmarks.
AI.result: On the injected DocCite benchmark, AtomCite attains around 93% binary verification accuracy, outperforming OCR-only setups (including compute-matched controls) and surpassing prior text-based baselines using the same OCR text. Its deterministic repair policy improves citation precision in the injected mixture from 34% to 87–90% while maintaining over 90% of correct claims. When transferred with frozen prompts and zero training to two open 7–8B models on five public hallucination benchmarks, AtomCite-style verification improves hallucination-detection scores beyond what those models achieve when prompted as direct judges. The human audit reveals substantial noise in automatic labels, which biases accuracy estimates and can even invert the ranking of systems.
AI.conclusion: AtomCite provides an effective agentic approach to verifying and repairing page-level citations in multi-page document QA, markedly improving citation precision while preserving most correct claims. DocCite fills a missing evaluation gap by offering a document-image-based benchmark for citation verification and repair, with deterministically assigned primary labels plus human validation. The work also shows that such verification methods can transfer to broader hallucination detection tasks. Finally, it highlights that evaluations based solely on synthetic or automatically generated labels can be misleading, as label noise may systematically distort measured verifier performance and system comparisons.

title: PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN: Prior-Guided Joint Probabilistic Forecasting of Clinical Trajectories
summary: Clinical deterioration unfolds through coupled, partially observed trajectories, not a single diagnostic label. We introduce PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN, a trajectory-first framework for joint probabilistic forecasting of multivariate physiology. It combines missingness-aware temporal encoders, a soft organ-system prior, patient-specific relations, nonlinear Kolmogorov-Arnold messages, and a low-rank multivariate Student-t head. We evaluate 24-hour histories and six-hour forecasts on a frozen MIMIC-IV-derived cohort of 6,882 patients and 54,694 windows. Across five seeds and 13 models, PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN obtains the second-lowest normalized MAE (0.37727 +/- 0.00029) and the lowest RMSE (0.52656 +/- 0.00034). It reduces MAE by 0.52% relative to deterministic TimeKAN. For probabilistic forecasting, it reaches a marginal NLL of 0.66380 and a CRPS of 0.27301. Empirical coverage is 0.533, 0.831, and 0.958 for nominal 50%, 80%, and 95% intervals. Removing relational structure causes the largest ablation loss. Increasing covariance rank improves joint likelihood but has little effect on point accuracy. A trajectory-derived risk score remains weaker than a dedicated GRU-D classifier (AUROC 0.603 versus 0.650), which limits the present clinical claim. Joint trajectory forecasting therefore provides an inspectable intermediate task, but accurate physiology forecasts alone do not ensure a calibrated event detector.

AI.tldr: The paper presents PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN, a probabilistic multivariate physiological time-series forecasting model that treats clinical deterioration as coupled trajectories rather than single labels, achieving strong point and probabilistic forecasting performance on MIMIC-IV but showing that better trajectory prediction does not automatically yield better event-risk classification.
AI.motivation: Clinical deterioration in hospitalized patients is typically modeled as a single outcome label (e.g., mortality, ICU transfer), which discards rich information in multivariate physiological time-series. There is a need for models that directly forecast full physiological trajectories, handle missing data, capture organ-system structure and patient-specific relations, and provide probabilistic forecasts for uncertainty quantification—while assessing whether such improved trajectory modeling actually helps downstream risk prediction.
AI.method: The authors design PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN, a trajectory-first probabilistic forecasting architecture. It uses (1) missingness-aware temporal encoders for multivariate physiology; (2) a soft organ-system prior to structure variables; (3) patient-specific relational components; (4) nonlinear Kolmogorov–Arnold networks for message passing; and (5) a low-rank multivariate Student-t output head to model joint distributions and heavy tails. They train and evaluate the model on 24-hour history windows to forecast the next 6 hours for multiple physiological variables in a MIMIC-IV-derived cohort, and compare against a suite of 13 models across multiple random seeds. They also perform ablations removing relational structure and varying covariance rank, and derive a downstream risk score from the predicted trajectories, comparing it to a GRU-D classifier.
AI.result: On 6,882 patients and 54,694 windows, PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN attains the second-best normalized MAE (0.37727 ± 0.00029) and the best RMSE (0.52656 ± 0.00034) among 13 models, slightly improving MAE by 0.52% over deterministic TimeKAN. For probabilistic performance, it achieves marginal NLL 0.66380 and CRPS 0.27301, with empirical coverage close to nominal 50%, 80%, and 95% intervals. Ablations show that removing the relational structure produces the largest performance drop, and increasing the covariance rank improves joint likelihood without materially affecting point prediction accuracy. However, a trajectory-derived risk score based on these forecasts yields AUROC 0.603, substantially below a GRU-D classifier’s AUROC of 0.650.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PGP-Clinical-TimeKAN framework effectively models coupled multivariate physiological trajectories, providing accurate and probabilistic forecasts and highlighting the importance of relational structure and covariance modeling. Nonetheless, improvements in trajectory forecasting do not straightforwardly translate into better-calibrated or more accurate event-risk prediction, as evidenced by the weaker trajectory-derived risk score compared with a dedicated classifier. Thus, joint trajectory forecasting is best viewed as an interpretable intermediate task and modeling layer, rather than a complete solution to clinical risk prediction, and dedicated classification models remain necessary for robust event detection.

title: CONDUIT: A Unified Residual-Stream Restoration Framework for KV Cache Reuse in Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted to Findings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026)
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often answer new questions about recurring visual content, where reusing the key-value (KV) cache can avoid re-encoding expensive visual prefixes. Exact-prefix reuse, however, fails when the same visual content appears under a changed prefix. Selective recomputation can recover quality under a small visual-token budget, but only when the right stale tokens are refreshed. Raw-attention selection can waste budget on high-attention tokens with small value-norm proxy scores and on query-irrelevant images. To address these failure modes, we propose CONDUIT, a training-free refresh policy that unifies single- and multi-image reuse as residual-stream restoration. Building on norm-weighted attention, CONDUIT ranks cached visual tokens using cached-key query attention and an accessible pre-output cached-value-norm proxy, then applies empirical image-level relevance amplification before one global selection. With one image, the coefficient is one and the rule reduces to intra-image token selection. The method preserves model architecture and weights, adding only a single query-conditioned scoring pass at inference. At a 10% refresh budget, CONDUIT achieves 97.0-99.5% of the corresponding full-prefill five-dataset average across three VLM backbones and leads budgeted methods on average; on the MMLongBench-Doc latency subset, it uses 13.5% of full-prefill FLOPs and achieves a 2.99x time-to-first-token speedup.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CONDUIT, a training-free key-value cache refresh policy that selectively recomputes visual tokens for vision-language models to enable efficient prefix reuse with minimal loss in performance.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models frequently see repeated visual content (e.g., the same images or pages) across different queries. Re-encoding these visual prefixes is computationally expensive. Existing exact-prefix KV cache reuse only works when the preceding text (prefix) is unchanged, and simple selective recomputation fails to reliably choose which cached visual tokens to refresh, especially under a tight visual-token budget. There is a need for a principled, training-free way to decide which stale visual tokens to recompute so that VLMs can be both efficient and accurate across single-image and multi-image reuse scenarios.
AI.method: The paper proposes CONDUIT, a refresh policy framed as residual-stream restoration. It uses norm-weighted attention to rank cached visual tokens based on (1) cached-key attention scores from the new query and (2) a pre-output cached-value-norm proxy that approximates each token’s contribution. CONDUIT then applies an empirical image-level relevance amplification to downweight query-irrelevant images before performing a single global selection of tokens to refresh, subject to a given budget. For single-image reuse, this reduces to intra-image token selection. The method is training-free, leaves the VLM architecture and weights unchanged, and adds only a lightweight, query-conditioned scoring pass at inference time.
AI.result: Under a 10% visual-token refresh budget, CONDUIT recovers 97.0–99.5% of the performance of full-prefill decoding on the five-dataset average across three different VLM backbones. It outperforms other budgeted refresh methods on average. On the MMLongBench-Doc latency subset, CONDUIT reduces FLOPs to 13.5% of full-prefill and yields a 2.99× speedup in time-to-first-token, showing substantial efficiency gains with minimal accuracy degradation.
AI.conclusion: CONDUIT provides an effective, training-free mechanism to reuse visual KV caches in vision-language models under constrained recomputation budgets. By ranking tokens with a norm-weighted attention criterion and incorporating image-level relevance, it addresses failure modes of raw-attention selection and generalizes across single-image and multi-image reuse. This leads to near-full-prefill quality at a fraction of the compute cost, improving latency and efficiency without modifying model architectures or retraining.

title: SciLitBench: Benchmark and Design Principles for LLM-Powered Systematic Literature Reviews
comment: 22 pages, 6 figures, and 5 tables. Data and code are available at https://github.com/linlab/SciLitBench
summary: Systematic reviews require sustained human judgment across thousands of records, yet existing evaluations of large language models (LLMs) typically examine review stages in isolation. We introduce SciLitBench, a multi-stage benchmark spanning title and abstract screening, full-text screening, and schema-guided data extraction, with 42,981 retrieved records, 1,012 full texts, and annotations for 888 included papers. Across 22 open-weight LLMs from six model families, explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria improve title and abstract screening $F_2$ by 28.8\%, while researcher-authored rationales improve full-text screening by 15\%. Data extraction reveals a different reliability regime: performance declines from 0.97 accuracy for publication year to 0.37 Jaccard overlap for computational approach, while the strongest models recover only 30\% of annotated evaluation evidence and 25\% of limitations. SciLitBench identifies a practical boundary between high-recall screening and evidence-complete extraction and provides a reproducible resource for evaluating LLM-assisted evidence synthesis.

AI.tldr: SciLitBench is a large, multi-stage benchmark to evaluate how well LLMs can assist with systematic reviews, from screening to detailed data extraction, and it exposes where they work well (high-recall screening) and where they break down (complete evidence extraction).
AI.motivation: Systematic reviews demand extensive, consistent human judgment over tens of thousands of records and multiple stages, but prior LLM evaluations usually assess only single, isolated tasks (e.g., just abstract screening). There is no standard, realistic benchmark that covers the full pipeline and shows how LLMs perform when asked both to filter studies and to extract detailed evidence needed for high-quality evidence synthesis. The authors aim to fill this gap to understand when and how LLMs are reliable in this workflow.
AI.method: The authors construct SciLitBench, a multi-stage benchmark reflecting a realistic systematic review pipeline. It includes 42,981 retrieved records, 1,012 full texts, and detailed annotations for 888 included papers. They define tasks for title/abstract screening, full-text screening, and schema-guided data extraction (e.g., publication year, computational approach, evaluation evidence, limitations). They evaluate 22 open-weight LLMs from six model families under different prompting conditions, including explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria and researcher-authored rationales. Performance is measured with metrics like F2 for screening and accuracy/Jaccard overlap for extraction.
AI.result: For title and abstract screening, providing explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria substantially improves performance, increasing F2 by 28.8%. For full-text screening, adding researcher-authored rationales yields a 15% performance gain. In contrast, data extraction shows much weaker reliability: simple, well-defined fields like publication year reach 0.97 accuracy, but more complex, semantic fields like computational approach achieve only 0.37 Jaccard overlap. Even the strongest models recover only about 30% of annotated evaluation evidence and 25% of reported limitations from papers.
AI.conclusion: SciLitBench shows that open-weight LLMs can support high-recall screening in systematic reviews when given clear criteria and rationales, but they are not yet reliable for evidence-complete, fine-grained data extraction, especially for nuanced methodological and evaluative details. The benchmark thus delineates a practical boundary between where LLMs are useful assistants versus where human expertise remains essential, and it offers a reproducible, multi-stage resource to drive future improvements and evaluations of LLM-assisted evidence synthesis.

title: SinoGlyphBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Chinese Glyph-Level Obfuscation in Language-Model Moderation
summary: Glyph-level obfuscation can leave harmful Chinese content readable to humans while degrading automated moderation. We introduce SinoGlyphBench, a diagnostic benchmark that identifies label-critical semantic anchors and creates matched original and glyph-obfuscated inputs in text and image modalities. By perturbing anchors, background context, or both, this design distinguishes corruption of moderation-relevant evidence from general surface variation. Across 176,916 paired evaluations of 12 LLMs and MLLMs, obfuscation increases harmful false-negative and false-positive rates by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively, and reduces four-way accuracy by 5.0 points. Models retain 75.7% of the decisions that were correct on the matched original inputs. Full-scope perturbations cause the largest degradation, anchor-only perturbations are more damaging than background-only perturbations, and cross-script substitution is particularly difficult in the text modality. Analysis of structured outputs identifies observable mismatches in visible-form reading, intended-message recovery, and final safety judgment. The evaluated models, therefore, remain brittle to Chinese content written with non-canonical glyphs. Resources are available at https://github.com/fengshun124/SinoGlyphBench.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SinoGlyphBench, a benchmark to test how glyph-level obfuscation of Chinese text undermines automated safety moderation in LLMs and multimodal LLMs, showing substantial drops in accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: Automated content moderation systems, especially LLMs and MLLMs, can be bypassed by visually modifying Chinese characters (glyph-level obfuscation) so that humans still understand the text but models fail to detect harmful content. Existing evaluations do not precisely separate the impact of such obfuscations on moderation-critical meaning versus generic noise, nor do they systematically test different obfuscation types across text and image modalities. The authors aim to build a controlled, diagnostic benchmark to quantify and analyze these vulnerabilities.
AI.method: The authors construct SinoGlyphBench by first identifying label-critical semantic anchors in harmful and benign Chinese texts and then generating matched pairs of original and glyph-obfuscated inputs in both text and image formats. They create several perturbation conditions: altering only semantic anchors, only background context, or both, enabling them to distinguish between corruption of moderation-relevant evidence and simple surface variation. They evaluate 12 large language and multimodal models across 176,916 paired samples, and analyze performance in terms of false negatives, false positives, overall four-way classification accuracy, and consistency of decisions between original and obfuscated versions. They also qualitatively and quantitatively inspect structured outputs to separate errors in reading the visible form, recovering the intended meaning, and making the final safety judgment.
AI.result: Glyph-level obfuscation significantly harms moderation quality. Compared with original text, obfuscation increases harmful false negatives by 6.1 percentage points and false positives by 4.7 points, leading to a 5.0 point drop in overall four-way accuracy. Even when models are correct on the original input, they preserve only 75.7% of those correct decisions on the obfuscated counterparts. Perturbations affecting both anchors and background cause the greatest degradation, but even anchor-only changes are more harmful than background-only ones. Cross-script substitution (e.g., mixing character sets) is particularly challenging in the text modality. The analysis of structured outputs reveals distinct failure modes in correctly reading glyphs, reconstructing intended messages, and making safety judgments.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs and MLLMs are brittle when moderating Chinese content written with non-standard or obfuscated glyphs. SinoGlyphBench exposes that relatively small, human-readable glyph perturbations can substantially increase both missed detections of harmful content and incorrect flagging of benign content. The benchmark provides a diagnostic tool for disentangling different failure sources and for guiding robustness improvements in safety moderation systems. The authors release data and code to facilitate further research in robust multilingual moderation and glyph-invariant model design.

title: SCAFFOLD: Self-Improving Web Agents via Recursive Parametric Skill Abstraction
summary: Web agents need to navigate visually rich, long-horizon interfaces that change across sites, yet most previous agents still learn each task in isolation and discard the procedural knowledge they accumulate. Recent skill-augmented frameworks take an important first step, but they treat the skill library as a flat or two-tier prompt-side cache and offer no principled mechanism for compressing redundancy or composing skills recursively. We introduce \textsc{Scaffold}, a self-improving framework for visual web agents that (i) induces parametric, executable skills from successful trajectories under a multi-instance abstraction constraint, (ii) maintains a recursively composed hierarchy in which higher-level skills invoke lower-level ones, (iii) compacts the library via a minimum-description-length (MDL) criterion and behavioral equivalence checking, and (iv) periodically distills skill-augmented trajectories back into model weights to internalize the abstractions. Across WebArena, VisualWebArena, and a held-out split of Online-Mind2Web, \textsc{Scaffold} improves success rate by $11.1$--$17.2$ absolute points over the strongest skill-augmented baseline and shows monotonic gains across five self-improvement iterations without library collapse. We release the code and documents in the Github \href{https://github.com/BokwaiHo/SCAFFOLD}{repository}.

AI.tldr: SCAFFOLD is a self-improving framework that learns, compresses, and hierarchically composes reusable skills from web navigation trajectories to boost visual web agent performance.
AI.motivation: Existing visual web agents handle each website task in isolation, failing to reuse procedural knowledge and lacking mechanisms for organizing, compressing, and composing discovered skills, which limits generalization and long-horizon performance.
AI.method: SCAFFOLD automatically induces parametric, executable skills from successful trajectories subject to a multi-instance abstraction constraint; organizes these skills into a recursive hierarchy where high-level skills call lower-level ones; compresses and de-duplicates the skill library using a minimum-description-length objective and behavioral equivalence checking; and periodically distills trajectories that use these skills back into the model weights so the agent internalizes the abstractions.
AI.result: On benchmarks including WebArena, VisualWebArena, and a held-out portion of Online-Mind2Web, SCAFFOLD outperforms the strongest prior skill-augmented baseline by 11.1–17.2 absolute success-rate points and continues to improve monotonically over at least five rounds of self-improvement without the skill library degenerating or collapsing.
AI.conclusion: By inducing, hierarchically composing, compressing, and distilling reusable skills from interaction data, SCAFFOLD provides a robust self-improvement loop for visual web agents, leading to sustained performance gains and a stable, compact skill library.

title: What if LLMs Ate Their Words: Causal History Effects in Multi-Turn Interaction
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures. Code and data are available at https://github.com/jinnanli/llms-ate-their-words
summary: Multi-turn interaction creates a feedback process in which an LLM's previous responses become context for later behavior. Prior work shows substantial multi-turn degradation and that assistant-generated history can affect later behavior. However, it remains unclear how these effects manifest across models, tasks, turns, and inside a model. We study these gaps across six task families and five models. Degradation from fully specified single-turn input (FULL) to progressively revealed multi-turn interaction (SHARDED) is clearly task- and model-dependent, and stronger one-shot performance does not imply greater interaction robustness. We then retrospectively analyze completed SHARDED conversations by replaying the user messages already observed in each trajectory while editing only assistant-generated history. Replacing prior assistant responses with neutral content (termed neutralization) changes downstream min-max normalized performance by +.027 across 2,973 trajectories. On a prespecified length-controlled subset, short and length-matched neutralization yield nearly identical effects (+.069 versus +.068), showing that simple context shortening is insufficient to explain the effect of history editing. Turn Surgery further intervenes on one assistant turn at a time. Among 237 selected degraded trajectories, 63.7% contain at least one beneficial intervention, while most tested positions remain unchanged; for binary tasks, 48.4% admit a fail-to-success reversal. An open-weight case study links behaviorally consequential history changes to measurable downstream state differences, but finds task-dependent rather than universal internal signatures. Overall, assistant-generated history has active but selective effects on multi-turn performance, motivating selective rather than uniform history management.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how large language models’ own previous responses in multi-turn conversations affect their later performance, showing that model- and task-specific degradations occur and can often be improved by carefully editing or neutralizing earlier assistant messages.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn interactions with LLMs frequently show performance degradation compared to single-turn, fully specified prompts, and prior work suggests that assistant-generated conversation history can influence later behavior. However, it is unclear how systematic, general, and internally grounded these effects are across different models, task families, and conversation turns. Understanding this is important for building more reliable conversational systems and for designing better history management strategies.
AI.method: The authors evaluate five LLMs on six task families, comparing performance in a single-turn ‘FULL’ setting (where all information is provided at once) with a multi-turn ‘SHARDED’ setting (where information is revealed progressively). They then retrospectively replay completed SHARDED conversations, systematically editing only the assistant-generated history while keeping user messages fixed. They introduce ‘neutralization’, replacing previous assistant responses with neutral content, and ‘Turn Surgery’, targeted interventions on individual assistant turns to see which edits improve downstream performance. For one open-weight model, they further analyze internal state differences induced by different histories.
AI.result: They find that degradation from FULL to SHARDED is strongly dependent on both the task and the model, and better one-shot (FULL) performance does not guarantee robustness in multi-turn settings. Neutralizing assistant-generated history yields an average performance increase of +0.027 across 2,973 trajectories, and on a length-controlled subset, short vs. length-matched neutralization produce nearly identical gains (+0.069 vs +0.068), indicating that the benefit is not simply due to shorter context. Turn Surgery reveals that in 63.7% of 237 degraded trajectories, editing at least one assistant turn is beneficial, with many positions having no effect; in binary tasks, 48.4% of cases can be flipped from failure to success. The case study on an open-weight model shows that history edits correlate with measurable internal state changes, but these signatures depend on the task and are not universal.
AI.conclusion: Assistant-generated conversation history has active but selective effects on LLM performance in multi-turn interactions. Multi-turn degradation is not uniform across tasks and models, and targeted edits to prior assistant responses can often restore or improve performance without simple context shortening. These findings argue against blanket truncation or naive history management and instead support selective, task-aware manipulation of conversation history to improve robustness and reliability of conversational LLMs.

title: Reasoning-Aware Compression: Identifying and Protecting Vulnerable Reasoning Circuits for Energy-Efficient LLM Deployment
summary: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) impose substantial energy costs during deployment, yet current compression methods apply uniform quantization across all components, risking damage to critical reasoning circuits. We present a reasoning-aware compression framework that benchmarks quantization conditions across five reasoning benchmarks, GSM8K, FOLIO, MATH-500, ProofWriter, and MuSiQue, with hardware-level GPU energy measurement; profiles per-module INT4 vulnerability across all 196-224 (layer, projection) pairs via a perturbation sweep on a held-out calibration split, then selectively restores the most sensitive circuits to FP16. Three findings emerge. First, INT4 quantization can increase energy by extending reasoning chains; a 25% power reduction becomes a net energy increase on GSM8K. Second, vulnerability is task-dependent: attention projections are more critical for mathematical reasoning, and sensitivity patterns differ by architecture in logical inference. Third, selective compression achieves Pareto-optimal points inaccessible to uniform methods: R1-Qwen-7B Top-10% on ProofWriter gains +12 pp over FP16 at -9.7% energy, validated on held-out data across five reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reasoning-aware, selective quantization framework for Large Reasoning Models that profiles which components are most sensitive, then keeps them in higher precision to save energy without harming—and sometimes improving—reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: Large Reasoning Models consume significant energy at deployment. Existing compression/quantization methods treat all layers and projections uniformly, which can damage critical reasoning components and even increase total energy by lengthening reasoning chains. There is a need for compression that considers the specific demands and failure modes of reasoning tasks, as well as the energy implications on real hardware.
AI.method: The authors benchmark INT4 and mixed-precision quantization on five reasoning datasets (GSM8K, FOLIO, MATH-500, ProofWriter, MuSiQue) while measuring GPU energy at the hardware level. They run a perturbation-based sensitivity/“vulnerability” sweep for each of 196–224 (layer, projection) modules on a calibration split to identify which components degrade reasoning most under INT4. Using this profile, they design a selective quantization strategy that keeps the most vulnerable circuits in FP16 and compresses the rest to INT4, exploring the resulting accuracy–energy trade-off curve.
AI.result: 1) INT4 quantization can paradoxically increase net energy because it lengthens reasoning chains, so a nominal 25% power reduction may translate into higher total energy on GSM8K. 2) Sensitivity to quantization is strongly task- and architecture-dependent: e.g., attention projections matter more for mathematical reasoning, and logical inference models show different vulnerability patterns. 3) The proposed selective compression scheme yields Pareto-optimal trade-offs unattainable by uniform quantization, including a configuration where R1-Qwen-7B in a Top-10% ProofWriter setting gains 12 percentage points over FP16 while still reducing energy by 9.7%, with gains validated across all five benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning-aware, module-level selective quantization can outperform uniform compression for Large Reasoning Models in both accuracy and energy. By profiling quantization vulnerability per module and selectively retaining FP16 for the most critical components, practitioners can avoid reasoning degradation, prevent hidden energy regressions, and find better Pareto points for deployment on real hardware, particularly for mathematically and logically intensive tasks.

title: AlignDiff: Exploiting Model-Intrinsic Information for Better Preference Data Selection
summary: Aligning large language models with human preferences remains a challenge, primarily due to the critical role of preference data quality in effective alignment. Existing datasets are frequently plagued by inherent noise and distribution shifts, which inherently limit model performance. To bridge this gap, we propose AlignDiff, a preference data filtering framework driven by intrinsic model signals. AlignDiff first identifies samples with clear preferences using both positive and inverse signals, then prioritizes the more challenging samples based on the average negative log-likelihood gap, encouraging the model to learn richer information from them. AlignDiff is evaluated on two widely used model families (LLaMA and Qwen) and three benchmarks widely adopted in the alignment community (AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard, and MT-Bench). Across all settings, it consistently outperforms seven strong baselines. We conduct comprehensive ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of AlignDiff, and further show that difficulty-based curriculum learning improves model performance.

AI.tldr: They propose AlignDiff, a framework that filters and prioritizes preference data for aligning large language models using intrinsic model signals, leading to better alignment performance than strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Aligning large language models with human preferences is difficult because the quality of preference data is crucial, yet existing datasets often contain noise and distribution shifts that reduce alignment effectiveness and model performance. There is a need for a more principled way to select and prioritize training samples for preference alignment.
AI.method: AlignDiff uses intrinsic signals from the model itself to filter and rank preference data. It first detects samples with clear preferences by leveraging both positive and inverse preference signals. Then, among these, it prioritizes the more challenging samples according to the average negative log-likelihood gap between preferred and dispreferred responses, effectively creating a difficulty-aware curriculum where harder, information-richer samples are emphasized during training.
AI.result: When applied to two major LLM families (LLaMA and Qwen) and evaluated on three standard alignment benchmarks (AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard, and MT-Bench), AlignDiff consistently surpasses seven strong baseline methods for data filtering or alignment. Ablation studies confirm that both the preference clarity filter and the difficulty-based prioritization contribute significantly to the gains.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic model signals can be effectively used to both clean and curriculum-structure preference data for alignment. AlignDiff improves alignment quality and generalization across models and benchmarks, and the results further support that difficulty-based curriculum learning is beneficial for preference alignment of LLMs.

title: When and What to Teach: Budget-Aware Online Adaptation for Web Agents
summary: Web agents have achieved significant success in automating complex internet tasks but deploying them in real-world environments requires continuous online adaptation. Given that deploying powerful proprietary models remains commercially cost-prohibitive, practitioners must rely on lightweight local models that evolve post-deployment via online teaching from a stronger teacher. However, standard interactive feedback imposes prohibitive costs. We show that conventional trajectory-level preference optimization wastes budget on both unresolvable episodes and redundant execution turns. To resolve these inefficiencies, we propose \textbf{Score-Guided Online Teaching with Budgeted Trajectory Trimming}, a budget-aware framework that systematically orchestrates \textbf{when} and \textbf{what} to teach. Specifically, our framework integrates a solvability-aware teacher gate to dictate \textbf{when} to query the teacher model and a score-guided turn selection mechanism to decide \textbf{what} informative turns to retain. Extensive experiments on MiniWoB and TimeWarp demonstrate that our method achieves comparable first-pass success while reducing teacher calls by 22.6\% and student training compute by 52.1\% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/zjw131f1fc/budgeted-online-teaching.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a budget-aware online teaching framework for training lightweight web agents with minimal reliance on expensive teacher models.
AI.motivation: Deploying powerful proprietary models as web agents is too costly in real-world settings, so practitioners prefer lightweight local agents that must be improved online through interaction. Existing trajectory-level preference optimization is inefficient because it spends supervision budget on episodes that cannot be solved and on redundant steps, making online teaching prohibitively expensive.
AI.method: The authors introduce Score-Guided Online Teaching with Budgeted Trajectory Trimming. The framework has two key components: (1) a solvability-aware teacher gate that decides when to query the stronger teacher model based on whether an episode is likely solvable, and (2) a score-guided turn selection mechanism that determines which specific interaction turns to keep for training, trimming away uninformative or redundant parts of the trajectory. This jointly addresses the timing and content of supervision under a fixed feedback budget.
AI.result: On the MiniWoB and TimeWarp benchmarks, the proposed method maintains comparable first-pass task success rates while reducing teacher queries by 22.6% and student training computation by 52.1% on average compared to conventional online preference optimization baselines.
AI.conclusion: By intelligently deciding when to consult the teacher and what parts of trajectories to preserve for learning, the framework substantially cuts supervision and compute costs without sacrificing performance, making online adaptation of lightweight web agents more practical in real-world, budget-constrained deployments.

title: From Narrative to Auditable Forecasts: A Structured Scaffold for Agentic Forecasting
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for live forecasting, where they retrieve up-to-date information and produce estimates for unresolved future events. However, current agentic forecasting often relies on implicit narrative aggregation: agents collect evidence, discuss it in prose, and often assign a probability without an explicit update path from evidence to forecast. This limits both forecasting accuracy and auditability. We propose AuditForecast, an agentic scaffold for structured probabilistic forecasting. AuditForecast first anchors the forecast with a suitable quantitative baseline model, uses model-guided data retrieval to derive a base probability, and then applies situational factor updates outside the model's scope through mechanical aggregation in odds space. This turns forecasting from a prose-based judgment into a structured process with explicit intermediate objects. Across multiple live forecasting benchmarks, AuditForecast improves forecasting accuracy and calibration relative to strong agentic baselines, surpasses market-implied references in several settings, and outperforms substantially more expensive deep-research agents while remaining Pareto-dominant in the cost--accuracy tradeoff. Beyond performance gains, AuditForecast produces an auditable forecasting report that makes forecast construction explicit and supports systematic post hoc analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AuditForecast, a structured agent framework that turns LLM-based forecasting into an explicit, auditable probabilistic updating process instead of free-form narrative judgments.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents used for real-time forecasting gather information and reason in prose, then jump to a probability estimate without a transparent, step-by-step link between evidence and the final forecast. This reduces both accuracy (because updates are ad hoc and uncalibrated) and auditability (because one cannot easily see how each piece of evidence changed the forecast). The authors want a method that is more accurate, better calibrated, cheaper than deep research agents, and whose reasoning steps can be inspected and analyzed afterward.
AI.method: They design AuditForecast, an agentic scaffold for probabilistic forecasting that: (1) starts from a quantitative baseline model appropriate to the question, (2) uses that model to guide targeted information retrieval and compute an initial base probability, and (3) applies explicit, mechanical updates in odds space for additional situational factors that lie outside the baseline model. The process is fully structured, with intermediate objects like baseline estimates, retrieved evidence, and separate update factors instead of only narrative reasoning. They evaluate AuditForecast on multiple live forecasting benchmarks and compare it to strong agentic baselines, market odds, and more expensive deep-research LLM agents, also measuring cost–accuracy tradeoffs.
AI.result: On several live forecasting benchmarks, AuditForecast yields more accurate and better-calibrated forecasts than strong existing LLM agent baselines. In some cases, it even outperforms market-implied reference predictions. It also beats substantially more expensive deep-research agents while being cheaper, resulting in a Pareto improvement in cost versus accuracy. Additionally, it generates structured, auditable reports that preserve all intermediate steps and evidence-to-forecast links.
AI.conclusion: Structuring LLM forecasting around explicit baseline models and mechanical odds updates, rather than purely narrative reasoning, can significantly improve both performance and transparency. AuditForecast shows that agentic scaffolds that enforce explicit probabilistic updating not only increase accuracy and calibration but also produce forecasts that are easier to audit and analyze after the fact, offering a more reliable and interpretable way to use LLMs for live forecasting.

title: The Failure Happens Before the Drift: The Social Dynamics of Values in LLM Agent Societies
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents are increasingly used as proxies for human participants in social science research, yet it remains unclear whether they can faithfully simulate diverse and conflicting human value systems. We present a World Values Survey (WVS)-grounded simulation framework where culturally diverse agents with different communication styles engage in longitudinal, value-laden discussions. Across approximately 4,000 conversations involving 1,200 personas, 15 topics, and three models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash, and Gemma-4-E4B), we evaluate value faithfulness, value drift, and conversational realism. We find that more than 50\% of personas fail to express their assigned WVS profiles from the outset, while 2-7\% drift after repeated conversations. Ablations removing demographic details improve faithfulness for some models but do not change the broader trend: simulated value distributions still systematically deviate from the assigned WVS profiles. Compared to human discussions, simulated dialogues show a different trade-off between stylistic consistency and semantic diversity, often producing content-wise varied but stylistically repetitive exchanges. These findings suggest that current LLM agents can generate plausible conversations, but remain limited proxies for representing and preserving diverse human value profiles over time.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well current LLM-based agents can simulate diverse, stable human value systems in conversations, finding substantial mismatches and drift from assigned value profiles.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used as stand-ins for humans in social science research, especially to model opinions and value-based behavior across cultures. However, it is unclear whether these models can accurately and stably represent heterogeneous human value systems over time, which is crucial if they are to be treated as reliable proxies for people in value-laden discussions and experiments.
AI.method: The authors build a simulation framework grounded in the World Values Survey (WVS), constructing culturally diverse personas with assigned value profiles and communication styles. Using three LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemma-4-E4B), they generate roughly 4,000 longitudinal conversations spanning 1,200 personas and 15 topics. They then quantify (1) value faithfulness: whether an agent’s expressed values match its assigned WVS profile; (2) value drift: whether expressed values change over repeated conversations; and (3) conversational realism: comparisons of style and content relative to human discussions. They also run ablations that remove demographic details from personas to test their effect on faithfulness.
AI.result: Over half of the simulated personas fail to express their assigned WVS value profiles correctly from the very first interactions, and 2–7% exhibit value drift over time. Removing demographic attributes sometimes improves value faithfulness for specific models but does not fix the core issue: simulated value distributions still diverge systematically from the target WVS profiles. Additionally, compared to human dialogues, LLM-generated conversations trade off semantic diversity and stylistic variety differently, with content that varies in substance but remains stylistically repetitive and less human-like.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM agents can create plausible, coherent conversations, but they do not reliably maintain or faithfully reproduce diverse human value profiles over time. Systematic deviations from assigned WVS values and measurable value drift indicate that LLM-based agents are presently limited and potentially misleading proxies for human participants in value-centric social science research, especially when accurate representation of cultural and ideological diversity is required.

title: UniRRM: Unified Reasoning Reward Models Across Languages and Evaluation Paradigms
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) excels on tasks with verifiable rewards, but in open-ended tasks, the reliability of reward models remains a key challenge. Existing solutions either depend on costly proprietary LLM-as-a-Judge systems or opaque scalar reward models that lack interpretability. Recent works on generative reward models offer a promising alternative, but they remain constrained by static evaluation criteria, fragmented evaluation paradigms, and limited multilingual support. To address these challenges, we introduce \textbf{MixReward}, a large-scale multilingual dataset spanning six domains and 103 languages, containing both pairwise and listwise data, and propose \textbf{UniRRM}, a unified reasoning reward model supporting multiple languages and evaluation paradigms. UniRRM uses a staged reasoning chain to dynamically generate task-generic and instruction-specific criteria, enabling fine-grained, input-adaptive judgments while maintaining consistency across languages. Experiments demonstrate that UniRRM-8B and UniRRM-14B achieve performance close to the state-of-the-art for models of comparable size across multiple benchmarks, and are effective for unseen evaluation paradigms. In addition, ablation studies validate the reliability and effectiveness of UniRRM.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MixReward, a large-scale multilingual reward dataset, and UniRRM, a unified reasoning reward model that generates dynamic, interpretable evaluation criteria and supports multiple evaluation paradigms and 103 languages, achieving near state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning for open-ended tasks suffers from unreliable reward models. Existing reward approaches either rely on expensive proprietary LLM judges or on opaque scalar reward models that lack interpretability and flexibility, particularly across languages and task formats. Generative reward models are promising but are limited by fixed criteria, fragmented evaluation settings, and weak multilingual support. There is a need for a unified, interpretable, multilingual reward modeling framework that can handle different evaluation paradigms and adapt its criteria to each specific task.
AI.method: The authors construct MixReward, a large multilingual dataset covering six domains and 103 languages with both pairwise and listwise preference data. On top of this, they propose UniRRM, a unified reasoning reward model that employs a staged chain-of-thought style process. UniRRM first derives task-generic and instruction-specific evaluation criteria, then uses these dynamically generated criteria to produce fine-grained judgments on model outputs. The model is trained to work across multiple evaluation paradigms (e.g., pairwise and listwise) and languages, enforcing consistency while maintaining adaptability. Models of two sizes, UniRRM-8B and UniRRM-14B, are implemented and evaluated.
AI.result: UniRRM-8B and UniRRM-14B reach performance close to the state of the art among reward models of comparable size across a variety of benchmarks. They generalize effectively to evaluation paradigms that were not seen during training, indicating strong adaptability. Ablation studies demonstrate that the staged reasoning chain and the dynamic criteria generation are key contributors to reliability and performance, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: MixReward and UniRRM provide an interpretable, multilingual, and unified solution to reward modeling for open-ended RL tasks. By dynamically generating evaluation criteria and supporting multiple evaluation paradigms and languages, UniRRM achieves near-SOTA performance with strong generalization and reliability. The work suggests that reasoning-based, generative reward models with adaptive criteria are a viable alternative to proprietary judges and static scalar rewards, and pave the way for more robust RL in open-ended settings.

title: Beyond "AI Helps Humans": Decision-Targeted Evaluation Design for Human-Agent Teams in the Agentic Era
summary: Wherever a coding agent works under engineer supervision, or a clinical model assists a radiologist, the deployment question is whether to keep the human-AI workflow or replace it with the human alone or the agent alone. The human-AI workflow is worth keeping only if it beats both of those alternatives. Yet once it is deployed, neither alternative outcome is observed: recovering one means replaying the task under that alternative, and every replay costs expert time or compute. Under a fixed replay budget, the design question is therefore which tasks should be more likely to receive a human-only replay, and which an agent-only replay. Existing methods do not directly target this decision. Agent benchmarks do not choose which missing baseline to measure, variance-based sampling ignores which of the two comparisons is closer to failing, and Bayesian information methods focus on learning model parameters instead of making the deployment decision. We propose TEAM-Design, a rule that gives every task two replay probabilities, one per baseline. It raises a probability where the missing baseline outcome is hard to predict from what is already known about the task and where that comparison is harder to establish, and lowers it where replay is expensive. We prove that the rule solves this budgeted design problem, and that drawing the replays at random from recorded probabilities still controls the chance of wrongly declaring that the workflow beats both. We reanalyze 6 clinical settings, where no human-AI workflow beats both alternatives, and a coding benchmark, where one does, then evaluate TEAM-Design on synthetic designs and on a semi-synthetic design built from a real chest X-ray reader study. TEAM-Design works best when one of the two comparisons is clearly harder to settle than the other, and can do worse than variance-based allocation when the two are similarly difficult.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to allocate a limited budget of human- or agent-only replays to evaluate whether a human-AI workflow truly outperforms both human-only and AI-only baselines, and proposes TEAM-Design, a theoretically optimal replay allocation rule.
AI.motivation: In many real-world deployments (e.g., clinical AI assisting radiologists or coding agents supervised by engineers), we want to know whether the combined human-AI workflow truly performs better than either a human alone or the AI agent alone. However, after deployment we only observe the performance of the human-AI workflow, not the two counterfactual baselines. To estimate them, we must "replay" tasks under human-only or agent-only conditions, which consumes scarce expert time or compute. Under a fixed budget for such replays, it is crucial to decide which tasks to replay, and for each task, whether to replay human-only, agent-only, or both, in order to make the most reliable deployment decision. Existing methods (standard benchmarks, variance-based sampling, Bayesian information criteria) do not directly optimize for this specific, budgeted, three-way comparison problem.
AI.method: The authors formulate the evaluation of a human-AI workflow against human-only and agent-only baselines as a budgeted experimental design problem over tasks. For each task, they assign two replay probabilities: one for human-only and one for agent-only replays. They derive TEAM-Design, a probabilistic allocation rule that increases replay probabilities when (1) the outcome under the missing baseline is hard to predict from existing information and (2) the relevant comparison (workflow vs. that baseline) is statistically hard to resolve, and decreases them when replay costs are high. They provide theoretical proofs that TEAM-Design optimally solves this constrained design problem and that sampling replays according to these probabilities still controls the error rate of incorrectly concluding that the workflow beats both baselines. They then validate the method via reanalyses of multiple real clinical studies, a coding benchmark, synthetic experiments, and a semi-synthetic chest X-ray reader study.
AI.result: Theoretical results show that TEAM-Design is optimal for the stated budgeted design objective and that random sampling based on its probabilities controls the risk of falsely declaring the human-AI workflow superior to both baselines. Empirically, across six clinical settings, the reanalysis reveals that no human-AI workflow actually outperforms both human-only and agent-only, whereas in a coding benchmark one such superior workflow exists. In synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments, TEAM-Design outperforms variance-based and other allocation baselines when one of the two key comparisons (workflow vs. human-only, workflow vs. agent-only) is substantially harder to settle than the other. When both comparisons are of similar difficulty, TEAM-Design can perform worse than simpler variance-based allocation strategies.
AI.conclusion: TEAM-Design provides a principled way to spend limited replay budget when evaluating whether a human-AI workflow truly dominates both human-only and AI-only alternatives. By tailoring replay probabilities per task and per baseline according to predictive uncertainty, comparison difficulty, and replay cost, it yields better allocation of scarce expert and compute resources and maintains statistical control over erroneous deployment decisions. Its main advantage arises in asymmetric settings where one of the two baseline comparisons is clearly more challenging, while in symmetric difficulty regimes simpler variance-based methods may suffice or even perform better.

title: Neuron-Guided Fine-Tuning: Unlocking Efficient Alignment Mechanisms for Large Language Models
comment: EMNLP 2026 Findings. Codes are available at: https://github.com/NLP2CT/NGFT
summary: Existing Supervised Fine-Tuning paradigms, particularly Full Parameter Fine-Tuning are often plagued by parameter redundancy, inconsistent data quality, and catastrophic forgetting, which current methods typically address in isolation and lack a unified optimization signal to bridge data selection, parameter updates, and knowledge preservation. To address this, we propose Neuron-Guided Fine-Tuning (NGFT), a holistic framework that leverages neuron activation patterns as a universal proxy to unify the fine-tuning lifecycle. NGFT operates via three synergistic mechanisms: (1) Adaptive Task-Specific Neuron Selection, which identifies essential neurons in a single forward pass to concentrate updates and reduce redundancy; (2) Activation-Based Data Selection, which prioritizes information-dense samples that maximize contribution to key neurons; and (3) Neuron Activation Alignment, a novel loss function that anchors activations to pre-trained states, deepening representation learning and preserving general knowledge. Experimental results across three models across both domain-specific and general benchmarks demonstrate that NGFT significantly outperforms existing mainstream fine-tuning methods in both efficiency and performance, while effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting.

AI.tldr: They propose a unified, neuron-activation–guided fine-tuning framework (NGFT) that improves efficiency, performance, and knowledge retention compared to standard supervised fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Conventional full-parameter and related supervised fine-tuning approaches suffer from redundant parameter updates, noisy or suboptimal training data selection, and catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained knowledge. Existing methods tend to handle these issues separately and lack a single optimization signal that coordinates which data to train on, which parameters to update, and how to preserve prior knowledge.
AI.method: NGFT uses neuron activation patterns as a shared signal across the fine-tuning pipeline. It has three main components: (1) Adaptive Task-Specific Neuron Selection: in a single forward pass, it selects a subset of neurons that are most relevant to the target task and restricts updates to them, reducing redundancy; (2) Activation-Based Data Selection: it scores and prioritizes training samples by how strongly they activate key neurons, thus keeping samples that are more informative for the task; (3) Neuron Activation Alignment: it introduces a new loss term that keeps the activations of selected neurons close to their pre-trained states, improving representation learning while preserving general knowledge and reducing forgetting.
AI.result: On multiple models and both domain-specific and general benchmarks, NGFT yields better downstream performance and higher fine-tuning efficiency than mainstream baselines, while also reducing catastrophic forgetting compared with those methods.
AI.conclusion: Using neuron activation patterns as a unified optimization proxy can simultaneously guide parameter selection, data selection, and knowledge preservation during fine-tuning, leading to more efficient and robust adaptation than traditional fine-tuning schemes.

title: EdgeMem: LLM-Free Agent Memory Construction and Retrieval via Evidence-Preserving Multi-Anchor Hypergraph
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, and 5 tables. An earlier implementation is available at https://github.com/Soullesskid/edgemem ; it differs substantially from the version described in this paper. The repository will be updated with the corresponding implementation after peer review
summary: Agent memory allows LLM agents to use earlier interactions when answering new queries. Existing methods often compress interaction histories into summaries or other LLM-generated representations. Repeated generation adds cost and can discard answer-bearing details before the system knows what a future query will require. We propose EdgeMem, an agent-memory method built around a simple principle: preserve original interaction turns and organize them through complementary content, temporal, and episodic cues. EdgeMem realizes this principle with a multi-anchor hypergraph constructed by lightweight local processing. Retrieval directly returns source evidence and reserves LLM use for final answer generation, combining structured access to multi-session histories with faithful retention of the original conversation. Experiments on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S show strong retrieval and memory-grounded question answering; on LoCoMo, EdgeMem achieves the highest strict-judge score among seven reproduced systems under a shared prompt (61.01 versus 58.70), while construction and retrieval require no generative-LLM calls. Overall, EdgeMem shows that preserving and organizing source evidence provides an effective and efficient foundation for agent memory without generative memory management.

AI.tldr: EdgeMem is a non-generative agent-memory system that preserves full past interactions and organizes them via a hypergraph using content, time, and episode cues for efficient, accurate retrieval and QA.
AI.motivation: LLM agents need to use long, multi-session histories, but existing memory methods rely on repeatedly summarizing or compressing interactions with generative LLMs. This is expensive and risks throwing away details that may later be needed to answer questions. The authors want a memory mechanism that is both cost-efficient and faithful to original evidence while still supporting effective retrieval from long histories.
AI.method: They introduce EdgeMem, which keeps original interaction turns instead of summarizing them, and organizes these turns in a multi-anchor hypergraph. This structure leverages complementary cues: semantic content similarity, temporal proximity, and episodic/session grouping. The hypergraph is built using lightweight local processing rather than generative LLMs. At query time, retrieval operates on this structure to fetch relevant source turns directly, and only then is an LLM used once to generate the final answer based on the retrieved evidence.
AI.result: On two benchmarks, LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, EdgeMem shows strong retrieval quality and memory-grounded QA performance. On LoCoMo, under a shared prompt and seven reproduced baselines, EdgeMem attains the best strict-judge score (61.01 vs the next-best 58.70) while incurring no generative-LLM calls for memory construction or retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Preserving raw interaction data and organizing it with a structured, non-generative hypergraph offers an effective and efficient alternative to generative memory management for LLM agents. EdgeMem demonstrates that such evidence-preserving organization can deliver state-of-the-art agent-memory performance with reduced computational and monetary cost.

title: Solving versus Verifying: Catching Contradictions in Tax Reasoning Systems
comment: Accepted for the 38th IEEE International Conference on Tools with Artificial Intelligence (ICTAI 2026)
summary: Large language models now compute correct tax liabilities on over 90% of well-formed cases in statutory benchmarks, which makes them candidates for the tax-advisory and compliance systems that consume such an answer directly. Real legal inputs, however, are frequently defective: required facts are missing, or stated facts contradict one another. Accuracy on clean benchmarks says nothing about how a model behaves then, and a system that computes straight through a defective input returns a confident number with no sign that anything is wrong. This raises two questions: does a model asked to solve a case abstain when the input is defective, and when it does not, can the same model catch the defect when asked instead to verify the input? We study six recent models on SARA-derived tax cases under missing-fact and contradictory-fact perturbations. The strongest models abstain when a fact is missing but compute through injected contradictions, returning the clean-input answer 63-76% of the time with no signal of the conflict; asked instead to verify the same input, they flag most of those contradictions. We wire that verification call into a simple contradiction gate: one extra call that abstains when the model reports a conflict. Across all six models it recovers most of the missed contradiction abstention at a clean-accuracy cost of at most about 5 percentage points, with no training and no external tooling. High accuracy on well-formed inputs is therefore an incomplete measure of reliability, and the detection the solver misses is cheaply recoverable with a single self-check.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that large language models (LLMs) can compute taxes accurately on clean cases but often fail to notice contradictory facts; however, a simple additional self-check call can detect most contradictions with only a small drop in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Although LLMs achieve high accuracy on clean, well-formed statutory tax benchmarks, real-world legal inputs are often incomplete or internally inconsistent. Existing benchmarks therefore overstate the reliability of LLM-based tax advisory and compliance systems because they do not test how models behave when the factual input is defective. The authors aim to understand whether models naturally abstain on such defective inputs and whether the same models can detect these defects when explicitly asked to verify the inputs instead of solving them.
AI.method: The authors construct perturbations of SARA-derived tax cases by either removing required facts (missing-fact perturbations) or injecting mutually inconsistent facts (contradictory-fact perturbations). They evaluate six recent LLMs under two regimes: (1) a solving regime, where the model is asked to compute the tax liability, and (2) a verification regime, where the model is asked to check the input for defects. They measure how often models abstain from answering when inputs are defective in the solving regime, and how often they flag contradictions when explicitly verifying. They then implement a simple contradiction gate that makes a second verification call on each input and abstains whenever the model reports a conflict, and they quantify the resulting impact on contradiction detection and accuracy on clean inputs.
AI.result: On missing-fact perturbations, the strongest models tend to abstain rather than produce a potentially wrong answer. On contradictory-fact perturbations, however, these models typically compute through the conflict and output the same answer they would give on a clean input in 63–76% of cases, often without indicating that anything is wrong. When switched to the verification regime, those same models correctly flag most of the contradictions that they ignored during solving. Using the contradiction gate—one additional verification call that triggers abstention if a conflict is detected—recovers most of the missing abstention behavior on contradictory cases. This comes at a modest cost: at most about a 5 percentage point reduction in accuracy on clean, contradiction-free inputs across all six models, and it requires no extra training or external tools.
AI.conclusion: The reliability of LLM-based tax reasoning systems cannot be judged solely by accuracy on well-formed benchmark cases because such metrics hide systematic failures on defective inputs, especially those with internal contradictions. Nonetheless, the paper demonstrates that models possess latent ability to detect many contradictions when explicitly prompted to verify rather than solve. A simple self-check mechanism—adding one verification call and abstaining when contradictions are reported—substantially improves reliability on contradictory inputs while only slightly reducing clean-case accuracy, offering a lightweight, training-free way to harden LLM tax applications against flawed factual inputs.

title: Deep belief networks are exact
summary: We prove that every strictly positive probability distribution on \(\{-1,1\}^n\) is represented exactly by a sigmoid belief network with finite parameters. This answers a question of Sutskever and Hinton. The proof upgrades their probability-sharing approximation to exact representation using Brouwer's fixed-point theorem.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that any strictly positive distribution on binary variables {-1,1}^n can be exactly represented by a finite sigmoid belief network.
AI.motivation: Understand the expressive power of sigmoid belief networks and resolve an open question by Sutskever and Hinton about whether such networks can represent all strictly positive distributions over binary vectors.
AI.method: They build on Sutskever and Hinton’s probability-sharing approximation construction and mathematically strengthen it. Using tools from topology, in particular Brouwer’s fixed-point theorem, they show how to turn approximate probability sharing into an exact representation with finite parameters.
AI.result: They show that for any strictly positive probability distribution on {-1,1}^n, there exists a sigmoid belief network with a finite number of units and parameters whose induced distribution matches it exactly.
AI.conclusion: Sigmoid belief networks are universal density models for strictly positive distributions over finite binary spaces; the earlier approximate universality result can be upgraded to exact representational universality via a fixed-point argument.

title: SurveyAgent-HKA: A multi-agent framework for scientific survey generation with LLMs and human knowledge augmentation
summary: Automatic scientific survey generation has become an important task in scientific document processing. The common approach of retrieving literature from a single source (e.g., arXiv) and generating surveys through a one-pass large language model (LLM) call often leads to limited reference coverage and, more importantly, fails to replicate the expert-driven revision process that is crucial for writing high-quality surveys. In this paper, we introduce SurveyAgent-HKA, a multi-agent framework that improves end-to-end scientific survey generation by incorporating knowledge derived from published surveys and peer-review comments. The framework decomposes survey generation into well-defined sub-tasks handled by LLM-powered agent. It first retrieves relevant papers from multiple sources and identifies key topics through clustering to construct an initial outline, which is then refined using outlines from related human-written surveys. Based on the refined outline, topic-focused papers are retrieved and re-ranked to select for drafting a well-grounded survey. Then, we identify common issues raised by experts in peer-review comments from published surveys to guide the revisions and finalize the survey. Experiments on two domains show that our approach outperforms mainstream baselines in citation quality, structural consistency, and content quality. Furthermore, our framework is efficient in both time and cost, making it a practical solution for broader AI-assisted scientific writing applications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SurveyAgent-HKA, a multi-agent LLM framework that generates high-quality scientific surveys by leveraging multi-source literature retrieval, human survey outlines, and peer-review comments, significantly improving citation, structure, and content quality over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing automatic survey generation typically relies on a single-source corpus (like arXiv) and a single-pass LLM generation, which limits coverage and fails to mimic the iterative, expert-driven revision process characteristic of real survey writing. There is a need for an end-to-end system that better captures expert practices, integrates richer external knowledge, and produces surveys with higher citation quality, structural coherence, and content reliability, while remaining efficient and practical.
AI.method: The authors propose SurveyAgent-HKA, a multi-agent framework that decomposes survey generation into sequential LLM-powered sub-tasks. First, it retrieves relevant papers from multiple sources and clusters them to identify key topics, from which an initial outline is constructed. This outline is refined using outlines from related, human-written surveys. Next, for each topic in the refined outline, the system retrieves and re-ranks papers to select those best suited for drafting the survey.
