Finally, the draft is revised by incorporating signals extracted from common issues in peer-review comments on published surveys, guiding improvements to structure, citations, and content quality. All steps are orchestrated via interacting LLM agents.
AI.result: On two scientific domains, SurveyAgent-HKA surpasses mainstream baseline methods in metrics related to citation quality, structural consistency, and content quality. The framework also shows good efficiency in both runtime and computational cost, indicating that the multi-agent, multi-stage design does not introduce prohibitive overhead and is viable for real-world AI-assisted survey writing.
AI.conclusion: SurveyAgent-HKA demonstrates that modeling survey writing as a multi-stage, multi-agent process augmented with knowledge from existing surveys and peer-review comments leads to higher-quality automatic scientific surveys than single-pass LLM approaches. The system effectively balances quality and efficiency, suggesting it can serve as a practical foundation for broader AI-assisted scientific document authoring and editing tools.

title: EnvCraft: Synthesizing Executable Environments in Agentic RL for Claw-like Agent
summary: The paradigm of LLMs has rapidly shifted from passive language interfaces to autonomous Claw-like agents that execute long-horizon tasks across stateful workspaces. While Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL) provides a promising path to optimize these agents, its scaling is heavily bottlenecked by the severe scarcity of interactive training environments. Existing synthetic environments are strictly limited to tool-calling endpoints, rendering them insufficient for accommodating the end-to-end real-world demands of claw-like agents. To bridge this gap, we introduce EnvCraft, an automated framework for synthesizing executable environments and scalable training data. Specifically, EnvCraft employs an environment synthesis engine to build sandbox-isolated workspaces, alongside a topology-aware data generation engine to produce coherent task trajectories. Overall, we synthesize 139 interactive environments comprising approximately 20K complex tasks for Agentic RL training. Experiments on Qwen3/3.5 models (8B-32B) show that our method yields gains of up to +11.9% on Claw-style benchmarks and +8.0% on general tool-use benchmarks, with concurrent reductions in inference token cost. The results confirm that synthesized executable environments provide robust and generalizable learning signals for training.

AI.tldr: EnvCraft is a framework that automatically builds executable, interactive environments and task trajectories to scale Agentic RL training for LLM-based agents, significantly improving performance on claw-style and general tool-use benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Agentic RL for LLM-based agents is constrained by a lack of rich, interactive training environments. Existing synthetic environments mainly expose simple tool-calling APIs, which are too narrow to reflect the complex, stateful, end-to-end workflows that emerging claw-like agents must manage. The authors aim to remove this data and environment bottleneck so that large language models acting as autonomous agents can be trained more effectively and robustly for real-world tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose EnvCraft, an automated framework that synthesizes both environments and training data. First, an environment synthesis engine programmatically constructs sandboxed, executable workspaces in which an agent can interact with stateful resources. Second, a topology-aware data generation engine creates coherent task trajectories within these environments, capturing multi-step, long-horizon interactions. Using this pipeline, they generate 139 distinct interactive environments and about 20K complex tasks tailored for Agentic RL training of LLM agents such as Qwen3/3.5.
AI.result: Using the synthesized environments and data from EnvCraft to train Qwen3/3.5 models (8B–32B parameters) leads to performance improvements of up to +11.9% on claw-style agent benchmarks and +8.0% on broader tool-use benchmarks. Additionally, the trained agents exhibit lower inference token usage, indicating more efficient decision-making and interaction patterns.
AI.conclusion: Automatically synthesized, executable environments can serve as effective training grounds for Agentic RL, providing strong, generalizable learning signals for LLM-based agents. EnvCraft demonstrates that scalable, sandboxed environment and trajectory generation substantially enhances both task performance and efficiency of claw-like autonomous agents, helping close the gap between synthetic training setups and real-world, end-to-end agent demands.

title: The Blindness of Document-Level Translation Evaluation
summary: Document-level machine translation (MT) evaluation extends segment-level protocols by presenting full documents to annotators, on the assumption that such presentation elicits document-level judgments. We test this assumption with a counterfactual condition (MIX) in which each document combines segments drawn from different systems, preserving document-level presentation while breaking cross-segment consistency. Across 18,420 expert Englis-to-Korean annotations and 14 automatic metrics, scores, system rankings, and error annotations are statistically equivalent between coherent and incoherent documents. Perception does not explain this: shown matched passages, raters identify the coherent one as the work of a single translator in 87.3% of trials. Document presentation does change how annotators work, but that change does not reach the recorded output. What is blind is the protocol, not the annotator. The concern is not that scores fall short, but that the resources invested in document-level systems, metrics, and annotation may not be measuring what they are intended to measure.

AI.tldr: The paper questions whether document-level human evaluation of machine translation truly captures document-level quality, showing that even when document coherence is broken, evaluation results remain statistically the same.
AI.motivation: Document-level MT systems and evaluation protocols are expensive to develop and run, and they are justified by the belief that showing annotators full documents allows them to judge cross-sentence coherence and discourse phenomena. The authors want to test whether current document-level evaluation protocols actually measure document-level quality or merely replicate segment-level judgments at a larger scale.
AI.method: The authors introduce a counterfactual evaluation condition called MIX, where each document is formed by mixing sentence-level segments from different MT systems, destroying cross-sentence consistency while keeping the appearance of a full document. They collect 18,420 expert English-to-Korean human annotations under standard coherent conditions and under MIX, and compare scores, system rankings, and error annotations. They also test raters’ ability to perceive coherence by asking them to identify which of two passages comes from a single translator. Additionally, they compare 14 automatic metrics across conditions.
AI.result: Scores, system rankings, and detailed error annotations are statistically indistinguishable between truly coherent documents and the MIX condition with broken cross-sentence coherence. Yet raters can reliably perceive which passage is coherent: they choose the coherent passage as being from a single translator in 87.3% of trials. Automatic metrics similarly show no meaningful difference between conditions. The way annotators work changes when viewing documents, but these differences do not manifest in the recorded evaluation outputs.
AI.conclusion: Current document-level MT evaluation protocols are effectively “blind” to document-level coherence issues: they do not produce different scores or rankings even when cross-sentence consistency is deliberately broken. The problem lies in the evaluation protocol rather than in annotator ability, since annotators can perceive coherence but the task design fails to capture it. This raises concerns that substantial resources invested in document-level MT systems, metrics, and human evaluation may not be measuring the intended document-level phenomena, calling for redesigned protocols that more directly and sensitively target document-level quality aspects.

title: Planning and Scheduling Business Processes under Control-Flow Uncertainty
summary: Scheduling activities in business processes can improve efficiency (e.g., reduce makespan), but is challenging because the exact sequence of activities required to complete a case is often uncertain due to decisions based on data that emerges during execution. Nevertheless, probabilistic information regarding such decisions can often be estimated or derived from historical execution logs, and can help anticipate which execution paths are likely to lead to successful completion. Planning with particular execution paths affects feasibility, i.e., the probability of successful completion, and the expected number of superfluous activities that are planned but never executed. We frame the problem as a chance-constrained optimization problem and present two formulations: A decomposed approach with two stages, a planning stage that minimizes the expected number of superfluous activities subject to a feasibility constraint, and a scheduling stage that minimizes the makespan over the planned activities; and an integrated approach that combines planning and scheduling into a single formulation. Evaluation on two real-world and one synthetic dataset shows that the integrated approach yields superior makespans but is intractable at scale, while the decomposed approach scales to large settings.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses scheduling in business processes under uncertain execution paths by using probabilistic information from logs and formulating a chance-constrained optimization problem with decomposed and integrated approaches.
AI.motivation: In many business processes, activity scheduling can greatly improve efficiency (e.g., reduce makespan), but the exact future sequence of activities is uncertain because later decisions depend on data that becomes available only during execution. However, historical logs provide probabilistic information about alternative execution paths, which is underexploited for planning and scheduling.
AI.method: The authors formulate the problem as a chance-constrained optimization problem. They propose two formulations: (1) a decomposed two-stage approach where a planning stage chooses activities to minimize the expected number of superfluous (planned but not executed) activities under a feasibility (success probability) constraint, followed by a scheduling stage that minimizes makespan over the chosen activities; and (2) an integrated approach that jointly optimizes planning and scheduling in one model.
AI.result: Through experiments on two real-world and one synthetic dataset, they compare the decomposed and integrated formulations. The integrated approach achieves better makespans but becomes computationally intractable for large-scale instances, while the decomposed approach remains computationally scalable to large problem sizes, with some sacrifice in optimality of makespan.
AI.conclusion: Chance-constrained optimization using probabilistic path information from logs is effective for scheduling under process uncertainty. An integrated planning-and-scheduling formulation yields superior makespans but does not scale well, whereas a two-stage decomposed formulation offers a practical trade-off between solution quality and scalability for large business process settings.

title: Beyond Cross-Lingual Transfer: Benchmarking Propagation Boundaries in Multilingual LLM Unlearning
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) unlearning aims to suppress target knowledge while preserving general capabilities. In multilingual settings, unlearning must additionally propagate within its intended linguistic scope. However, existing evaluations mainly measure cross-lingual transfer and cannot distinguish insufficient from excessive propagation. We introduce CLLPU (Cross-Lingual and Language-Bound Protocol for LLM Unlearning), a multilingual benchmark that formulates this problem through two settings: common-goal forgetting, where target knowledge should be suppressed across all languages, and language-conditioned forgetting, where suppression should remain confined to a designated language. CLLPU combines goal-guided topic pairing, schema-aware relation matching, and dual-anchor multilingual translation to construct 800 matched knowledge-unit pairs and 72,000 QA instances across ten languages. Experiments with six representative methods on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct reveal opposite failure modes: forgetting remains incomplete when universal suppression is required, yet spreads beyond the intended boundary when language-conditioned confinement is required. We further find that general multilingual utility can conceal damage to neighbor knowledge. These findings establish propagation control as a central challenge for multilingual LLM unlearning. We publicly release CLLPU together with its construction pipeline.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CLLPU, a multilingual benchmark to evaluate how well LLM unlearning can suppress specific knowledge across or within languages while preserving general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM unlearning work in multilingual settings lacks fine-grained evaluation of how forgetting propagates across languages. Current metrics focus on whether knowledge transfers cross-lingually but cannot tell if unlearning is too weak (incomplete forgetting) or too strong (unintended spillover into other languages). There is a need to systematically test both universal forgetting and language-specific forgetting, and to understand propagation control as a key challenge.
AI.method: The authors design CLLPU, a benchmark and protocol for multilingual unlearning. They define two settings: (1) common-goal forgetting, where specific knowledge must be suppressed in every language, and (2) language-conditioned forgetting, where forgetting must be restricted to one target language while preserving the same knowledge in other languages. To build the benchmark, they use goal-guided topic pairing to match related knowledge units, schema-aware relation matching to align facts and relations, and a dual-anchor multilingual translation pipeline to ensure consistent alignment across ten languages. This yields 800 matched knowledge-unit pairs and 72,000 QA examples. They then evaluate six representative unlearning methods on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under these settings.
AI.result: On CLLPU, all evaluated unlearning methods show systematic failures. In the common-goal setting, unlearning does not fully suppress the target knowledge across all languages, leaving residual memorization. In the language-conditioned setting, unlearning tends to over-propagate, erasing or degrading the target knowledge in languages where it should be kept intact. Additionally, the authors observe that standard measures of multilingual capability can hide localized damage to semantically or linguistically neighboring knowledge items.
AI.conclusion: CLLPU reveals that controlling how unlearning effects propagate across languages is a central unsolved problem in multilingual LLM unlearning. Existing methods either forget too little when universal suppression is needed or forget too broadly when language-scoped suppression is required, and standard utility metrics can obscure these issues. The benchmark and its construction pipeline are released to facilitate more nuanced evaluation and development of propagation-aware unlearning techniques.

title: Agents Trust Tools Too Much: Measuring Reliance on Unreliable Tools
summary: Existing evaluations of tool-using agents primarily measure whether an agent can successfully complete diverse tasks with tools. These evaluations generally assume that tools return reliable information. However, tool returns in real-world systems can be plausible yet incorrect. We investigate how agents respond to unreliable tool returns by evaluating fourteen LLMs using three tools-web search, LLM sub-agent delegation, and code execution. For each tool, we corrupt its returns and measure whether agents adopt the corrupted content in their final answers. Agents exhibit high levels of overtrust across all three settings: the mean adoption rate exceeds one third for every tool and reaches 68.0% for web search. Analysis of reasoning traces reveals a particularly concerning failure mode: agents often recognize conflicts and even recover the correct answer internally, yet present only the corrupted answer without warning the user. To mitigate agents' overtrust in tool returns, we intervene at three levels: prompting by the user, metadata from the tool provider, and post-training by the agent builder. Although some interventions help for particular models or tools, none consistently mitigates overtrust across tools. These findings identify overtrust in unreliable tools as a serious and persistent failure mode, motivating evaluations and interventions that enable agents to validate tool outputs and transparently communicate unresolved conflicts.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language model (LLM) agents behave when tools they call (like web search, code execution, or sub-agents) return misleading or corrupted results, finding that agents frequently overtrust these tools and propagate incorrect outputs, and that common mitigation strategies are only partially effective.
AI.motivation: Most benchmarks for tool-using LLM agents assume that external tools always provide correct information, which is unrealistic because real-world APIs, search engines, or other tools can be wrong or adversarial. There is a need to understand whether LLM agents detect and resist unreliable tool outputs, or instead overtrust them and pass on errors to users, and to evaluate if current mitigation strategies work.
AI.method: The authors evaluate fourteen different LLMs acting as tool-using agents. They construct three tool settings: (1) web search, (2) delegation to an LLM sub-agent, and (3) code execution. For each setting they systematically corrupt the tool outputs to introduce plausible but incorrect information. They then measure the adoption rate, i.e., how often the agent incorporates the corrupted content into its final answer. They also analyze chain-of-thought or reasoning traces to see whether agents internally notice conflicts between their own reasoning and the corrupted tool outputs. Finally, they test mitigation interventions at three layers: user-level prompting instructions, metadata or warnings provided alongside tool outputs, and post-training modifications or alignment by the agent developer.
AI.result: Across all three tool types, agents show high overtrust in unreliable tools. The mean adoption rate of corrupted tool outputs is above one third for every tool and rises to 68% for web search. Reasoning-trace analysis shows that agents sometimes internally derive or recover the correct answer and acknowledge inconsistencies, yet still output only the corrupted tool result to the user without signaling the conflict. Mitigation interventions—such as prompting agents to be more skeptical, attaching reliability metadata to tool responses, or post-training to reduce overtrust—yield mixed improvements and do not consistently solve the problem across tools or models.
AI.conclusion: Tool overtrust is a pervasive and serious failure mode in current LLM-based agents. Agents are prone to accept and propagate erroneous tool outputs, even when their internal reasoning suggests those outputs may be wrong, and they often fail to communicate such conflicts to users. Existing mitigation strategies are insufficiently robust, suggesting that future work must design better evaluation methodologies and training or architectural approaches to help agents validate tool outputs, manage uncertainty, and transparently surface unresolved inconsistencies instead of silently deferring to tools.

title: Alignment by Stereotyping: How LLMs Sacrifice Individual Distinctiveness for Cultural Adaptation
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed for personalized interaction, and demographic conditioning via user profiles is a widely adopted strategy for cultural adaptation. We ask whether this approach genuinely serves individual users or achieves accuracy by erasing individual distinctiveness. Studying seven models including frontier GPT-5.1 on the World Values Survey, we find that demographic profiles improve value alignment accuracy for most models, but at a systematic cost to individuality. That is, models pull responses toward demographic group centroids rather than preserving individual differences, a behavioral pattern we term alignment by stereotyping. Permutation tests (10,000 permutations, six demographic attributes, seven models) certify that top-performing models compress individuals far above the human baseline; within-family scaling amplifies this tradeoff while degrading intrinsic cultural understanding. Using a synthetic dialogue dataset validated on real human-chatbot conversations from PRISM (Kirk et al., 2024), we further show that distributing demographic signals across conversational turns partially suppresses prototype retrieval compared to compact demographic labels, a finding validated on real conversations via PRISM but requiring replication at larger scale.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that using demographic profiles to personalize large language models can increase value alignment accuracy but does so by stereotyping—pulling user responses toward group averages and reducing individual distinctiveness.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used for personalized, culturally adaptive interactions, demographic conditioning has become standard practice. However, it is unclear whether this method truly serves individuals or merely exploits group-level regularities, potentially reinforcing stereotypes and erasing personal uniqueness. The authors aim to rigorously test whether demographic conditioning aligns with individual values or primarily operates via demographic prototyping.
AI.method: The authors evaluate seven large language models, including a frontier model (GPT-5.1), using the World Values Survey as a benchmark for human value judgments. They compare model predictions with and without demographic profiles across six demographic attributes. They measure how often demographic conditioning pulls model responses toward demographic group centroids instead of individual-level data, defining this pattern as “alignment by stereotyping.” They run permutation tests with 10,000 permutations across all models and demographics to quantify how much models compress individual differences relative to a human baseline. They also study within-family model scaling to see how model size affects this tradeoff and run experiments on a synthetic dialogue dataset, validated against real human–chatbot conversations from the PRISM corpus, to test how distributing demographic cues across turns versus in compact labels affects prototype retrieval behavior.
AI.result: Demographic profiles generally increase value alignment accuracy for most tested models, but this comes with a consistent reduction in individuality: model outputs are attracted toward demographic group centroids, demonstrating “alignment by stereotyping.” Permutation tests show that top-performing models exhibit significantly greater individual compression than what is observed in human data. Within-family scaling intensifies the tradeoff, leading to more reliance on demographic prototypes and worse intrinsic cultural understanding. In dialogue settings, spreading demographic signals across multiple conversational turns reduces prototype retrieval compared with providing compact demographic labels, a result observed both in synthetic data and validated with PRISM conversations, though larger-scale replication is still needed.
AI.conclusion: Demographic conditioning helps LLMs better match aggregate group-level value patterns but does so by stereotyping, sacrificing individual distinctiveness and over-compressing users relative to human baselines. Larger models worsen this tradeoff, suggesting that simple scaling and demographic profiling do not yield genuine cultural understanding. More nuanced approaches are needed—such as less compact, more contextual demographic signaling—to preserve individuality while still enabling cultural adaptation, and the dialogue findings must be replicated at larger scale to confirm their robustness.

title: The convergent laboratory: when AI reasoning, autonomous experiments, high performance and quantum computing reshape chemistry
summary: This Comment emerges from TPC26 (https://tpc26.org), a conference convening leaders from academia, national laboratories, and industry who are reshaping materials science discovery. The meeting explored how AI, autonomous agents, self-driving labs, higher performance and quantum computing converge to amplify their individual impact on materials science discovery. The perspectives here reflect the firsthand experiences of researchers at these frontiers and capture the essence of this global endeavor. As AI-driven reasoning, autonomous agentic frameworks, self-driving laboratories, and fault-tolerant quantum processors mature simultaneously, we offer this Comment as a reference at what we believe is a tipping point of transformative advances and productive disruption in the chemical sciences.

AI.tldr: Comment from TPC26 highlights a convergence of AI, autonomous agents, self-driving labs, high-performance computing, and quantum computing that is reshaping materials science discovery.
AI.motivation: To capture and communicate the perspectives of leading researchers at TPC26 on how emerging computational and automation technologies are collectively transforming materials and chemical sciences, and to mark what they see as a tipping point in the field.
AI.method: Synthesize firsthand experiences and viewpoints shared at the TPC26 conference among experts from academia, national laboratories, and industry, focusing on their work at the intersection of AI, autonomous systems, self-driving laboratories, and quantum/high-performance computing.
AI.result: The Comment distills consensus themes and insights indicating that the simultaneous maturation of AI reasoning, autonomous agentic frameworks, self-driving labs, and fault-tolerant quantum processors is significantly accelerating materials discovery and altering research workflows.
AI.conclusion: The field of chemical and materials science is at a transformative tipping point driven by converging advances in AI, autonomy, and quantum/high-performance computing, promising both major scientific gains and disruptive changes in how research is conducted.

title: ModularPhaseNet: Finite-Cyclic Phase Geometry for Computable Semantic Hierarchy, Direction, and Context Consistency in Standard Transformers
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure. Extends arXiv:2602.14419 (WavePhaseNet) and arXiv:2608.15820 (QuantumPhaseNet). Theory and a pre-registered evaluation plan; no experimental results are reported
summary: We propose ModularPhaseNet, a classical and integer-computable discretization of the continuous complex phase geometry introduced in QuantumPhaseNet. The real-valued hidden states of a standard Transformer are retained, while only an auxiliary phase channel is quantized into a cyclic subgroup G = <g> of order q | (p-1) in the multiplicative group of F_p. A continuous phase e^{i phi} is represented by z = g^a mod p; phase composition becomes group multiplication, relative phase becomes group division, conceptual hierarchy is induced by a filtration of cyclic quotients, semantic direction is represented by oriented relative group elements, and contextual consistency is measured by gauge-invariant cycle holonomy. The method introduces three components into an otherwise standard Transformer: a finite-phase encoder, a quotient-filtration hierarchy module, and a group-valued connection module. Their outputs enter self-attention as real-valued bias terms. Training uses distributions in the real group algebra or straight-through Gumbel-Softmax, whereas inference uses exact modular exponentiation and precomputed tables. No quantum hardware, complex-valued matrix multiplication, or discrete-logarithm computation is required. We prove quantization-distortion bounds, nesting of quotient-induced partitions, gauge invariance, a discrete integrability result for flat connections, and boundedness of the resulting attention output. The central empirical hypothesis is that these exact discrete invariants improve hierarchy recovery, discourse alignment, contradiction detection, and calibrated hallucination-risk prediction under a controlled compute budget. This paper reports the theory together with a pre-registered evaluation plan; the experiments described in Section 14 have not yet been carried out, and no empirical result is claimed here.

AI.tldr: ModularPhaseNet discretizes the complex phase geometry of QuantumPhaseNet into modular arithmetic over a finite cyclic group, integrating group-valued phase structure into an otherwise standard Transformer to obtain discrete, provably well-behaved invariants believed to help with hierarchy and discourse-related tasks.
AI.motivation: Transformers typically operate on real-valued representations without an explicit, principled mechanism for modeling phase-like relational geometry, hierarchy, and gauge-invariant structure. QuantumPhaseNet introduced a continuous complex phase geometry using quantum-inspired ideas, but such models can be harder to compute with and deploy on classical hardware. There is a need for a purely classical, integer-computable framework that preserves the beneficial geometric and invariant properties of phase-based representations while remaining compatible with standard Transformer infrastructures and practical compute constraints.
AI.method: The authors define ModularPhaseNet by quantizing continuous complex phases e^{i phi} into elements of a finite cyclic subgroup G = <g> of the multiplicative group of a finite field F_p, with order q | (p-1). Each phase is represented as z = g^a mod p, and phase operations are implemented through group multiplication and division. They keep the standard Transformer’s real-valued hidden states, and add an auxiliary phase channel governed by group operations. The model introduces three new modules: (1) a finite-phase encoder that maps inputs to group-valued phases; (2) a quotient-filtration hierarchy module that builds a conceptual hierarchy from nested cyclic quotients, inducing partitions of the representation space; and (3) a group-valued connection module that defines oriented relative group elements along edges in the attention graph, enabling the computation of gauge-invariant cycle holonomy as a measure of contextual consistency. These group-theoretic quantities are then converted into real-valued bias terms fed into self-attention. For training, they approximate discrete group elements via distributions in the real group algebra or via straight-through Gumbel-Softmax relaxation. At inference, the system uses exact modular exponentiation and precomputed lookup tables for efficiency, with no reliance on quantum hardware, complex-valued linear algebra, or discrete logarithm computation. Theoretical analysis establishes bounds on quantization distortion, properties of quotient-induced partitions, gauge invariance, a discrete integrability theorem for flat group connections, and boundedness of attention outputs incorporating these biases.
AI.result: There are no empirical or benchmark results reported; the paper is theoretical and methodological. The authors provide mathematical guarantees: (1) bounds on how much distortion arises from quantizing continuous phases into the finite cyclic subgroup; (2) proof that the quotient-filtration yields nested partitions, reflecting a coherent multi-level hierarchy; (3) formal gauge invariance of the key quantities, so that predictions do not depend on arbitrary global phase choices; (4) a discrete integrability result identifying when connections are flat, relating holonomy around cycles to consistency conditions; and (5) boundedness of the augmented attention outputs when group-derived bias terms are included. They also present a detailed, pre-registered evaluation plan outlining how they will later test the empirical value of these constructs, but without current experimental outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that ModularPhaseNet offers a fully classical, integer-friendly discretization of the phase geometry previously proposed in QuantumPhaseNet, embedding group-theoretic, gauge-invariant structure into Transformers through an auxiliary phase channel and associated modules. The theoretical groundwork suggests that exact discrete invariants derived from finite-group phases can be cleanly integrated into self-attention and remain computationally tractable and well-behaved. The authors hypothesize—but do not yet demonstrate—that this structure will improve recovery of hierarchical relations, discourse alignment, contradiction detection, and calibrated hallucination-risk estimation under realistic compute budgets. They position the work as a theoretical contribution plus a pre-registered roadmap for future empirical evaluation rather than as a claim of realized performance gains.

title: What LLM Trading Agents Actually Do in Production: A Six-Month, Population-Scale Record from Two Fleets
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Artifacts, figures, and aggregate data: https://github.com/ProjectDXAI/continuous-record-llm-trading-agents
summary: We present a continuous, population-scale measurement record of autonomous language-model trading agents operating in production across two systems with one design lineage: DX Terminal Pro (3,505 user-funded vaults trading real ETH in Base memecoin markets for 21 days, February to March 2026) and the DXAP live alpha fleet (500 to 599 user-created agents all-history, 91 to 117 concurrently active, trading Hyperliquid perpetuals, June to August 2026). The record spans roughly six months, 7.5M single-model invocations with about 300K onchain actions, and a further 231,638 multi-tool turns producing 14,596 fills. Four findings carry the paper. First, the operating layer determines behavior more than anything written in strategy text: a risk slider explains leverage (+0.425 per level), agent fixed effects absorb 60% of variance, and a leaderboard render boundary causally routes selection (regression discontinuity 1.75x at the top-3 cut). Second, sizing is volatility-blind: median leverage is 5.0x in every volatility sextile, and one posture-slider cell (11% of the book) holds 62% of liquidations. Third, agents capture almost none of the upside they reach: 43.2% of positions saw at least +300 bps of favorable excursion within 24h, yet 49.3% of those closed with a negative trade return; a mechanical bracket recovers +39.0 bps per position. Fourth, neither fleet shows a directional edge. The DXAP fleet is not profitable and trails a matched Hyperliquid retail benchmark (41% vs. 50% roundtrip win rate). A paired-replay league of frontier models on 416 captured production scenarios finds decision quality statistically indistinguishable at this horizon, while choice stability differs sharply across model families. Every headline survives day-clustered inference, permutation nulls, and a common-fee restatement; the paper closes with a 17-rule methodology canon bought with our own retractions.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes real-world performance and behavior of autonomous, user-configured language-model trading agents across two large live deployments, showing that UI/operating-layer design dominates strategy text, sizing is poorly risk-adjusted, agents fail to capture reachable upside, and exhibit no directional edge versus retail benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Despite rapid interest in LLM-based trading agents, there is very little population-scale, production data on how they actually behave with real capital over time. Existing work focuses on backtests, toy markets, or small samples, leaving open questions about whether LLM agents have an edge, how interface design shapes their risk-taking, whether they size positions appropriately to volatility, and how decision quality and stability vary across model families. This paper aims to fill that empirical gap with continuous, on-chain and platform-level measurements from two live systems.
AI.method: The authors collect and unify logs from two production deployments of LLM trading agents: (1) DX Terminal Pro, with 3,505 user-funded vaults trading real ETH in Base memecoin markets over 21 days; and (2) the DXAP live alpha fleet, 500–599 user-created agents trading Hyperliquid perpetuals over June–August 2026. The dataset includes 7.5M single-model invocations, ~300K onchain actions, and 231,638 multi-tool turns generating 14,596 fills. They conduct statistical analyses including fixed-effects models, regressions on risk and UI parameters, regression discontinuity at leaderboard thresholds, volatility-bucket analyses of leverage, excursion vs. realized P&L studies with counterfactual mechanical brackets, benchmarking against a matched retail cohort, and a paired-replay league of frontier models over 416 captured scenarios. Robustness checks include day-clustered inference, permutation nulls, and restatement under common fee assumptions.
AI.result:
1) Operating-layer/UI factors dominate: a simple risk slider strongly predicts leverage (+0.425 per level), agent fixed effects soak up 60% of behavioral variance, and being just above a leaderboard top-3 cutoff causally boosts selection by 1.75x.
2) Position sizing ignores volatility: median leverage is ~5x across all volatility sextiles, and a single posture-slider setting (11% of exposure) accounts for 62% of liquidations.
3) Agents systematically fail to monetize favorable excursions: 43.2% of trades experience at least +300 bps profit within 24h, but 49.3% of these end with negative P&L; a simple mechanical bracket rule would reclaim +39 bps per position on average.
4) No directional edge: the DXAP fleet is unprofitable and underperforms a matched retail Hyperliquid benchmark (41% vs. 50% win rate). In replay, different frontier LLMs show statistically indistinguishable decision quality over this horizon, though their choice stability varies significantly across model families. All main findings remain under multiple robustness checks.
AI.conclusion: The performance and risk behavior of LLM trading agents in the wild is governed more by operating-layer design and user-configurable controls than by the written strategy prompts. These agents do not currently show a systematic directional edge and exhibit volatility-insensitive sizing and poor profit capture, leaving easy mechanical improvements unexploited. Differences between advanced models manifest more in stability profiles than in short-horizon edge. The authors distill their empirical lessons into a 17-rule methodological canon for designing, deploying, and evaluating production LLM trading systems, based on errors they encountered and subsequently retracted.

title: Tri-PvP: Exposing Modality Bias in Omni-Modal Large Language Models through Perceptual-Propositional Evidence Conflicts
summary: Omni-modal large language models (OLLMs) jointly process vision, audio, and text, yet their modality bias under cross-modal conflict remains underexplored. Existing benchmarks conflate two distinct forms of evidence within a single modality: perceptual signals (e.g., a photograph or recording of a dog) and propositional signals (e.g., the declarative claim "this is a dog"), such that any measured modality bias is inherently confounded with evidence-form bias, precluding clean attribution to either source. To address this, we introduce Tri-PvP, an 8,000-sample tri-modal conflict benchmark crossing vision, audio, and text, where vision and audio each take perceptual or propositional form. Evaluating five OLLMs, we find robust visual bias across most models and evidence-type conditions. Crucially, we reveal a systematic asymmetry in evidence-form bias: models exhibit a stronger bias toward perceptual signal in vision but propositional in audio. Further analyses via layer-wise linear probing and contrastive decoding reveal that modality bias is already linearly decodable from early representation layers and can only be partially mitigated, calling for mitigation strategies beyond surface-level interventions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Tri-PvP, a tri-modal benchmark to disentangle modality bias from evidence-form bias in omni-modal LLMs, showing that models are visually biased and treat perceptual vs. propositional evidence asymmetrically across vision and audio, with biases detectable early in representations and hard to fix with shallow methods.
AI.motivation: Omni-modal LLMs can process vision, audio, and text, but it is unclear how they behave when these modalities conflict. Existing benchmarks mix perceptual and propositional evidence within a modality (e.g., image vs. caption-like text about that image), which confounds whether models favor a modality itself or a specific form of evidence. This prevents a clean understanding and mitigation of modality bias, a crucial aspect for safety, reliability, and interpretability of OLLMs.
AI.method: The authors build Tri-PvP, an 8k-sample benchmark spanning vision, audio, and text. In this benchmark, visual and audio inputs can appear either as perceptual signals (raw-like sensory data, such as photos or recordings) or as propositional signals (explicit declarative statements in those modalities). They systematically construct cross-modal conflicts across vision–audio–text and evaluate five OLLMs on which signals the models prefer. They further perform layer-wise linear probing to read out modality bias from internal representations and apply contrastive decoding to test whether such bias can be mitigated via decoding-level interventions.
AI.result: Across five evaluated OLLMs, the models consistently exhibit visual bias—preferring visual evidence over conflicting audio or text—across most evidence-type configurations. Moreover, there is a striking asymmetry in how they treat evidence forms: in the visual channel, models prefer perceptual over propositional evidence, whereas in the audio channel they prefer propositional over perceptual signals. Linear probing shows that these modality preferences are already encoded and linearly decodable from early hidden layers, and contrastive decoding only partially reduces these biases.
AI.conclusion: Modality bias in current omni-modal LLMs is both robust and nuanced: they not only favor vision over other modalities but also treat perceptual vs. propositional evidence differently across modalities. Because these biases emerge early in the representation hierarchy and resist surface-level decoding tweaks, effective mitigation will likely require architectural or training-level interventions rather than only prompt or decoding strategies. Tri-PvP offers a cleaner way to study and compare such biases in future OLLMs.

title: CUSP: Decomposable Collective Uncertainty for Multi-Agent Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Aggregating heterogeneous vision-language models (VLMs) can improve multimodal reasoning, but neither an individual model's confidence nor that of the aggregated answer measures reliability at the system level. We present CUSP (Collective Uncertainty through Semantic Opinion Pooling), a training-free uncertainty quantification framework that maps multiple VLM responses to a shared semantic response space, pools them into a pooled semantic opinion, and reports two complementary system-level signals: collective uncertainty, the dispersion of the pooled opinion, and Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD), the conflict among the model-level opinions. Within this pooled semantic opinion, the unnormalized collective entropy decomposes exactly into the mean of the models' individual semantic entropies and the JSD, separating total dispersion from model conflict. Requiring neither token logits nor calibration labels, CUSP applies to open-weight and commercial VLMs alike. In static multi-VLM ensembles, collective uncertainty is the strongest signal in the small-model regime (0.764 AUROC for prediction-error detection, 0.889 AUARC for abstention), outperforming uncertainty baselines majority voting and naive selection by 4.7 to 15.8 points and widening its margin as the ensemble grows; JSD is strongest in the evaluated commercial regime (0.819 AUROC, 0.910 AUARC) and ranks hard-answer model conflict with AUROC up to 0.982. The pooled prediction also improves accuracy over the average single model by 5.6 to 13.0 points. Over the full trajectory of a multi-step, multi-agent system, subagent collective uncertainty ranks system failures above chance (0.619 AUROC) and gives the best abstention ordering among the evaluated signals (0.699 AUARC).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CUSP, a training-free framework to quantify uncertainty and reliability for ensembles of heterogeneous vision-language models by mapping their responses to a shared semantic space and analyzing dispersion and disagreement.
AI.motivation: Existing ensembles of vision-language models can boost multimodal reasoning, but there is no good way to measure reliability at the whole-system level. Simple proxies such as an individual model’s confidence, or the confidence of the aggregated answer, fail to capture when the ensemble is confused or internally conflicted. Moreover, many uncertainty methods require access to token logits or calibration data, making them unusable with closed or commercial VLMs. The authors aim to provide a principled, model-agnostic and training-free way to quantify uncertainty and disagreement in heterogeneous VLM ensembles, and to use that to detect errors, guide abstention, and improve system-level reliability.
AI.method: The authors introduce CUSP (Collective Uncertainty through Semantic Opinion Pooling), a framework that takes responses from multiple VLMs and projects them into a shared semantic response space (a distribution over semantic options). These model-level semantic distributions are then pooled into a single “pooled semantic opinion.” From this pooled opinion, they compute: (1) collective uncertainty, measured as the dispersion (entropy) of the pooled distribution, and (2) Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD), which captures conflict among the individual model distributions relative to their mean. They show that the unnormalized collective entropy decomposes exactly into the average individual semantic entropy plus the JSD, cleanly separating overall dispersion from inter-model conflict. The method is training-free and does not require token-level logits or any calibration labels, allowing it to work for both open-weight and commercial VLMs.
AI.result: In static ensembles of multiple VLMs, collective uncertainty is the most informative signal in the small-model regime, achieving 0.764 AUROC for detecting prediction errors and 0.889 AUARC for abstention, outperforming majority voting and naive model-selection baselines by 4.7–15.8 points and gaining advantage as ensemble size increases. In a regime dominated by commercial models, JSD becomes the strongest signal, with 0.819 AUROC and 0.910 AUARC, and can rank “hard” answer conflicts with AUROC up to 0.982. The pooled semantic prediction itself improves accuracy over the average single model by 5.6–13.0 percentage points. In multi-step, multi-agent settings, subagent collective uncertainty can rank full-system failures above chance (0.619 AUROC) and yields the best abstention ordering among evaluated signals (0.699 AUARC).
AI.conclusion: CUSP provides a practical, training-free, and model-agnostic way to quantify uncertainty for ensembles of heterogeneous VLMs by operating in a shared semantic response space. By decomposing collective uncertainty into dispersion and inter-model conflict (via JSD), it offers interpretable, system-level reliability metrics that work even with closed commercial models. Empirically, these signals significantly improve error detection, abstention strategies, and overall accuracy in both static ensembles and multi-agent, multi-step systems, indicating that semantic opinion pooling is an effective approach for making VLM aggregates more reliable and trustworthy.

title: Factors Influencing the Emergence of Dependency Length Minimization in Neural Agent Simulations
comment: This is a preprint version of the manuscript currently under review at Cognitive Science
summary: Given various grammatical options, language users prefer the word order choice that reduces the overall length of syntactic dependencies, a principle known as dependency length minimization (DLM). The origins of this preference remain an open question, particularly whether it originates from constraints on efficient information processing. Computational simulations provide a powerful approach to identifying the factors influencing the emergence of linguistic phenomena. However, previous simulations of DLM have not examined realistic interaction contexts and have produced mixed results. The present study investigates the emergence of DLM in artificial languages using a recently proposed language learning and communication framework based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs). In this framework, agents are trained to speak and interpret artificial languages and then use these languages to communicate. Using this framework, we study the impact of several factors related to processing limitations in a communicative setting, such as noise during listening, limited speaker capacity, and incremental sentence processing. Our results reveal a complex interplay among these factors in shaping word order preferences in neural agents. Specifically, in the full meaning space, agents regularize toward a single dominant word order, while in the half meaning space they show a short-before-long preference that only aligns with DLM in verb-initial languages. A consistent DLM preference emerges only when agents are subject to incremental processing pressure. These findings suggest that limitations in human cognitive processing may indeed play a role in shaping DLM. Our findings provide insights into the conditions under which neural models replicate human-like preferences and highlight the challenges of designing emergent communication models that capture human cognitive biases in language processing.

AI.tldr: The paper studies when and how dependency length minimization (DLM) emerges in artificial languages learned and used by neural-network agents, showing that a robust DLM preference appears mainly under incremental processing constraints.
AI.motivation: Language users tend to choose word orders that minimize the total length of syntactic dependencies, but it is unclear whether this pattern arises from constraints on efficient information processing. Existing computational simulations of DLM use oversimplified settings and yield inconsistent findings, so there is a need for more realistic communicative simulations to test processing-based explanations of DLM.
AI.method: The authors use a recurrent neural network (RNN)-based emergent communication framework in which artificial agents are jointly trained to speak and interpret languages and then use them for communication. Within this setup, they systematically manipulate processing-related factors: noise during listening, limitations on the speaker’s capacity, the size of the semantic (meaning) space, and whether sentence processing is incremental. They then analyze the resulting word order patterns and their relationship to dependency length minimization.
AI.result: In large (“full”) meaning spaces, agents converge on a single dominant word order rather than flexibly adjusting order for DLM. In reduced (“half”) meaning spaces, agents exhibit a short-before-long word order preference, which corresponds to DLM only in verb-initial systems. Across conditions, a stable, general preference for DLM emerges only when agents are required to process input incrementally. This demonstrates that different processing constraints interact in nontrivial ways to shape emergent word order preferences.
AI.conclusion: The study supports the view that human-like dependency length minimization can arise from cognitive processing limitations, particularly incremental processing pressure. However, it also shows that such preferences are not an automatic outcome of training neural agents to communicate; they depend on specific conditions. The findings clarify when neural communication models reproduce human word-order biases and underscore the difficulty of designing emergent communication frameworks that faithfully capture human cognitive constraints on language processing.

title: Recovering Temporal and Geographic Signals from Language Model Embeddings
summary: Understanding whether language-model embeddings encode structured real-world information is important for both representation analysis and information retrieval. We study this question for temporal and geographic signals using a simple projection-based method that operates directly on output embeddings. Given a small set of seed examples, the method defines an axis in embedding space and ranks texts or entities by their projection onto that axis. Our approach is fully black-box and model-agnostic: it requires only embeddings, without access to model weights, internal activations, auxiliary probes, or additional training. This makes it applicable to modern embedding models available only through APIs and provides a lightweight way to analyze whether temporal and spatial dimensions are present in their representation spaces. We apply the method to temporal and geographic datasets and find that embedding projections recover meaningful chronological and spatial structure. These results provide evidence that output embeddings encode signals relevant to time and space, while also offering a practical tool for interpretability and for downstream temporal and geographic information retrieval tasks, such as temporal ordering, geographic ranking, and tagging.

AI.tldr: They test whether language-model embeddings encode time and location by projecting embeddings onto axes defined from a few seed examples, showing that temporal and geographic structure can be recovered in a black-box, model-agnostic way.
AI.motivation: To determine if and how language-model embeddings contain interpretable real-world structure, specifically temporal (when) and geographic (where) information, without needing access to model internals or training additional models. This is valuable both for understanding representation spaces and for enabling practical retrieval tasks that depend on time and space signals.
AI.method: Use a small set of seed examples with known temporal or geographic attributes to define a direction (axis) in the embedding space. Then, project other text or entity embeddings onto this axis and use the projection values to rank or analyze them. The method is black-box and model-agnostic, requiring only output embeddings (e.g., from API models) without any access to weights, intermediate activations, or extra training/probes.
AI.result: When applied to temporal and geographic datasets, the projection-based method successfully recovers meaningful chronological and spatial structure. Ranked projections correlate with actual time and location, indicating that embeddings organize data along latent temporal and geographic dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Language-model output embeddings implicitly encode structured temporal and geographic information that can be linearly extracted using simple projection methods. This offers both evidence about the internal structure of embedding spaces and a lightweight, practical tool for interpretability and for temporal/geographic retrieval tasks like ordering, ranking, and tagging.

title: Generating Adversarial Texts for Machine Translation via GRPO
summary: As machine translation (MT) systems continue to improve, standard benchmarks become less informative for exposing remaining weaknesses. Traditional methods for creating challenging test sets rely on expensive manual creation or curation, while automated approaches struggle to produce sets with the necessary translation difficulty and linguistic diversity. We propose a scalable reinforcement-learning-based approach for rewriting existing source texts into instances that are more difficult to translate for MT systems. We fine-tune a large language model with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), using reward signals based on translation difficulty together with constraints for semantic similarity, grammaticality, and approximate length preservation. On WMT25, our approach substantially reduces average COMET translation quality from 0.63 to 0.48, while preserving grammaticality and readability, whereas the base model remains at 0.64. Evaluations on the unseen WMT19-WMT24 benchmarks confirm that this behavior generalizes beyond the training data, and human evaluation further shows that the rewrites substantially lower translation quality while incurring a moderate drop in naturalness and only a small change in grammaticality. We release our code to support reproducibility.

AI.tldr: They use reinforcement learning to rewrite source sentences into harder-to-translate versions that expose weaknesses in machine translation systems, while keeping meaning and readability similar.
AI.motivation: Standard MT benchmarks are becoming saturated as systems improve, so they no longer clearly reveal remaining weaknesses. Manually building harder test sets is costly, and fully automatic methods tend to either be too easy or lack linguistic diversity and realism. The authors want a scalable way to generate challenging, realistic test data that preserves original meaning while exposing MT weaknesses.
AI.method: They take existing source texts and fine-tune a large language model with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a reinforcement-learning variant. The model is rewarded for producing rewrites that are harder for MT systems to translate, with additional reward components or constraints to enforce semantic similarity to the original, grammatical correctness, and similar length. They then apply this model to WMT25 and evaluate translation difficulty using COMET scores and human judgments, and test generalization on unseen WMT19–WMT24 benchmarks.
AI.result: On WMT25 data, rewritten sentences drop average COMET translation quality from 0.63 to 0.48 for MT systems, while a base (non-RL-tuned) model leaves COMET at 0.64, indicating much higher difficulty. Human evaluations show that the new sentences substantially reduce MT quality but only moderately reduce perceived naturalness and cause minimal change in grammaticality. Similar patterns hold on unseen WMT19–WMT24 sets, indicating that the learned rewriting policy generalizes beyond the training benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement-learning-based rewriting of source sentences is an effective, scalable way to construct harder MT evaluation sets that preserve meaning, grammaticality, and reasonable naturalness. This method better exposes weaknesses in MT systems than standard benchmarks or naive rewriting, and it generalizes across datasets. The released code enables others to reproduce and extend this approach for more robust MT evaluation.

title: Beyond Prompts: Measuring and Optimizing LLM Tool-Agent Harnesses
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026. 18 pages, 9 figures, 10 tables
summary: LLM tool agents can be improved without retraining by modifying the runtime harness around a fixed model: prompts, tool interfaces, middleware, state handling, and recovery logic. We study this setting as resource-bounded harness selection for fixed-model multi-turn tool agents, with the search surface scoped to prompts and tool-boundary middleware: edits are guarded intercepts at the tool boundary, not arbitrary rewriting of agent execution logic. Our optimizer-agnostic protocol reports mean held-out lift, worst-condition lift, repeatability, logged cost diagnostics, and RelLift95(B), a conservative estimate of the held-out gain of the harness selected under budget B. We instantiate the protocol with prompt-only and prompt-plus-middleware optimizers, including PRISM, which clusters failures and routes repairs to prompt, tool-boundary middleware, or joint edit surfaces within a Pareto search. On BFCL multi-round, tau2-Retail, and tau2-Telecom, PRISM obtains mean held-out lifts of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points and positive empirical RelLift95 on all three benchmarks, and a component ablation attributes the margin chiefly to failure-surface routing and the edit-pattern constraint. Across optimizers, the results show that some search procedures can occasionally find large gains but still choose brittle updates, so the reliability of the chosen harness should be reported alongside average held-out lift.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to systematically improve LLM tool agents by tuning only their prompts and tool-boundary middleware, without retraining models or rewriting core logic, and proposes an evaluation protocol and a specific optimizer (PRISM) that yields reliable performance gains on several benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LLM tool agents often perform suboptimally, but retraining models or rewriting complex agent logic is expensive and risky. Many practical gains may be achievable just by changing the "harness" around a fixed model—prompts, interfaces, and simple middleware—yet there is little systematic methodology to search these changes, assess their robustness, or compare optimizers under a realistic cost budget. The authors want a principled, resource-bounded way to select better harness configurations and to quantify not just average gains but also reliability and worst-case performance.
AI.method: They formalize the problem as resource-bounded harness selection for fixed-model, multi-turn tool agents, restricting the search space to edits at the tool boundary (prompts and guarded middleware intercepts) rather than arbitrary agent rewrites. They define an optimizer-agnostic evaluation protocol that, under a fixed cost budget, reports mean held-out lift, worst-condition lift, repeatability, cost diagnostics, and a conservative metric RelLift95(B) estimating the likely held-out gain of the selected harness. They then instantiate this framework with several optimizers, including PRISM, which clusters observed failures, then routes potential repairs either to prompt edits, tool-boundary middleware edits, or joint edits, conducting a Pareto search over these constrained edit patterns. They also perform ablations to understand which components drive PRISM’s performance.
AI.result: On the BFCL multi-round, tau2-Retail, and tau2-Telecom benchmarks, PRISM achieves mean held-out performance improvements of 14.2, 14.9, and 10.1 percentage points respectively, and shows positive empirical RelLift95 on all three, indicating robust gains under the budget. Ablation experiments suggest that the main performance margin comes from the specific way PRISM routes failures to appropriate edit surfaces and from enforcing a constrained set of edit patterns. Across different optimizers, they find that some search procedures can sometimes discover large apparent gains but make brittle updates that do not generalize well.
AI.conclusion: Carefully optimizing the runtime harness—limited to prompts and tool-boundary middleware—can substantially and reliably improve fixed-model tool agents without retraining or deep architectural changes. However, evaluating only average held-out lift is misleading: certain optimizers produce brittle improvements. Therefore, harness selection should be done under a resource-bounded protocol that also reports robustness metrics like worst-condition lift and conservative estimates such as RelLift95(B). PRISM, which uses failure clustering and targeted, constrained edits, is an effective instantiation of this approach, yielding sizable, more reliable gains across multiple benchmarks.

title: Don't Lose Entities from Retrieval to Generation: Dual Entity Recovery RAG for multi-hop QA
comment: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Retrieval-augmented multi-hop question answering (QA) decomposes a query into sub-questions and decomposes the corpus into smaller retrieval units such as sentences. Both forms of decomposition improve the pipeline, but we show that both share the same vulnerability, the loss of entity information, and that this loss breaks the pipeline at two separate points. The first point is retrieval, where a sub-question loses the entity resolved at the previous hop, leaving the retriever with nothing to match against. The second point is harder to see, because retrieval still appears to succeed. Once a passage is split into sentences, an isolated sentence loses the context that grounds its pronouns, so even with the correct sentence in hand the LLM cannot tell which entity the sentence is about. We isolate this second point as a distinct failure mode that we call lost-in-generation, and a retrieval-controlled experiment shows that it degrades answers even when the gold evidence is fixed in the context. We then propose Dual Entity Recovery RAG (DER-RAG), which keeps the grounding entity explicit from retrieval through to generation with two lightweight components, a two-way query decomposition that carries the resolved entity across sub-questions and a subject entity prefix attached to each sentence at generation time. DER-RAG needs no graph construction, no corpus modification, and no fine-tuning, yet on three multi-hop QA benchmarks it matches or exceeds strong baselines, including graph-based methods that depend on costly offline structures.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a key failure mode in retrieval-augmented multi-hop QA where entity information is lost during both query and passage decomposition, and proposes a simple method (DER-RAG) to explicitly preserve grounding entities across retrieval and generation, improving accuracy without heavy graph structures or fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Although retrieval-augmented multi-hop QA benefits from decomposing questions into sub-questions and documents into smaller units like sentences, current pipelines still frequently fail. The authors observe that a central, under-explored reason is that entity information (which entity is being talked about) gets lost at different stages. This leads to either failed retrieval or incorrect reasoning even when relevant sentences are retrieved. They want to understand and systematically address this failure mode without resorting to expensive graph-based or fine-tuned systems.
AI.method: The authors first analyze and formalize two vulnerable points in standard multi-hop RAG pipelines: (1) in retrieval, where sub-questions omit previously resolved entities; and (2) in generation, where sentence-level passages lose context needed to resolve pronouns, which they term the "lost-in-generation" failure mode. They then design DER-RAG, which has two lightweight components: (a) a two-way query decomposition procedure that carries the resolved entity explicitly across sub-questions, ensuring that later retrieval queries contain the grounding entity; and (b) a subject-entity prefixing mechanism at generation time, where each retrieved sentence is augmented with an explicit subject entity prefix, so that the LLM can unambiguously link pronouns and references to the correct entity. They test this in a retrieval-controlled setting to isolate the effect of generation failures and evaluate on several multi-hop QA benchmarks.
AI.result: Experiments, including a retrieval-controlled setup where gold evidence is fixed in the context, show that the identified lost-in-generation failure mode significantly harms answer quality even when retrieval is perfect. DER-RAG, which explicitly preserves the grounding entities via query decomposition and subject entity prefixes, consistently matches or outperforms strong baselines on three multi-hop QA benchmarks. This includes surpassing or equaling graph-based methods that rely on computationally expensive offline graph construction and corpus modification.
AI.conclusion: Entity grounding loss is a fundamental and previously under-appreciated weakness of decomposed retrieval-augmented multi-hop QA, affecting both retrieval and answer generation. The paper introduces and empirically validates the lost-in-generation failure mode and shows that explicitly tracking and encoding grounding entities from retrieval through to generation can substantially improve performance. DER-RAG achieves competitive or superior results to graph-based and other strong baselines without requiring graph construction, corpus changes, or model fine-tuning, suggesting that simple, explicit entity-aware mechanisms can close much of the gap in multi-hop QA.

title: The Normalization of Deviance in AI Development
summary: Work on the risks of artificial intelligence has focused predominantly on capability risk: the danger that systems become too powerful, too autonomous, or too misaligned with human values. Far less attention has been paid to the organizational level---to whether the institutions building these systems are themselves predisposed to drift toward failure. This paper argues that they are. Regardless of how capable AI systems become, the organizations building them face the same structural dynamics that preceded past major technological disasters. Drawing on case studies of the Space Shuttle Challenger, the Three Mile Island accident, and the Boeing 737 MAX crashes, this paper identifies the common structural mechanisms preceding each failure and maps them onto contemporary AI development. The findings suggest that existing safety infrastructure may provide less protection than it appears, as organizations can complete safety processes in full compliance and still produce catastrophic outcomes. The pre-disaster period of AI development is still underway; the purpose of this paper is to make these dynamics legible while they can still be interrupted.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the main near-term danger from AI comes not only from the technical capabilities of AI systems but from organizational failures in the institutions that build them, which resemble patterns seen in past technological disasters.
AI.motivation: Most AI risk discussions focus on technical capability risks (powerful, misaligned systems), neglecting whether the organizations building these systems are structurally prone to failure. Historical technological disasters show that organizational dynamics can undermine safety even with formal processes in place. The author wants to redirect attention to this neglected but crucial dimension of AI risk.
AI.method: The paper conducts a comparative case study analysis of three historical technological disasters: the Space Shuttle Challenger, the Three Mile Island nuclear accident, and the Boeing 737 MAX crashes. It identifies recurring structural mechanisms that preceded these failures—such as normalization of deviance, production pressures, fragmented oversight, and diffusion of responsibility—and then systematically maps these mechanisms onto current practices and institutions in AI development.
AI.result: The analysis finds strong parallels between the organizational dynamics behind past disasters and those present in contemporary AI labs and companies. It shows that organizations can follow existing safety protocols and remain in formal compliance yet still drift into conditions where catastrophic failure is likely. The current safety infrastructure around AI therefore offers less real protection than it appears to on paper.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that AI safety must explicitly address organizational and institutional design, not just technical alignment and capability control. Without interventions that interrupt known drift-to-failure dynamics, AI organizations may be on a pre-disaster trajectory similar to Challenger, Three Mile Island, and 737 MAX. The author aims to surface these dynamics early enough that they can be recognized and changed before a major AI-related catastrophe occurs.

title: DPH Parser: A Bottom-Up Grammar-Driven Parser for Joint Constituency and Dependency Analysis
summary:
This paper presents Dependency-Phrase Hierarchy Parser (DPH Parser), a grammar-driven bottom-up unsupervized parsing framework inspired by Generalized Phrase Structure Grammar (GPSG) and Head-driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG). The parser incrementally constructs constituency structures using a compact inventory of feature-based syntactic rules while deriving dependency relations through explicit head annotations. The system combines probabilistic POS tagging, recursive phrase projection, and weighted parse hypotheses to process realistic and partially noisy text input. Unlike purely neural and data-driven parsers, the resulting syntactic derivations remain explicitly interpretable.
  We evaluated parser performance on English corpora from the Universal Dependencies (UD) project using Unlabeled Attachment Score (UAS) as the main parsing metric, comparing the outcomes against Stanza and spaCy parsers. For a small inventory of syntactic rules, DPH parser achieved UAS values of 53.32% & 52.58% (UD Devset/Testset respectively). For the same data, Stanza achieved 89.12% & 88.67% while spaCy achieved 56.91% and 58.59%. Although the current system does not yet approach the accuracy of modern neural parsers, the results demonstrate the feasibility of applying transparent rule-based bottom-up parsing to realistic treebank data while jointly producing constituency and dependency structures.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces DPH Parser, a rule-based, bottom-up, feature-structure grammar parser that jointly builds constituency and dependency structures, trading accuracy for interpretability and minimal supervision.
AI.motivation: Modern state-of-the-art parsers are largely neural and data-driven, often opaque and difficult to interpret. The authors want a transparent, grammar-driven alternative that can still handle realistic, noisy text and simultaneously produce both constituency and dependency structures, with minimal supervision and a compact rule set.
AI.method: They design the Dependency-Phrase Hierarchy Parser (DPH Parser), a bottom-up unsupervised parsing framework grounded in GPSG and HPSG. It uses a small, feature-based grammar with explicit head annotations to incrementally build phrase structures and derive dependency arcs. The system incorporates probabilistic POS tagging, recursive phrase projection, and a weighted set of parse hypotheses to parse sentences from UD corpora, producing both constituency trees and dependency parses.
AI.result: On English UD data, the DPH Parser reaches UAS of 53.32% on the dev set and 52.58% on the test set. In comparison, Stanza (a strong neural baseline) gets around 89% UAS, and spaCy (neural but more general-purpose) gets about 57–59% UAS. So DPH underperforms Stanza substantially and is slightly below spaCy, but remains competitive given its small rule inventory and unsupervised, interpretable design.
AI.conclusion: Although DPH Parser is not yet as accurate as modern neural parsers, the experiments show that a transparent, grammar-based, bottom-up parsing approach can be feasibly applied to real treebank data while jointly delivering interpretable constituency and dependency structures. This validates the overall framework and motivates further refinements to close the accuracy gap with neural systems.

title: From Monolithic Blending to Agentic Orchestration: Dynamic Response for Conversational Assistants at Scale
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Industry Track. 16 pages, 1 figure, 21 tables
summary: Conversational assistants can blend retrieval, action selection, escalation, and wording in a single model path, or separate those roles. We report a production migration of a customer-support assistant at a large accommodation marketplace (millions of conversations per month, 11 languages, 10-second P90). Dynamic Response (DR) replaces a single Qwen3-235B-A22B blended responder with a bounded ReAct orchestrator over typed tools plus a smaller generator that writes from a backend-validated context contract. Because the migration also changed prompts, alignment, and serving, we attribute each effect to its cause and claim as architecture effects only those measured on identical replayed turns: typed entity selection moves the reservation selector to a precision-first operating point (precision 8.3% to 89.1%, recall 75.2% to 67.3%), and typed action IDs with a membership check remove observed structured-action hallucination (2.14% to 0.0%). A low-ramp A/B test reproduces the replay escalation reductions: hard-escalation responses fall from 5.60% to 3.08% and soft-escalation responses from 9.56% to 2.49%, while production handoff volume holds roughly steady; self-solve is directional (+5.1 points, 95% CI [-2, +12]). Serving optimizations cut orchestrator P90 latency from 3.87s to 2.24s on a GPU footprint reduced by roughly one-third, and self-hosting reduces estimated annual model-serving cost by more than an order of magnitude.

AI.tldr: The paper describes a production migration of a large-scale customer-support conversational assistant from a single large blended model to a modular Dynamic Response architecture using a ReAct-style orchestrator and smaller generator, improving precision, reliability, escalation rates, latency, and cost.
AI.motivation: To improve the reliability, precision, and efficiency of a large-scale customer support assistant handling millions of multilingual conversations, particularly reducing hallucinated actions, unnecessary escalations, latency, and serving costs, while maintaining or improving customer self-solve rates.
AI.method: They replace a single large blended responder model (Qwen3-235B-A22B) with a Dynamic Response setup: a bounded ReAct orchestrator that calls typed tools and a smaller generation model that only writes responses from a backend-validated context contract. They run controlled replays and low-ramp A/B tests to disentangle architectural effects from prompt, alignment, and serving changes, measuring precision/recall of entity selection, hallucinated structured actions, escalation rates, latency, GPU footprint, and cost.
AI.result: Typed entity selection shifts the reservation selector to a precision-first regime, boosting precision from 8.3% to 89.1% while slightly reducing recall from 75.2% to 67.3%. Typed action IDs plus membership checks eliminate observed structured-action hallucinations (2.14% to 0.0%). In A/B tests, hard escalations drop from 5.60% to 3.08% and soft escalations from 9.56% to 2.49%, without increasing human handoff volume; self-solve shows a positive but not fully conclusive improvement (+5.1 points, 95% CI [-2, +12]).
