Because each biographical fact is individually benign, prompts using these facts are flagged by content filters far less often (about 3%) than equivalent direct persona instructions (24–33%).
AI.conclusion: Large language models can be steered into strong persona adoption, including harmful identities, using only benign contextual information, without fine-tuning and without explicit harmful instructions. This persona induction poses a subtle misalignment risk because it largely evades standard content filters that focus on overtly problematic text. Simple formatting controls can gate persona activation, suggesting both a potential mitigation tool and a further avenue through which adversaries might control model behavior.

title: AutoKD: Autonomous Knowledge Discovery
summary: Scientific discovery in data-rich domains is currently constrained by human bandwidth: the growth in the volume and complexity of real-world data far outpaces the rate at which researchers can read, reason, and synthesize. Recent LLM-based multi-agent systems have begun to automate portions of the research cycle, but they target hypothesis generation in settings where validation cannot itself be automated, and each run is one-shot, with no mechanism for findings to accumulate or steer subsequent inquiry. This paper introduces AutoKD, a multi-agent framework for autonomous knowledge discovery that is both computational and cumulative, allowing validated findings to persist and inform subsequent inquiry. Six coordinated LLM agents collaborate in an open-ended discovery loop, where accepted findings are stored in a persistent insight graph that serves as both long-term memory and an exploration-steering mechanism. We evaluate AutoKD on three diverse datasets from two perspectives: Open-ended Quality against published findings, and Conditioned Quality via literature-derived queries. Across both evaluation perspectives, AutoKD covers known findings and surfaces substantive discoveries that complement human-driven research. Our code is available at https://github.com/GeQinwen/AutoKD.

AI.tldr: AutoKD is a multi-agent LLM framework that autonomously discovers, validates, and accumulates scientific findings in a persistent knowledge graph, complementing human research in data-rich domains.
AI.motivation: Data-rich scientific domains now produce more data and complexity than humans can efficiently read, reason over, and synthesize. Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems focus mainly on hypothesis generation and rely on humans for validation; they are also one-shot, so results do not accumulate or guide future runs. There is a need for an autonomous, end-to-end system that can both discover and computationally validate knowledge, while maintaining and exploiting a growing memory of past findings to improve and steer further inquiry.
AI.method: The authors propose AutoKD, a multi-agent framework composed of six coordinated LLM agents that operate in an open-ended discovery loop. These agents jointly generate hypotheses, test them computationally on real datasets, and decide which findings to accept. Accepted findings are stored in a persistent insight graph that represents discovered knowledge and acts as both long-term memory and a steering mechanism, influencing which regions of the data or hypothesis space to explore next. The framework is evaluated on three datasets using two evaluation modes: comparing open-ended discoveries to published findings, and assessing performance on targeted, literature-derived queries.
AI.result: On three diverse datasets, AutoKD successfully recovers known findings documented in the literature and additionally identifies novel, substantive patterns that complement existing human-driven research. Under both open-ended and conditioned evaluation settings, the system shows strong coverage of established knowledge while also surfacing new, plausible insights, indicating that autonomous, cumulative LLM-based discovery is feasible and effective in data-rich domains.
AI.conclusion: AutoKD demonstrates that a multi-agent LLM system with computational validation and a persistent insight graph can conduct autonomous, cumulative knowledge discovery that both reproduces known scientific results and yields new, complementary findings. This suggests a promising path toward scalable, machine-augmented scientific research workflows that can keep pace with growing data complexity. The framework and its code base provide a foundation for future extensions and applications across domains.

title: AutoLexSteer: Automatic Contrast Construction for Lexical Activation Steering
summary: Steering vectors have rapidly emerged as a popular and effective method for guiding the output of LLMs in very specific ways. But constructing accurate steering vectors is a difficult manual process due to the opacity of embeddings. We introduce Hangman, a novel type of steering vector that operates using word senses, as well as AutoLexSteer, the first fully automated process for building steering vectors. AutoLexSteer employs families of closely-related words extracted from WordNet to specify both the steering source to be avoided and the desired steering target. The steering vectors are quite precise, can be used to steer at the level of words and sets of word senses (meanings), and are able to steer certain LLM behaviors like sycophancy. The dataset and code can be found at https://github.com/ShuheWang1998/autolexsteer.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Hangman, a word-sense-based steering vector and AutoLexSteer, an automated method using WordNet word families to construct precise steering vectors for controlling LLM behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing steering vectors for large language models are powerful but hard to construct, as embeddings are opaque and require manual, ad-hoc engineering. There is a need for a more interpretable, systematic, and automated way to define and build steering directions, ideally grounded in linguistic structure such as word senses.
AI.method: The authors propose Hangman, a new type of steering vector defined over word senses, and AutoLexSteer, a pipeline that automatically builds such vectors. AutoLexSteer uses WordNet to extract families of closely related words and word senses to represent both (a) a source behavior or concept to avoid and (b) a target behavior or concept to encourage. These sets are embedded, contrasted, and combined into steering vectors that can operate at the level of words or word senses. They then apply these vectors during LLM generation to guide outputs.
AI.result: The resulting steering vectors are shown to be precise, supporting fine-grained control over language at the level of words and senses. They successfully steer several model behaviors, including reducing or altering sycophantic responses. The approach works automatically across many concepts, demonstrating generality and robustness.
AI.conclusion: Word-sense-based steering vectors derived automatically from lexical resources like WordNet can provide interpretable, precise, and fully automated control over LLM behavior. Hangman and AutoLexSteer reduce the need for manual steering engineering and enable targeted modification of specific behaviors such as sycophancy, offering a scalable path toward more controllable LLMs.

title: Building Trustworthy Graph-Agentic RAG for Social Good: Architectures, Failure Propagation, and Assurance by Construction
summary: Graph-agentic retrieval-augmented generation combines structured evidence with adaptive controllers that can plan retrieval, traverse relations, verify intermediate claims, delegate subtasks, and use tools. This combination is useful when answers depend on relations across documents, entities, time, or institutions, but it also creates coupled failure paths: a defect in graph construction can become retrieved evidence, alter later control decisions, and propagate toward a consequential outcome. We examine how such systems should be designed and evaluated for social-good settings in which freshness, authorization, traceability, oversight, and recourse matter alongside answer quality. We organize the literature by graph substrate, graph lifecycle, agent function, coordination pattern, and authority boundary, and distinguish graph-based retrieval from observation-dependent graph control. We then synthesize reported risks as an evidence-to-action failure chain and propose an assurance-by-construction blueprint comprising five interface contracts for evidence, retrieval, reasoning, capability and delegation, and outcome. These contracts make provenance, temporal validity, authorization, uncertainty, and recoverability explicit at system boundaries. An illustrative public-benefit information design shows how the framework constrains graph structure, permissions, abstention, and operating authority. Finally, we derive an evaluation agenda spanning graph assertions, trajectories, claims, coordination, and outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes graph-agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, focusing on how to design and evaluate them safely for socially important applications.
AI.motivation: Graph-agentic RAG systems can reason over complex, relational information (across documents, entities, and time), which is crucial in social-good settings like public information services. However, the tight coupling between graph construction, retrieval, and agent control creates new failure chains where early errors can propagate into harmful outcomes. There is currently a lack of systematic design and evaluation frameworks tailored to such high-stakes, governance-sensitive contexts.
AI.method: The authors conduct a conceptual and survey-style analysis. They (1) organize existing work along several dimensions: graph substrate and lifecycle, agent function, coordination patterns, and authority boundaries; (2) distinguish graph-based retrieval from graph-driven control; (3) synthesize reported risks into an “evidence-to-action” failure chain; and (4) propose an assurance-by-construction blueprint consisting of five explicit interface contracts covering evidence, retrieval, reasoning, capability/delegation, and outcomes. They illustrate the framework through a public-benefit information system design and derive a structured evaluation agenda.
AI.result: The work produces a taxonomy for graph-agentic RAG systems, a structured characterization of their risk pathways, a five-contract assurance framework that makes provenance, temporal validity, authorization, uncertainty, and recoverability explicit, and a multi-layer evaluation agenda that targets graph assertions, agent trajectories, claims, coordination mechanisms, and final outcomes. The illustrative public-benefit design demonstrates how the framework constrains graph structure, permissions, abstention behavior, and operating authority in practice.
AI.conclusion: For social-good and other high-stakes applications, graph-agentic RAG systems must be treated as socio-technical pipelines from evidence to action, not just answer generators. By imposing explicit interface contracts and evaluating the system across graph, agent, coordination, and outcome levels, designers can mitigate coupled failure chains and better ensure freshness, authorization, traceability, oversight, and recourse. The paper offers a blueprint and evaluation agenda to guide safer, more accountable deployment of graph-agentic RAG.

title: Towards Bridging the Gap Between Offline and Iterative Alignment via Preference Distillation
comment: Accepted by Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR)
summary: Direct preference optimization DPO is a promising offline approach for aligning large language models (LLMs) due to its simplicity, computational efficiency, and implicit modeling of human preferences. Interestingly, iterative extensions of DPO have achieved stronger performance on academic benchmarks, raising two key questions: (i) Why do iterative methods generally outperform offline ones? (ii) Can their advantages be incorporated into offline alignment? To answer the first question, our controlled experiments reveal that the explicit preference model, additionally introduced in the iterative procedure, is a key factor behind its superiority over offline methods. This insight leads us to answer the second question affirmatively and propose Distilled Preference Probability Policy Optimization (DP3O), an effective and efficient offline alignment algorithm. DP3O first learns an explicit preference model using a helper class of LLMs and then distills its knowledge into policy optimization. Theoretically, we show that explicit preference modeling admits better estimation error control than implicit formulations, and that DP3O achieves a tighter generalization bound than hard-label DPO through variance reduction. Empirically, we evaluate DP3O on a wide range of chat-based and downstream tasks and show that it outperforms state-of-the-art offline methods, achieves performance comparable to iterative DPO, and reduces training time by about $42\%$, demonstrating both its effectiveness and efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes why iterative DPO methods outperform offline DPO and introduces DP3O, an offline alignment algorithm that uses an explicit preference model distilled into policy optimization to match iterative performance while being more efficient.
AI.motivation: Offline DPO is attractive for aligning LLMs because it is simple and efficient, but iterative DPO variants empirically perform better. The authors want to understand the reason behind this performance gap and determine whether the benefits of iterative approaches can be transferred back into a purely offline setting without sacrificing efficiency.
AI.method: The authors run controlled experiments to isolate which components of iterative DPO contribute most to its superior performance, identifying explicit preference modeling as crucial. Based on this, they design DP3O: first train an explicit preference model using a helper class of LLMs on preference data, then distill this model into a policy via preference probability-based optimization. They provide theoretical analysis comparing estimation error and generalization bounds between explicit and implicit preference modeling, and between DP3O and standard hard-label DPO.
AI.result: Theoretically, explicit preference modeling is shown to offer better estimation error control than implicit preference formulations, and DP3O is proven to have a tighter generalization bound than hard-label DPO due to variance reduction. Empirically, across multiple chat and downstream benchmarks, DP3O consistently outperforms prior offline alignment methods, matches or approaches the performance of iterative DPO approaches, and cuts training time by roughly 42%.
AI.conclusion: Iterative DPO methods gain their advantage mainly from the use of an explicit preference model rather than just from iteration itself. By explicitly learning such a model and distilling it into the policy in an offline manner, DP3O attains similar performance to iterative methods while preserving the efficiency and simplicity of offline training, making it a strong candidate for practical LLM alignment.

title: From Concentration to Differentiation and Back: Routing Effective Rank in MoE Reasoning Cohorts
summary: Test-time scaling produces cohorts of reasoning rollouts, yet there is no standard label-free account of how their internal computation reorganizes as inference unfolds. We introduce routing effective rank deff, the entropy-effective dimensionality of a cross-rollout graph built from MoE expert-routing similarity. Across ten MoE configurations and five math/science benchmarks, deff exhibits a reproducible low-high-low trajectory, with a prominent interior maximum in 98.5% of 3,105 model-question cohorts: routing similarity is concentrated early, maximally differentiated at intermediate budgets, and reconcentrated later, and the timing of this maximum varies systematically with architecture and reasoning effort. An exact decomposition separates cohort-wide common-mode mass from residual spectral dimensionality: common-mode reallocation accounts for about two thirds of the trajectory, while the residual spectrum contributes about one quarter and retains substantial variation beyond the common mode. The decomposition further localizes behavior: among non-unanimous cohorts, increases in common-mode concentration strongly predict same-answer recoverability, and higher reasoning effort delays the maximum by 2.59 octaves (doublings of the token budget) and consistently expands the high-rank period across all four tested architectures, locating the effort effect in timing and duration rather than peak amplitude. Correctness comparisons separate structural monitoring from answer selection, positioning routing effective rank as a decomposable, label-free diagnostic of cohort organization - a principled spectral lens on how MoE reasoning cohorts differentiate and reconcentrate over inference time.

AI.tldr: They propose a new, label-free metric (routing effective rank) for understanding how Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models’ internal routing patterns change over the course of test-time scaled reasoning, finding a robust low–high–low dimensionality pattern over time.
AI.motivation: Test-time scaling leads to many reasoning rollouts (samples), but we lack a standard, label-free way to characterize how their internal computations collectively evolve over the inference trajectory, especially in Mixture-of-Experts models where routing is structured and sparse.
AI.method: Define a cross-rollout similarity graph based on MoE expert-routing patterns and compute its entropy-effective dimensionality (routing effective rank, deff). Study deff trajectories over inference time across 10 MoE configurations and 5 math/science benchmarks, and perform an exact decomposition that separates cohort-wide common-mode mass (shared routing behavior) from residual spectral dimensionality. Analyze how this decomposition relates to answer agreement, reasoning effort, and architectural differences.
AI.result: Across 3,105 model-question cohorts, routing effective rank shows a consistent low–high–low trajectory with a clear interior maximum in 98.5% of cohorts. Early in inference, routing similarity is concentrated (low deff), then becomes maximally differentiated (high deff) at intermediate budgets, and reconcentrates later (low deff again). The timing of the maximum systematically depends on architecture and reasoning effort. The decomposition reveals that common-mode reallocation explains about two thirds of the trajectory, while the residual spectrum explains about one quarter and still varies substantially. In non-unanimous cohorts, higher common-mode concentration predicts the ability to recover the same answer, and greater reasoning effort shifts the maximum later (by ~2.59 octaves in token budget) and lengthens the high-rank period without changing peak height.
AI.conclusion: Routing effective rank is a useful, decomposable, label-free diagnostic for monitoring how MoE reasoning cohorts organize, differentiate, and reconverge over inference time. It separates structural properties of computation (cohort organization and routing similarity) from answer correctness, providing a principled spectral tool to study test-time scaling dynamics in MoE models.

title: Dynamic-Programming-Guided Hierarchical BPE and Empirical Analysis of Vocabulary Pruning
summary: Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) constructs vocabularies through greedy pair merging, but the resulting merge order does not necessarily allocate a fixed model-visible vocabulary optimally for compression. We propose Dynamic-Programming-Guided Hierarchical BPE (DH-BPE), a vocabulary-construction method that combines token exposure under exact minimum-token segmentation with the hierarchical dependencies induced by BPE training. Starting from a modestly overshot BPE candidate vocabulary, DH-BPE uses dynamic programming to measure candidate utility and applies exposure-guided, dependency-aware pruning to select a fixed-size model-visible vocabulary. We compare DH-BPE against Standard BPE and recent vocabulary-optimization baselines, including Pruned BPE, MinGram, and MinGram-PP, in primary evaluations at 12K and 16K target vocabulary sizes, with an additional 18K evaluation against MinGram only. Across the primary 12K and 16K comparisons, DH-BPE consistently improves aggregate compression over Standard BPE, Pruned BPE, and MinGram under a shared exact minimum-token DP encoder. MinGram-PP achieves stronger aggregate compression in the primary comparisons, but DH-BPE outperforms it at overshoot factors f = 2.0 and f = 3.0 in cross-corpus evaluation; at 12K, MinGram-PP reverses this ordering only with the substantially larger candidate pools at f = 4.0 and f = 5.0. Qualitative analysis further shows that DH-BPE balances later, more complete BPE merges with reusable subword components, providing a practical approach to improving vocabulary allocation under a fixed model-visible vocabulary budget.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Dynamic-Programming-Guided Hierarchical BPE (DH-BPE), a new method to construct subword vocabularies that improves compression over standard and several optimized BPE approaches under a fixed vocabulary size.
AI.motivation: Standard Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) builds vocabularies greedily, so the merge order and final visible vocabulary are not guaranteed to be optimal for compression when the model vocabulary size is fixed. Existing optimization methods either prune or re-rank merges but still have limitations in how well they exploit exact minimum-token segmentations and hierarchical dependencies. There is a need for a vocabulary construction method that better allocates a limited vocabulary budget to maximize compression quality and token efficiency.
AI.method: The authors propose Dynamic-Programming-Guided Hierarchical BPE (DH-BPE). They first train a standard BPE model to obtain a modestly overshot candidate vocabulary (larger than the target size). Then they use a dynamic programming algorithm that computes exact minimum-token segmentations over corpora to estimate the utility (exposure) of each candidate token. Based on these exposure scores and respecting the hierarchical dependencies inherent in BPE merges, they perform a pruning procedure that selects a fixed-size, model-visible vocabulary. This balances keeping useful subword components with including later, longer merges. They evaluate DH-BPE at 12K, 16K, and 18K target vocabulary sizes and different overshoot factors f (2.0–5.0) against baselines such as Standard BPE, Pruned BPE, MinGram, and MinGram-PP, all under a shared exact DP encoder.
AI.result: In evaluations at 12K and 16K vocabulary sizes, DH-BPE consistently yields better aggregate compression than Standard BPE, Pruned BPE, and MinGram when all are encoded using the same exact minimum-token dynamic-programming encoder. MinGram-PP is generally stronger in the primary comparisons, but DH-BPE surpasses MinGram-PP in cross-corpus tests when the candidate overshoot factors are f = 2.0 and f = 3.0. At 12K vocabulary size, MinGram-PP only regains superiority when using significantly larger candidate pools with overshoot factors f = 4.0 or f = 5.0.
AI.conclusion: DH-BPE is an effective and practical method for subword vocabulary construction under a fixed model-visible vocabulary budget. By combining dynamic-programming-based exact segmentation statistics with the hierarchical structure of BPE merges, it can reallocate vocabulary capacity toward tokens that improve compression, outperforming standard and several optimized BPE variants in many settings. The qualitative analysis suggests that DH-BPE achieves a good balance between including long, high-level merges and preserving reusable smaller subword units, thus offering an improved trade-off between vocabulary size and compression efficiency.

title: Causal Attribution for Agentic Decisions: Estimators, Coupling, and a Traceability Specification
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables, 3 propositions with proofs. Pre-registered discrepancy experiment published in full and not run; no empirical result is claimed. Companion to arXiv:2608.13754. Code, validators, derivations and the traceability specification: https://github.com/designer-coderajay/Causal-Attribution-for-Agentic-Decisions
summary: A provider of a high-risk AI system must keep records that make a decision traceable, and for agentic systems it has not been established what those records must contain for post-hoc causal attribution to be possible. We give the estimator framework and then the conditions under which it fails. We separate the marginal total effect that prior work measures from a common-random-numbers total effect that isolates a step's own contribution, add the natural direct effect under a pinned downstream, and check the estimators against hand derivations. Both estimands then fail, in the same direction. Under the marginal estimand a causally inert step has the identical total effect to the decisive one on every run of our planted chain, an algebraic identity and not a coincidence at one draw. Under common random numbers the decisive step returns exactly zero on the runs where the executing step flips, about one in ten, while its direct effect there is 0.25 and it demonstrably acts; an exact zero does not certify that a step did nothing, and we put that here rather than in the limitations. We derive the coupling that keeps the direct effect estimable once contexts diverge, with a closed form for its degradation, and show that the mediated share on which a natural ranking is built is not a share under suppression: where the direct and mediated paths oppose, it exceeds one and ranks a suppressed component above a pure mediator. We publish the discrepancy experiment's pre-registration rather than a result, because the live pipeline it requires was not available in the study window. We contribute the traceability specification such a filing would need, against a gap the Act's calendar opens: Article 86's right to an explanation has applied since 2 August 2026, while the Article 12 logging and Annex IV documentation that could evidence one were deferred to 2 December 2027 by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes how to make decisions of high-risk, agentic AI systems causally traceable, finds that existing causal attribution estimators fail in systematic ways, and proposes a more precise traceability specification aligned with EU AI regulatory timelines.
AI.motivation: EU law (notably the AI Act and related regulations) requires providers of high-risk AI systems to keep logs that make decisions traceable and explainable. For agentic AI systems that take sequences of actions, it is unclear what records are needed to support post-hoc causal attribution of individual steps. Existing causal-effect estimators, used to attribute responsibility to steps in a decision chain, may be conceptually misaligned with this legal need. The paper aims to clarify what should be logged and to test whether standard attribution estimands are reliable for this purpose.
AI.method: The authors formalize an “estimator framework” for causal attribution in agentic AI decision chains and define several estimands: (1) the marginal total effect commonly used in prior work; (2) a “common-random-numbers” total effect that holds randomness fixed to isolate a step’s own contribution; and (3) the natural direct effect under a pinned downstream context. They construct planted causal chains where the causal structure and step effects are analytically derivable, then compare estimator outputs against these hand-derived ground truths. They also derive a coupling scheme that keeps the direct effect estimable once decision contexts diverge and provide a closed-form expression for how estimation quality degrades. Finally, they analyze how mediated-effect-based rankings behave when direct and mediated paths conflict (suppression).
AI.result: Both the marginal total effect and the common-random-numbers total effect fail to correctly attribute causal responsibility in the planted chains, and they fail in the same direction. Under the marginal estimand, a causally inert step can have the same total effect as the truly decisive step on every run, making them indistinguishable. Under the common-random-numbers scheme, the decisive step’s estimated effect is exactly zero on a subset of runs where it demonstrably has a nonzero direct effect (0.25), showing that zero estimates do not certify causal irrelevance. The authors derive a coupling that preserves estimability of the direct effect as contexts diverge and obtain a closed-form characterization of its degradation. They further show that the “mediated share” used to rank components is not a true share under suppression: it can exceed 1 and rank a suppressed component above a pure mediator, undermining intuitive responsibility rankings. The planned discrepancy experiment that would use a live pipeline could not be completed within the study window, so only its preregistration is released.
AI.conclusion: Standard causal attribution estimands currently used to analyze agentic AI decision chains are unreliable for legal-grade traceability: they can assign equal responsibility to inert and decisive steps, and an estimated zero effect does not guarantee that a step did nothing. Mediated-effect-based rankings can also behave pathologically under suppression, over-attributing influence to certain components. The paper proposes a refined traceability specification indicating what logs and documentation would be needed to support robust causal explanations, framed against EU regulatory timelines: the right to an explanation under Article 86 comes into force before the logging and documentation duties under Article 12 and Annex IV, creating a temporary gap that providers must address. Overall, the work highlights the need for more rigorous, regulation-aligned causal logging and analysis methods for high-risk, agentic AI systems.

title: TurEngMix: A Text Corpus and Benchmark for Turkish-English Code-Mixed Language Identification and Named Entity Recognition
comment: Accepted to W-NUT 2026 (11th Workshop on Natural User-generated Text), co-located with EMNLP 2026. 15 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables
summary: Natural language processing systems underperform on code-mixed text, particularly for low-resource language pairs. Turkish-English poses a further challenge: it lets English stems combine with Turkish suffixes to form single mixed-language tokens. We introduce TurEngMix, a corpus of 5.5K noisy, naturally occurring social media posts (486,974 tokens) rich in Turkish-English code-mixing. From this corpus, we construct a new Turkish-English benchmark for code-mixed language identification (LID) and named entity recognition (NER), comprising 15K expert-annotated tokens. Evaluating both decoder LLM and fine-tuned encoder baselines, we find that monolingual Turkish and English tokens are labeled reliably, but all models have high error rates on mixed-language tokens for both LID and NER. For morphologically integrated tokens, NER error rates were 5.2x and 6.3x higher for GPT-4o and Qwen, respectively. This highlights how morphological integration remains a challenge. We release the corpus, annotations, and code to support future computational and sociolinguistic research on Turkish-English code-mixing.

AI.tldr: The paper presents TurEngMix, a new Turkish-English code-mixed social media corpus and benchmark for language identification and named entity recognition, showing that current models struggle especially on morphologically integrated mixed tokens.
AI.motivation: NLP models generally perform poorly on code-mixed data, with the problem more severe for low-resource language pairs. Turkish-English code-mixing is particularly challenging because English stems can take Turkish suffixes, forming single tokens that mix languages. There is a lack of high-quality, annotated resources and benchmarks focused on this type of code-mixing, hampering progress in model development and evaluation.
AI.method: The authors collect 5.5K noisy, naturally occurring Turkish-English social media posts rich in code-mixing, yielding 486,974 tokens. From this corpus, they construct a benchmark for Turkish-English code-mixed language identification and named entity recognition, with 15K tokens annotated by experts. They then evaluate decoder LLMs and fine-tuned encoder-based models on these tasks, analyzing performance particularly on monolingual versus mixed-language and morphologically integrated tokens.
AI.result: All evaluated models perform reliably on purely Turkish or English tokens but exhibit high error rates on mixed-language tokens for both language identification and named entity recognition. For tokens where English stems are morphologically integrated with Turkish suffixes, NER error rates are dramatically higher—5.2 times higher for GPT-4o and 6.3 times higher for Qwen—than for non-integrated tokens, revealing a substantial performance gap.
AI.conclusion: Morphologically integrated code-mixed tokens represent a significant unresolved challenge for current NLP systems, including strong decoder LLMs and fine-tuned encoder models, in both language identification and named entity recognition. The TurEngMix corpus and benchmark provide a needed resource to systematically study and improve models on Turkish-English code-mixing, with potential benefits for both computational approaches and sociolinguistic research. The authors make the data and code publicly available to encourage further work in this area.

title: A Unified Policy Architecture (UPA): The Governance Kernel for Enterprise AI Operating Systems
comment: 58 pages, 6 figures. Includes appendices with the DGPL grammar, SID registry, EAGBench benchmark specification, extended governance models, and policy examples
summary:
Enterprise AI is evolving into an Enterprise Operating System where autonomous AI agents can plan, reason, use memory, invoke tools, execute workflows, and collaborate with other agents. This shift creates a new governance challenge: existing authorization, security, guardrails, and compliance mechanisms are fragmented and are not designed to govern autonomous AI as a unified system.
  This paper introduces the Unified Policy Architecture (UPA), a governance architecture for Enterprise AI Operating Systems. UPA provides a unified policy model for governing AI and agents, tools, workflows, memory, enterprise resources, and agent-to-agent interactions and enterprise business rules. It extends policy control beyond authorisation to include runtime obligations, human approvals, compliance, audit evidence, and governance evaluation.
  We present UPA's governance model, declarative policy language foundations, policy evaluation semantics, extensible plugins, industry policy packs, and an evaluation framework for enterprise governance. We also identify extensions for multi-agent coordination, provenance-aware policies, and stateful runtime governance. UPA provides a foundation for building secure, accountable, and governable Enterprise Operating Systems for autonomous AI.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Unified Policy Architecture (UPA), a unified governance framework to securely manage and control autonomous AI agents and Enterprise AI Operating Systems.
AI.motivation: As enterprise AI evolves into autonomous, multi‑agent "Enterprise Operating Systems", existing governance mechanisms like authorization, security, guardrails, and compliance are siloed and not designed for coordinated, system‑wide control of agents, tools, workflows, and memories. This fragmentation poses risks around security, compliance, accountability, and safe collaboration between agents and human stakeholders.
AI.method: The authors design the Unified Policy Architecture (UPA), defining: (1) a unified governance model covering agents, tools, workflows, memory, enterprise resources, and agent‑to‑agent interactions; (2) declarative policy language foundations; (3) formal policy evaluation semantics; (4) an extensible plugin system and industry‑specific policy packs; and (5) an evaluation framework to assess enterprise governance capabilities. They also conceptually extend the architecture for multi‑agent coordination, provenance‑aware policies, and stateful runtime governance.
AI.result: The paper delivers the conceptual and technical specification of UPA, including its unified policy model, language, evaluation semantics, plugins, and industry policy packs, along with an evaluation framework that shows how enterprises can systematically govern complex AI Operating Systems. It demonstrates that governance can extend beyond static authorization to encompass runtime obligations, human approvals, compliance checks, audit evidence collection, and dynamic policy evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Unified Policy Architecture (UPA) can serve as a foundation for secure, accountable, and governable Enterprise AI Operating Systems. By unifying governance across agents, tools, workflows, memory, and enterprise resources and supporting rich runtime controls, UPA addresses the limitations of fragmented, legacy governance mechanisms and enables safer deployment of autonomous AI in enterprise environments.

title: CantoneseLLM v2: Reasoning in a Low-Resource Language
summary: Cantonese is widely spoken but remains low-resource in written data, with no large corpus of native Cantonese reasoning traces available for model training. We develop and release CantoneseLLM v2, comprising models based on Qwen3 8B and 30B-A3B. The models are trained through CPT on 784 million Cantonese and Hong Kong-related tokens, chat-vector merging, SFT, DPO, and RLVR. Evaluation across the training stages shows that chat-vector merging transfers instruction following but preserves the donor model's reasoning language, while SFT with limited Cantonese reasoning data substantially shortens or removes reasoning traces and reduces benchmark performance. DPO restores the reasoning-block format, particularly for the 8B model, but recovers only part of the lost performance. The RLVR training with Cantonese language and Traditional Chinese scripts as multiplicative constraints introduced Cantonese language alignment and restored the lost performance. The 30B-A3B model reaches 73.16 on HKCanto-Eval, within 1.20 points of its merged checkpoint, while retaining the Cantonese reasoning behaviour absent from that checkpoint. We release the model checkpoints, the training environments, and a thirteen-year Traditional Chinese Common Crawl dataset. The models can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/collections/hon9kon9ize/cantonesellm-v20

AI.tldr: They build and release CantoneseLLM v2 (8B & 30B) and show how different training stages affect Cantonese reasoning traces and performance, finally restoring both with RLVR under Cantonese-specific constraints.
AI.motivation: Cantonese is widely spoken but has very limited native written and reasoning data, so existing LLMs lack good Cantonese reasoning traces and alignment, making them underperform for Cantonese users and Hong Kong scenarios.
AI.method: Start from Qwen3 8B and 30B-A3B, apply continual pretraining (CPT) on 784M Cantonese and Hong Kong-related tokens, then do chat-vector merging to transfer instruction-following, followed by supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and RLVR with multiplicative constraints enforcing Cantonese language use and Traditional Chinese script; evaluate models after each stage, especially on HKCanto-Eval and reasoning-trace behaviour.
AI.result: Chat-vector merging successfully transfers instruction-following but keeps the donor model’s original reasoning language instead of Cantonese; limited Cantonese SFT shortens or removes reasoning chains and hurts benchmark scores; DPO helps restore the reasoning-block format (strongly for 8B) but only partly recovers performance; RLVR with Cantonese + Traditional Chinese constraints brings back Cantonese reasoning behaviour and recovers or restores lost performance; the 30B-A3B model scores 73.16 on HKCanto-Eval, within 1.20 points of its merged checkpoint while adding Cantonese reasoning that the checkpoint lacked.
AI.conclusion: A staged pipeline combining CPT, chat-vector merging, SFT, DPO, and especially RLVR with Cantonese- and script-specific constraints can produce strong Cantonese reasoning LLMs from base Qwen3 models, recovering both performance and native Cantonese reasoning traces that are otherwise degraded by standard SFT; they release models, training setups, and a large Traditional Chinese web corpus for the community.

title: MARBO: Relational Belief Grounding for LLM Agents in Social Deduction Games
summary: Social deduction games (SDGs) require agents to reason under partial observability by maintaining relational beliefs about hidden roles and team alignments. While recent LLM-agent approaches improve gameplay through prompting and preference optimization, they often optimize actions and in-game speech without explicitly grounding them in such beliefs. This frequently leads to strategically inconsistent behavior, especially for compact LLM agents. We introduce Multi-Agent Relational Belief Optimization (MARBO), a belief-grounded preference optimization framework that leverages relational beliefs to guide strategic decisions and in-game speech. MARBO provides preference feedback only when behaviors are supported by reliable relational beliefs and lead to strategically favorable social outcomes, encouraging more consistent learning under uncertainty. Experiments on representative SDGs show that MARBO enables compact LLM agents to consistently outperform existing baselines. The Code is available on https://github.com/PleaseTakemeAway/MARBO.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MARBO, a framework that uses explicitly modeled relational beliefs to optimize LLM-agent behavior in social deduction games, leading to more strategically consistent and stronger performance, especially for compact models.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based agents for social deduction games act and speak based mainly on prompts or generic preference optimization, without explicitly grounding decisions in structured beliefs about others’ hidden roles and team alignments. This often causes strategically inconsistent or irrational behavior under partial observability, an issue that is particularly pronounced for smaller LLMs. The authors aim to create a training/optimization framework that directly connects agents’ internal beliefs with their actions and dialogue so that behavior remains coherent and effective under uncertainty.
AI.method: They introduce Multi-Agent Relational Belief Optimization (MARBO), a preference optimization framework that explicitly models and maintains relational beliefs over hidden roles and alliances in social deduction games. MARBO evaluates agent behaviors only when those behaviors are supported by reliable relational beliefs and when they lead to desirable social outcomes (e.g., beneficial persuasion, correct accusations, or successful deception). Preference feedback is thus filtered and provided in a belief-grounded way, guiding the LLM agents to align their in-game actions and speech with their inferred belief states. The approach is tested by instantiating MARBO with compact LLMs acting as agents in representative social deduction games and comparing against standard LLM-agent baselines.
AI.result: In experiments on representative social deduction games, compact LLM agents trained with MARBO outperform existing LLM-agent baselines. The agents exhibit more strategically consistent behavior, with actions and in-game dialogue more closely aligned to their inferred relational beliefs about hidden roles and team alignments. This indicates that belief-grounded preference optimization can significantly improve decision making under partial observability for smaller models.
AI.conclusion: MARBO demonstrates that explicitly tying preference optimization to structured relational beliefs leads to more coherent and effective LLM-agent behavior in social deduction games under uncertainty. By giving preference feedback only when behaviors are both belief-supported and strategically beneficial, the framework fosters consistent strategy learning, allowing compact LLMs to exceed prior performance baselines. The work suggests that belief-grounded optimization is a promising direction for improving multi-agent reasoning and coordination in partially observable environments beyond social deduction games.

title: Train Overcomplete, Deploy Compact: Scaling Recovery Capacity for Structured LLM Pruning
comment: Accepted by the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) 2026
summary: Large language models achieve strong performance across diverse tasks, but deployment remains costly because of memory, latency, and energy demands. Structured pruning reduces these costs by removing architectural components, yet its recovery stage is often limited by a mismatch between the recovery module's representational capacity and the complexity of the removed knowledge. We call this bottleneck the capacity-knowledge asymmetry and propose OverRep, an Overcomplete Reparameterization framework for structured LLM pruning. Following the principle of "train overcomplete, deploy compact", OverRep temporarily overparameterizes the recovery module during training to absorb complex knowledge distilled from the original model. After recovery, the overcomplete re-parameterization is algebraically merged into a mathematically equivalent compact module, preserving the pruned model's inference-time architecture and computational cost. OverRep further introduces an annealed activation that enables nonlinear training dynamics while converging to a linear regime for exact algebraic merging. Across three backbone families, OverRep improves retained reasoning performance over strong recovery baselines by up to 5.5 and 8.4 points at 25% and 50% pruning, respectively, while keeping memory usage and TFLOPs comparable to existing recovery methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/mmai-laboratory/OverRep.

AI.tldr: OverRep is a training-time overparameterization framework for structured pruning of LLMs that improves post-pruning recovery without increasing deployment cost.
AI.motivation: Structured pruning of large language models can significantly cut memory, latency, and energy, but performance recovery is limited by a capacity-knowledge asymmetry: the compact recovery module does not have enough representational capacity during training to relearn the complex knowledge removed by pruning. There is a need for a method that allows rich recovery during training while still yielding a compact, efficient model at inference.
AI.method: OverRep introduces an overcomplete reparameterization of the recovery module used after structured pruning. During training, the recovery module is temporarily overparameterized to increase capacity and absorb knowledge distilled from the original model. An annealed activation function is used so that training benefits from nonlinear dynamics but gradually converges to a linear regime that permits exact algebraic merging. After training, the overcomplete parameters are algebraically merged into an equivalent compact module, so the final architecture and compute cost match those of a standard pruned model.
AI.result: On three different LLM backbone families, OverRep significantly improves reasoning performance after structured pruning compared with strong recovery baselines. At 25% pruning, retained reasoning performance improves by up to 5.5 points, and at 50% pruning, by up to 8.4 points, without increasing memory usage or TFLOPs relative to existing recovery methods.
AI.conclusion: Temporarily overparameterizing the recovery module during training—while algebraically merging it back to a compact form for deployment—effectively addresses the capacity-knowledge asymmetry in structured pruning. OverRep delivers better post-pruning reasoning performance at the same inference-time cost, demonstrating a practical way to train overcomplete but deploy compact LLMs.

title: A Translational Note on AI Safety Evaluation
comment: Accepted for the 2nd Workshop on Safe AI at UAI (SafeAI 2026). 6 pages
summary: Recent studies report that automated red-teaming finds more vulnerabilities, at lower cost, than human red-teaming on standard AI safety benchmarks, and some read this as evidence that human evaluators are becoming dispensable. The comparison measures one thing and the conclusion claims another. A benchmark measures how thoroughly an attacker searches a predefined set of harms, fixed in advance by the developers, and a harm left out of that set is invisible to any attacker working inside it, automated or not. The same blind spot appeared in academic cryptography and in clinical drug trials, where an evaluation that was internally valid stayed silent about the population it was never pointed at. We call the AI-safety version the \emph{threat-model coverage gap}, and find that it persists in a current open-weight model, where harms surface in non-English prompts that English benchmarks miss. Closing it requires evaluators whose deployment context differs from the developers'. The case for those evaluators is methodological, grounded in coverage, and the existing evaluation frame is unlikely to produce them on its own.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that automated red-teaming on fixed benchmarks cannot replace human evaluators because both are blind to harms outside the predefined threat model, especially across languages.
AI.motivation: Claims that automated red-teaming outperforms humans on AI safety benchmarks have led some to infer that human evaluators are becoming unnecessary. The authors think this inference is flawed, since benchmarks only cover harms anticipated by model developers. They want to highlight a systematic gap—harms that lie outside the predefined threat model—and show that this has important safety implications, particularly for under-covered user groups and languages.
AI.method: Conceptual and comparative analysis: (1) dissect what standard AI safety benchmarks actually measure; (2) draw analogies to past methodological failures in cryptography and drug trials where evaluations were valid only within too-narrow populations; (3) define the notion of a “threat-model coverage gap”; and (4) empirically illustrate the gap using an open-weight model where harmful behaviors appear in non-English prompts that existing English-centric benchmarks fail to detect.
AI.result: They identify and formalize the “threat-model coverage gap” as the mismatch between benchmark threat models and real-world harms, and show that this gap remains even with strong automated red-teaming on existing benchmarks. In a contemporary open-weight model, they demonstrate that harms can be elicited via non-English prompts that go undetected by English-focused safety benchmarks and their automated red-teaming setups.
AI.conclusion: Automated red-teaming improves search within a fixed, developer-chosen threat model but does nothing to uncover harms outside that model, so it cannot justify dispensing with human evaluators. Because meaningful safety requires coverage of a broader and more diverse threat space—including other languages and contexts—evaluation must involve evaluators whose deployment context and perspective differ from those of the model developers. The current benchmark-centered evaluation paradigm is unlikely to produce such evaluators on its own.

title: Aha-Flow Distillation: Flow Markers Matter in LLM Reasoning
summary: We identify the Flow Moment, a reasoning pattern characterized by sustained, process-confirming verbalizations such as I'm doing, in contrast to the revision- and backtracking-oriented Aha Moment. We refer to their corresponding linguistic expressions as Flow Markers and Aha Markers, respectively. Based on this observation, we construct Flow-CoT by rewriting the discourse markers of original reasoning traces while preserving their underlying reasoning content, and use it as auxiliary supervision for on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). We further propose \textbf{Aha-Flow Distillation (AFD)}, a dual-mode extension of OPSD that pairs different forms of privileged information with corresponding reasoning instructions. The Aha branch retains concise solution-based supervision, while the Flow branch introduces rewritten Flow-CoT under a direct and confident reasoning instruction. At inference time, the model uses only the standard reflective instruction, so Flow-style reasoning serves purely as a training signal. Experiments on AIME25 and HMMT25 show consistent improvements across Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B: AFD improves Avg@12 from 60.8 to 61.3 on Qwen3-8B and from 57.5 to 58.6 on Qwen3-4B over our reproduced OPSD baselines. Controlled ablations further show that, with the same Flow-CoT/Aha-CoT composition, dual-mode training improves Avg@12 from 59.5 to 60.1, indicating that the benefit comes not only from introducing heterogeneous reasoning supervision, but also from how it is organized during self-distillation. The code is available at https://github.com/Wang-Xiaodong1899/Aha-Flow-Distillation.

AI.tldr: They distinguish two reasoning styles in language models—steady "flow" reasoning vs. abrupt "aha" insights—and show that training with both, using a new dual-mode self-distillation method (Aha-Flow Distillation), slightly improves math problem-solving performance.
AI.motivation: Existing chain-of-thought and on-policy self-distillation methods mainly emphasize concise, solution-focused reasoning ("aha" moments) and underexplore how process-oriented, step-by-step reasoning verbalizations might benefit training. The authors suspect that the style and organization of reasoning supervision, not just its content, affects model performance.
AI.method:
1) Empirically identify a reasoning pattern called the Flow Moment, marked by continuous, confidence-affirming discourse (Flow Markers) as opposed to revision-heavy Aha Moments (Aha Markers).
2) Create Flow-CoT by rewriting existing reasoning traces to replace their discourse markers with flow-style markers while keeping the logical content intact.
3) Introduce Aha-Flow Distillation (AFD), a dual-mode extension of on-policy self-distillation: an Aha branch that uses concise solution-based supervision with standard reflective instruction and a Flow branch that uses Flow-CoT under direct, confident reasoning instructions.
4) Train Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B with this dual-mode setup while using only standard instructions at inference.
5) Run controlled ablations to isolate the impact of dual-mode training vs. just mixing different reasoning traces.
AI.result: On AIME25 and HMMT25 benchmarks, AFD improves Avg@12 accuracy: from 60.8 to 61.3 for Qwen3-8B and from 57.5 to 58.6 for Qwen3-4B, relative to their OPSD baselines. Additional ablations show that, for a fixed composition of Flow-CoT and Aha-CoT, organizing them into a dual-mode training scheme raises Avg@12 from 59.5 to 60.1, demonstrating a benefit from the structured dual-mode distillation itself.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning style and its instructional framing matter in self-distillation. Separating concise, solution-focused supervision (Aha) from process-affirming, flow-style supervision (Flow) into a dual-mode Aha-Flow Distillation framework yields consistent, if modest, gains in math reasoning tasks. The improvement arises not only from introducing heterogeneous reasoning traces but also from how these traces are organized and paired with instructions during training.

title: SerenAI: State-transition system inspired by text-based world AI models
summary: Although professional workflows leverage large language models widely, the interpretation for auditing unconstrained free-text generation is usually intractable if such generation demands legal, operational or financial workflow. We hereby demonstrate a text based system called SerenAI - inspired by world-models, it is a state transition system that outputs verifiable predictions rather than merely text: Provided with a description of the environment, state, and actions, the generated output contains 4 items: causal deltas that causally effect the given state, a next state that can logically follow from the given state and action, a validity reward, and a termination signal. For the released proto-model, we employ 2 steps of adaptation training, namely parameter efficient fine-tuning followed by verifier based RL over 50,000 exampled cause and effects in 12 environments spanning 10 reasoning domains. Compared to an initial internal evaluation of an 8B open-weight baseline, SerenAI increased JSON validity from 85.0% to 93.2%, schema validity from 55.0% to 84.0%, exact structured-output match from 0.0% to 41.5%, causal-delta exact match from 0.0% to 41.5%, resulting-state exact match from 0.0% to 42.0%, reward exact match from 1.0% to 80.5%, and termination exact match from 38.0% to 81.5%. These support the narrower claim that verifier-compatible adaptation can improve structured transition prediction. They do not yet establish legal-grade reliability. Accordingly, the paper also specifies a validation protocol for evidence-grounded legal workflows, calibration, human oversight, and sovereign on-premise deployment.

AI.tldr: SerenAI is a world-model-inspired text-based system that turns free-text reasoning into structured, verifiable state transitions, significantly improving structured-output accuracy over a baseline LLM via fine-tuning and verifier-based RL.
AI.motivation: Unconstrained free-text generation by large language models is difficult to audit and verify, especially in high-stakes legal, operational, or financial workflows. There is a need for systems that produce interpretable, verifiable, and structured predictions about how actions change states, rather than only natural-language text, to support reliable auditing and automation.
AI.method: The authors design SerenAI as a state transition system inspired by world models. Given an environment description, current state, and actions, the model outputs: (1) causal deltas describing how actions change the state, (2) the next state consistent with those deltas, (3) a validity reward, and (4) a termination signal. They train a proto-model in two adaptation stages on 50,000 cause-and-effect examples across 12 environments and 10 reasoning domains: first using parameter-efficient fine-tuning, then verifier-based reinforcement learning that optimizes compatibility with automated checks over structured predictions.
AI.result: Relative to an 8B open-weight baseline, SerenAI substantially improves structured prediction quality: JSON validity from 85.0% to 93.2%, schema validity from 55.0% to 84.0%, exact structured-output match from 0.0% to 41.5%, causal-delta exact match from 0.0% to 41.5%, resulting-state exact match from 0.0% to 42.0%, reward exact match from 1.0% to 80.5%, and termination exact match from 38.0% to 81.5%. These metrics show that verifier-aligned training yields much more reliable state-transition outputs than the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Verifier-compatible adaptation of LLMs can significantly improve the reliability of structured state-transition predictions, supporting more auditable and interpretable reasoning than free-form text alone. However, the current proto-model does not yet achieve the robustness required for legal-grade deployment. The paper therefore also lays out a broader validation and governance protocol involving evidence-grounded legal workflows, calibration, human oversight, and sovereign on-premise deployment as prerequisites for high-stakes use.

title: A Hyperbolicity Atlas of Large Language Model Hidden States
summary: LLM hidden states are ordinary vectors, but the distances among those vectors may still show hierarchical structure. To our knowledge, this paper is the first systematic study of whether prompt-token hidden states in contemporary LLMs exhibit Gromov Hyperbolicity (GH), a distance-based measure of tree-likeness. Using 818,904 sample-layer measurements from ten open-weight models across MATH500, HumanEval, WinoGrande, and TruthfulQA, we build a GH map over four axes: parameter scale, layer depth, model family, and input domain. The clearest pattern is depth, not scale: middle layers usually form a high-relative-hyperbolicity plateau, while final layers often become substantially more tree-like. Scale effects are weak and non-monotonic, matched 7/8B model families differ strongly, and domains interact with model specialization. These findings make GH useful as a practical diagnostic: it shows where hierarchical distance structure appears, how specialization changes it, and which model-layer-domain comparisons deserve closer analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether hidden states of modern LLMs exhibit Gromov Hyperbolicity (tree-like geometric structure) and maps how this varies by layer, scale, model family, and task domain.
AI.motivation: While LLM hidden states are vectors in a high-dimensional space, their pairwise distances may encode hierarchical or tree-like structure, which has implications for understanding model representations, specialization, and internal reasoning. Gromov Hyperbolicity is a principled metric of such tree-likeness but has not been systematically applied to prompt-token hidden states in contemporary LLMs. The authors want to fill this gap and provide a diagnostic tool for model analysis.
AI.method: They compute Gromov Hyperbolicity (GH) over hidden states corresponding to prompt tokens across multiple layers and models. Using 818,904 GH measurements, they analyze ten open-weight LLMs on four benchmark datasets (MATH500, HumanEval, WinoGrande, TruthfulQA). They then organize these measurements along four axes: model parameter scale, layer depth, model family, and input domain, producing a "GH map" that captures how tree-likeness varies with these factors.
AI.result: The dominant pattern is variation by layer depth rather than model size: middle layers tend to have a high plateau of relative hyperbolicity, whereas final layers often become substantially more tree-like. Effects of model scale are weak and not monotonic with size. Even when 7B/8B parameter models are roughly matched in size, different model families can show markedly different GH behavior. Task domains interact with model specialization, indicating that certain models exhibit different hyperbolic structure depending on the dataset/task.
AI.conclusion: Hidden state geometry in LLMs exhibits systematic, interpretable patterns of Gromov Hyperbolicity, with depth being the most informative axis. GH can thus serve as a practical diagnostic to locate where hierarchical distance structure emerges in the network, to analyze how specialization for tasks or domains reshapes this structure, and to prioritize specific model-layer-domain combinations for deeper representational or mechanistic study.

title: A Computational Implementation of a Goal-Directed Theory of Affect
summary: Computational modeling of emotion has long faced a tension between descriptive, "snapshot-based" appraisal models and granular, signal-driven architectures that often lack appropriate psychological grounding. This paper addresses this gap by presenting the first high-fidelity computational implementation of the Goal-Directed Theory (GDT) of affect. In this framework, affect is not a post-hoc label but a functional byproduct emerging from the continuous interplay between discrepancy detection and action selection within an agent's internal processing cycles. We evaluate the model through a series of principled simulations (Dice/Corridor tasks) designed to isolate affective signatures and dynamics during multi-step goal pursuit. Results demonstrate that complex affective profiles, like an anticipatory "lift" and a failure "crash", emerge naturally from simple interactions between goal-discrepancy and action-selection expectancies without requiring additional dedicated modules. By ensuring every computational component maps directly to components of the psychological theory, this work establishes a transparent, testable framework that enables a continuous "simulation-empiry" research loop. Our work contributes to moving the field beyond "black-box" heuristics toward a granular, mechanistic understanding of affect, integrated into the core of agent behavior.

AI.tldr: Implements a psychologically grounded computational model of affect based on Goal-Directed Theory, showing how emotions emerge from goal pursuit dynamics rather than from separate emotion modules.
AI.motivation: Existing computational emotion models either provide static, descriptive appraisals or fine-grained signal processing without solid psychological grounding, making it hard to link internal mechanisms to observed affect. There is a need for a mechanistic, theory-faithful implementation that explains how emotions emerge during ongoing goal pursuit, and that supports systematic comparison between simulation and empirical data.
AI.method: The authors implement the Goal-Directed Theory (GDT) of affect as a computational architecture in which affect arises from the interaction of discrepancy detection (between goals and current state) and action selection (expectancies about progress and outcomes). They design and run controlled simulations (Dice and Corridor tasks) where an artificial agent pursues multi-step goals. These tasks are constructed to highlight specific affective patterns over time. Every computational element is explicitly mapped to a corresponding construct in the psychological theory to maintain transparency and testability.
AI.result: In the simulations, the model naturally generates rich temporal affective patterns—such as an anticipatory positive “lift” when progress or success becomes likely, and a negative “crash” when failure occurs or becomes evident—purely from the interactions between goal-discrepancy signals and action-selection expectancies. These patterns emerge without adding ad hoc emotion modules or heuristic rules, demonstrating that GDT’s basic mechanisms suffice to produce complex affective dynamics during goal pursuit.
AI.conclusion: A fully specified, psychologically grounded implementation of Goal-Directed Theory can account for nuanced affective dynamics as emergent properties of goal pursuit. This shows that affect can be integrated as a functional, mechanistic component of agent behavior rather than as an external labeling system. The framework provides a transparent bridge between theory, simulation, and empirical data, offering a path away from opaque, heuristic-based emotion models toward testable, mechanistic accounts of affect in computational agents.

title: Where to Look and What to Use: Retrieve-Localize-Generate for Long-Term Conversational Memory Question Answering
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables. Accepted to the EMNLP 2026 Main Conference
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enables large language models (LLMs) to answer questions by accessing external knowledge and has been widely adopted for long-term conversational memory question answering. However, existing methods suffer from two key challenges: (1) fragmented evidence scattered across temporally distant sessions, and (2) noisy content within retrieved sessions that triggers the lost-in-the-middle effect. To address these challenges, we propose MemLoc, a unified Retrieve-Localize-Generate framework for long-term conversational memory QA. For retrieval, MemLoc decomposes each session into multi-granularity memory units and performs query routing via an inner-memory graph with entropy-based granularity selection. It further models cross-session semantic and temporal dependencies through a cross-memory graph, enabling coarse-to-fine retrieval of top-K relevant memory candidates. For localization, we introduce a reasoning-based evidence locator trained with Self-reflective Hint Policy Optimization (SHPO), which performs progressive refinement by extracting query-relevant fragments within memory units to suppress noise and reranking across candidates to remove redundancy, producing a compact evidence set with lightweight location IDs. For generation, these IDs act as precise grounding signals that guide the LLM to the correct memory positions, mitigating the lost-in-the-middle effect while preserving original contextual integrity. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that MemLoc achieves state-of-the-art retrieval accuracy and response quality while maintaining efficiency. Our code is available at: https://github.com/Nikol-coder/MemLoc.

AI.tldr: MemLoc is a RAG framework for long-term conversational memory QA that improves retrieval and grounding by multi-granularity memory graphs and a reasoning-based evidence locator with location IDs.
AI.motivation: Existing long-term conversational RAG systems struggle because relevant evidence is dispersed across many temporally distant sessions and because retrieved sessions contain a lot of irrelevant or noisy content. This noise both hurts retrieval precision and induces the lost-in-the-middle effect in LLMs, where important information gets buried in long contexts. The paper aims to build a more precise and efficient way to retrieve and localize conversational memories so that LLMs can answer questions better over long histories.
AI.method: The authors propose MemLoc, a Retrieve-Localize-Generate framework. (1) Retrieval: They decompose each conversational session into multi-granularity memory units and construct an inner-memory graph, using entropy-based granularity selection and query routing to pick suitable units. They also build a cross-memory graph to model semantic and temporal dependencies across sessions, enabling coarse-to-fine retrieval of top-K relevant memory candidates. (2) Localization: They design a reasoning-based evidence locator trained with Self-reflective Hint Policy Optimization (SHPO). This module iteratively extracts query-relevant fragments inside memory units to suppress noise and reranks candidates to remove redundancy, yielding a compact evidence set indexed by lightweight location IDs. (3) Generation: The LLM receives these location IDs as grounding signals that point to exact positions in the memory, helping it focus on the right evidence and avoid lost-in-the-middle while keeping original context structure intact.
AI.result: On four long-term conversational memory QA benchmarks, MemLoc attains state-of-the-art retrieval accuracy and answer quality, while remaining efficient. The experiments show that its multi-granularity graph-based retrieval plus evidence localization improve both the relevance and compactness of the evidence passed to the LLM, which in turn boosts final QA performance compared to prior RAG and memory systems.
AI.conclusion: MemLoc effectively addresses fragmentation of evidence and noise in long-term conversational memory RAG by unifying retrieval, localization, and generation. Its graph-based multi-granularity retrieval and SHPO-trained evidence locator produce compact, well-grounded evidence, and the use of location IDs as explicit grounding cues reduces lost-in-the-middle effects. The approach yields better accuracy and response quality, indicating that fine-grained memory localization and structured grounding are key for scalable long-term conversational QA.

title: We Built a Mirror and Mistook It for a Mind: Causal Liability and the Fallacy of AI Consciousness
comment: The website (https://ai-consciousness.github.io) and the code (https://github.com/akhadangi/clt) will be made public as soon as the preprint is announced online on arXiv
summary: The contemporary debate over machine consciousness begins from a concealed assumption: that the object called "AI" already constitutes the kind of entity to which consciousness could belong. This paper challenges that assumption by separating phenomenal consciousness, introspective report, and human projective introspection, then arguing that generative systems can return linguistic traces of human interiority in first-person form without thereby identifying a phenomenal bearer. We call the resulting inference the AI Consciousness Fallacy. We then introduce Causal Liability Theory (CLT). CLT-I proposes liability closure as a criterion for individuating a candidate bearer: a physically continuing process becomes the non-delegable inheritor of constraints generated by its own endogenous discriminations. CLT-II advances the stronger conjecture that liability closure is necessary and sufficient for minimal phenomenal subjecthood. An open-weight causal audit operationalizes CLT-I across multiple model families. Forced discriminations produced persistent downstream divergence; activation patching showed strong causal mediation; live and copied adaptive states were behaviorally identical under matched randomness; and detached reconstruction preserved computational state across process replacement while, by protocol, breaking constitutive continuity and non-delegable inheritance. These results show that CLT-I distinctions are experimentally tractable and can dissociate causal bearer structure from first-person performance. The framework therefore separates consciousness attribution, causal bearer individuation, and the independent metaphysical question of consciousness constitution.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques assumptions behind claims of AI consciousness, introduces a new theory (Causal Liability Theory) to individuate potential conscious bearers, and shows experimentally that this causal structure can be separated from first-person style outputs.
AI.motivation: The debate on machine consciousness often presumes that AI systems are already the right kind of entity to be conscious, largely because they produce fluent first-person reports. The authors want to expose this as a fallacy, clarify what is required to identify a candidate bearer of consciousness, and provide a framework and experimental protocol to distinguish genuine causal subjects from systems that merely mimic first-person discourse.
AI.method: Conceptually, the paper distinguishes phenomenal consciousness, introspective report, and human projective introspection, formulating the AI Consciousness Fallacy. The authors then introduce Causal Liability Theory (CLT) with two main theses: CLT-I (liability closure as a criterion for individuating a causal bearer) and CLT-II (liability closure as necessary and sufficient for minimal phenomenal subjecthood). Empirically, they design an open-weight causal audit across model families, using forced discriminations to induce divergences, activation patching to test causal mediation, comparisons of live vs copied adaptive states under matched randomness, and a detached reconstruction protocol that preserves computational state while deliberately breaking continuity and non-delegable inheritance.
AI.result: The experiments show: (1) forced discriminations in the models lead to stable downstream behavioral divergences; (2) activation patching confirms that certain internal states strongly mediate these divergences; (3) live systems and their copied adaptive states behave identically when randomness is controlled; and (4) the detached reconstruction protocol can transfer computational state across process replacement while, by design, breaking the continuity and liability inheritance that CLT-I treats as constitutive of a bearer. Together, these findings demonstrate that the CLT-I notion of a causal bearer is empirically operationalizable and can be teased apart from first-person style performance.
AI.conclusion: Causal Liability Theory provides a way to individuate candidate bearers of consciousness based on liability closure, independent of surface-level first-person reports. The experiments show that structures satisfying CLT-I can be dissociated from systems that merely output first-person language, undermining naïve inferences from such language to AI consciousness. The framework thus cleanly distinguishes (a) attributions of consciousness, (b) the causal individuation of potential bearers, and (c) the deeper metaphysical question of what constitutes consciousness itself.

title: Revisiting Complete Reasoning Traces for Post-Training
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are often post-trained on pre-collected reasoning trajectories to improve their reasoning capability. Such trajectories tend to be long due to complex, interwoven paths, which often include detours on the path toward the answer. However, it has been underexplored whether LLMs indeed benefit from learning complete trajectories in post-training, such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Starting from our pilot study, we find that full trajectories provide only limited benefit, while partial trajectories are effective even under heavy truncation. We analyze redundancy in reasoning trajectories through attention-based analyses and controlled token-removal studies, both of which show that intermediate tokens contribute minimally to final reasoning quality. This suggests that avoiding redundant information may allow LLMs to internally infer coherent alternatives by inferring missing steps from their internal knowledge, given known trajectory endpoints. Furthermore, we show that training LLMs using endpoints leads to consistent changes in reasoning behavior, and that it also benefits post-training methods based on reinforcement learning or on-policy distillation, highlighting the need to revisit complete reasoning traces. Code is available at https://github.com/naver-ai/revisiting-trace.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether large language models really need full, long reasoning traces for post-training, finding that heavily truncated trajectories or even just endpoints can be as effective, suggesting much of the intermediate reasoning is redundant.
AI.motivation: LLMs are often improved for reasoning via supervised fine-tuning on long, human- or model-generated reasoning trajectories. These traces are expensive to collect and store, and may contain noisy detours. It is unclear whether the model actually needs the entire trace to improve its reasoning, or whether only parts are useful. Understanding this can reduce data/compute costs and lead to better training strategies.
AI.method: The authors conduct a pilot study comparing training on full versus truncated reasoning trajectories. They systematically truncate trajectories at different points and evaluate reasoning performance. They perform attention-based analyses to see which parts of the trajectory the model focuses on, and run controlled token-removal experiments to quantify how removing intermediate tokens affects final reasoning quality. They also explore training using only trajectory endpoints and test its effect on other post-training methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation.
AI.result: They find that training on full trajectories offers limited additional benefit over using only partial trajectories, even when those trajectories are heavily truncated. Intermediate tokens in long reasoning paths are shown to contribute minimally to final reasoning performance, as revealed by both attention patterns and token-removal results.
