Training on endpoints alone induces consistent changes in reasoning behavior and improves the effectiveness of reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation methods.
AI.conclusion: Much of the content in long reasoning trajectories is redundant for improving LLM reasoning via post-training. LLMs can infer missing intermediate steps from internal knowledge when given sufficient endpoint information. As a result, it is not always necessary to train on complete reasoning traces; focusing on endpoints or shorter segments can be more efficient and can even enhance other post-training techniques. This calls for a rethinking of current practice that relies on full reasoning trajectories.

title: Monte Carlo-Based Ex-Ante Assessment of the Green Benefits of an AI-Driven Smart Agriculture Platform in Hainan
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables; bilingual (Chinese title page with Chinese abstract, English full text); all results are ex-ante Monte Carlo simulation intervals, not field measurements
summary: Smart agriculture platforms are widely regarded as key carriers for implementing China's pesticide and fertilizer reduction, water-saving and carbon-reduction agendas, yet a unified quantitative framework for assessing their green value is still lacking. Taking an AI-driven decision platform for tropical agriculture as the object (integrating large-language-model question answering, multimodal pest diagnosis, IoT sensing, satellite remote sensing, and a closed-loop field record system), this study builds a cradle-to-farm-gate agricultural carbon accounting model covering pesticide and fertilizer production, field N2O, irrigation electricity and paddy CH4, translates platform interventions into quantifiable transmission parameters, and propagates parameter uncertainty by Monte Carlo simulation over three Hainan scenarios (mango, winter vegetable, rice/nanfan, area-weighted 40%:30%:30%). Under full adoption, median reductions are 23.5% (90% interval 15.0%-33.2%) for pesticide use, 21.0% (13.8%-28.9%) for fertilizer, 16.5% (10.9%-23.5%) for irrigation water, and 21.5% (16.1%-27.2%) for carbon intensity. Attainment probabilities are high for fertilizer reduction >=15% (90.6%) and clear carbon decline (98.1%), but only about 20% for aggregate water saving >=20%, favoring scenario-specific statements. Sobol first-order indices show soil-test recommendation and organic substitution jointly explain about 83% of the variance of aggregate carbon-intensity reduction. Convergence tests show 10,000 iterations stabilize all statistics; conservative/baseline/optimistic scenario bounds are reported. The framework offers a reproducible, calibration-ready methodology for ex-ante green-value assessment and pilot observation design.

AI.tldr: The paper develops and applies a unified quantitative framework to estimate how much an AI-driven smart agriculture platform can reduce pesticide, fertilizer, water use, and carbon intensity in tropical agriculture, using a carbon accounting model and Monte Carlo uncertainty analysis across multiple crop scenarios in Hainan.
AI.motivation: Although smart agriculture platforms are promoted as key tools for reducing pesticides, fertilizers, water use, and carbon emissions, there is no standardized, quantitative method to evaluate their actual green benefits. Policymakers and investors need a reproducible framework that can translate digital-ag interventions into measurable environmental outcomes, with uncertainties explicitly characterized, to support targets like pesticide/fertilizer reduction and carbon peaking in agriculture.
AI.method: The study takes an AI-based decision platform for tropical agriculture as a case, integrating LLM Q&A, multimodal pest diagnosis, IoT sensing, satellite data, and field records. It constructs a cradle-to-farm-gate agricultural carbon accounting model that includes upstream agrochemical production, field N2O, irrigation electricity, and paddy CH4. Platform interventions (e.g., soil testing, organic substitution) are parameterized as transmission factors that affect input rates and emissions. A Monte Carlo simulation with at least 10,000 iterations propagates uncertainties in these parameters over three crop scenarios in Hainan (mango, winter vegetables, rice/nanfan) with specific area weights, and Sobol sensitivity indices are used to identify key drivers of variance in carbon-intensity reduction. Scenario-based conservative, baseline, and optimistic bounds are reported.
AI.result: Under full adoption of the platform, median reductions are estimated at 23.5% for pesticide use, 21.0% for fertilizers, 16.5% for irrigation water, and 21.5% for carbon intensity, with 90% uncertainty intervals reported for each indicator. The probability of achieving at least 15% fertilizer reduction is about 90.6%, and the probability of clear carbon decline is about 98.1%, whereas the probability of reaching 20% or more aggregate water savings is only about 20%. Sensitivity analysis shows that soil-test-based recommendation and organic-input substitution jointly account for roughly 83% of the variance in overall carbon-intensity reduction. Convergence checks indicate 10,000 Monte Carlo iterations are sufficient to stabilize the statistics.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the proposed framework is effective for ex-ante assessment of the green value of smart agriculture platforms, yielding quantitative, uncertainty-aware estimates of reductions in agrochemical use, water consumption, and carbon intensity. It highlights that fertilizer-related interventions, especially soil testing and organic substitution, dominate the variance in carbon outcomes, and that water-saving effects are more uncertain and context-dependent. The authors argue the methodology is reproducible and ready for calibration with field data, and can guide pilot design and policy communication through scenario-specific and probabilistic statements about expected environmental benefits.

title: The Illusion of Debiasing: Persona Steering Redistributes Rather Than Reduces Bias in LLMs
summary: Prompt-based interventions: system prompts, personas, role instructions, reliably reshape what a language model says, but it is unclear which layer they reach. Do they reconfigure internal structure, or only modulate the output channel? We use persona conditioning as a controlled probe, measuring its effects along a depth axis from self-report, through open-ended generation, to word-level parametric association, across three instruction-tuned models. We find a graded dissociation. Personas are legible but not structural: models follow single-trait instructions yet fail to reproduce human inter-trait covariance. The dissociation deepens with depth: personas hold or amplify closed-form QA bias, shift absolute tone while leaving between-group disparity unchanged, and barely perturb an already saturated associative baseline. Prompt-based steering thus operates in the output channel and has a structural reach limit that surface manipulability can mask.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how prompt-based persona instructions affect language models, finding they mainly alter outputs rather than deep internal representations, with effects weakening at deeper representational levels.
AI.motivation: To determine whether system prompts and persona instructions truly change internal model structure or just superficially steer outputs, clarifying the depth and limits of prompt-based control over language models.
AI.method: Use persona conditioning as a controlled probe across three instruction-tuned models, measuring effects at multiple depths: self-reported traits, open-ended text generation, and word-level parametric associations, then compare to human-like covariance between traits and biases.
AI.result: Models follow single-trait persona instructions and show clear changes in self-report and surface behavior, but fail to reproduce human-like inter-trait covariance; the influence of personas decreases with representational depth, leaving deeper associative structures largely unchanged and existing disparities intact.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-based steering primarily operates on the output channel with limited structural reach into a model’s internal representations; surface controllability can mask deep-seated, largely unaltered associative patterns and biases.

title: Simulating the Marginal Green Contribution of AI Modules in a Smart-Agriculture Platform: Evidence from Two Monte Carlo Experiments
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables; bilingual (Chinese title page with Chinese abstract, English full text); companion to platform-level green-value assessment; all results are ex-ante Monte Carlo simulation intervals, not field measurements
summary: Smart agriculture platforms usually bundle AI diagnosis, IoT sensing and decision push into a single package, so the green benefit attributable to each component remains unclear and resource-allocation decisions lack quantitative evidence. Building on a previous platform-level Monte Carlo assessment, this paper makes the components explicit and runs two controlled simulation experiments. Experiment 1 follows the chain from AI capability to farmer behavior to agrochemical input reduction, modeling pesticide/fertilizer reduction as avoidable blind-application share times prescription effectiveness times decision-touch coverage times adoption rate, and compares an experienced-extension mode with the AI mode: the probability of reaching 20% pesticide reduction is essentially zero in the extension mode but 20.7% at baseline, up to 49% with diagnosis accuracy 0.95 and adoption 0.85 under AI; the probability of 15% fertilizer reduction rises from near zero to 52.0%. Experiment 2 compares current practice (P0), IoT engineering retrofit (P1), and P1 plus AI irrigation scheduling (P2): median aggregate water saving rises from 7.8% (P0) to 11.0% (P1) and 16.0% (P2), with AI adding 5.0 percentage points beyond engineering; paddy CH4 reduction reaches 30.5% under AI scheduling versus 19.8% under manual operation, and the rice irrigation-methane subsystem carbon intensity declines 27.9%. Sensitivity analyses of both experiments consistently indicate that the primary bottleneck for meeting green targets is farmer adoption rather than algorithm accuracy, and that AI data fusion is robust to soil-moisture sensing errors. This work provides a reproducible simulation framework for component-level green-value evaluation and promotion-strategy optimization of smart agriculture platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper quantitatively disentangles the green benefits of AI diagnosis, IoT sensing, and farmer decision support in smart agriculture using component-level Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.motivation: Most smart agriculture platforms bundle AI, IoT sensing, and decision-push tools, so it is unclear how much each component contributes to environmental benefits such as reduced chemicals, water, and emissions. This lack of component-level evidence makes it difficult to optimize investments, design promotion strategies, and target the true bottlenecks for achieving greener agriculture.
AI.method: The authors extend an earlier platform-level Monte Carlo framework into two controlled simulation experiments that isolate individual components. Experiment 1 models the pathway from AI diagnosis capability to behavior change and reductions in pesticide and fertilizer use. It represents pesticide/fertilizer reduction as the product of avoidable blind-application share, prescription effectiveness, decision-touch coverage, and adoption rate, then compares a traditional extension-service mode with an AI-diagnosis mode across parameter ranges. Experiment 2 constructs three scenarios for irrigation systems: current practice (P0), IoT engineering retrofit (P1), and P1 plus AI irrigation scheduling (P2). It simulates water savings, methane emissions from paddy fields, and carbon intensity of the irrigation-methane subsystem. Sensitivity analyses test the impact of adoption rates, algorithm accuracy, and sensor error on green outcomes.
AI.result: In Experiment 1, under traditional extension the probability of achieving 20% pesticide reduction is effectively zero, whereas under baseline AI settings it reaches 20.7% and can rise to 49% when diagnosis accuracy is 0.95 and adoption is 0.85. For fertilizer, the probability of achieving 15% reduction increases from near zero in the extension mode to 52.0% under AI. In Experiment 2, median water saving increases from 7.8% in current practice (P0) to 11.0% with IoT engineering retrofit alone (P1) and 16.0% when AI irrigation scheduling is added (P2), meaning AI contributes an additional 5 percentage points beyond engineering improvements. Paddy CH4 reduction under AI scheduling reaches 30.5% compared with 19.8% under manual operation, and the carbon intensity of the rice irrigation-methane subsystem falls by 27.9%. Sensitivity analyses show farmer adoption is the dominant constraint on achieving green targets, while AI’s data fusion remains robust to soil-moisture sensor errors and algorithm accuracy is a secondary bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that AI components in smart agriculture platforms can substantially enhance pesticide, fertilizer, water, and methane reduction beyond what is achievable by traditional extension services or hardware retrofits alone. However, farmer adoption, not algorithmic performance, is the main limiting factor for realizing these green benefits. The authors provide a reproducible, component-level Monte Carlo simulation framework that allows stakeholders to quantitatively evaluate the environmental value of individual platform components and to design promotion and investment strategies that focus on improving adoption while leveraging the robustness of AI data fusion to sensing imperfections.

title: PTCG: Persona-guided Tree-based Counterargument Generation
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 30 pages, 13 figures, 15 tables
summary: The ability to generate counterarguments is important for critical thinking and balanced discourse, yet existing approaches typically produce only a single counterargument, failing to capture the diversity and persuasiveness required in real-world debates. To address this limitation, we propose Persona-guided Tree-based Counterargument Generation (PTCG), a framework that combines Tree-of-Thoughts-inspired step-wise generation and pruning with speaker persona selection. By estimating the author's persona from the original argument and incorporating speaker personas representing distinct perspectives, PTCG operationalizes perspective-taking and enables the generation of diverse counterarguments. Results from LLM-as-a-Judge, classifier-based assessment, and human evaluations indicate that PTCG shows consistent improvements in both the diversity and persuasiveness of counterarguments compared to baseline methods.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PTCG, a persona-guided, tree-based framework for generating multiple diverse and persuasive counterarguments, outperforming existing single-counterargument approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing counterargument generation methods usually output only one counterargument, which fails to reflect the diversity of viewpoints and persuasive strategies found in real debates. There is a need to model multiple perspectives and systematically search for better counterarguments to support critical thinking and balanced discourse.
AI.method: The authors propose Persona-guided Tree-based Counterargument Generation (PTCG). First, the system estimates the author’s persona from the original argument. Then, it uses a set of speaker personas that represent different perspectives. Counterarguments are generated step-wise in a Tree-of-Thoughts-like structure, where branches represent alternative reasoning paths or perspectives. A pruning mechanism selects the most promising partial counterarguments, guided by the personas, to expand further. This combination of persona modeling and tree-based exploration aims to produce multiple, varied, and persuasive counterarguments.
AI.result: Using evaluations from LLM-as-a-judge, automated classifier metrics, and human annotators, PTCG consistently outperforms baseline methods on diversity and persuasiveness of the generated counterarguments. The improvements are robust across these different evaluation protocols.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating explicit persona modeling with tree-based, stepwise exploration effectively enhances counterargument generation, leading to more diverse and persuasive outputs than traditional single-shot methods. This suggests that perspective-taking and structured search are key ingredients for more realistic and useful argumentation systems.

title: Reason Through the Latent! Making Latent Visual Reasoning Necessary
summary: Latent visual reasoning aims to perform multimodal reasoning through hidden-state computation rather than explicit textual chains of thought. However, visual information being present in a latent state does not imply that the model actually relies on that state when producing its answer, especially when alternative image-conditioned paths remain available. We introduce \textbf{C}ausal \textbf{V}isual \textbf{R}ecurrent \textbf{R}easoning (CVRR), which preserves pretrained visual competence while making recurrent computation the required image-conditioned path to prediction. CVRR initializes recurrence from the question hidden state after the pretrained vision-language model has incorporated the image, then repeatedly updates this state while re-reading the same fixed visual evidence. Before decoding, visual states and the original multimodal KV cache are removed so that only the final recurrent state carries image-conditioned information to the answer. Across the $V^*$, MMVP, BLINK, and MME-RealWorld-Lite benchmarks, CVRR retains strong performance under this strict interface, while compatible latent reasoners fail to recover comparable visual competence even when retrained under the same constraint. Causal interventions further show that predictions remain sensitive to recurrent content when the question is held fixed, and that persistent visual evidence causally revises the recurrent trajectory. These results distinguish latent informativeness from latent computation that is actually used for prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Causal Visual Recurrent Reasoning (CVRR), a method that forces multimodal models to actually use latent visual reasoning for predictions rather than just storing visual information in hidden states.
AI.motivation: Existing latent visual reasoning approaches may encode visual information in hidden states but do not guarantee that this information is causally used when producing answers, because models can exploit shortcut paths or alternative image-conditioned representations. The authors want a way to: (1) constrain the model so that recurrent latent computation is the only image-conditioned route to the final answer, and (2) empirically distinguish between representations that merely contain information and those that are truly used for prediction.
AI.method: They introduce CVRR, a modification of pretrained vision-language models where: (1) the model first processes the image and question as usual to obtain a multimodal question hidden state; (2) this hidden state initializes a recurrent reasoning process that repeatedly updates while attending to the same fixed visual features; (3) before generating the answer, all visual states and the original multimodal key–value (KV) cache are discarded, so the only image-conditioned information available to the decoder is the final recurrent state; (4) they train/evaluate this under a strict interface across multiple benchmarks and compare to other latent-reasoning baselines trained under the same constraint; (5) they perform causal interventions on the recurrent trajectory and visual evidence to test sensitivity and causal influence on predictions.
AI.result: Across V*, MMVP, BLINK, and MME-RealWorld-Lite benchmarks, CVRR largely preserves the original model’s visual competence despite the strict constraint that only the final recurrent state can carry image-conditioned information to the answer. Competing latent reasoning methods, when retrofitted with the same constraint, suffer substantial performance drops and cannot match CVRR. Causal experiments show that holding the question fixed while perturbing recurrent content changes predictions, and that re-presenting persistent visual evidence causally alters the recurrent trajectory, confirming that recurrent states are actively used in prediction.
AI.conclusion: CVRR successfully enforces a causal bottleneck whereby recurrent latent computation becomes the necessary image-conditioned path to answers, demonstrating that it is possible to preserve strong visual performance under this constraint. The causal analyses show that not all informative latent states are functionally used for prediction, and that methods like CVRR are needed to ensure latent visual reasoning is genuinely involved in decision-making rather than being a passive repository of image information.

title: Line-Coupled Language Model
summary: Autoregressive language models generate one token per decoding step, limiting the useful output of each forward pass. Although diffusion models, insertion-based decoding, and multi-token prediction enable parallel generation, they either incur additional training-time token traffic or struggle to predict strongly dependent future tokens. We introduce the Line-Coupled Language Model (LCLM), an autoregressive model that advances multiple text lines together by predicting the next token for every active line while coupling the lines through shared causal context. LCLM interleaves line tokens into a single causal sequence and uses line-staggered rotary positions, retaining the standard next-token objective and causal attention. Controlled experiments show that cross-line targets are substantially less dependent than consecutive same-line targets, supporting lines as parallel generation units. With 881M parameters, LCLM produces an average of 2.94 content tokens per forward pass with a validation cross-entropy loss of 2.44, compared with 1.00 token per forward pass and a loss of 2.39 for the vanilla autoregressive baseline. Most notably, even when LCLM generates 16 tokens per forward pass, its loss is only 0.09 higher than that of the vanilla autoregressive baseline (2.34 vs. 2.25).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Line-Coupled Language Models (LCLM), which generate multiple lines of text in parallel while preserving a standard autoregressive next-token objective, significantly increasing tokens per forward pass with only a small degradation in perplexity.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive language models are limited by generating only one token per forward pass, which restricts decoding speed. Existing parallel-generation approaches (diffusion, insertion-based decoding, multi-token prediction) either require extra training-time token traffic or have difficulty modeling strong dependencies between future tokens. The authors seek a way to parallelize generation without changing the standard training objective and while maintaining strong local dependencies.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Line-Coupled Language Model (LCLM), where text is organized into multiple lines that are advanced together. At each decoding step, the model predicts the next token for every active line in parallel, while all lines share a single causal context. Technically, line tokens are interleaved into one causal sequence, and line-staggered rotary positional embeddings are used to preserve order and enable coupling. Training still uses the conventional next-token prediction objective with causal attention, but targets are spread across multiple lines rather than along a single sequence.
AI.result: Controlled experiments show that prediction targets across different lines are substantially less mutually dependent than consecutive tokens on the same line, validating lines as effective units for parallel generation. A model with 881M parameters achieves an average of 2.94 generated content tokens per forward pass with validation cross-entropy 2.44, versus 1.00 token per pass and loss 2.39 for a vanilla autoregressive baseline. When configured to generate as many as 16 tokens per forward pass, LCLM’s loss remains close to the baseline, increasing by only 0.09 (2.34 vs 2.25).
AI.conclusion: LCLM demonstrates that organizing text into coupled lines, and interleaving their tokens into a shared causal sequence with line-staggered positions, can substantially increase the number of tokens produced per forward pass while retaining the standard autoregressive training setup and keeping perplexity degradation minimal. This offers a practical path to faster generation with minimal architectural and objective changes compared to standard language models.

title: Improving Proficiency and Efficiency of Android GUI Agents via Self-Generating Tool Actions
summary: Android agents using a hybrid action space that combines GUI actions and tool actions (e.g., accessing application data via APIs) remain largely underexplored, mainly due to the excessive effort required to create tools. To address this gap, we introduce DroidTool, a framework for augmenting the agents with self-generated tools, which are realized as Python functions operating on application states (e.g., a database). To create tools with minimal human labor, DroidTool employs an agentic workflow featuring stages: proposal, implementation, test generation and execution, and repair. Notably, when testing the created tools for verification, it constructs relational tests across relevant tools for natural preparation of appropriate test preconditions and improved test coverage, rather than testing each tool separately. The GUI agents augmented with the generated tools achieved approximately 4.47%p higher performance with approximately 20.05% fewer interactions than the GUI-only agents, averaged across representative benchmarks: AndroidWorld, B-MoCA, and MobileSafetyBench.

AI.tldr: DroidTool is a framework that automatically generates Python tool functions for Android GUI agents, enabling a hybrid action space (GUI + tools) and improving task success and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Hybrid agents that can both operate the GUI and call tools over app data are powerful but underused on Android because creating and maintaining such tools is very labor-intensive. There is a need to automate tool creation so that Android agents can leverage structured access to application state (e.g., databases) without heavy human engineering.
AI.method: DroidTool defines an agentic workflow to automatically create tools as Python functions over application states. The workflow has multiple stages: (1) proposal – the system proposes useful tools the agent might need; (2) implementation – it synthesizes Python implementations of these tools; (3) test generation and execution – it automatically generates tests and runs them to verify tool correctness; and (4) repair – it debugs and fixes tools that fail tests. A key novelty is that tests are constructed relationally across multiple related tools so that test preconditions are naturally set up and test coverage is improved, instead of validating each tool in isolation.
AI.result: On Androidagent benchmarks (AndroidWorld, B-MoCA, and MobileSafetyBench), GUI agents augmented with DroidTool-generated tools achieved on average about 4.47 percentage points higher performance and required about 20.05% fewer interactions than agents restricted to GUI-only actions.
AI.conclusion: Automated generation and verification of application-specific tools for Android agents is feasible and beneficial. DroidTool’s agentic workflow and relational testing improve both success rate and interaction efficiency of Android GUI agents, demonstrating that hybrid action spaces can be practically realized without heavy manual tool engineering.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Prompt Ensemble for Minor-Grain Breeding Information Extraction
comment: Accepted at CCL 2026 (China National Conference on Computational Linguistics)
summary: This paper presents our system for CCL2026-Eval Task 5: Minor-Grain Breeding Information Extraction (MGBIE), which jointly extracts 12 entity types and 6 relation types from minor-grain breeding literature. We propose RAME (Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Prompt Ensemble), a training-free framework that elicits multiple LLM outputs under controlled diversity and aggregates them by majority voting to obtain high-confidence predictions. RAME combines (i) retrieval-augmented few-shot selection via a hybrid BM25-embedding retriever, (ii) a three-prompt ensemble (Strict, Relaxed, Balanced) spanning the precision to recall spectrum, and (iii) large-scale repeated sampling with majority voting to filter noisy predictions. Built on DeepSeek-V4-Flash, RAME achieves a Total Score of 0.499 (NER 0.730, RE 0.346) on the leaderboard, ranking 1st and surpassing the official Track-A baseline powered by GPT-5.5 (0.448), representing an 11.4% relative improvement. Code is available at https://github.com/king-wang123/CCL26-RAME.

AI.tldr: They build a training-free, retrieval-augmented multi-prompt ensemble on top of a DeepSeek model to jointly extract entities and relations from minor-grain breeding literature, achieving state-of-the-art results on CCL2026-Eval Task 5.
AI.motivation: Minor-grain breeding literature contains rich structured knowledge about entities and relations, but extracting this information (12 entity types and 6 relation types) is challenging and costly to annotate. Existing baselines, even those powered by strong LLMs, leave room for improvement in accuracy and robustness. The authors aim to design a simple, training-free framework that can better exploit LLMs for domain IE and outperform the official competition baseline.
AI.method: They propose RAME (Retrieval-Augmented Multi-Prompt Ensemble), a training-free framework built on DeepSeek-V4-Flash. RAME: (1) uses a hybrid BM25-embedding retriever for retrieval-augmented few-shot example selection; (2) employs a three-prompt ensemble (Strict, Relaxed, Balanced) to span a precision–recall tradeoff; and (3) performs large-scale repeated sampling to generate multiple outputs and aggregates them with majority voting, filtering out noisy or inconsistent predictions and yielding higher-confidence entity and relation extractions.
AI.result: On the CCL2026-Eval Task 5 leaderboard, RAME achieves a Total Score of 0.499, decomposed into 0.730 for named entity recognition (NER) and 0.346 for relation extraction (RE). It ranks 1st overall and surpasses the official Track-A baseline system based on GPT-5.5, which scores 0.448, corresponding to an 11.4% relative improvement in total score.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that a training-free, retrieval-augmented multi-prompt ensemble can effectively leverage LLMs for joint entity and relation extraction in specialized domains like minor-grain breeding. Their RAME framework significantly outperforms a strong GPT-5.5 baseline on CCL2026-Eval Task 5, demonstrating that carefully designed prompting, retrieval, and ensemble strategies can yield robust high-confidence IE without additional model training.

title: Unsound Search with Policy and Value Networks in Legends of Code and Magic
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Also available as a Zenodo preprint, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22547763
summary: Decision-time search in perfect and imperfect information games with enumerable belief states are effective methods for game AI. Collectible card games are imperfect information games with large belief states. Legends of Code and Magic is a collectible card game competition where the belief states are $2^{101}$. The Legends of Code and Magic (LoCM) champion, ByteRL, plays with no search. Other works claim sound enumeration-based search is unusable in the genre due to the number of belief states. We measured three previously defined properties that predict where theoretically unsound perfect information Monte Carlo's defects are cheap and found LoCM sits in the favorable region. Starting with imitation learning of the runner-up policy, NeteaseOPD, we created a policy and value feed-forward network. Our agent searches over worlds sampled from a prior over the opponent's deck built from the runner-up's drafts. Using our strictest configuration in the battle phase we beat ByteRL with a win percentage of 51.35% 95% CI [50.37, 52.33], over 10,000 pre-registered games using the LoCM official referee and time limit. Search is not a minor factor on the matchup between our agent and ByteRL. Without search this agent scores 26.8% and adding search adds +24.6 points. Unsound search in imperfect information games could be exploitable. We replicate a published best-response attack against ByteRL. We then apply the same attack protocol to two search configurations of our agent, and each one resists it better than ByteRL at every iteration. In LoCM unsound search gives us a stronger and more resilient agent.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that “unsound” decision-time search using perfect-information Monte Carlo over sampled hidden states can still be very effective in a large imperfect-information card game, beating the reigning champion bot.
AI.motivation: Previous work and the reigning LoCM champion ByteRL suggest that search, especially belief-state enumeration or perfect-information Monte Carlo, is impractical or unusable in large imperfect-information games like collectible card games due to enormous belief spaces (e.g., 2^101 possible opponent decks/states). The authors want to test whether theoretically unsound but practical search methods can still yield strong play and whether such search makes agents more vulnerable to exploitation.
AI.method: 1) Analyze Legends of Code and Magic (LoCM) along three previously proposed properties that indicate when perfect-information Monte Carlo’s theoretical defects are practically small, showing LoCM lies in the favorable regime. 2) Train a policy and value feed-forward neural network by imitation learning from the runner-up bot NeteaseOPD. 3) Construct a prior over hidden opponent decks from NeteaseOPD’s draft data and at decision time sample concrete “worlds” (opponent decks/states) from this prior. 4) Run search over these sampled worlds using an unsound perfect-information Monte Carlo style decision-time search guided by the network. 5) Evaluate against the champion ByteRL under official competition conditions over 10,000 preregistered games. 6) Evaluate exploitability by reproducing a known best-response attack against ByteRL and then applying the same protocol to the new search-based agent.
AI.result: With the strictest (most limited) search configuration during the battle phase, the new agent beats the reigning champion ByteRL with a 51.35% win rate (95% CI [50.37, 52.33]) over 10,000 official-referee games under time constraints. The same architecture without search wins only 26.8% of games versus ByteRL, so adding search yields roughly +24.6 percentage points in win rate, indicating search is a major performance factor. In the exploitability analysis, the previously published best-response attack significantly harms ByteRL, but both tested search configurations of the new agent withstand this attack better than ByteRL at all iterations, indicating increased robustness rather than increased exploitability.
AI.conclusion: Contrary to prior claims that search is impractical or ineffective in large imperfect-information collectible card games, this study demonstrates that a carefully designed, theoretically unsound decision-time search over sampled belief states can substantially outperform a strong no-search champion agent and even be more robust to targeted best-response exploitation. In Legends of Code and Magic, such unsound search yields a stronger, more resilient agent, suggesting that practical performance can trump theoretical concerns about soundness in many-game AI settings.

title: Vishing-Tactics-Bench: Forecasting Exploitation Trajectories in Voice Phishing Calls
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Voice phishing (vishing) unfolds in real time; by the time a call has ended and post-hoc classification is possible, the harm has already been done. The more actionable question is which concrete harm (Information Gathering or Financial Exploitation) an ongoing call is tactically progressing toward. We present Vishing-Tactics-Bench, a benchmark grounded in Endsley's situation-awareness (SA) framework that recasts vishing defense from after-the-fact fraud classification to harm projection: predicting at each turn whether the call will reach either terminal harm. We adapt MITRE ATT&CK to vishing as a 6-tactic taxonomy (Vishing-Tactics) and label 35,340 scammer utterances across 5,645 synthetic Chinese calls. We define Exploitation Trajectory Forecasting, a survival-style protocol over the two terminal harms with three metrics: AP@k, C-index, and divergence error. Baselines ranging from a Markov heuristic to fine-tuned LLMs show that the tactical trajectory serves as an interpretable representation of the call's tactical state, supporting harm-specific forecasting, which can then be used for the downstream application of intervention selection; a stratified lead-time analysis at a tight false-alarm budget further identifies at what point in a call the trajectory signal yields early warning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Vishing-Tactics-Bench and a new prediction task to forecast, during an ongoing phone scam, whether it will lead to information theft or financial loss.
AI.motivation: Existing vishing defenses typically classify calls as fraudulent only after they end, which is too late to prevent harm. The authors aim to enable real-time understanding of what concrete harm a scammer is progressing toward, so systems can intervene early and appropriately.
AI.method: They build Vishing-Tactics-Bench, a benchmark based on Endsley’s situation-awareness framework and an adapted MITRE ATT&CK-style 6-tactic taxonomy for vishing. They label 35,340 scammer utterances from 5,645 synthetic Chinese scam calls with these tactics. They then define a new task, Exploitation Trajectory Forecasting, which treats the progression toward two terminal harms (Information Gathering, Financial Exploitation) as a survival-style prediction problem and evaluate models using AP@k, C-index, and divergence error. They test baselines from simple Markov models to fine-tuned LLMs, using the evolving tactical trajectory as a representation of call state.
AI.result: Experiments show that modeling the call’s tactical trajectory is an informative and interpretable state representation that supports accurate, harm-specific forecasting of whether the call will reach information or financial exploitation. The benchmark and protocol allow comparison of diverse methods, and empirical results demonstrate that the trajectory signal can provide early warnings under strict false-alarm constraints.
AI.conclusion: Framing vishing defense as real-time harm projection instead of post-hoc fraud detection, and representing calls via a vishing tactic trajectory, enables earlier and more targeted interventions. Vishing-Tactics-Bench and the Exploitation Trajectory Forecasting task provide a standardized foundation for developing and evaluating models that anticipate concrete harms during scam calls.

title: Formation of structural attractors in neuromorphic systems
summary: This paper examines the theory of Invariant Structural Learning (ISL), which proposes a non-optimization approach to concept formation. Learning is interpreted as convergence to structural attractors in a hypergraph space, rather than as the minimization of a global loss function. The paper presents the ISL model, including its mathematical formalization, computational verification, and a hypothetical neurobiological interpretation. The mathematical section introduces the formal apparatus of the structural reduction process and proves its finite convergence, the existence and uniqueness of class structural attractors, and the self-organization of attractor maps. The computational section demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed approach on classical image recognition tasks, utilizing the proposed learning mechanism without backpropagation and with extremely small training datasets. Finally, the neurobiological section formulates hypotheses regarding the possible implementation of structural attractors in dendritic trees, neural coding as a projection of internal attractor dynamics, and the development of neural architectures supporting the proposed learning concept. These hypotheses are discussed in the context of modern experimental data in the fields of dendritic computations, synaptic plasticity, and the structural organization of neural circuits. The proposed neurobiological mechanisms are presented as testable hypotheses rather than established biological facts. The results demonstrate the mathematical consistency and computational feasibility of the proposed model, while the neurobiological hypotheses outline potential directions for its experimental verification.

AI.tldr: Introduces and analyzes Invariant Structural Learning (ISL), a non-optimization approach where learning is convergence to structural attractors in a hypergraph, provides math proofs of convergence and uniqueness, computational image-recognition demos without backprop and with tiny datasets, and testable neurobiological hypotheses for how such attractors might be implemented in real neural tissue.
AI.motivation: To propose and validate an alternative to standard optimization-based learning (e.g., backprop-driven deep learning) that may better reflect biological learning and work effectively with small data, by framing learning as structural self-organization toward attractors instead of loss minimization.
AI.method: 1) Theoretical: formalize a structural reduction process in a hypergraph space, define structural attractors, and prove properties such as finite convergence, existence/uniqueness of class-specific attractors, and self-organization of attractor maps. 2) Computational: implement ISL on classical image recognition tasks, using its structural learning rules without backpropagation and with very small training datasets to test feasibility. 3) Neurobiological: formulate mechanistic hypotheses that map structural attractors onto dendritic trees, interpret neural coding as projections of internal attractor dynamics, and discuss how neural architectures and plasticity rules could realize ISL, comparing these ideas with contemporary experimental findings.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows that the structural reduction dynamics converge in finite time to unique structural attractors for each class and that attractor maps self-organize. Computational experiments indicate that the ISL mechanism can successfully perform classical image recognition tasks without backpropagation and using extremely small training sets. Neurobiological analysis yields a set of concrete, testable hypotheses relating ISL constructs to dendritic computation, synaptic plasticity, and circuit organization, consistent with but not proven by current experimental data.
AI.conclusion: Invariant Structural Learning is mathematically sound and computationally viable as a non-optimization-based learning paradigm, capable of solving standard recognition tasks with minimal data. While the biological implementation remains hypothetical, the model generates specific, experimentally testable predictions about dendritic and circuit-level mechanisms, positioning ISL as both a novel machine learning framework and a candidate theory for aspects of biological learning and neural coding.

title: FreqBLiMP: Frequency-Controlled Minimal Pairs Reveal Robustness and Fragility of LLMs Under Lexical Rarity
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. Repo link: https://github.com/TimeTravelerTy/freqblimp-generation
summary: Minimal-pair benchmarks such as BLiMP evaluate linguistic knowledge by testing whether language models (LMs) prefer acceptable sentences over minimally different unacceptable ones. However, these benchmarks largely ignore lexical frequency variation, despite lexical frequency being a pervasive and highly skewed property of natural language use. Consequently, existing evaluations do not test whether grammatical preferences remain stable when contrasts involve rare lexical items. We introduce FreqBLiMP, a frequency-controlled extension of BLiMP that regenerates all 67 paradigms under explicit Zipf-frequency regimes while preserving each minimal-pair's grammatical contrast. Evaluating multiple open-weight LLM families across scales, we find that decreasing lexical frequency produces a consistent, monotonic decrease in sentence likelihood, but only a modest reduction in overall contrastive acceptability accuracy. However, this aggregate stability masks substantial variation across linguistic phenomena, with LLMs remaining robust on overt morphosyntactic generalization while degrading on phenomena that require lemma-specific information.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FreqBLiMP, a frequency-controlled version of the BLiMP benchmark, to test whether language models’ grammatical judgments stay reliable when sentences contain rare words.
AI.motivation: Existing minimal-pair benchmarks like BLiMP evaluate whether language models prefer grammatical over ungrammatical sentences, but they largely ignore how lexical frequency—especially rare words—affects these preferences. Since lexical frequency in natural language is highly skewed (Zipfian), a model’s performance on common words may overestimate its true grammatical competence. The authors want to know if grammatical preferences are stable when the same syntactic contrasts are instantiated with rare lexical items.
AI.method: They construct FreqBLiMP, an extension of BLiMP that regenerates all 67 original minimal-pair paradigms under explicitly controlled Zipf-frequency bands for the lexical items, while preserving the original grammatical versus ungrammatical contrasts. They then evaluate multiple open-weight LLM families of different scales on this benchmark, measuring how sentence likelihoods and contrastive acceptability accuracies change as lexical frequency decreases.
AI.result: As lexical frequency decreases, models give consistently lower probabilities to sentences overall (both grammatical and ungrammatical), showing a monotonic drop in sentence likelihood. However, the accuracy with which models prefer grammatical over ungrammatical sentences only declines modestly in aggregate. This global stability hides strong differences by phenomenon: models remain robust on overt morphosyntactic generalizations but show notable degradation on phenomena that depend on lemma-specific information.
AI.conclusion: LLMs’ overall grammatical discrimination, as measured by BLiMP-style minimal pairs, is relatively stable even when lexical items become rare. Nonetheless, lexical frequency matters unevenly: phenomena tied to specific lexical items are more vulnerable to rarity than more abstract morphosyntactic patterns. FreqBLiMP thus reveals that frequency-controlled evaluation is necessary for a nuanced understanding of LMs’ syntactic and lexical generalization behavior.

title: NormViz: A Benchmark and Framework for Grounding Multimodal Reasoning in Global Cultures
comment: Accepted to Conference on Language Modeling (COLM) 2026. 37 pages, 23 figures
summary: AI systems are used worldwide, but they struggle to serve the needs of culturally diverse populations. Prior work on cultural understanding evaluates AI systems on text-only settings or on visual artifact recognition (e.g. foods, clothing). The ability to reason about visually observable behaviors through local social norms, which we call visual norm understanding, remains unexamined. We introduce NormViz-Bench, a high quality, human-validated benchmark of 3,268 contrastive image pairs (6,536 images) spanning 16 countries. Each pair varies only in the culturally relevant behavior (e.g., objects, attributes, spatial relations, and actions) that alters how each image is interpreted. Each image is labeled as conforming to, violating, or irrelevant to local social norms, and pair-level evaluation requires both images to be correctly classified, thereby preventing reliance on superficial visual shortcuts. Even the strongest VLMs, Gemini 3.0 Flash and Qwen2.5 VL 7B, succeed on only 26.6% and 21.6% of pairs, struggling most with identifying violating and culturally benign visual behaviors. Towards bridging this, we introduce NormViz-Train, a training dataset of 64k images paired with explanations. Though absolute performance remains low (<30%), finetuning on NormViz-Train improves pair accuracy relatively by up to 125% and 36% Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B respectively, showing a path forward to teach models to connect visual perception to cultural significance. Together, NormViz-Bench and NormViz-Train establish visual norm understanding as a challenging and consequential frontier for multimodal AI.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NormViz-Bench and NormViz-Train to evaluate and improve AI models’ ability to recognize and reason about culturally grounded social norms from images, revealing that current vision-language models perform poorly and that targeted finetuning offers meaningful gains.
AI.motivation: AI systems are deployed globally but often fail to capture or respect the social norms of culturally diverse populations. Prior evaluations have focused on text-only cultural understanding or on recognizing static cultural artifacts (like food or clothing), leaving unexplored the harder problem of interpreting visually observable human behaviors in context. The authors aim to systematically study this gap, termed visual norm understanding, to show how current multimodal models fall short and to provide resources to push progress.
AI.method: The authors construct NormViz-Bench, a human-validated benchmark of 3,268 contrastive image pairs from 16 countries, where each pair differs only in a culturally salient behavior (objects, attributes, spatial relations, or actions). Each image is labeled as conforming to, violating, or irrelevant to local social norms. Evaluation is pair-level: a model must correctly classify both images in a pair, discouraging reliance on superficial cues. They evaluate several state-of-the-art vision-language models on this benchmark. To improve performance, they build NormViz-Train, a 64k-image training dataset that pairs images with explanations about their normative status, and then finetune specific models (Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B) on this data.
AI.result: On NormViz-Bench, strong baseline models such as Gemini 3.0 Flash and Qwen2.5 VL 7B achieve only 26.6% and 21.6% pair accuracy respectively, with particular difficulty in identifying norm violations and culturally benign behaviors. After finetuning on NormViz-Train, models still have low absolute accuracy (<30%), but they show substantial relative gains: up to 125% improvement for Qwen3-VL 4B and 36% for Qwen3-VL 8B. These results demonstrate both the difficulty of the task and the potential for data-driven improvement in visual norm understanding.
AI.conclusion: Visual norm understanding—interpreting culturally dependent social norms from images—is a challenging, underexplored capability for multimodal AI. NormViz-Bench provides a rigorous, behavior-focused benchmark that exposes major weaknesses in current vision-language models, while NormViz-Train and the associated finetuning experiments illustrate a promising path to better align models with local social norms. Together, these resources define a new research frontier at the intersection of computer vision, multimodal reasoning, and cultural AI alignment.

title: In-Place Instruction Following in Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) generate text via bidirectional iterative denoising, naturally supporting user-specified constraints anchored at arbitrary output positions, a paradigm known as In-place Prompting (IPP). We formalize this as the In-place Instruction Following (IIF) task and construct IIF-Bench, a hierarchical benchmark spanning literal, style, and discourse-function constraints, paired with a rubric-based local-global evaluation protocol. An inference-time attention-bias probe suggests that vanilla dLLMs often under-prioritize constraint spans during denoising. We then propose GRAFT, an IPP-oriented post-training framework combining constraint-aware SFT and preference optimization. On four representative dLLMs, GRAFT raises the average IIF score from 57.75 to 73.10 (+15.35 points), with absolute gains of 15.91 and 15.57 points on literal and discourse-function constraints, while preserving general generation ability.

AI.tldr: They define and benchmark a new task for diffusion LLMs—following constraints at specific positions in text—and propose a training framework that significantly improves performance on this task without hurting general text quality.
AI.motivation: Diffusion LLMs generate text via iterative denoising and can, in principle, naturally respect constraints at arbitrary positions in the text (In-place Prompting). However, there was no formal task definition, no systematic benchmark to measure how well these models follow such localized constraints, and preliminary evidence suggests that standard diffusion LLMs do not sufficiently prioritize constraint spans during generation. This gap motivates building a proper benchmark and a training method to make dLLMs reliably obey in-place constraints.
AI.method: 1) Formalize the problem as In-place Instruction Following (IIF), where the model must honor user-specified constraints anchored to specific output spans. 2) Build IIF-Bench, a hierarchical benchmark with constraints spanning literal constraints (exact content), style constraints, and discourse-function constraints (e.g., rhetorical roles), together with a rubric-based evaluation that looks at both local constraint satisfaction and global text quality. 3) Use an attention-bias probe at inference time to analyze how much dLLMs actually focus on constraint spans. 4) Propose GRAFT, a post-training pipeline for diffusion LLMs that combines constraint-aware supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference optimization specifically targeted at in-place prompting behavior. 5) Evaluate GRAFT on four representative diffusion LLMs on IIF-Bench and standard generation benchmarks.
AI.result: The attention-bias probe shows that unmodified diffusion LLMs tend to under-attend to constraint spans during denoising, which correlates with poor adherence to in-place constraints. After applying GRAFT, the average score on the IIF-Bench increases from 57.75 to 73.10, a gain of 15.35 points overall. The improvements are particularly strong on literal constraints (+15.91 points) and discourse-function constraints (+15.57 points). At the same time, general text generation ability is maintained, indicating that the specialized post-training does not significantly degrade broad language modeling performance.
AI.conclusion: In-place Instruction Following is a meaningful, measurable capability for diffusion LLMs, and standard models are not yet optimized for it. By formalizing the task, introducing IIF-Bench, and proposing the GRAFT post-training framework, the paper demonstrates that diffusion LLMs can be substantially improved at honoring localized constraints across literal, stylistic, and discourse levels, without sacrificing overall generation quality. This positions diffusion-based LLMs as strong candidates for controllable text generation with fine-grained, position-specific instructions.

title: Learning transferable human physiology from two million hours of sleep with SleepFM-2
summary: Sleep provides a nightly window into health by capturing coordinated activity across the brain, heart, muscles and respiratory system. We introduce SleepFM-2, a sleep foundation model developed and evaluated on 282,511 polysomnography recordings from 26 cohorts, including 235,865 used for pretraining. These data span more than two million hours of multimodal physiology. Compared with SleepFM, SleepFM-2 improves disease prediction and sleep scoring, supports arousal, limb movement and respiratory event detection, and transfers to wearable sensing and subjective sleep phenotypes. A model combining its PSG representation with age, sex and BMI met a prespecified discrimination and significance criterion for 215 subsequently recorded EHR phenotypes in two held-out cohorts, including one health system unseen during pretraining. For 155 phenotypes, the PSG representation added reproducible information beyond demographics. SleepFM-2 also outperformed a 480-feature baseline derived from the same recordings. Its disease scores revealed a reproducible principal component associated with reduced sigma-band spatial coupling and increased hypnodensity entropy. The frozen encoder performed within the observed range of expert scorers for sleep events and transferred to wakeful EEG, headband and in-ear EEG, wrist PPG and wrist accelerometry. It improved sleep staging across six accelerometry cohorts and achieved disease-prediction performance in UK Biobank similar to models pretrained directly on accelerometry. Finally, SleepFM-2 captured aspects of subjective sleep not recovered by conventional PSG summaries, particularly reports of the recorded night. These results show that multimodal sleep physiology can provide a transferable representation of human health across diseases, clinical tasks, sensors and subjective experience.

AI.tldr: SleepFM-2 is a large-scale sleep foundation model trained on over two million hours of polysomnography that learns a general physiological representation useful for disease prediction, sleep event detection, and transfer to multiple sensors and subjective sleep measures.
AI.motivation: Current sleep analysis relies on hand-crafted features, manual scoring, and task-specific models, which limits scalability, generalizability, and the ability to capture subtle, shared physiological signatures of health and disease across cohorts, sensors, and tasks. A unified, transferable representation of multimodal sleep physiology could improve disease prediction, automate sleep scoring, and better link objective measures with subjective sleep experience.
AI.method: The authors pretrain a foundation model, SleepFM-2, on 235,865 polysomnography (PSG) recordings (over two million hours) from 26 cohorts, learning a shared representation of multimodal physiology (EEG, EOG, EMG, ECG/PPG, respiration, etc.). They evaluate it on 282,511 PSGs in total for multiple downstream tasks: disease prediction for hundreds of EHR phenotypes in held-out cohorts, automated sleep staging and detection of arousals, limb movements and respiratory events, and transfer learning to other sensor modalities (headband/in-ear EEG, wrist PPG and accelerometry) and subjective sleep outcomes. They compare against a 480-feature baseline derived from the same PSGs and analyze latent disease scores and physiological signatures (e.g., sigma-band coupling and hypnodensity entropy).
AI.result: SleepFM-2 improves disease prediction and sleep scoring relative to the prior SleepFM model and a strong 480-feature PSG baseline. A simple model combining its PSG representation with age, sex and BMI met predefined discrimination and significance criteria for 215 EHR phenotypes in two held-out cohorts, including an unseen health system; for 155 phenotypes the learned representation added reproducible information beyond demographics. The model operates at expert-like performance for detecting sleep events using a frozen encoder and identifies a principal component of disease scores associated with reduced sigma-band spatial coupling and increased hypnodensity entropy. The representation transfers well to wakeful EEG and multiple wearable sensors (headband and in-ear EEG, wrist PPG and accelerometry), improves sleep staging in six accelerometry cohorts, and achieves disease-prediction performance in UK Biobank comparable to models pretrained directly on accelerometry. It also captures aspects of subjective sleep—especially about the recorded night—that conventional PSG summary measures miss.
AI.conclusion: A large-scale, multimodal sleep foundation model can learn a compact physiological representation that generalizes across diseases, clinical tasks, sensor types, and subjective experiences. SleepFM-2 demonstrates that night-time polysomnography encodes broad, transferable health information beyond standard sleep metrics and demographic variables, offering a scalable basis for automated sleep analysis, multi-disease risk stratification, and integration of clinical PSG with consumer wearables and patient-reported outcomes.

title: CircuitLens: Reasoning Circuits as Data Selection Signals for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
comment: Accepted at EMNLP 2026 Findings. Long paper. 9 pages + references + appendix
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is sensitive to which problems a model trains on, yet existing selection criteria--difficulty filtering, hand-curation, reward-trajectory scoring--assess data value as an intrinsic property of problems, independent of the model that will learn from them. We introduce Circuit Reasoning Score (CRS), a selection signal derived from 46 reasoning-sensitive attention heads identified via contrastive ablation, computed in a single forward pass on the frozen base model without reward labels or rollouts. CRS runs against the intuitive hypothesis that stronger reasoning-circuit engagement produces better training data: on Qwen2.5-Math-7B, the lowest-engagement decile improves over random selection on three medium-difficulty benchmarks (GSM8K +2.0 pp, OlympiadBench +1.6 pp, Minerva +2.9 pp), while the highest-engagement decile gains less and is indistinguishable from the middle decile. The advantage has boundary conditions: on a domain-curated pool no selection method separates from the others; at 1.5B scale the useful direction differs; and the lowest-reward training condition produces the strongest downstream generalization. Within the Qwen2.5-Math settings tested, RLVR data selection appears regime-dependent rather than reducible to a static ranking of problem quality.

AI.tldr: They propose a model-dependent data-selection metric (CRS) for RL with verifiable rewards and find that, counterintuitively, problems that least engage certain reasoning circuits can give better downstream performance than those that strongly engage them, showing data value is regime-dependent.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR data-selection methods treat problem quality as intrinsic and independent of the learner, but performance in RLVR is highly sensitive to which problems a particular model trains on. The authors want a data-selection signal that is cheap (no rollouts or rewards needed), tied to the actual model’s internals, and can reveal how problem choice affects generalization.
AI.method: They identify 46 ‘reasoning-sensitive’ attention heads in a base model (Qwen2.5-Math variants) using contrastive ablation. For each candidate training problem, they compute a Circuit Reasoning Score (CRS) in a single forward pass that measures engagement of these heads, without using reward labels or trajectories. They then partition data by CRS deciles and compare how training RLVR on different deciles affects performance across several math benchmarks and scales, as well as under different reward strengths and data pools.
AI.result: On Qwen2.5-Math-7B and a broad problem pool, using the lowest-CRS decile as training data yields better benchmark performance than random selection (e.g., +2.0 percentage points on GSM8K, +1.6 on OlympiadBench, +2.9 on Minerva). High-CRS data brings smaller gains and is statistically similar to mid-CRS data. However, when the pool is already domain-curated, all selection methods perform similarly; for a 1.5B model, the beneficial CRS direction reverses; and surprisingly, training with the lowest reward strength leads to the best downstream generalization.
AI.conclusion: Data value in RLVR depends strongly on the training regime and model scale, not on a fixed, model-agnostic ranking of problem ‘quality.’ CRS demonstrates that internal circuit engagement provides a meaningful but nuanced selection signal: lower reasoning-circuit activation can be more useful than higher activation in some settings. Consequently, effective RLVR data selection must be model- and regime-aware rather than relying on static difficulty or handcrafted criteria.

title: A visual large language foundational model for medical image recognition using clinician-oriented social media
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across diverse domains, showing considerable potential in medicine. However, their application in medical settings remains limited by the scarcity of visual question answering (VQA) datasets that capture clinical reasoning and explicit image-text alignment. Here, we leverage de-identified medical images and expert commentaries shared on clinician-oriented social media. By combining an advanced LLM with clinician-in-the-loop verification, we established a rigorous pipeline to construct ThoughtMed-1M, a long-form medical VQA dataset containing over one million VQA pairs and designed to capture structured clinical logic and medical image-text alignment. To demonstrate its utility, we developed a FOundational LLM Trained on ThoughtMed-1M (FOLTMed). FOLTMed achieved state-of-the-art performance across 42 medical VQA benchmark datasets, with a macro accuracy of 85.4%, and generated more clinically coherent responses on the ThoughtMed-1M test set. It outperformed state-of-the-art models by 3--5% across factuality and similarity metrics, highlighting a scalable paradigm for advancing research on clinically grounded multimodal LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ThoughtMed-1M, a large-scale, long-form medical visual question answering (VQA) dataset built from de-identified clinician social media posts, and shows that an LLM trained on it (FOLTMed) achieves state-of-the-art performance on many medical VQA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: While large language models show promise in medicine, their use in real clinical settings is constrained by the lack of visual question answering datasets that both reflect real clinical reasoning and align images with detailed textual explanations. Existing datasets are often small, shallow, or do not capture the step-by-step logic physicians use when interpreting medical images. This gap prevents training and evaluating multimodal LLMs that can reason clinically from images and text together.
AI.method: The authors collect de-identified medical images and expert commentaries from clinician-focused social media platforms. Using an advanced LLM plus clinician-in-the-loop verification, they build a pipeline that transforms these posts into structured, long-form VQA pairs, emphasizing explicit clinical reasoning and image-text alignment. This process yields ThoughtMed-1M, a dataset with over one million VQA pairs. They then train a foundational multimodal LLM, FOLTMed, on this dataset and evaluate it across a large suite of existing medical VQA benchmarks as well as on their own test set, measuring accuracy, clinical coherence, factuality, and similarity to expert responses.
AI.result: The resulting dataset, ThoughtMed-1M, comprises more than one million structured, long-form medical VQA pairs. The model trained on it, FOLTMed, achieves state-of-the-art performance on 42 medical VQA benchmark datasets, with a macro accuracy of 85.4%. On the ThoughtMed-1M test set, FOLTMed produces more clinically coherent answers than competing systems and surpasses state-of-the-art baselines by 3–5% on factuality and semantic similarity metrics.
AI.conclusion: By leveraging de-identified clinician-generated content and a human-verified LLM pipeline, the paper provides a scalable approach for constructing large, clinically grounded medical VQA datasets. Training on ThoughtMed-1M enables FOLTMed to achieve strong, state-of-the-art performance and more clinically aligned reasoning, suggesting that similar pipelines can significantly advance multimodal LLMs for medical applications that require robust image-text reasoning.

title: SIFTING: A Novel LLM-Based Framework for Structured and Transparent Information Extraction from Clinical Free-Text Reports, with Application to Tumor Staging in Lung Cancer
summary:
Background: Large language models (LLMs) show promise for extracting information from clinical free-text documents, but their outputs are often unstructured and lack traceability, complicating validation and adoption in clinical workflows. In this work we introduce SIFTING, an LLM-based framework designed to address these shortcomings.
  Methods: SIFTING combines the language comprehension capabilities of LLMs with segment-level processing and structured prompts with strict output control, linking findings to the source text to enable both accurate and transparent information extraction. To demonstrate its capabilities, we applied the framework to the task of extracting tumor T-stage information from 130 lung cancer radiology reports (SIFTING-T-stage). A compact 4-bit quantized version of the open-source LLM Llama-3.3-70B (35 GB) was used in a fully self-hosted setup, providing full control over data and model. Performance was evaluated against a reference standard created by four clinical experts and compared with a range of LLMs as used in a conventional single-prompt approach, using bootstrap resampling to estimate confidence intervals.
  Results: SIFTING-T-stage achieved an accuracy of 90% (95% CI: 84-95) against the reference standard. We found its performance to be comparable to even the largest state-of-the-art LLMs with reasoning capabilities and to be interchangeable with clinical experts (p < 0.001), while at the same time offering full traceability through source text references.
  Conclusion: SIFTING enables accurate, structured, and traceable information extraction from clinical free-text documents. It ensures data control, reproducibility, and verifiable outputs that can support clinical validation and workflow integration.

AI.tldr: The paper presents SIFTING, an LLM-based, fully self-hosted framework that extracts structured and traceable clinical information from free-text documents, achieving expert-level performance for lung cancer T-stage extraction.
AI.motivation: Clinical free-text documents contain rich information, but existing LLM-based extraction approaches often produce unstructured, non-traceable outputs that are hard to validate and integrate into clinical workflows. There is a need for a method that yields structured, verifiable data, preserves data control, and can match clinical expert performance.
AI.method: The authors propose SIFTING, which uses large language models with segment-level document processing and tightly controlled, structured prompts. The system enforces strict output formats and links each extracted finding back to its originating text segment, enabling traceability. They implement SIFTING-T-stage for extracting lung tumor T-stage from 130 radiology reports using a compact 4-bit quantized, self-hosted Llama-3.3-70B model. Performance is compared to several LLMs used in a standard single-prompt manner and to a multi-expert reference standard, with bootstrap resampling used to estimate confidence intervals.
AI.result: SIFTING-T-stage reached 90% accuracy (95% CI: 84–95) compared to the expert reference standard. Its performance was comparable to that of state-of-the-art reasoning-capable LLMs and statistically interchangeable with clinical experts, while uniquely providing explicit source-text references for each extracted item.
AI.conclusion: SIFTING provides a practical, expert-level solution for extracting accurate, structured, and traceable information from clinical free text under full local data and model control. Its verifiable outputs and reproducibility make it suitable for clinical validation and facilitate integration into clinical workflows.

title: When and Why LLM Causal Priors Help: Closed-Loop Prior Selection for Amortized Causal Inference
summary: Causal effect estimation asks how an outcome would change under an intervention, and medicine, economics, and public policy all treat it as a foundational task. Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) amortize the task: a model trained on large numbers of programmatically generated synthetic causal tasks reads a new problem's observational data into context and returns an interventional-effect estimate in a single forward pass. The capability of such models is largely determined by the synthetic training prior, which is currently designed by hand, a bottleneck acknowledged by both Do-PFN and CausalPFN. Large language models (LLMs) can now ``draw'' plausible causal graphs for a given domain, suggesting that LLM-distilled graphs could serve as prior material. Whether injecting such graphs helps at all, where any gain comes from, and when injection helps. Practice has so far relied on manual trial and error. We propose a \emph{closed-loop prior selection framework} that casts prior injection as a budget-constrained optimization over a candidate prior pool. Candidates undergo cheap post-training and are scored by a composite metric dominated by real-domain generalization; the winner then receives full training and paired statistical validation. On a 7.34M-parameter Do-PFN, the framework's winner attains a formally significant $2.75\times$ gain on the primary evaluation domain, and its error falls below that of the uninjected official base. Generalization on an adjacent monitoring domain improves significantly, and no monitored capability degrades. Mechanism experiments show that the gain depends on the semantic content of the distilled graph rather than its structural diversity alone does not produce it (directional evidence). With this framework and this regularity in hand, the use of LLM causal priors stops being manual trial and error and becomes an empirically verifiable selection problem.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a closed-loop framework to automatically select and train better synthetic priors for PFN-based causal effect estimators using LLM-generated causal graphs, yielding large accuracy gains without harming other capabilities.
AI.motivation: Prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) can estimate causal effects in a single forward pass, but their performance heavily depends on synthetic training priors that are currently crafted by hand. With LLMs now able to propose plausible causal graphs, there is an opportunity to use them as richer priors. However, current use of such LLM-based causal priors is ad hoc, relying on manual trial and error, with no systematic way to know whether and when they help. The paper aims to turn this trial-and-error process into a principled, data-driven selection procedure.
AI.method: The authors build a closed-loop prior selection framework that treats the design of synthetic training priors as a budget-constrained optimization over a set of candidate priors, many of which are derived from LLM-distilled causal graphs. Each candidate prior is subjected to cheap post-training of a relatively small PFN and evaluated with a composite metric that is primarily driven by performance on real-domain generalization. Based on these scores, the best prior is selected and then used for full-scale training and paired statistical evaluation. Additionally, they run mechanism experiments to disentangle whether performance gains come from the semantic content of the LLM-generated causal graphs or merely from increased structural diversity.
AI.result: On a 7.34M-parameter Do-PFN model, the prior chosen by the framework delivers a statistically significant 2.75× improvement on the main evaluation domain, achieving error lower than the standard, uninjected base PFN. It also yields significant improvements on a nearby monitoring domain, and no tracked capability is degraded. Mechanism studies provide directional evidence that the observed gains are due to the meaningful, domain-relevant structure encoded in the LLM-distilled graphs, rather than just adding structurally diverse but semantically arbitrary graphs.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that LLM-generated causal graphs can be turned into effective synthetic priors for PFN-based causal effect estimation, provided they are selected through a systematic closed-loop process rather than manual guesswork. Their framework converts prior injection into an empirically testable selection problem under a computation budget, and the evidence suggests that the semantic quality of the LLM-distilled graphs is what drives the performance gains. This makes the integration of LLM causal priors both practical and principled, with substantial improvements in real-domain causal effect estimation and no observed trade-offs on monitored tasks.

title: CEDAR: Error-Bounded Residual Routing for Efficient Long-Context Attention
summary: Post-hoc sparse attention accelerates long-context prefill by routing each query to a small set of token-level interactions. Hard selection, however, assigns zero probability to every omitted chunk: a routing miss cannot be recovered, and a fixed expansion budget spends the same work on easy and ambiguous queries. We introduce Coarse-to-fine Error-aware Dynamic Attention Routing (CEDAR), a coarse-to-fine method that keeps the language model frozen while preserving global coverage. Each semantic chunk contributes a cheap key--value summary to a residual attention path; chunks with high estimated approximation error are then expanded to exact token attention. Exact and summarized contributions are combined in a single softmax normalization, so refinement replaces, rather than duplicates, coarse evidence. We derive an output-error bound governed by within-chunk key/value dispersion and use it to allocate a variable refinement budget. A controlled clustered-attention study shows that residual summaries reduce reconstruction error by more than 98% relative to hard dropping at equal exact-chunk budgets. Experiments on long-context benchmarks demonstrate that CEDAR recovers most of the quality lost by hard sparse routing while maintaining approximately $3\times$ kernel speedup at 128K context.

AI.tldr: CEDAR is a coarse-to-fine, error-aware attention routing method that speeds up long-context prefill while preserving coverage and quality, by combining cheap chunk summaries with selective exact token attention under a single softmax.
AI.motivation: Existing post-hoc sparse attention methods accelerate long-context prefill by routing each query to a small subset of tokens, but they rely on hard selection: tokens or chunks not selected receive zero probability mass. This creates unrecoverable routing misses and wastes computation by treating easy and ambiguous queries equally under a fixed expansion budget.
