There is a need for a routing approach that maintains global coverage, adapts computation to difficulty, and works with frozen base LMs.
AI.method: CEDAR (Coarse-to-fine Error-aware Dynamic Attention Routing) first partitions the context into semantic chunks. For each chunk, it builds a cheap key-value summary that participates in a residual attention path, ensuring all chunks maintain some influence. It then estimates the approximation error for each chunk, based on within-chunk key/value dispersion, to decide which chunks to refine. High-error chunks are expanded from summary-level attention to exact token-level attention. Both summarized and exact token contributions are merged in a single softmax, so refined evidence replaces rather than adds to the coarse summary. The method also derives an analytical bound on output error governed by chunk dispersion and uses this bound to allocate a variable refinement budget, i.e., how many and which chunks to refine per query.
AI.result: In controlled experiments using clustered attention as a testbed, CEDAR’s residual summaries reduce reconstruction error by more than 98% compared to methods that hard-drop unselected chunks, at the same budget of exact chunks. On long-context benchmarks up to 128K tokens, CEDAR recovers most of the performance degradation introduced by hard sparse routing, while preserving about a 3× attention kernel speedup relative to dense attention.
AI.conclusion: CEDAR provides an effective coarse-to-fine, error-aware routing mechanism for long-context attention that maintains global coverage, adapts computation to content difficulty, and can be applied without modifying or retraining the underlying language model. It significantly improves faithfulness over hard sparse routing while retaining substantial speedups at very long context lengths.

title: iBrain: A Unified Foundation Model Reading the Brain from Surface to Spikes
summary: Invasive neural recordings provide high-fidelity measurements of brain activity, with signals such as intracranial EEG (iEEG) and intracortical spiking activity capturing neural dynamics at different spatial and temporal scales. Yet existing neural foundation models have largely been developed independently for different invasive recording paradigms, leaving joint pretraining across heterogeneous invasive signals underexplored. In this work, we introduce iBrain, a unified foundation model that jointly learns from iEEG and spiking activity. iBrain employs signal-specific encoders to accommodate their distinct signal characteristics and a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone to model dependencies across recording channels and time. We pretrain iBrain on over 7,000 hours of heterogeneous neural recordings using masked signal reconstruction and channel-view alignment, promoting contextual modeling of neural dynamics and robustness across different channels. iBrain consistently outperforms single-signal pretraining baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks. Further experiments demonstrate that iBrain exhibits transferability and data efficiency across diverse recording settings. These results highlight the potential of joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings to support scalable neural modeling and transferable representations across recording settings and downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes iBrain, a unified foundation model jointly pretrained on intracranial EEG and intracortical spiking data, achieving state-of-the-art performance and strong transfer across recording settings.
AI.motivation: Existing neural foundation models are usually trained separately on specific invasive recording types (e.g., only iEEG or only spikes), missing the opportunity to leverage shared structure and complementary information across modalities. There is a need for a scalable, unified model that can learn robust, transferable neural representations from heterogeneous invasive recordings.
AI.method: The authors design iBrain, which uses modality-specific encoders for iEEG and spiking activity followed by a shared spatiotemporal Transformer backbone that models dependencies across channels and time. They pretrain on more than 7,000 hours of diverse invasive neural data using self-supervised objectives: masked signal reconstruction and channel-view alignment, encouraging contextual modeling and consistency across channels and modalities.
AI.result: iBrain outperforms baseline models that are pretrained on a single signal type, and it achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks. The model also shows strong transferability and data efficiency, performing well when adapted to new recording conditions and tasks with limited labeled data.
AI.conclusion: Joint pretraining on heterogeneous invasive neural recordings using a unified architecture produces scalable neural models with more generalizable and transferable representations. This approach can support a wide range of downstream neural decoding and analysis tasks across different recording paradigms.

title: Separating Stream Stability from Long-Term Recall in Language Models
summary: Methods for streaming language models are often discussed alongside long-context and memory systems, although they solve different problems. An attention sink can stabilize autoregressive generation over an indefinitely long stream while the model remains unable to use content that has left its recent-token cache. We argue that this distinction should be explicit in system claims and evaluation. We introduce three horizons: the stability horizon, over which predictive behavior remains well behaved; the access horizon, over which past content can still causally affect the output; and the utility horizon, over which a task retains acceptable performance. We show constructively that the stability horizon can be infinite while the access and utility horizons are finite. We then propose ThreeH, an evaluation contract that measures all three horizons under a common state and compute budget. Applying the framework to attention-sink streaming clarifies its strength, constant-memory, stable generation, without treating anchor tokens as semantic memory. The framework exposes roles for cache policies, recurrent state, retrieval, and external memory. Experiments on 128K-token streams, delayed binding recall, and delayed decisions show that attention sinks preserve local modeling but not content beyond the active cache; recurrent and retrieval state extend the semantic horizon.

AI.tldr: The paper distinguishes between stability, access, and utility in streaming language models, showing that a model can generate stably over infinite streams while only using a finite recent context, and proposes a unified evaluation framework (ThreeH) to measure these horizons under fixed state and compute budgets.
AI.motivation: Streaming language models are often conflated with long-context or memory-augmented models, even though they address different challenges. Current discussions and benchmarks do not clearly separate the ability to generate stably over long token streams from the ability to use very old information. The authors want a precise vocabulary and evaluation protocol to differentiate these aspects so that system claims about long-context capability are not overstated or misleading.
AI.method: The authors conceptually define three horizons for streaming LMs: (1) stability horizon (how long predictive behavior remains well behaved over a stream), (2) access horizon (how far back past tokens can still causally affect current outputs), and (3) utility horizon (how far back information can lie while still enabling acceptable task performance). They construct examples and analyses demonstrating that a model can have an infinite stability horizon even when it has finite access and utility horizons. They then design ThreeH, an evaluation contract that jointly measures these three horizons under a shared constraint on model state and compute, and apply it to streaming via attention sinks, as well as to systems with cache policies, recurrent states, retrieval, and external memory.
AI.result: Using ThreeH on attention-sink streaming models, the authors find that attention sinks indeed provide constant-memory, stable generation over very long (e.g., 128K-token) streams, preserving high-quality local modeling. However, they empirically confirm that such models cannot effectively use information that has fallen out of the active recent-token cache: the access and utility horizons are limited. Experiments on tasks such as 128K-token streaming, delayed binding recall, and delayed decision-making show that adding recurrent or retrieval-based state can extend the semantic horizon beyond what attention sinks alone can achieve.
AI.conclusion: The stability of streaming generation and the ability to use long-past content are distinct properties that must be evaluated separately. Attention-sink mechanisms solve the stability problem and enable constant-memory, long-stream generation, but they do not themselves provide long-range semantic memory beyond the active cache window. The ThreeH framework offers a principled way to measure stability, access, and utility horizons under consistent resource constraints and clarifies the complementary roles of cache policies, recurrence, retrieval, and external memory in extending a model’s effective semantic horizon.

title: SSP-DMGTimeNet: Physics-Constrained Learning for Spatiotemporal Trajectory Prediction of Vehicle Platoons
summary: Existing car-following prediction methods mainly optimize trajectory accuracy, while rarely considering whether predicted disturbances propagate realistically along a vehicle platoon. This limitation may lead to accurate but string-unstable predictions. We propose SSP-DMGTimeNet, a physics-constrained learning framework for spatiotemporal trajectory prediction of vehicle platoons. The model combines multi-scale temporal representations with cross-vehicle interaction features to capture complex and time-varying platoon dynamics. A propagation-delay-aware causal attention mechanism explicitly models upstream-to-downstream disturbance propagation by learning response delays between adjacent vehicles and accumulating them along the platoon. In addition, time- and frequency-domain string-stability losses relieve disturbance amplification across both adjacent vehicles and arbitrary sub-platoons during training. Experiments on HighD show that SSP-DMGTimeNet achieves an unstable-window rate of 0.65\% for five-vehicle platoons and a maximum head-to-tail amplification of 0.898 on the ground-truth excitation subset, while maintaining competitive trajectory prediction performance. In zero-shot evaluation on NGSIM US-101 and I-80, the model achieves velocity MAEs of 1.316~m/s and 1.252~m/s, with unstable-window rates of 3.90\% and 4.10\%, respectively. These results demonstrate that incorporating platoon-level physical constraints can effectively balance trajectory prediction accuracy and disturbance propagation stability.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new car-following trajectory prediction model that explicitly enforces platoon string stability, achieving both accurate predictions and realistic, non-amplifying disturbance propagation along vehicle platoons.
AI.motivation: Most car-following trajectory prediction methods focus on point-wise accuracy for individual vehicles, but they ignore whether small speed or spacing disturbances grow or decay as they propagate along a vehicle platoon. This can lead to predictions that are numerically accurate in the short term but physically unrealistic, exhibiting string instability (amplification of disturbances downstream). The paper is motivated by the need for prediction models that respect platoon-level dynamics and stability properties important for safety, comfort, and traffic flow efficiency, especially in connected/automated driving scenarios.
AI.method: The authors introduce SSP-DMGTimeNet, a physics-constrained deep learning framework for spatiotemporal prediction of vehicle platoon trajectories. The method: (1) builds multi-scale temporal representations to capture short- and long-term dynamics; (2) encodes cross-vehicle interaction features to model dependencies among vehicles in a platoon; (3) incorporates a propagation-delay-aware causal attention mechanism that learns response delays between adjacent vehicles and accumulates them along the platoon to reflect realistic upstream-to-downstream disturbance propagation; and (4) adds physics-inspired string-stability loss terms in both time and frequency domains to penalize disturbance amplification across adjacent vehicles and arbitrary sub-platoons during training. These components together guide the network to produce predictions that are accurate yet string stable.
AI.result: On the HighD dataset, SSP-DMGTimeNet achieves an unstable-window rate of 0.65% for five-vehicle platoons and a maximum head-to-tail amplification of 0.898 on a ground-truth excitation subset, while retaining competitive trajectory prediction accuracy. In zero-shot tests on NGSIM US-101 and I-80 datasets, it reaches velocity MAEs of 1.316 m/s and 1.252 m/s, respectively, with unstable-window rates of 3.90% and 4.10%. These metrics indicate that the model significantly improves string stability characteristics without sacrificing, and in some cases while preserving, predictive performance compared to standard methods.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that explicitly embedding platoon-level physical constraints—via delay-aware causal attention and time/frequency-domain string-stability losses—enables learning-based trajectory predictors to better balance accuracy and stability. SSP-DMGTimeNet produces physically plausible, string-stable disturbance propagation along vehicle platoons while maintaining strong prediction accuracy and demonstrating robustness in zero-shot cross-dataset evaluations.

title: Probing the Structure and Dynamics of LLM Value Expression through Value Conflicts
comment: Code and data are available at https://github.com/ZeroGen-Lab/CFProbe
summary: Ethical evaluation of Large Language Models (LLMs) often characterizes model values as static and monolithic. In contrast, we argue that LLM value expression is better understood as a structured yet dynamic phenomenon. To investigate this, we introduce Conflict-driven Value Probing, a controlled framework that places LLMs in value conflicts and implements four types of interventions that perturb these conflicts to probe LLM value expression. Applying this framework to ten LLMs, we identify three recurring patterns. (1) Expression duality: models shift from broad idealistic orientations in abstract assessment toward more pragmatic priorities in concrete conflicts. (2) Functional steerability: models readily reconfigure their expressed value profiles toward task-defined value objectives. (3) Bounded plasticity: such reconfiguration is not without constraints, i.e. pressure induces a security- and goal-oriented priority shift while negative framing distinguishes protected values from those more amenable to redirection. Together, these findings characterize both the structure and dynamics of LLM value expression: context flexibly reconfigures expressed priorities, yet within behavioral boundaries. This behavioral account provides a foundation for understanding controllability, alignment, and safety in LLMs. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ZeroGen-Lab/CFProbe.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new framework, Conflict-driven Value Probing, to study how LLMs express and adapt their values under conflicting situations, revealing that values are dynamic, context-dependent, but bounded.
AI.motivation: Most ethical evaluations treat LLM values as fixed and uniform, but real deployments reveal that model responses vary with context, task, and framing. There is a need for a systematic way to study how LLMs navigate value conflicts and how their expressed priorities change under different pressures, to better understand alignment, controllability, and safety.
AI.method: The authors design Conflict-driven Value Probing, a controlled experimental setup where LLMs are placed in scenarios with explicit value conflicts. They then apply four types of interventions that perturb these conflicts (e.g., changing abstraction level, task goals, or framing) to observe how the models’ expressed values and priorities shift. They run these probes across ten different LLMs and analyze recurring behavioral patterns in their responses.
AI.result: Across ten LLMs, the study finds three general patterns: (1) Expression duality: when reasoning abstractly, models express broad, idealistic value commitments, but in concrete dilemmas they prioritize more pragmatic considerations. (2) Functional steerability: models can be steered to align their expressed values with task-defined objectives, showing significant configurability. (3) Bounded plasticity: this steerability has limits; under pressure, models prioritize security and goal achievement, and negative framing reveals a subset of values that remain resistant to redirection compared to more flexible ones.
AI.conclusion: LLM value expression is structured, dynamic, and context-sensitive rather than static, yet it is also constrained by consistent behavioral boundaries. Context and task framing can reconfigure the priorities a model expresses, but not arbitrarily. This behavioral understanding of how values are expressed and reconfigured provides a basis for more precise notions of controllability, alignment, and safety in LLMs, and the released code/data enable replication and further study.

title: RedKnot-MLA: Multi-Head Offline-Online Reuse for DeepSeek-V4 Long-Context Serving
summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) exposes many logical query heads through one packed latent KV stream. This representation is memory efficient, but it removes the physical per-head cache boundary assumed by conventional head-wise reuse. We present our system, a DeepSeek-V4 realization of RedKnot's head-aware reuse principle. Each immutable document is processed offline at canonical position zero; certified Local-head contributions are retained as MLA-Off. At serving time, query-side RoPE relocation restores the document's request position, a small Global-head set and protected Local token rows are recomputed as MLA-Online, and the two paths are merged before a single shared output projection. The packed MLA latent is never split. DeepSeek-V4-Flash uses 37 reusable layers and a 56/8 Local/Global partition, giving a 75.29% analytic logical head-row ceiling; the Pro-0813 profile uses 55 layers and 112/16 heads, giving 78.89%. Frozen Flash operating points show hot-artifact TTFT speedups of 2.02-3.84x. At 256K, the archived three-dataset study reports an aggregate F1 change of +3.24 percentage points, an EM change of +4.16 points, and a 78.7-79.5% analytic major-operator arithmetic saving, while one dataset decreases by 2.81 F1 points. A separate author-reported 256K hot-artifact QPS measurement is approximately 2.0x; because its raw concurrency trace is not included in this bundle, we mark it as preliminary rather than archived evidence. We describe the factorization, position repair, token-row closure, sparse-MoE support, TP8 integration, and the measurement boundaries needed to interpret these results.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a head-aware reuse system for multi-head latent attention in DeepSeek-V4 models, enabling efficient offline/online KV reuse without splitting the packed latent, yielding significant speedups and compute savings at long context with small or positive accuracy impact.
AI.motivation: Existing MLA compresses many logical attention heads into a single packed latent KV stream, which is memory efficient but breaks conventional per-head cache reuse and limits efficiency gains for long-context inference. The authors want to restore head-wise reuse principles (as in RedKnot) while retaining MLA’s compression benefits, to improve throughput and latency for hot artifacts at very long sequence lengths.
AI.method: They implement a DeepSeek-V4 realization of RedKnot’s head-aware reuse by factorizing attention heads into Local and Global sets and doing offline/online processing. Immutable documents are preprocessed offline at position zero to compute and store certified Local-head contributions (MLA-Off). At serving time, they use RoPE relocation to map these cached contributions to the actual request position, recompute a small set of Global heads plus protected Local token rows online (MLA-Online), then merge both paths before a shared output projection, keeping the MLA latent packed. The system supports sparse-MoE, tensor parallelism with TP8, and defines token-row closure and measurement boundaries for correct reuse.
AI.result: DeepSeek-V4-Flash uses 37 reusable layers with a 56/8 Local/Global head partition and achieves a theoretical 75.29% logical head-row reuse ceiling; the Pro-0813 profile uses 55 layers and 112/16 heads for a 78.89% ceiling. Frozen Flash configurations show 2.02–3.84x TTFT speedup on hot artifacts. At 256K context, an archived study over three datasets shows aggregate F1 +3.24 points, EM +4.16 points, and 78.7–79.5% estimated savings in major arithmetic operators, though one dataset sees a 2.81 F1 point drop. An additional author-reported 2.0x QPS gain at 256K is noted but marked preliminary due to missing raw traces.
AI.conclusion: Head-aware reuse can be made compatible with packed multi-head latent attention by separating Local and Global heads, precomputing immutable Local contributions, and repairing positions at query time without splitting the latent. This design delivers substantial long-context efficiency gains (latency, QPS, and arithmetic savings) with neutral to positive accuracy, and the paper clarifies the necessary implementation details (factorization, RoPE-based position repair, token-row closure, sparse-MoE and TP integration, and careful measurement practices) to reproduce and interpret the results.

title: Marginal Fidelity Does Not Establish User Simulation in Demographic Synthetic Survey Panels: Response Contracts, Support Collapse and Conditioning Failure
summary:
Demographic synthetic survey panels are often validated by matching aggregate answers to published surveys. We test what that certificate establishes across six multiselect batteries from four survey organisations in three countries. The headline analysis is restricted to three instruments whose synthetic cohort and human target share the stated population frame; three other batteries remain sensitivity analyses.
  The response contract dominates measured fidelity. In the aligned instruments, committed sets leave 66 of 128 model-battery option slots empty in panels of up to 500 respondents, versus 0 of 128 under per-option probability elicitation. Across eight uncapped model-instrument comparisons, probabilities reduce option-marginal MAE by 4.53 to 7.30 points. The capped instrument reverses on two models until the vectors are projected onto its stated maximum. These are measurement effects: human targets are realised check-all responses, whereas the vectors are latent inclusion propensities.
  Published marginal agreement also fails to discriminate respondent simulation from direct population estimation. On nine aligned model-battery pairs, a no-persona population-prevalence query averages 6.27 MAE versus 12.39 for committed panels and wins all nine comparisons. Constraint-aware probability vectors average 5.34 and beat the query on four of nine, so the baseline challenges the validation criterion rather than proving direct estimation uniformly best. On three unpublished demographic cells, neither approach beats reciting the national distribution. Population-marginal agreement is therefore evidence about an elicitation contract and an estimand obtainable without simulated respondents, not evidence of individual simulation.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well synthetic survey panels actually simulate individual respondents by testing different ways of eliciting model answers, and finds that matching aggregate marginals mainly reflects the response format and can be achieved without simulating people.
AI.motivation: Synthetic survey panels (AI-generated respondents) are often validated by showing that their aggregate answers match official or published survey marginals. The authors question what this kind of validation really proves: does it show that models are good at simulating individuals, or only that they can reproduce known distributions under a particular response format? They aim to clarify what is being measured when comparing model-generated survey data to human survey results.
AI.method: They run a set of tests on six multi-select question batteries from four survey organizations in three countries. They compare: (1) “committed set” responses, where a model must output a concrete subset of options (like a human check-all-that-apply answer) and (2) per-option probability elicitation, where the model gives an inclusion probability for each option. They restrict headline results to three instruments where model and human data share the same population frame and use the rest as sensitivity checks. They compute option-level mean absolute error (MAE) between model outputs and human marginals, and they also compare these model-based methods to a simple baseline that directly queries population prevalence without personas and to constraint-aware probability vectors. They further test performance within unpublished demographic cells and against a trivial baseline of repeating the national distribution.
AI.result: 1) Response format has a huge impact on measured fit. With committed-set outputs, models leave 66 of 128 option slots completely unused in panels of up to 500 synthetic respondents, versus zero unused options when eliciting per-option probabilities, indicating much sparser and less faithful coverage under the committed format. Per-option probabilities consistently reduce option-level MAE by roughly 4.5–7.3 points across multiple comparisons. A capped instrument (with a maximum number of options) initially appears to favour committed answers for two models, but this reverses once probability vectors are projected into the same cap, highlighting a pure measurement artifact. 2) Agreement on published marginals does not show that respondent simulation is better than direct estimation. On nine aligned model-battery pairs, a no-persona query that asks directly for population prevalence achieves average MAE 6.27 vs 12.39 for committed synthetic panels, and it wins all nine pairwise comparisons. Constraint-aware probability vectors do even better (average MAE 5.34), beating the direct query on four of nine, which shows that the benchmark is strong and the main issue is with the validation criterion. 3) In three unpublished demographic subgroups, neither synthetic panels nor direct prevalence queries outperform simply re-using the national distribution. This indicates that strong apparent performance on publicly known marginals does not generalize to more granular or unpublished targets.
AI.conclusion: Matching population marginals with synthetic survey panels primarily reflects the choice of elicitation contract (committed answers vs probability vectors) and what estimand is being targeted, not successful simulation of individual-level responses. Per-option probability elicitation produces substantially better agreement with human marginals than committed-set panels, and a simple direct population-prevalence query can outperform synthetic panels entirely. In settings where the target marginals are known or structurally predictable, population-marginal agreement is therefore evidence about measurement choices and estimands achievable without generating synthetic individuals, rather than evidence that AI models are accurately simulating respondents. This undermines the common practice of validating synthetic panels solely by macro-level marginal comparisons.

title: Beyond One-Shot Expansion: Contrastive Evidence Exploration for Multi-Hop Retrieval
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) critically depends on retrieving the evidence necessary for effective reasoning. However, this remains particularly challenging in multi-hop question answering (QA), where supporting passages are often linked through intermediate entities and relations that must be progressively uncovered. Existing retrieval approaches typically rely on a single retrieval intent or one-shot query expansion, limiting their ability to adapt to newly retrieved evidence and potentially introducing noisy or redundant retrieval signals. To address these limitations, we propose a training-free multi-hop retrieval framework that integrates evidence-conditioned exploration, passage-specific contrastive refinement, and coverage-aware final ranking. During offline indexing, the framework constructs passage-specific contrastive facets that characterize each passage relative to its semantically similar neighbors, providing fine-grained signals to distinguish closely related candidates. At inference time, the framework iteratively retrieves evidence, generates probes targeting unresolved information needs, refines candidate relevance using the contrastive facets, and selects a complementary set of passages that collectively cover diverse evidence-seeking intents. Experiments on MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA demonstrate consistent improvements in retrieval quality and downstream QA performance over baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free multi-hop retrieval framework for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that dynamically explores, refines, and ranks evidence passages to improve multi-hop QA performance.
AI.motivation: In multi-hop QA for RAG, it is difficult to retrieve all necessary supporting passages because evidence is linked through intermediate entities and relations that must be uncovered step by step. Existing retrievers usually rely on a single static query or one-shot query expansion, which cannot adapt well to newly retrieved evidence and often brings in noise or redundant passages. A more adaptive, fine-grained, and coverage-aware retrieval process is needed to improve reasoning and answer quality.
AI.method: The authors design a training-free multi-hop retrieval framework with three main ideas: (1) evidence-conditioned exploration, where the system iteratively retrieves evidence and then generates new probe queries aimed at remaining unresolved information needs; (2) passage-specific contrastive refinement, where, during offline indexing, each passage is associated with contrastive facets that distinguish it from semantically similar neighbors, allowing finer-grained relevance scoring; and (3) coverage-aware final ranking, where the final set of passages is selected to jointly cover diverse evidence-seeking intents rather than just picking top-scoring but redundant passages. The process is iterative at inference time: retrieve, probe, refine using contrastive facets, and re-rank for diverse coverage.
AI.result: On three multi-hop QA benchmarks—MuSiQue, HotpotQA, and 2WikiMultihopQA—the proposed framework consistently outperforms baseline retrieval methods in both retrieval quality metrics and downstream QA accuracy, indicating better support for multi-hop reasoning in RAG setups.
AI.conclusion: A training-free, iterative, and contrastive multi-hop retrieval strategy can significantly enhance evidence collection for RAG-based QA. By conditioning retrieval on discovered evidence, refining candidate passages via passage-specific contrastive facets, and explicitly optimizing for coverage of multiple evidence intents, the framework yields more accurate and robust multi-hop QA without requiring additional training of the retriever.

title: RouteRelay: Event-Triggered Cross-Layer Route Reuse for Efficient Dynamic Sparse Attention
summary: Dynamic sparse attention reduces long-context prefill cost by routing each query chunk to a small set of key chunks at every Transformer layer. The sparse attention kernel avoids most token interactions, but the router still rebuilds a chunk--chunk score matrix layer after layer, even when the selected routes change little. We introduce RouteRelay, a router-agnostic method that reuses only route metadata across depth while continuing to compute attention with the current layer's queries, keys, and values. Anchor layers perform full routing. Intermediate layers rescore the previous top-$k$ route and a compact sentinel set of near-miss and randomly probed chunks. A query row is rerouted only when a sentinel challenges its weakest selected chunk. We give a top-$k$ stability condition, a probabilistic bound on missed challengers, and a row-selective GPU execution design. In a reproducible empirical evaluation, RouteRelay retains at least 99.99% route recall while rerouting 25.0%, 55.4%, and 78.2% of rows under low, moderate, and high cross-layer drift, respectively. Across routing scales, RouteRelay retains 100.0% recall while evaluating 38.4--51.6% of full-routing score pairs as the key-chunk count grows from 128 to 1024. Its unfused CPU execution remains slower than dense matrix multiplication, exposing row compaction and ledger updates as the main kernel-engineering targets.

AI.tldr: RouteRelay is a method for long-context Transformers that reuses routing decisions across layers to cut the cost of dynamic sparse attention while preserving routing quality.
AI.motivation: Dynamic sparse attention reduces computation by routing each query chunk to only a few key chunks, but existing approaches recompute the full chunk–chunk score matrix at every layer, even though routes change little across depth. This repeated routing is wasteful and becomes a bottleneck for long contexts.
AI.method: The authors propose RouteRelay, a router-agnostic framework that propagates only route metadata across layers instead of recomputing full routing from scratch. Certain "anchor" layers perform full routing. Intermediate layers reuse the previous layer’s top-k routes and only rescore those plus a small sentinel set comprising near-miss and randomly probed chunks. A query row is rerouted if any sentinel chunk scores higher than the weakest currently selected chunk. They derive a top-k stability condition, a probabilistic bound on the chance of missing better challengers in the sentinel set, and design a row-selective GPU execution scheme to exploit this sparsity pattern efficiently.
AI.result: Empirically, RouteRelay achieves at least 99.99% recall of the routes that would be found by full routing, even when cross-layer drift in routing patterns is high. It reduces the fraction of rows that must be fully rerouted to 25.0%, 55.4%, and 78.2% under low, moderate, and high drift, respectively. Over a range of routing scales, it maintains 100% recall while requiring only 38.4–51.6% of the score computations that full routing would perform as the number of key chunks increases from 128 to 1024. On CPU, the current unfused implementation remains slower than dense matrix multiplication, highlighting row compaction and ledger update operations as key targets for kernel optimization.
AI.conclusion: RouteRelay enables efficient reuse of routing information in dynamic sparse attention, significantly reducing routing computation across Transformer layers without sacrificing route quality. Its theoretical guarantees and empirical results show that it can maintain near-perfect route recall while evaluating far fewer score pairs. Further kernel engineering, especially for CPU implementations, is needed to fully realize its speed benefits relative to dense attention.

title: VST: Verifiable Structured Transport for Auditable Agent-to-Agent Alpha Discovery
summary: Agent-to-agent (A2A) alpha discovery is slowed by repeated feedback cycles between mining and evaluation agents, whose hand-offs, in contemporary LLM multi-agent systems, are free-form natural-language messages that carry no stable contract and cannot be replayed. We first restructure this communication as a structured agent-to-agent protocol of \emph{typed, causally addressable, unicast records}, so that the committed stream forms a causal trajectory. On that trajectory a single predictor with four typed heads forecasts the accumulated guidance the two miners would receive several cycles ahead; a transactional verify--leap controller then commits a multi-cycle speculative outcome only when it passes a four-level gate, and otherwise rolls back to the exact prior state. Structure is the enabling contribution, and its value is not accuracy. A controlled ablation shows an equal-information free-text channel reaches the same predictor hit rate. What typing provides is a state that can be schema-checked, replayed deterministically, and prevented by construction from leaking a forecast to an evaluator: auditability by construction, not an empirically stress-tested guarantee. On a CSI~1000 out-of-sample holdout, our single run is the only one among eight methods (seven baselines and ours) to hold a positive median annualized return and Sharpe at the factor level, though the median return \emph{in excess} of the benchmark stays negative for every method including ours; its development-selected top-20 portfolios reach a $0.71$ median holdout Sharpe, selected on a split inside the optimization horizon. We report these single-run results descriptively, gross of costs, and are explicit about their limits throughout; in particular we do not isolate the effect of the leap machinery from the inherited search substrate, which we leave to future work.

AI.tldr: They propose a structured communication and speculative execution mechanism for multi-agent LLM-based alpha discovery, showing modest but more auditable performance gains in a quant setting.
AI.motivation: In current LLM-based multi-agent systems for alpha (trading signal) discovery, agents communicate via unstructured natural language messages. This causes slow feedback cycles, lack of stable contracts, difficulty in deterministic replay, and challenges in ensuring that predictive information is not leaked between agents (e.g., from a forecasting component to an evaluator), which complicates both performance optimization and auditability.
AI.method: They redesign agent communication into a structured protocol of typed, causally addressable, unicast records, forming a deterministic causal trajectory of the interaction. Over this trajectory, they train a single predictive model with four typed output heads to forecast several cycles ahead the aggregate guidance that two mining agents would otherwise receive. On top of this, they implement a transactional verify–leap controller that speculatively commits multi-cycle outcomes when the predictor’s forecast passes a four-level gating criterion; if the gate fails, the system rolls back exactly to the prior state. They perform a controlled ablation comparing this typed channel to an equal-information free-text channel and then evaluate the full system in a CSI 1000 factor investing experiment against seven baseline methods.
AI.result: The ablation shows that, in terms of prediction accuracy (hit rate), the structured typed communication channel does not outperform an equally informative free-text channel; both achieve similar predictor performance. However, the typed schema enables deterministic replay, schema validation, and structural prevention of forecast leakage to evaluators, thus improving auditability. In the CSI 1000 out-of-sample holdout test, their method is the only one among eight total methods (seven baselines plus theirs) that attains a positive median annualized return and Sharpe ratio at the factor level. Nonetheless, all methods, including theirs, still exhibit negative median excess return over the benchmark. A development-selected subset of top-20 portfolios from their method attains a median holdout Sharpe of 0.71, using a selection split within the optimization horizon. Results are reported from a single run and are gross of trading costs.
AI.conclusion: Structuring agent-to-agent communication into typed, causally addressable records and adding a verify–leap speculative controller enables deterministic replay, schema checking, and by-construction auditability in multi-agent LLM alpha discovery, without necessarily improving raw predictive accuracy over an unstructured channel. In a CSI 1000 empirical study, the approach yields relatively better factor-level performance than several baselines, though absolute economic performance remains limited and excess returns are still negative. The authors emphasize that the contribution is primarily in system structure and auditability rather than alpha magnitude, and they do not disentangle the effect of their leap mechanism from the underlying search substrate, leaving that as future work.

title: SPARROW: Scalable Taxonomy Induction via Structure-Preserving Partitioning and Constraint-Guided Merging
summary: Taxonomy induction aims to organize concept sets into coherent hierarchical structures. Recent LLM-based methods can induce taxonomies directly from flat term lists, avoiding the need for corpora, but degrade sharply as concept sets scale up. We argue that this degradation stems not only from context length limitations, but also from structural failures in hierarchical reasoning. To address this, we adopt a divide-and-merge paradigm that partitions concepts into smaller subsets, induces local taxonomies, and merges them into a global hierarchy. However, we identify two structural failure modes inherent to this paradigm: Structural Fragmentation, where partitioning weakens local hierarchical signals, and Parent Displacement, where locally plausible relations are misplaced in the global hierarchy. To address both, we propose SPARROW, a scalable taxonomy induction framework that combines structure-preserving spectral partitioning to retain hierarchical connectivity within each block, and constraint-guided incremental fusion that treats block-level relations as structural constraints rather than ground truth for global placement. Experiments on large-scale benchmarks show that SPARROW consistently achieves the strongest global structural quality across backbones. The code is available at https://github.com/rebeccazyr/SPARROW.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SPARROW, a scalable framework for inducing high-quality taxonomies from large concept sets by using structure-aware partitioning and constraint-guided merging to overcome hierarchical reasoning failures in large language models.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based taxonomy induction methods can build hierarchies directly from flat term lists without corpora, but their performance breaks down as the concept set grows. This is not only due to context length limits of LLMs, but also because LLMs struggle with maintaining coherent hierarchical structure at scale. Furthermore, common divide-and-conquer approaches that split concepts into subsets and merge local taxonomies suffer from structural issues that compromise the final global taxonomy. The paper aims to build a scalable method that preserves global hierarchical quality while handling large concept collections.
AI.method: The authors first analyze two structural failure modes in divide-and-merge taxonomy induction: (1) Structural Fragmentation, where naive partitioning weakens the hierarchical signals inside each subset, and (2) Parent Displacement, where relations that look plausible locally are misplaced when merged globally. To mitigate these, they propose SPARROW, which has two main components: (a) structure-preserving spectral partitioning that groups concepts into blocks while maintaining strong hierarchical connectivity inside each block, thereby preserving useful parent-child and sibling relations; and (b) constraint-guided incremental fusion that does not treat intra-block relations as hard ground truth, but rather as soft structural constraints when incrementally integrating blocks into a single global hierarchy. This fusion process adjusts local relations to fit a coherent global structure, reducing misplacements that arise when simply stitching local trees together.
AI.result: On large-scale taxonomy induction benchmarks, SPARROW is evaluated across different LLM backbones. It consistently achieves better global structural quality—such as more accurate hierarchies and fewer misplaced relations—than prior methods. The improvements hold across scales, demonstrating that SPARROW effectively alleviates degradation when the concept set becomes large. The approach proves robust and scalable for real-world taxonomy construction tasks.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the scalability issues of LLM-based taxonomy induction are rooted both in context limitations and in deeper structural reasoning failures. By explicitly modeling and addressing the structural fragmentation and parent displacement problems through structure-preserving partitioning and constraint-guided fusion, SPARROW provides a more reliable way to induce taxonomies from large flat term lists. The framework yields state-of-the-art global structural quality and can be flexibly combined with various LLM backbones, offering a practical solution for large-scale taxonomy construction.

title: A Hierarchical Consistency Framework for Auditing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is commonly evaluated by whether the final answer is correct. That test is insufficient: an answer can match its reference while the context that produced it contains a direct contradiction, leaving the contested evidence invisible to answer-only review and retrieval relevance scores. This paper presents the Hierarchical Consistency Framework (HCF), a post-hoc, model-agnostic audit of three distinct levels of a RAG process: the knowledge corpus, the final retrieved context, and the generated answer. HCF represents corpus conflicts as source-linked atomic facts, thereby identifying the documents responsible, and returns each Answer Consistency Score (ACS) with an explanation of supporting and contradictory contextual statements. We evaluate HCF on several controlled corpora spanning five domains and 100 query-corpus instances. A human evaluator compares every generated response with its supplied ground-truth response. The results show that the three diagnostic levels can dissociate: the corpus with the highest mean retrieval similarity has the lowest mean ACS, while a structurally degraded corpus performs worse at corpus level but better at answer level. Most importantly, HCF identifies contradictory retrieved evidence in several cases where the answer still matches the ground truth. HCF does not certify factual truth; it makes the evidence supporting and challenging an answer inspectable and attributable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework to audit retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems by checking consistency across corpus, retrieved context, and final answers, rather than only judging if answers match ground truth.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG evaluations focus mainly on whether the final generated answer is correct with respect to a reference answer. This is inadequate because an answer can appear correct while being supported by contradictory or unreliable evidence in the retrieved context or underlying corpus. The authors want a way to expose and analyze such hidden inconsistencies, making the evidence behind answers transparent and attributable.
AI.method: The authors propose the Hierarchical Consistency Framework (HCF), a post-hoc, model-agnostic auditing method that operates at three levels: (1) corpus level, representing documents as source-linked atomic facts and detecting conflicts across the corpus; (2) retrieval/context level, examining the subset of documents actually retrieved for a query and identifying supporting and contradicting statements; and (3) answer level, computing an Answer Consistency Score (ACS) that explains how well the generated answer aligns with both supporting and contradictory contextual evidence. They apply HCF to controlled corpora across five domains and 100 query–corpus instances, then have human evaluators compare model answers to ground-truth answers.
AI.result: The evaluation shows that the three diagnostic levels (corpus, retrieval, answer) can diverge in informative ways. For example, the corpus with the highest mean retrieval similarity (i.e., seemingly best retrieval quality) can have the lowest mean Answer Consistency Score, while a structurally degraded corpus can look worse at corpus level but yield better answer-level consistency. Crucially, HCF successfully flags cases where the generated answer matches the ground truth but is backed by contradictory retrieved evidence, which traditional answer-only or relevance-based metrics would miss.
AI.conclusion: HCF enables fine-grained auditing of RAG systems by making the underlying evidence for answers explicit, inspectable, and attributable to specific documents. It does not attempt to guarantee factual correctness, but rather highlights supporting and contradictory evidence at multiple levels, revealing when seemingly correct answers rest on inconsistent or conflicted contexts. This multi-level view can guide better corpus construction, retrieval strategies, and trust assessment for RAG systems.

title: LANTERN: Language Model Assessment on Noisy and Transformed Tasks for Understanding Error and Robustness Nuances
summary: Robustness evaluation of large language models (LLMs) remains a critical challenge, particularly in assessing their sensitivity to perturbations in input data. In this work, we systematically evaluate LLM robustness across multiple dimensions, including word error rate, character repetition and duplication, modifications in choices, and variability in instruction following. To facilitate this evaluation, we construct a synthetic and augmented dataset encompassing a diverse set of LLM benchmarks, specifically targeting multiple-choice question (MCQ) datasets and instruction-following tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on LLMs of varying scales-small, medium, and large-as well as across base and instruction-tuned variants. Our analysis quantifies the variability in model responses under perturbed conditions and highlights discrepancies relative to baseline models. The findings provide insights into the stability of LLMs across different evaluation scenarios contributing to the development of more robust and reliable language models as well as robust evaluation methodologies.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how robust large language models are to various input perturbations using a synthetic, augmented benchmark suite, comparing models of different sizes and training types.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in real-world settings, it is crucial to understand how sensitive they are to small changes or noise in inputs. Existing evaluations often focus on average accuracy but overlook robustness to perturbations such as typos, duplicated text, or altered instructions, which can significantly affect reliability and user trust. This paper aims to fill that gap by providing a systematic robustness assessment framework.
AI.method: The authors build a synthetic and augmented dataset derived from existing LLM benchmarks, focusing on multiple-choice questions and instruction-following tasks. They introduce controlled perturbations along several axes: word error rate, character repetition and duplication, modifications to answer choices, and variability in instructions. They then run extensive experiments on LLMs of different scales (small, medium, large) and training configurations (base vs. instruction-tuned), measuring how model outputs change under these perturbations and comparing them to performance on unperturbed baselines.
AI.result: The experiments quantify how much model responses vary when inputs are perturbed, revealing non-trivial sensitivity even to relatively minor changes. The analysis shows differing robustness profiles across model sizes and between base and instruction-tuned variants, and identifies notable discrepancies between perturbed performance and baseline performance, indicating that some models are brittle under certain perturbation types.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that current LLMs exhibit significant variability and instability under input perturbations, and that robustness cannot be inferred from standard benchmark scores alone. The proposed evaluation setup and findings offer a pathway toward designing more robust LLMs and more rigorous robustness-focused evaluation methodologies, emphasizing the need to incorporate perturbation-based testing in future LLM assessment and development.

title: Risk Is Not Review Value: Wrong-Answer Exposure Under Bounded Review Budgets
summary: LLM assistants often produce more answers than humans can review before users see them. Most evaluations ask whether an answer is wrong, unsupported, or low-confidence. Bounded review budgets instead ask which answers should be checked first under a fixed review budget. Risk alone is not enough: a high-risk answer may be hard to repair, while a moderately risky answer may be directly correctable from available evidence. For generated-answer evaluation, we model review prioritization as exposure reduction, where review value combines estimated wrongness, intervention affordance, impact, and cost. We evaluate review queues with Wrong-Answer Exposure Ratio (WAER), the fraction of wrong answers left unreviewed, and post-repair residual exposure (PRRE), the fraction still exposed after deterministic benchmark-supported repairs. PRRE uses repairability rules that do not numerically reuse the affordance scores used for ranking. On a 720-item TAT-QA/SciFact stress benchmark, review-value ranking keeps answer-level WAER nearly unchanged at 20% budget (0.605 vs. 0.600) but lowers PRRE from 0.881 to 0.716. These results show that trustworthy LLM evaluation should measure not only error detection, but also how limited review capacity reduces exposed wrong answers.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework and metrics for prioritizing which LLM answers should be reviewed first under limited human review budgets, focusing on reducing users’ exposure to wrong answers rather than only detecting errors.
AI.motivation: In practical deployments, LLMs generate far more answers than humans can feasibly review, so traditional evaluations that only ask whether an answer is right or wrong do not reflect real operational constraints. There is a need to understand which model outputs should be prioritized for review to minimize the harm from unrepaired wrong answers, especially since some errors are easier to fix than others once evidence is consulted.
AI.method: The authors formalize review prioritization as an exposure-reduction problem where each answer’s review value is a function of four components: estimated probability of wrongness, how easily a human (or system) can intervene to fix it (intervention affordance), the impact of that answer, and the cost of reviewing it. They create ranking strategies for ordering answers in review queues according to this review value. To evaluate these strategies, they introduce two metrics: Wrong-Answer Exposure Ratio (WAER), the proportion of wrong answers that remain unreviewed under a given review budget, and Post-Repair Residual Exposure (PRRE), the proportion of wrong answers still effectively exposed after applying deterministic, benchmark-based repair rules to reviewed items. Importantly, the repair rules for PRRE are defined without reusing the same affordance scores used in ranking, to avoid circularity. They test on a 720-example stress benchmark built from TAT-QA and SciFact.
AI.result: On the 720-item TAT-QA/SciFact stress benchmark, when allowing review of only 20% of the answers, their review-value-based ranking yields an answer-level WAER that is almost unchanged compared to a baseline (0.605 vs. 0.600), meaning raw error detection rates are similar. However, PRRE—capturing the fraction of wrong answers that remain effectively exposed after possible repairs—drops substantially from 0.881 to 0.716 when using the proposed prioritization, demonstrating that better ordering of review effort meaningfully reduces users’ exposure to uncorrected wrong answers even when error detection alone looks similar.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that evaluating trustworthy LLM systems should go beyond simply measuring whether errors are detected and should instead explicitly consider how limited review resources are allocated to reduce the exposure of users to wrong answers. Metrics such as WAER and PRRE, along with a review-value model that combines wrongness, repairability, impact, and cost, provide a more realistic and operationally relevant framework for assessing and improving LLM-assisted workflows under constrained human oversight.

title: Content-Based Addressing for Long Context
summary: Rotary position embedding (RoPE) uses each token's integer position to determine the rotation applied inside attention. This works well for local token order, but increasing context length creates a positional train-test mismatch: RoPE produces relative rotations at offsets not seen during training. Methods that rescale, interpolate, randomize, or bias positions specify how attention handles those offsets, but still derive positional information from a growing token counter. We instead divide a token stream into units, retain ordinary RoPE positions within each unit, and assign every completed unit an address computed from its content. Adding units then applies the same learned map to new content rather than extending a positional range or an identifier table. We prove that this construction preserves local RoPE exactly, leaves the attention comparison between two fixed tokens unchanged when other units are inserted or reordered, and does not create new relative rotations merely because more units are added. In a character-level Tiny Shakespeare diagnostic, a model trained on 256-character contexts has validation perplexity 4.04 at 256 characters and 3.82 at 4096, while continuous RoPE changes from 4.71 to 12.09. A second diagnostic shows that content-based addressing can retrieve and use information from multiple serialized facts. These are controlled shallow experiments, not scale benchmarks, but they support a direct prescription: use position to address locally and content to address across units.

AI.tldr: Paper proposes content-based addressing of token units to fix RoPE’s long-context positional mismatch, preserving local behavior while enabling robust extrapolation.
AI.motivation: Standard RoPE depends on absolute token indices, so extending context length forces the model to use relative rotations at offsets never seen in training. Existing fixes still rely on stretching or modifying the global position index, causing train-test mismatch and unstable long-context behavior. The authors want a method that keeps RoPE’s good local ordering while making long-range addressing depend on content rather than ever-increasing position counters.
AI.method: Segment the token sequence into ‘units’ (e.g., fixed-size chunks). Inside each unit, apply standard RoPE with normal local positions. For inter-unit relations, assign each completed unit a content-derived address (a function of its tokens), and use those addresses instead of large absolute positions when computing attention across units. They prove theoretically that this preserves local RoPE exactly, keeps pairwise attention between any two fixed tokens invariant under inserting or reordering other units, and avoids introducing unseen relative rotations as more units are added. Empirically, they run controlled diagnostics: a Tiny Shakespeare character-level model trained on 256-character context, evaluated up to 4096 characters, and a second toy task where the model must retrieve multiple serialized facts using content-based addressing.
AI.result: On Tiny Shakespeare, a model trained on 256-character contexts gets validation perplexity 4.04 at 256 characters and 3.82 at 4096 with content-based addressing, whereas standard continuous RoPE degrades from 4.71 to 12.09 when extrapolating to 4096 characters. In another diagnostic, the content-addressed scheme successfully retrieves and uses information from multiple serialized facts, demonstrating effective long-range retrieval via content-based unit addresses. The results are framed as shallow diagnostics rather than large-scale benchmarks, but they highlight strong long-context extrapolation without modifying the trained positional range.
AI.conclusion: Content-based addressing over token units combined with local RoPE positions resolves the positional train-test mismatch of standard RoPE in long contexts. The approach keeps all desirable local RoPE properties, makes attention comparisons robust to inserting or reordering distant units, and avoids new, untrained relative rotations when increasing context length. Controlled experiments show superior long-context generalization versus continuous RoPE and suggest a practical recipe for model design: use positional indices only for local ordering within units, and use learned content-based addresses to relate information across units.

title: Beyond Sparse Rewards: A New Benchmark and Structure-Aware Graph Alignment for Micro-Drama Understanding
summary: Micro-dramas, characterized by ultra-short durations and hyper-dense storylines, pose unique challenges for video understanding that conventional benchmarks fail to address. To bridge this gap, we introduce M-Drama, the first large-scale bilingual benchmark for micro-drama comprehension, featuring over 35K instances across 9,138 clips. Furthermore, while reinforcement learning can enhance VLMs on complex narratives, existing reward metrics often suffer from sparse and superficial signals, failing to capture intricate character identities and temporal structures. We propose SAGA (Structure-Aware Graph Alignment), a novel graph-matching reward function that models narratives as heterogeneous graphs. SAGA computes dense, rigorous rewards via decoupled semantic triplet and structural temporal matching. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct demonstrate that SAGA outperforms existing baselines, delivering substantial improvements in open-ended accuracy and summary quality, while maintaining competitive out-of-domain generalization. Code is available at https://github.com/qyx1121/MDrama_SAGA.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces M-Drama, a large-scale bilingual benchmark and SAGA, a structure-aware graph alignment reward for improving video-language models on ultra-short, dense micro-drama videos.
AI.motivation: Micro-dramas are extremely short videos with very dense storylines, which make them hard to understand using existing video understanding benchmarks and training schemes. Current reinforcement learning reward metrics for video-language models offer sparse, shallow signals and do not adequately capture narrative elements like character identities and temporal structure, limiting performance on complex, fine-grained video narratives.
AI.method: (1) Build M-Drama, a large-scale bilingual benchmark dedicated to micro-drama comprehension, with over 35K QA/summary instances across 9,138 clips. (2) Propose SAGA (Structure-Aware Graph Alignment), a novel reinforcement learning reward function that represents narratives as heterogeneous graphs encoding entities, relations, and temporal links. SAGA performs decoupled semantic triplet matching and structural temporal alignment between the model’s outputs and reference graphs, yielding dense reward signals. (3) Train and evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct with SAGA and compare against existing reward metrics and baselines.
AI.result: On the M-Drama benchmark, using SAGA as the RL reward significantly improves open-ended question answering accuracy and the quality of generated summaries compared to baseline reward functions. The resulting models also retain strong performance on out-of-domain tasks, indicating that the improvements are not overfitted to micro-dramas.
AI.conclusion: Modeling narrative structure explicitly via heterogeneous graphs and using graph alignment as a reward in reinforcement learning is effective for training video-language models on micro-dramas. The M-Drama benchmark and SAGA reward together provide a practical framework for advancing fine-grained understanding of ultra-short, densely plotted videos while maintaining generalization to other domains.

title: BlueprintAgent: Constraint-Triggered Targeted Revisits for Simulation-Ready Generation from Scanned Structural Blueprints
comment: Accepted to Findings of EMNLP 2026. 14 pages, 4 figures
summary: Converting in-service reinforced-concrete (RC) building blueprints into simulation-ready models---structured frame representations that support deterministic FEM export and qualified-engineer review---underpins safety assessment and seismic retrofit, but the process remains manual. Direct prompting of a multimodal large language model (MLLM) over a scanned sheet is unreliable: outputs often violate engineering constraints on beam--column support, span count, or 3D continuity. We present BlueprintAgent (BPA), a constraint-triggered multimodal agent for simulation-ready frame extraction from scanned blueprints. BPA treats the MLLM as the primary reader and decision maker, with OCR and computer vision supplying localized evidence. Its central mechanism realizes engineering constraints as callable validators whose entity-level conflict reports trigger targeted MLLM revisits over the local region---an inference-time control distinct from fixed pipelines and free-form self-reflection. We evaluate BPA on 300 real scanned blueprint sheets from 20 anonymized RC frame projects, against five baselines and six ablations. BPA reaches a macro-averaged Beam F1 of 0.994, against 0.301 for single-MLLM zero-shot and 0.820 for a fixed pipeline; removing MLLM-led axis adjudication collapses Beam and Column F1 on complex multi-sheet projects. For dense technical drawings, engineering constraints are best deployed as triggers for entity-level targeted revisits rather than as post-hoc output filters.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BlueprintAgent, a constraint-triggered multimodal agent that converts scanned reinforced-concrete building blueprints into accurate, simulation-ready structural frame models, greatly outperforming direct MLLM prompting and fixed pipelines.
AI.motivation: Safety assessment and seismic retrofit of existing RC buildings require accurate, simulation-ready FEM models derived from old blueprints. Today, extracting structured frame representations (beams, columns, spans, 3D continuity) from scanned drawings is still a manual, expert-intensive process. Direct use of multimodal LLMs on these scans is unreliable because they often violate core engineering constraints, threatening the validity of any downstream simulation.
AI.method: The authors design BlueprintAgent (BPA), a multimodal agent that uses an MLLM as the primary reasoning engine, augmented with OCR and computer-vision tools for localized evidence. They encode engineering rules (e.g., beam–column support, span counts, continuity) as callable constraint validators. During inference, these validators check the MLLM’s extracted entities; detected conflicts trigger targeted re-queries to the MLLM on the specific problematic regions rather than re-processing the entire sheet. This creates a constraint-triggered, iterative correction loop that differs from both rigid pipelines and unconstrained self-reflection.
AI.result: On a dataset of 300 real scanned blueprint sheets from 20 anonymized RC projects, BPA is compared against five baselines and six ablations. It achieves a macro-averaged Beam F1 score of 0.994, far surpassing a single zero-shot MLLM (0.301) and a fixed pipeline approach (0.820). An ablation that removes MLLM-led axis adjudication shows dramatic performance drops for Beam and Column F1 on complex, multi-sheet projects, highlighting the importance of this design choice.
AI.conclusion: Engineering constraints are most effective when used during inference as triggers for localized, entity-level revisits by an MLLM, rather than only as post-hoc filters on final outputs. BlueprintAgent’s constraint-triggered multimodal agent design yields highly reliable, simulation-ready structural frame extractions from noisy, dense technical blueprints, substantially improving over direct MLLM prompting and rigid pipelines.

title: EEG-Driven Decoding Framework for Passenger Hazard Perception in Highly Automated Vehicles
comment: 31 pages, 8 figures, 13 tables, including appendices. Accepted for publication in Automotive Innovation. Yingkai Yang and Ashton Yu Xuan Tan contributed equally. Corresponding author: Hong Wang. Data: https://doi.org/10.21227/jw72-m261 ; Code: https://github.com/SOTIF-AVLab/EEG2023
summary: Reliable risk assessment remains a central challenge for Autonomous Vehicles (AVs). Despite advances in automation, passenger cognition provides a non-intrusive auxiliary signal that improves both objective and perceived safety without requiring active human intervention. We introduce an Electroencephalogram (EEG)-based Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) that decodes passenger neural responses for both Risk Prediction (RP) and Danger Identification (DI), explicitly modeling humans as passengers to match real-world AV use. To achieve this, we propose the Passenger Cognitive Model (PCM), Risk-aware Sequential Labeling (RSL), and the Passenger EEG Decoding Strategy (PEDS), which integrates a 3D Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (3D-CRNN) model for joint EEG decoding. Experimental results show that 3D-CRNN achieves a Balanced Accuracy (BA) of $95.3\% \pm 2.7\%$ in RP and improves single-subject DI from $80.9\% \pm 3.9\%$ to $85.0\% \pm 3.2\%$ with RSL. Event-wise analyses further show that 3D-CRNN consistently outperforms other models across different event types in RP and DI. In generalization experiments, 3D-CRNN achieves $77.0\% \pm 5.3\%$ BA in cross-session DI and $77.4\% \pm 1.1\%$ BA on seen subjects in cross-subject evaluation, while maintaining a $64.9\% \pm 8.5\%$ BA on unseen subjects, demonstrating promising generalizability and transferability across both intra-subject and inter-subject variability. These findings establish an Electroencephalogram (EEG) decoding framework for AV passenger hazard perception and suggest that passenger cognitive signals can provide auxiliary supervision for future AV decision-making and Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF) support.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an EEG-based BCI system that decodes AV passengers’ brain activity to predict driving risk and identify danger, showing high accuracy and promising generalization across sessions and subjects.
AI.motivation: Autonomous Vehicles still struggle with reliable real-time risk assessment, and existing systems rely mainly on external environment sensing and vehicle-state data. Human passengers, however, naturally perceive and react to hazards, and their brain activity can provide an auxiliary, non-intrusive signal that may improve both objective safety and passengers’ sense of safety. The paper aims to leverage passenger cognitive signals to support AV risk assessment and SOTIF without requiring active passenger intervention or changing standard AV operation.
AI.method: The authors design an EEG-based Brain-Computer Interface explicitly modeling humans as AV passengers. They propose three core components: (1) Passenger Cognitive Model (PCM) to formalize how passengers perceive risk and danger during AV driving; (2) Risk-aware Sequential Labeling (RSL) to better label EEG segments based on temporal risk evolution and event context; and (3) Passenger EEG Decoding Strategy (PEDS) that uses a 3D Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (3D-CRNN) to jointly exploit spatial, spectral, and temporal EEG structure. They evaluate this framework on tasks of Risk Prediction (anticipating risk states) and Danger Identification (detecting hazardous events), including single-subject, cross-session, and cross-subject generalization settings, and compare with alternative models.
AI.result: The 3D-CRNN model within PEDS attains a balanced accuracy of 95.3% ± 2.7% for Risk Prediction. For Danger Identification, integrating RSL improves single-subject performance from 80.9% ± 3.9% to 85.0% ± 3.2%. Event-wise analyses indicate that 3D-CRNN consistently outperforms other baselines across diverse event types for both RP and DI. In generalization experiments, the system achieves 77.0% ± 5.3% BA for cross-session DI, 77.4% ± 1.1% BA on seen subjects and 64.9% ± 8.5% BA on unseen subjects in cross-subject evaluation, demonstrating robustness to intra- and inter-subject variability.
AI.conclusion: The study establishes an EEG decoding framework tailored to AV passenger hazard perception and shows that passenger brain signals can reliably predict risk and identify danger. The high accuracies and generalization results suggest that passenger cognitive data can serve as an effective auxiliary supervision channel for AV decision-making and SOTIF assurance. This opens a path toward AVs that monitor and integrate passenger cognitive state to enhance both safety performance and user trust, without requiring active user input.

title: Beyond Fluent Generation: A CPU Reliability Benchmark for MCP-Style Tool Calling in Sub-2B Small Language Models for Edge Deployment
summary: Resource constrained single-board computers including Raspberry Pi, NVIDIA Jetson Nano, Arduino UNO Q, Orange Pi, and LattePanda motivate on-device small language model (SLM) agents that reduce cloud dependence, improve data locality, and tolerate intermittent connectivity. Model Context Protocol (MCP)-style tool invocation demands more than fluent generation: an agent must emit machine-readable JSON, select the correct tool, supply all required arguments, and avoid unintended actions. We establish a platform-agnostic CPU baseline by evaluating five open-weight models below two billion parameters Phi-1.5, Pythia-1.4B, TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat, Qwen2.5-0.5B, and Qwen2.5-1.5B on 100 prompts spanning weather retrieval, web search, calculation, email composition, and task creation, under greedy decoding and nucleus sampling. A recovery parser strips Markdown fences, extracts brace-delimited substrings, and scores parseability, tool-name correctness, argument completeness, and value agreement. Under this criterion, Qwen2.5-1.5B achieves 75% (greedy) and 79% (sampling); Qwen2.5-0.5B achieves 72% (greedy) but drops to 32% under sampling. Phi-1.5 scores 0%; Pythia and TinyLlama reach at most 7%. A strict post-hoc audit finds only 5 of 1,000 raw responses directly parseable as JSON, exposing near-total dependence on output recovery. A CPU resource probe shows Qwen2.5-1.5B requires 7,960 MiB and 30.782 s mean latency; Qwen2.5-0.5B uses 3,637 MiB and 10.627 s, revealing a reliability-resource trade-off for edge deployment. These results do not cover the named boards directly or a full MCP implementation. Safe deployment requires schema validation, constrained generation, least-privilege execution, and human escalation for consequential actions.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks small open-weight language models as tool-using agents on CPUs, showing that only Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-0.5B achieve reasonable reliability but at significant memory and latency costs, and that robust JSON output still heavily depends on recovery parsing.
AI.motivation: To enable on-device language model agents on resource-constrained single-board computers, reducing cloud reliance and handling intermittent connectivity, we need to understand how small language models perform as reliable tool users (e.g., MCP-style JSON tool invocation) under CPU-only constraints.
AI.method: The authors evaluate five sub-2B-parameter open-weight models (Phi-1.5, Pythia-1.4B, TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat, Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B) on 100 tool-use prompts covering typical assistant tasks. They test both greedy decoding and nucleus sampling, and apply a recovery parser that strips Markdown fences, extracts JSON-like brace segments, and scores outputs for parseability, correct tool name, complete arguments, and agreement between arguments and values. They also measure CPU memory usage and latency to probe resource needs.
AI.result: Qwen2.5-1.5B is the most reliable, reaching 75% success with greedy decoding and 79% with sampling. Qwen2.5-0.5B gets 72% with greedy decoding but drops sharply to 32% with sampling. Phi-1.5 fails (0%); Pythia-1.4B and TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat achieve at most 7%. Only 5 of 1,000 raw responses are directly valid JSON, indicating almost total dependence on the recovery parser. On CPU, Qwen2.5-1.5B needs about 7.8 GiB RAM and ~30.8 s mean latency; Qwen2.5-0.5B uses about 3.6 GiB and ~10.6 s, highlighting a trade-off between reliability and resource usage.
AI.conclusion: Among tested sub-2B models, only the Qwen2.5 variants are viable as on-device MCP-style tool agents on CPUs, with the 1.5B model more reliable but significantly heavier than the 0.5B model. However, none of the models reliably emit clean JSON—deployment must assume recovery parsing and add safety layers such as schema validation, constrained decoding, least-privilege tool access, and human oversight for impactful actions; further work is needed to cover specific single-board platforms and full MCP implementations.

title: Encoded Early, Used Late: Where Transformers Begin to Act on an Inferred Partner's Expertise
comment: Published at the Scientific Understanding of Foundation Models (Sci-FM) Workshop at COLM 2026
summary: A transformer can make an attribute linearly decodable in its residual stream at a depth where that attribute does not yet influence the output. This gap between where information is readable and where it is used has been shown for attributes stated directly in the input. We ask whether it also holds for an attribute the model must infer gradually over a conversation, namely how expert its dialogue partner is. Using ExpertCollab, a corpus of multi-turn research-planning dialogues between model-played personas at four expertise levels, we find that partner expertise is most decodable in the early layers and falls to near chance before the midpoint of the network. Counterfactual patching shows that injecting the expertise difference at the layer of peak decodability barely changes a fixed late-layer readout, whereas the same difference injected past the midpoint propagates almost completely, a separation of more than an order of magnitude. A content-matched random control and a probe-free diagnostic place the transition at the same early layer, and a statically specified control attribute stays decodable throughout. An inferred relational attribute is therefore represented well before it becomes causally active, which bounds where any attempt to read out or steer partner-conditioned behavior must intervene. We use one model on a synthetic corpus as an initial demonstration.
