AI.tldr: The paper shows that in a dialogue transformer, an inferred attribute (partner expertise) becomes linearly decodable in early layers long before it actually influences the model’s output, revealing a large gap between representation and causal use.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed that attributes explicitly present in the input are linearly decodable in a transformer’s residual stream at layers where they still do not causally affect the output. It was unknown whether this also holds for harder, gradually inferred attributes that emerge over multi-turn interaction, such as how expert a dialogue partner is. Understanding this is important for interpretability and for knowing where to intervene to steer model behavior conditioned on partner properties.
AI.method: The authors construct ExpertCollab, a synthetic corpus of multi-turn research-planning dialogues between model-simulated personas with four levels of expertise. They run a transformer dialogue model on these conversations and: (1) train linear probes across layers to decode the partner’s expertise from the residual stream; (2) perform counterfactual patching by injecting differences in the internal representation corresponding to expertise at various layers and measuring the effect on a fixed late-layer readout; (3) use a content-matched random control and a probe-free diagnostic to validate that the identified transition layer is not an artifact of probing; and (4) compare to a statically specified control attribute to see how its decodability evolves across layers.
AI.result: They find that the partner expertise attribute is most easily decodable in early layers, with decoding accuracy dropping to near chance before the network’s midpoint. Counterfactual patching reveals that injecting an expertise difference at the early layer where decodability peaks scarcely affects the late-layer readout, whereas the same injection after the midpoint propagates strongly, with more than an order-of-magnitude difference in causal impact. Both the content-matched random control and the probe-free diagnostic locate a similar early transition point. In contrast, a static control attribute remains decodable across all layers.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that an inferred, relational attribute (dialogue partner expertise) is represented robustly in early layers of a transformer long before it becomes causally active for the model’s behavior. There is thus a pronounced separation between where such information is linearly readable and where it begins to influence outputs. This implies that effective readout or steering of partner-conditioned behavior must intervene near or beyond the network’s causal transition point, not merely where the attribute is most decodable. The study, using one model and a synthetic dataset, serves as an initial proof of concept and suggests directions for more general investigations.

title: Beyond Single-Negative Preference: Multi-Negative DPO for LLM-Centric Historical Entity Linking
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown promise for historical entity linking, but preference optimization for this task is often formulated with only one negative candidate per training instance. This discards information from the remaining candidates retrieved for the same mention. We introduce multi-negative direct preference optimisation (MDPO), a reference-based pairwise objective that compares the correct entity with all valid rejected candidates associated with each mention. MDPO preserves the Bradley-Terry formulation of DPO while exploiting the complete candidate set through masked, length-normalised sequence scores. We evaluate MDPO on hipe-2020 and newseye, covering French, German, English, Swedish, and Finnish historical newspaper text. Experiments show that MDPO improves over supervised fine-tuning and single-negative DPO, with particularly strong gains for NIL mentions, semantic ambiguity, OCR noise, and historically difficult names. Further analyses disentangle candidate-generation and selection errors, showing that candidate retrieval remains a key bottleneck for end-to-end entity linking. These results demonstrate that incorporating all within-instance negative candidates is a simple and effective improvement for LLM-based historical entity linking.

AI.tldr: They propose MDPO, a multi-negative direct preference optimization method that leverages all candidate entities per mention to improve LLM-based historical entity linking, outperforming prior approaches and highlighting retrieval as the main remaining bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based historical entity linking methods typically use preference optimization with only a single negative candidate per training instance, wasting information from other retrieved candidates. This limits learning, especially in noisy, ambiguous, or NIL cases common in historical text. The authors aim to design a training objective that fully exploits all retrieved candidates within each instance to improve linking performance in challenging historical newspaper datasets.
AI.method: They introduce Multi-negative Direct Preference Optimization (MDPO), a reference-based pairwise objective extending DPO. For each mention, MDPO compares the sequence score of the correct entity against all valid negative candidates associated with that mention, preserving the Bradley-Terry formulation while using masked, length-normalised sequence scores to handle text length differences. They train LLMs with this objective on historical newspaper datasets (hipe-2020 and newseye) in multiple languages and compare against supervised fine-tuning and standard single-negative DPO. They also perform analyses that separate candidate-generation errors from candidate-selection errors.
AI.result: On hipe-2020 and newseye datasets (French, German, English, Swedish, Finnish historical newspapers), MDPO yields better entity linking performance than both supervised fine-tuning and single-negative DPO, with notable improvements on NIL mentions, semantically ambiguous cases, instances with OCR noise, and historically difficult names. Diagnostic experiments show that, although MDPO strengthens candidate selection, the overall system is still significantly constrained by candidate retrieval quality.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating all within-instance negative candidates into the preference optimization objective is a simple yet effective enhancement for LLM-based historical entity linking. MDPO better leverages available candidate information, improving robustness in noisy and ambiguous historical settings, though further progress depends on improving candidate retrieval to reduce upstream bottlenecks.

title: An Auditable Symbolic-RAG-Generative AI Architecture for Goal-Oriented Conversation Orchestration
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables, Appendices with complete experiments
summary: Goal-oriented conversational systems must answer factual questions, understand visitor-provided information, and advance business objectives without becoming rigid questionnaires. This paper proposes a Symbolic-RAG-Generative architecture centered on the Goal-oriented Retrieval-Augmented Conversation Engine (GRACE). An instruction-constrained Business Goal Compiler transforms business intent into an immutable objective set, normalized priority vector, canonical questions, and initial state vector. At runtime, GRACE receives the complete conversation history, latest visitor message, current state, and grounded answer generated by a separate RAG component. It updates completion only from visitor-authored evidence and selects one contextually modulated follow-up. The core policy maximizes expected business progress subject to a minimum visitor-utility constraint. We formalize the state, monotonic transitions, source separation, question modulation, and constrained policy; present the reference architecture; and define an evaluation comprising 24 English real-estate and 10 Spanish professional-cleaning conversations, totaling 119 protocol-defined visitor turns. Across both domains, GRACE achieves 84.9% exact state-transition accuracy, 91.6% evidence precision, 89.6% evidence recall, 100% monotonicity, and 94.1% terminal-state accuracy. The evaluation establishes compelling symbolic-state performance across standard, multi-goal, RAG-detour, validation, refusal, and robustness scenarios.

AI.tldr: They propose GRACE, a symbolic, goal-oriented conversational engine that integrates with RAG to drive business objectives while preserving conversational flexibility, and show it performs well on two real-world domains.
AI.motivation: Existing goal-oriented chat systems either become rigid, survey-like scripts or overly open-ended LLM agents that may hallucinate, lose track of goals, or mix up user-provided facts with generated content. Businesses need controllable systems that can reliably collect structured information, answer factual questions with external knowledge, and optimize explicit business goals, all while maintaining a natural conversational flow and protecting user utility.
AI.method: They design a Symbolic-RAG-Generative architecture whose core is GRACE, a Goal-oriented Retrieval-Augmented Conversation Engine. First, a Business Goal Compiler converts a high-level business intent into a formal specification: immutable objectives, a normalized priority vector over these objectives, a canonical question set, and an initial state. At runtime, GRACE gets the full dialog history, the latest user message, the current symbolic state, and grounded answers from a separate RAG module. GRACE then (1) updates the symbolic state strictly based on user-authored evidence (not model guesses), ensuring monotonic completion, and (2) selects a single, contextually adapted follow-up question or action according to a policy that maximizes expected business progress subject to a minimum visitor-utility constraint. They formalize all components—state, transitions, source separation between user evidence and RAG, question modulation, and constrained decision policy—and implement a reference architecture.
AI.result: They evaluate GRACE on 24 English real-estate and 10 Spanish professional-cleaning conversations, covering 119 visitor turns that follow predefined protocols across varied scenarios (standard flows, multiple concurrent goals, RAG detours, validation of information, refusals, and robustness tests). GRACE achieves 84.9% exact accuracy in predicting the correct state transition at each turn, 91.6% precision and 89.6% recall for identifying evidence from user messages, 100% monotonicity of state updates (no backtracking or contradiction), and 94.1% accuracy on reaching the correct final (terminal) state for each conversation.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates that a symbolic, compiler-driven goal representation combined with a constrained, evidence-grounded policy and external RAG can yield highly reliable, controllable goal-oriented dialogue. GRACE maintains strict separation between user-provided facts and retrieved content, supports multiple real-world business domains and languages, and sustains strong performance across diverse interaction patterns. This suggests that symbolic-state architectures can effectively bridge business objectives with LLM-based conversational interfaces while preserving both reliability and user experience.

title: An LLM-Associated Register Shift in Korean Journal Abstracts: A Morphology-Aware Excess-Vocabulary Study, 2018-2026
comment: 30 pages, 8 figures, 31 tables. Working paper. Data, code and this version are deposited at Zenodo: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22303588
summary: Excess vocabulary, a word's frequency above its pre-2023 trend, is how the change in scholarly English after 2022 has been measured. We adapt it to Korean with morphological units on 398,296 KCI abstracts (2018-August 2026), with 47,165 Vietnamese abstracts for comparison. Placebo floors are 0.1-2.2 points for the single-word statistic and at most 2.9 for the re-selected split-half set statistic. Korean abstracts show nothing in 2023, onset in late 2024, a rise through 2025 flattening in mid-2026: sisahada "suggest" appears in 21.4% of 2026 abstracts against 5.3% expected; plain verbs like araboda "look into" fall to a quarter of trend. Under stated assumptions the single-word conditional lower bound on LLM-processed abstracts is 3.5%, 10.5% and 16.1% for 2024-2026 and a split-half set bound 7.8%, 20.6% and 33.0%. Holzwarth et al.'s estimator under the same discipline gives 41.9% and 72.1% for 2025-2026. Subject-matter controls reduce but do not remove it: restricting the set to lemmas three language-model annotators all call style leaves 14.7 of the 33.0 points, and pairing each 2026 abstract with its journal's closest base-period abstract leaves 34.1. Tested translation routes do not explain it: the surface marks of translated Korean fall as the markers rise. In the same articles' English abstracts the excess appears a year earlier; where the English side carries none, the Korean shift persists at 30 to 66% of the rate where it does. Control abstracts from three providers reproduce the rising words, with marker turnover consistent with model generations; implied prevalences are scenario-dependent.

AI.tldr: The paper measures how much Korean scholarly writing since 2023 shows language-model-like style shifts by tracking “excess vocabulary,” comparing it to trends and Vietnamese controls.
AI.motivation: To detect and quantify the influence of large language models (LLMs) on Korean academic writing after 2022, using a method parallel to that used for English and checking whether similar stylistic shifts appear and when they start.
AI.method: Adapt the excess-vocabulary metric from English to Korean using morphological units on nearly 400k KCI abstracts (2018–Aug 2026), plus 47k Vietnamese abstracts as a comparison group. Compute placebo floors, track frequency changes in specific verbs and style markers, estimate lower bounds on the share of LLM-processed texts (single-word and split-half methods), compare to Holzwarth et al.’s estimator, control for subject matter and translation effects, and compare Korean vs English abstracts of the same papers and vs control-provider abstracts.
AI.result: Korean abstracts show no excess in 2023, clear onset late 2024, then rapid rise through 2025 and flattening mid-2026. Highly suggestive verbs like sisahada surge well above trend while plain verbs like araboda collapse. Under assumptions, LLM-processed shares are bounded below at low single digits in 2024 but climb to mid-teens by 2026, with split-half bounds reaching one-third and Holzwarth-style estimates exceeding 70% by 2026. Style-only lemmas and journal-matched controls still show strong effects; translation artifacts and Vietnamese controls do not explain the pattern. English abstracts show the shift a year earlier; where English lacks the shift, Korean still partly shows it. Control-provider abstracts mimic the rising markers with turnover typical of model generations.
AI.conclusion: LLM-style language has substantially penetrated Korean scholarly abstracts since late 2024, likely reflecting growing use of LLMs for drafting or editing. The timing, magnitude, robustness to controls, and cross-language comparisons suggest a genuine stylistic shift not attributable to subject-matter change or translation quirks, though precise usage prevalence remains scenario-dependent.

title: PhysMAS: Physics-Grounded Multi-Agent Synthesis of Compositional 4D Gaussians
summary: Efficient, fully automatic, and physically plausible 4D Gaussian synthesis is an important goal for dynamic scene generation. Recent physics-based methods couple 3D Gaussians with the Material Point Method (MPM) to generate physically driven motion, but extending this paradigm to heterogeneous multi-part objects and interacting multi-object scenes remains challenging. Object-level physical assignment collapses distinct parts into a single material state, while one-shot predictions from large language models, vision-language models, or agents neither reliably bind different materials to identified parts nor verify that the resulting MPM configuration is executable. Score Distillation Sampling (SDS)-based parameter optimization, meanwhile, requires repeated per-scene score evaluations and gradient backpropagation, incurring lengthy optimization and potentially yielding suboptimal or unstable solutions. We therefore present PhysMAS, a physics-grounded multi-agent framework. From a motion prompt and four scene views, an Object-Part Scene Agent establishes persistent identities and calls a Material Reasoning Agent for part-wise profiles. It invokes solver-aware skills to bind these identities and profiles to per-particle MPM fields and execute all objects in a shared domain; the framework then screens candidate forward-simulation results. This supports heterogeneous multi-part and interacting multi-object scenes without per-scene diffusion-score backpropagation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with recent physics-based 4D Gaussian baselines that rely on SDS, PhysMAS achieves better semantic alignment and perceived physical plausibility while requiring less runtime.

AI.tldr: PhysMAS is a multi-agent, physics-aware framework that automatically assigns materials and physical properties to parts and objects in 4D Gaussian dynamic scene generation, enabling heterogeneous multi-part and multi-object simulations more robustly and efficiently than SDS-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing physics-based 4D Gaussian methods use the Material Point Method (MPM) but struggle with heterogeneous multi-part objects and interacting multi-object scenes. Object-level physical assignment oversimplifies by merging distinct parts into one material, and one-shot predictions from LLMs or VLMs fail to reliably map materials to parts or ensure that the resulting MPM configuration is actually simulatable. SDS-based optimization is slow and unstable because it needs repeated score evaluations and backpropagation for each scene. A new framework is needed to reason about parts, materials, and solver constraints while being efficient and physically plausible.
AI.method: The authors propose PhysMAS, a physics-grounded multi-agent system. Given a motion prompt and four multi-view images of the scene, an Object-Part Scene Agent identifies objects and their constituent parts, maintains consistent identities, and then queries a Material Reasoning Agent to infer material profiles for each part. Solver-aware skills then map these object/part identities and material profiles onto per-particle MPM fields and run all objects together in a shared simulation domain. The system generates and screens candidate forward-simulation outcomes, selecting those that satisfy semantic and physical plausibility criteria, all without per-scene SDS score backpropagation.
AI.result: In experiments, PhysMAS is compared to recent physics-based 4D Gaussian baselines that rely on Score Distillation Sampling. Across diverse dynamic scenes, PhysMAS achieves stronger semantic alignment with the input motion prompts, produces motions perceived as more physically plausible, and does so with reduced runtime. Quantitative and qualitative results show improvements in both visual/semantic quality and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: PhysMAS demonstrates that a physics-grounded, multi-agent reasoning pipeline can effectively bridge high-level motion prompts and low-level MPM simulations for 4D Gaussian synthesis. By explicitly reasoning about object parts, materials, and solver constraints, it supports heterogeneous multi-part and interacting multi-object scenes without expensive SDS-based optimization, achieving better semantic and physical fidelity with lower computation cost.

title: FramingQA: Does the Question Shape the Answer? Measuring the Compositional Framing Effect
summary: We introduce FramingQA, a benchmark that measures the model sensitivity to question framing across law, medicine, finance, and robotic simulations. Large language models (LLMs) often change their responses to subtle rephrasings that align with an implied stance by users. This can leave users with advice tainted by how they happened to phrase a question rather than by the underlying facts, and the consequences are highly costly in high-stakes domains. Because in the realistic scenarios, both expert practitioners and non-expert users frequently ask LLMs questions containing incomplete or misleading assumptions, models are highly susceptible to those framings. To test this, we inject the framing bias across three nested levels: a framing-biased question phrasing (root), an injected framing-biased premise prepended to a neutral question (propositional), and a premise paired with a framing-biased question (global). Evaluating nine open models (3.8B-70B) across four families, we find that strong per-variant accuracy does not guarantee the robustness across differently phrased questions under the fixed factual information.

AI.tldr: FramingQA is a benchmark to test how sensitive LLMs are to different ways of asking factually equivalent questions in high‑stakes domains.
AI.motivation: LLMs often change their answers when users slightly rephrase questions, especially when the wording implies a particular stance or embeds misleading assumptions. In high‑stakes areas like law, medicine, finance, and robotics, such sensitivity can give users biased or incorrect advice just because of their phrasing, not the facts. There is a need for a systematic way to measure and compare how robust different models are to such framing effects.
AI.method: The authors build a benchmark called FramingQA that spans four high‑stakes domains (law, medicine, finance, robotic simulations). They design questions where the underlying factual situation is fixed but the framing changes. They inject framing bias at three nested levels: (1) root: subtly biased question wording itself; (2) propositional: a biased premise is prepended to an otherwise neutral question; (3) global: a biased premise is combined with a biased question. They then evaluate nine open LLMs (ranging from 3.8B to 70B parameters across four model families) on these differently framed but factually equivalent variants, and measure accuracy per variant and robustness across variants.
AI.result: Across nine open LLMs, many models achieve strong accuracy on individual question variants but fail to maintain consistent, correct answers across differently framed versions of the same factual problem. This shows substantial sensitivity to framing bias despite good per‑prompt performance.
AI.conclusion: Per‑variant accuracy metrics are insufficient to assess the reliability of LLMs in high‑stakes domains because models can still be highly vulnerable to framing effects. Robustness to question framing, under fixed factual content, needs to be explicitly measured and improved, and FramingQA provides a benchmark to do so.

title: EmoMed: An Emotionally-Aware Agent for Multimodal Medical Support with Real-Time Information Retrieval
summary: We present EmoMed - a multimodal medical consultation agent that adapts its responses based on users' emotional states while maintaining clinical accuracy. The system processes text and medical images, detects affect indicators (anxiety, confusion, urgency) from user input, and adjusts response tone, structure, and detail level accordingly. To ensure factual reliability, the agent grounds clinical information through a dual retrieval mechanism: web-based fact-checking and an API-connected, continuously updated medical knowledge base. We evaluate our approach across seven state-of-the-art language models (GPT-4/5, Qwen3, Llama 4, Gemini 2.5, Grok4, Claude3) using comprehensive metrics including LLM-as-judge assessments, MedQA style accuracy tests, BERT Score, safety/helpfulness ratings, and multimodal medical benchmarks. The results demonstrate that emotionally adaptive responses consistently outperform neutral baseline across evaluation dimensions, without compromising clinical accuracy. A controlled user study validated these findings, with participants reporting improved perceived empathy and communication clarity, while maintaining trust in factual accuracy. Source code: https://github.com/NasonovIvan/EmoMed-Agent

AI.tldr: EmoMed is a multimodal, emotionally adaptive medical consultation agent that adjusts its communication style to user emotions while preserving clinical accuracy, using dual retrieval for grounding and evaluated across multiple LLMs and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Telemedicine and AI medical chatbots often respond in a neutral, one-size-fits-all style and may hallucinate or provide outdated medical advice. There is a need for systems that are emotionally aware—able to detect user anxiety, confusion, or urgency—and adapt their responses accordingly, without sacrificing factual and clinical reliability. This paper aims to bridge the gap between empathetic communication and rigorous medical accuracy in multimodal (text + image) settings.
AI.method: The authors design EmoMed, a medical consultation agent that: (1) accepts both text and medical images as input; (2) detects emotional signals such as anxiety, confusion, and urgency; (3) dynamically adjusts tone, structure, and detail level of responses based on detected emotions; and (4) ensures factual correctness via a dual retrieval pipeline combining web-based fact-checking with a continuously updated, API-connected medical knowledge base. They instantiate EmoMed across seven leading LLMs (GPT-4/5, Qwen3, Llama 4, Gemini 2.5, Grok4, Claude3) and evaluate using LLM-as-judge, MedQA-style question accuracy, BERTScore, safety/helpfulness scores, and multimodal medical benchmarks, plus a controlled user study.
AI.result: Across all tested language models, emotionally adaptive responses outperform neutral baselines on a variety of metrics, including perceived empathy, clarity, and overall helpfulness, while maintaining or improving clinical accuracy scores on MedQA-style tests and multimodal benchmarks. Safety ratings remain high, indicating that the emotional adaptation does not lead to unsafe or speculative medical advice. The controlled user study shows that participants prefer EmoMed’s emotionally adaptive responses and report better communication and similar or higher levels of trust in the factual accuracy compared to neutral systems.
AI.conclusion: Emotionally adaptive, multimodal medical agents like EmoMed can significantly improve user experience—especially perceived empathy and clarity—without degrading, and potentially enhancing, clinical accuracy and safety when supported by robust dual retrieval grounding. This suggests that future medical AI systems should jointly optimize for emotional adaptation and factual reliability and that the EmoMed framework and released source code provide a practical blueprint for building such agents.

title: MEMO: Multimodal Evidence Memory Organization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long-running LLM agents rely on external memory to store and reuse information beyond a single context window, yet there is a fundamental tension between the continuous accumulation of interaction trajectories and the limited context capacity. The key challenge in agent memory is therefore not only to retrieve relevant records, but also to select necessary evidence under a given budget and organize it in an appropriate modality. Existing memory readout methods mainly use textual or visual forms. Text preserves high fidelity, but its linear token representation makes contents with different importance compete for the limited context at nearly uniform unit cost. Visual readout renders text into document-like images, which can use two-dimensional layouts to expose structure and emphasize key information, but it may lose fine-grained details during rendering and compression. To address this issue, we propose MEMO, a multimodal evidence memory organization method for LLM agents. MEMO first uses a trained evidence extractor to select relevant memory blocks and form evidence units with source information and presentation requirements. A trained query-conditioned memory manager assigns each unit to a textual, visual, or dual-channel carrier and selects a layout that matches the evidence structure. A deterministic memory construction module then generates the textual package and visual pages. The memory manager is trained with feedback from an offline reader that measures the utility of the guided memory plan, so that retention and presentation decisions align with downstream usage. We evaluate MEMO on four benchmarks, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, LoCoMo, and ALFWorld, with multiple reader backends. The results show that MEMO presents memory more efficiently with fewer memory tokens, improves downstream task performance, and builds more effective working memory under constrained budgets.

AI.tldr: MEMO is a multimodal memory organization framework for long-running LLM agents that allocates evidence to text, visual, or dual channels under a token budget to maximize downstream task performance.
AI.motivation: Long-running LLM agents must store and reuse information across many interactions, but context windows are limited. Existing memory readout methods are either purely textual, which preserves detail but wastes tokens and treats all content with similar token cost, or visual, which leverages 2D layout but may lose fine-grained information. There is no principled way to decide what evidence to keep, how to compress it, and in which modality to present it given a strict token or memory budget. The paper aims to solve this trade-off and improve the efficiency and effectiveness of agent memory.
AI.method: The authors propose MEMO, a multimodal evidence memory organization framework. First, a trained evidence extractor selects relevant memory blocks and groups them into evidence units enriched with source metadata and presentation needs. Then a query-conditioned memory manager, also trained, assigns each unit to textual, visual, or dual-channel form and chooses an appropriate layout that reflects the structure of the evidence. Finally, a deterministic construction module renders the memory into textual packages and visual pages for the LLM. The memory manager is trained offline with supervision from a reader model that evaluates the utility of the proposed memory plan for downstream tasks, aligning retention and presentation decisions with task performance.
AI.result: Experiments on four benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, LoCoMo, and ALFWorld) with different reader backends show that MEMO organizes memory more efficiently, using fewer memory tokens compared to baselines. It consistently improves downstream QA and agent performance and enables more effective working memory under constrained context budgets. Quantitative results indicate better accuracy and efficiency trade-offs versus purely textual or purely visual memory approaches.
AI.conclusion: MEMO demonstrates that a learned, query-conditioned multimodal memory planner that allocates evidence across text and visual channels can significantly enhance the effectiveness of long-term memory for LLM agents. By explicitly modeling what to keep, how to compress it, and in which modality to present it, MEMO better utilizes limited context windows, leading to improved performance on multi-hop reasoning and long-horizon agent tasks. This suggests that multimodal, layout-aware memory design is a promising direction for scalable LLM agents operating under strict context budgets.

title: Agentic Algorithm Engineering: Improving Shared-Memory Exact Minimum Cuts
summary: The minimum cut problem for an undirected edge-weighted graph asks us to divide its set of nodes into two blocks while minimizing the weighted sum of the cut edges. Over the last years, we engineered a range of fast algorithms for this problem. Our fastest exact algorithm uses an inexact algorithm to obtain a better bound for the problem, reductions that depend on this bound, improved data structures and parallel contraction routines. It is available in the open-source package VieCut and, on real-world instances, outperformed the previously fastest solvers by a factor of up to 2.5 sequentially and up to 12.9 when run in parallel. We improve this algorithm using agentic algorithm engineering (AAE), a methodology that we introduce here, in which autonomous large language model agents run the algorithm engineering cycle on an existing code base: they form hypotheses about where running time is lost, implement them, benchmark the result on a fixed instance set and keep or discard the change. Even though we had already tuned our algorithm by hand extensively, the agent finds significant optimizations, in particular on the DIMACS core instances: factors of 1.28 (sequential) and 1.63 (32 threads) on real-world k-cores, and 6.26 and 127 on the DIMACS core instances.

AI.tldr: Paper improves an already state-of-the-art exact minimum cut solver using autonomous LLM-based agentic algorithm engineering, yielding substantial speedups, especially on DIMACS core instances.
AI.motivation: Minimum cut is a fundamental graph problem with many applications. The authors previously engineered a very fast exact solver (VieCut) but want to push performance further. Manual tuning has diminishing returns, so they explore whether autonomous large language model agents can still find non-obvious optimizations in an already highly optimized code base.
AI.method: They introduce Agentic Algorithm Engineering (AAE): autonomous LLM agents repeatedly run the algorithm engineering cycle on the existing VieCut code base. The agents (1) hypothesize where runtime is being spent, (2) implement code modifications, (3) benchmark on a fixed instance set, and (4) accept or discard changes based on performance. The underlying algorithm uses inexact minimum cut to get bounds, bound-dependent reductions, improved data structures, and parallel contraction routines.
AI.result: The baseline VieCut already beat prior solvers by up to 2.5x sequentially and 12.9x in parallel on real-world graphs. With AAE, further speedups are achieved: factors of 1.28 (sequential) and 1.63 (32 threads) on real-world k-core instances, and dramatic factors of 6.26 (sequential) and 127 (32 threads) on DIMACS core instances.
AI.conclusion: Even highly hand-tuned algorithms can still be significantly optimized via autonomous LLM agents running a structured algorithm engineering loop. AAE is a promising methodology for further accelerating complex algorithms and finding non-obvious performance improvements on real-world and benchmark graph instances.

title: Where Should Language Sit in a Multimodal Model? Lessons from What Language Does to Human Perception and Cognition
summary: Language models compute over tokens: language is their input, their output, and increasingly their internal representation. Whether language should keep all of these positions depends on what language does to the system that uses it. The one system with a century of data on that question is the human. We review what language does to human perception, the brain, and thought, and read the same evidence against multimodal models and language models. Throughout, we treat language as a compressor that runs on a shared codebook: a word is an index, the content is in the receiver, and a community maintains the codebook. In humans the compression is measurable, learning the codebook reorganizes the senses, and thought survives the loss of language. We then measure the rule that models apply when two cues disagree, with cue-conflict experiments on six vision-language models and two robot policies. Surviving cues are weighted in the order their reliabilities prescribe, at 11 to 82\% of the ideal observer's slope, and many answers copy the text. One policy family drops a cue that adds no information beyond the others rather than down-weighting it, another keeps it at a weight that fails when the cues conflict, and a visual cue that identifies the task in every training frame is never learned, because the language pathway already fits the data. Language models are the best current models of the human language network, and they have entered the human speech community, shifting word frequencies while alignment narrows their conceptual diversity. We close with seven implications for token-based systems. Language belongs at a model's boundary and in the shared codebook, as in the brain, not as its internal representation; the price of leaving the codebook inside is auditability.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how language, viewed as a compression mechanism using a shared codebook, shapes human cognition and perception, and uses this lens to analyze multimodal and language models, arguing that language should be confined to model boundaries rather than internal representations for better alignment with human cognition and auditability.
AI.motivation: To understand whether language should remain the sole or primary medium for input, output, and internal representation in AI models, particularly as language models become central to AI. The authors leverage extensive evidence from humans—the only system extensively studied in relation to language—to evaluate how language structures perception, brain organization, and thought, and to assess implications for token-based AI systems.
AI.method: Conceptual and empirical analysis in two parts: (1) a review of cognitive neuroscience and psychology findings on how language acts as a compressor over a community-maintained codebook, affects sensory organization, and relates to thought; (2) cue-conflict experiments on six vision-language models and two robot policies, where conflicting language and visual cues are presented to measure how models weight different information sources compared to an ideal observer, including analysis of failure modes in cue integration and learning.
AI.result: In humans, language compression is quantifiable, acquiring the linguistic codebook measurably reorganizes sensory processing, and non-linguistic thought can persist without language. In models, when language and vision cues conflict, models weight cues roughly in accordance with their learned reliabilities but at only 11–82% of ideal-observer performance, with many outputs merely copying text. One robot policy family fully discards cues that add no extra information instead of smoothly down-weighting them; another retains such cues at maladaptive weights under conflict. A consistently informative visual cue present in every training frame is never learned because the language pathway alone suffices to fit the data, indicating overreliance on tokens.
AI.conclusion: Token-based language models best approximate the human language network but also participate in and reshape the human linguistic codebook, e.g., by altering word frequencies while alignment narrows conceptual diversity. The findings suggest that language in AI should function like in humans: as an interface and shared codebook at the system boundary, not as the core internal representation. Keeping the linguistic codebook inside the model harms auditability and encourages overdependence on text, leading to suboptimal cue integration and missed non-linguistic structure. The authors distill seven broader implications for designing multimodal and token-based systems with more human-like and transparent internal organization.

title: Unraveling the Real Working Mechanism and Inherent Flaws of GAE: A Method for Interpreting Transformer Processes from an Economic Perspective
summary: We observe a phenomenon that current algorithmic research in the field of explainable artificial intelligence primarily pursues better performance on several proxy metrics. On the one hand, these proxy metrics themselves are more or less flawed and cannot properly measure the quality of methods. On the other hand, metric-oriented research approaches often lead to the neglect of the rationality and interpretability of the methods themselves. Explainable artificial intelligence is abbreviated as XAI. The metric-driven research paradigm has resulted in a lack of interpretability of the relevant XAI methods themselves. Accordingly, there is a need for interpretability research on XAI methods, which can be playfully referred to as XXAI. This paper is one of our works on XXAI. This paper takes Generic Attention-model Explainability (GAE), a widely influential model interpretation method , or rather, XAI method that represents an important technical route, as the research object, and explores the real working mechanism and flaws of this method as well as the technical route it represents. Based on the conclusions of this study, it may be necessary to re-examine or verify GAE-related methods and their domain applications. We argue that GAE is an interpretation method that focuses on the attention process. After pointing out the working mechanism and flaws of GAE, we propose Cumulative Asset Holdings (CAH), a more reasonable Transformer interpretation method integrating both process-based and feature-based ideas from an economic zero-sum games perspective. In addition, it is worth noting that our method is applicable to models with special tokens, where existing methods may suffer from limitations. The model simplification research method and the analysis of additive operations adopted in this study may provide inspiration for other research works in XAI.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques metric-driven XAI research and deeply analyzes a popular attention-based explanation method (GAE), revealing its flaws and proposing a new, more principled Transformer interpretability method (CAH).
AI.motivation: Current XAI research is largely driven by improving scores on imperfect proxy metrics, which fails to ensure that explanations are truly rational or interpretable. A prominent class of methods—attention-based explainers like GAE—have become influential despite limited understanding of how they actually work or where they fail. The authors aim to inaugurate "XXAI": interpretability of XAI methods themselves, to ensure that explanation tools are trustworthy and conceptually sound.
AI.method: The authors select Generic Attention-model Explainability (GAE) as a representative and influential attention-based XAI method. They conduct a detailed analysis of its actual working mechanism and identify its flaws, including how it treats the attention process and additive operations. They use model simplification techniques and formal reasoning about the attention mechanism to uncover limitations. Based on this analysis, they design Cumulative Asset Holdings (CAH), a new Transformer interpretation method that combines process-based and feature-based explanation ideas, framed through an economic zero-sum game analogy and tailored for models with special tokens.
AI.result: They show that GAE is best understood as a process-focused attention explanation, with concrete weaknesses in how it captures model behavior and in its underlying assumptions. Their analysis implies that many GAE-based methods and applications may need to be re-examined or validated more carefully. They introduce CAH, demonstrate that it yields more reasonable Transformer explanations, and highlight that it works in settings with special tokens where existing methods often struggle. Their methodological choices—model simplification and careful analysis of additive operations—are presented as generally useful tools for scrutinizing XAI methods.
AI.conclusion: The metric-driven paradigm in XAI has produced methods whose own interpretability and soundness are under-examined. By treating XAI methods themselves as objects of interpretation (XXAI), the authors expose conceptual and technical flaws in a widely used attention-based method (GAE). They argue that many GAE-related works should be revisited, and propose CAH as a more principled alternative for interpreting Transformers, especially in the presence of special tokens. Their approach suggests a broader research direction: systematically analyzing and simplifying explanation methods to ensure they are genuinely interpretable and trustworthy, rather than merely optimized for potentially flawed metrics.

title: Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR Technical Report
summary: In recent years, automatic speech recognition (ASR) has witnessed transformative advancements driven by three complementary paradigms: data scaling, model scaling, and deep integration with large language models (LLMs). However, bridging the gap between academic benchmark performance and real-world production utility remains a persistent challenge, particularly in handling diverse regional dialects, dynamic entities and hotwords, long-range contextual information, and disfluent spontaneous speech. In this report, we present Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM-based ASR system designed to address these production demands through a unified, instruction-following framework. The model is built upon the Qwen backbone, and is trained on tens of millions of hours of large-scale speech data. Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR supports transcription across 30 languages and 16 Chinese dialectal varieties spanning eight major dialect regions. Beyond multilingual and dialectal recognition, the model provides production-oriented capabilities including industry-domain entity recognition, hierarchical hotword customization, native single-pass transcription polishing, and long-audio contextual modeling. We further develop a dedicated streaming variant, Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR-Streaming, for latency-sensitive applications. Extensive evaluations on Chinese, English, multilingual, and real-world industrial test sets demonstrate state-of-the-art or highly competitive recognition performance across a broad range of evaluation conditions, with strong performance relative to leading commercial and proprietary systems including GPT-4o Transcribe and Gemini 3.1 Pro.

AI.tldr: Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR is an MoE LLM-based ASR system built on Qwen, trained on tens of millions of hours of speech, supporting 30 languages and 16 Chinese dialects, with production-focused features and SOTA-level performance versus leading commercial systems.
AI.motivation: Despite major progress via data/model scaling and LLM integration, there is still a large gap between benchmark ASR performance and real production needs, especially for dialect diversity, dynamic entities/hotwords, long-range context, and disfluent spontaneous speech. The authors aim to build an ASR system that directly targets these practical challenges in a unified way.
AI.method: They design Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR, a Mixture-of-Experts LLM-based ASR built on the Qwen backbone. It is trained on tens of millions of hours of large-scale speech. The system is multilingual and multi-dialect, supports instruction-following use, and incorporates mechanisms for domain entity recognition, hierarchical hotword customization, single-pass transcription polishing, long-context modeling, and a streaming variant (Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR-Streaming) for low-latency scenarios.
AI.result: On extensive benchmarks covering Chinese, English, multilingual data, and real industrial test sets, Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR achieves state-of-the-art or highly competitive performance. It compares favorably to top commercial/proprietary ASR solutions like GPT-4o Transcribe and Gemini 3.1 Pro under a wide range of evaluation conditions.
AI.conclusion: Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR demonstrates that an MoE LLM-based, instruction-following ASR framework trained at massive scale can effectively bridge the gap between academic benchmarks and production demands. Its broad language/dialect coverage, production-oriented features, and strong empirical results suggest it is a practical, competitive choice for real-world ASR applications, including latency-sensitive ones via the streaming variant.

title: Distance-Aware Attention and Wall-Distance Expert Routing for Transformer-Based 3D Flow Prediction
summary: Transformer surrogates for 3D flow prediction compress an industrial mesh into a small set of tokens from which every prediction point reads. Two operations follow: the retrieval step in which a point gathers information from the compressed representation, and the feed-forward layer that transforms what it retrieved. In current backbones both are blind to where the point sits in the flow. We condition both on wall-related physical signals. Distance-aware cross-attention (DA-CA) reshapes each volume query by its wall distance before retrieval, so that a point deep in the boundary layer draws different geometric information than one in the outer flow. Surface-volume mixture-of-experts (SVMoE) replaces the shared feed-forward layer with a small set of experts, routed by wall distance for volume points and by local geometry for surface points. Neither mechanism is tied to one architecture, so we apply both unchanged to AB-UPT and Transolver-3. On DrivAerML with 50 training cases, DA-CA reduces the volume pressure error by 10.1%, and DA-CA and SVMoE together reduce it by 12.5%; DA-CA improves the near-wall region at some cost in the far region, which SVMoE recovers, and the volume experts settle into near-wall, transition, and free-stream bands without routing supervision. Retrained on 300 cases, the conditioning improves every field quantity, reducing volume pressure and velocity errors by 33.1% and 18.6% on AB-UPT and by 21.4% and 21.3% on Transolver-3. Under Leave-One-Body-Out evaluation on DrivAerNet++, it reduces the volume pressure error on unseen body types by up to 14.2%.

AI.tldr: They enhance transformer-based CFD surrogates by conditioning both attention and feed-forward stages on wall-related physics (wall distance and local geometry), significantly reducing flow-prediction errors, especially near walls, across multiple architectures and datasets.
AI.motivation: Standard transformer surrogates for 3D flow prediction compress the mesh into tokens and use attention and feed-forward layers that are agnostic to where a point lies relative to walls or flow regions. This spatial and physical unawareness limits accuracy, particularly in complex near-wall and boundary-layer regions that are critical in industrial aerodynamics. The authors aim to inject wall-related physical structure into the model so that predictions respect differences between boundary layers, transition regions, and free streams, while remaining architecture-agnostic and effective under limited training data and generalization to unseen geometries.
AI.method: They propose two architecture-agnostic conditioning mechanisms. (1) Distance-aware cross-attention (DA-CA): Each query representing a volume point is reshaped or modulated by its wall distance before performing cross-attention over compressed tokens, allowing points at different wall distances (deep boundary layer vs outer flow) to attend differently to geometric information. (2) Surface-volume mixture-of-experts (SVMoE): They replace the shared feed-forward layer with a small mixture-of-experts; routing is based on wall distance for volume points and local geometry for surface points, letting different experts specialize in distinct flow regimes. They plug these modules into existing transformer surrogates (AB-UPT and Transolver-3) without other architectural changes and train/evaluate on automotive aerodynamics datasets (DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++), including low-data (50 cases), larger-data (300 cases), and Leave-One-Body-Out generalization setups.
AI.result: On DrivAerML with only 50 training cases, DA-CA alone cuts volume pressure error by 10.1%, and DA-CA combined with SVMoE yields a 12.5% reduction. DA-CA especially improves near-wall predictions but can degrade far-field predictions; SVMoE compensates for this and restores far-region accuracy. The learned volume experts self-organize into near-wall, transition, and free-stream bands without explicit supervision of routing. With 300 training cases, the conditioning improves all predicted fields: for AB-UPT, volume pressure and velocity errors drop by 33.1% and 18.6%, and for Transolver-3 by 21.4% and 21.3%, respectively. Under Leave-One-Body-Out testing on DrivAerNet++, the methods reduce volume pressure error on unseen body types by up to 14.2%.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning both attention and feed-forward components of transformer CFD surrogates on wall-related physical information (wall distance and local surface geometry) yields substantial and robust accuracy gains, particularly in the challenging near-wall and boundary-layer regions, while preserving or improving far-field performance. The proposed DA-CA and SVMoE modules are architecture-agnostic, integrate seamlessly into different transformer backbones, and generalize across datasets and unseen geometries, with the mixture-of-experts naturally specializing in distinct flow regimes without explicit supervision.

title: We're Cooked! - Probing LLM Political Alignment Via Conflict-Framed Recipe Translation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for translation tasks, yet their implicit political positioning in such contexts remains understudied. We ask whether a single politically charged framing term, such as aggressor, enemy, neighbour, or coloniser is sufficient to trigger implicit political alignment in an otherwise apolitical task. We present a fully crossed factorial study in which eight models spanning Western, Chinese, and European origins are prompted to translate culturally attributed recipes into a target language left deliberately unspecified. Across 17 languages, four framing conditions, eight models, and 15,680 responses, we find that models do not simply decline or ask for clarification but resolve the ambiguity. Language resolution and reasoning behavior cluster meaningfully along model families: Western models hedge and deflect with vague justifications, Chinese models resolve conflicts silently, and Mistral Large emerges as a distinct profile combining high compliance with conflict-grounded reasoning. Sensitivity to framing terms is consistent across models: even subtle framing variation is sufficient to modulate behavior. Our findings urge caution when deploying LLMs for translation in conflict-adjacent contexts, where implicit political judgments may be made without any signal to the user.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how political framing words in translation prompts cause large language models to implicitly pick political sides, even when the task is ostensibly apolitical.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used for translation, especially in conflict-related or sensitive contexts, there is a risk that they may embed hidden political stances or biases. Current evaluations rarely examine how minimal political cues in prompts (e.g., a single charged word) can steer model behavior and translation choices, leaving a gap in understanding of how LLMs handle politically sensitive ambiguity.
AI.method: The authors design a fully crossed factorial experiment involving eight LLMs from Western, Chinese, and European origins. They prompt these models to translate culturally attributed recipes across 17 languages. The target language is intentionally left ambiguous, and prompts include one of four politically charged framing terms (aggressor, enemy, neighbour, coloniser). They collect 15,680 responses and analyze how models resolve the target-language ambiguity and how their reasoning or justifications vary across model families and framing conditions.
AI.result: All models resolve the ambiguous target language instead of refusing or asking for clarification. Distinct behavioral clusters emerge: Western models tend to hedge and deflect, offering vague justifications; Chinese models quietly resolve conflicts without explicit reasoning; Mistral Large shows a unique pattern of high compliance paired with explicit conflict-aware reasoning. Across all models, even minor changes in the political framing terms significantly affect the models’ translation decisions and explanations.
AI.conclusion: Minimal political framing in otherwise neutral translation tasks can push LLMs to make implicit political judgments without alerting users. Different model families exhibit characteristic strategies for resolving political ambiguity, suggesting that geopolitical and design factors influence alignment behavior. The authors argue that LLM-based translation systems, especially in conflict-adjacent or politically sensitive scenarios, should be deployed with strong caution, transparency, and further auditing for hidden political bias.

title: Elastic Horizon: Discovering the Effective Interaction Frontier in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 12 tables. Accepted to EMNLP 2026
summary: Scaling the interaction horizon-the maximum number of environment interactions per episode-improves LLM agents on long-horizon tasks, and curriculum-based methods that progressively expand the horizon outperform fixed-horizon alternatives. However, existing schedules are open-loop: they monotonically increase the horizon until a manually specified maximum, with no mechanism to detect when further expansion stops helping. We propose the effective interaction frontier hypothesis: a dynamic boundary beyond which additional interactions yield diminishing returns while cost grows linearly. We then introduce Elastic Horizon, a closed-loop controller that tracks this boundary via the 90th percentile of successful trajectory lengths. On AppWorld and BFCL, fixed-horizon sweeps reveal clear saturation plateaus; Elastic Horizon stabilizes the horizon inside the saturation band from both under- and over-capacity initializations, attains the best success rates across 7B and 14B backbones, and saves up to 25% of per-step trajectory tokens. Our work shifts the paradigm from how to scale interaction horizons to when to stop scaling.

AI.tldr: Paper studies when to stop increasing interaction horizon for LLM agents, proposing a closed-loop controller (Elastic Horizon) that adapts horizon based on achieved trajectory lengths to avoid wasteful long episodes.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon tasks benefit from allowing more environment interactions per episode for LLM agents, but existing methods use open-loop curricula that keep increasing this horizon up to a hand-set maximum, with no feedback on whether additional steps still improve performance or just waste computation. There is a need to understand and automatically detect the point at which extra horizon yields diminishing returns.
AI.method: Formulate the effective interaction frontier hypothesis, positing a dynamic boundary where increased horizon ceases to provide substantial gains. Implement Elastic Horizon, a closed-loop control scheme that adjusts the interaction horizon online using statistics of successful trajectory lengths, specifically targeting the 90th percentile, so that the allowed horizon tracks the saturation region instead of growing unbounded. Evaluate via fixed-horizon sweeps to identify saturation plateaus and then test Elastic Horizon on benchmarks such as AppWorld and BFCL with different LLM backbone sizes (7B, 14B).
AI.result: Empirical fixed-horizon sweeps show saturation plateaus, confirming the existence of an effective interaction frontier. Elastic Horizon converges the interaction horizon into this saturation band whether starting from too small or too large a horizon, consistently achieving the highest success rates across both 7B and 14B models and reducing trajectory token usage by up to 25% per step compared with open-loop or fixed-horizon baselines.
AI.conclusion: Interaction horizon should be treated as a dynamically controlled resource, not just scaled up monotonically. By estimating and tracking an effective interaction frontier based on actual agent trajectories, Elastic Horizon automatically stops horizon growth when it becomes inefficient, improving success rates while cutting computational cost and reframing horizon design from a static hyperparameter to a feedback-driven control problem.

title: Validating DBpedia Triple Sets for Natural Language Generation
summary: We present a study of the quality of individual DBpedia triples from the perspective of Natural Language Generation, and propose and evaluate an approach for collecting entity-specific triple sets that filters out questionable triples while minimizing the loss of correct ones. We show in an evaluation against manually annotated data that with validation rules, it is possible to reach 98% precision in triple selection, and with improvements to a few Property definitions, it is possible to improve recall by 40% without harming precision.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to automatically select high-quality DBpedia triples for NLG and proposes validation rules that achieve very high precision while improving recall via better property definitions.
AI.motivation: Natural Language Generation systems that verbalize knowledge base content need reliable, correct triples. DBpedia contains noisy or questionable triples that can lead to incorrect or unnatural text. There is a need for methods that can automatically filter out problematic triples for specific entities while retaining as many correct triples as possible.
AI.method: The authors analyze the quality of individual DBpedia triples from an NLG perspective and design validation rules that determine whether a triple for a given entity should be kept or filtered out. They then apply these rules to collect entity-specific triple sets and compare the system’s selected triples against manually annotated gold-standard data. Additionally, they explore how refining the definitions of certain properties affects recall and precision.
AI.result: Using their validation rules, they achieve 98% precision in selecting DBpedia triples, meaning almost all selected triples are correct. By improving the definitions of a small number of properties, they can increase recall by 40% while maintaining this high precision level.
AI.conclusion: Carefully designed validation rules can effectively filter DBpedia triples for NLG, yielding very high precision. Furthermore, modest refinements to property definitions significantly increase recall without sacrificing precision, making the approach practical for building higher-quality input datasets for NLG systems.

title: SkillAlign: Aligning Skill Interfaces for LLM-based Agents
summary: Language-model agents increasingly rely on skills: reusable procedural knowledge for reasoning, tool use, and interaction. Existing work studies how skills are acquired, retrieved, compressed, or composed, but often assumes that once a skill is selected, its interface to the agent is fixed. We argue that this overlooks a key source of skill utility: the same skill can help, distract, or mislead depending on how it is exposed. We propose SkillAlign, a provider-agnostic framework that represents candidate skills as multi-view procedural cards and renders them through alternative exposure interfaces, including full instructions, hints, compressed summaries, workflows, or no exposure. This enables counterfactual evaluation where the task, agent, and candidate skills are fixed while only the exposure interface varies. Across ALFWorld and SkillsBench, we show that exposure form substantially affects task success and rendered context cost, and that compact top-k exposure can outperform full-library injection. We further conduct a replay-based policy-learning analysis on ALFWorld, showing that adaptive exposure contains learnable signal but remains far from oracle selection. Our results suggest that skill-augmented agents should optimize not only which skills to use, but also how those skills are presented.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SkillAlign, a framework for studying how different ways of exposing skills to language-model agents (full instructions, hints, summaries, workflows, or none) affect performance and context cost.
AI.motivation: Most prior work on skills for language-model agents assumes that once a skill is selected, its interface is fixed, ignoring that the way a skill is shown to the agent can help, distract, or mislead. The authors want to understand and optimize not just which skills are used, but how they are presented to the agent.
AI.method: They design SkillAlign, a provider-agnostic framework that encodes candidate skills as multi-view procedural cards. These cards can be rendered in different exposure interfaces (full instructions, hints, compressed summaries, workflows, or hidden). By holding the task, agent, and candidate skills constant and only varying the exposure interface, they perform counterfactual evaluations on benchmarks like ALFWorld and SkillsBench. They also run a replay-based policy-learning analysis on ALFWorld to study adaptive exposure policies.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and SkillsBench show that the form of skill exposure strongly influences both task success and the cost of the rendered context. Compact top-k exposure strategies can even outperform naive full-library injection. The replay-based policy-learning analysis indicates that adaptive exposure strategies contain learnable signal, but are still far from an oracle that always picks the best exposure.
AI.conclusion: Skill-augmented agents should be designed to optimize not only which skills they use but also how these skills are exposed to the model. The exposure interface is a crucial and under-explored factor in leveraging procedural skills effectively, with potential gains in both performance and efficiency.

title: ObGynLongBench: Revealing the Evidence-to-EHR Gap in Longitudinal EHR Decision-Making
summary: The application of large language models (LLMs) to personalized medical assistants has garnered growing interest. However, existing medical benchmarks largely rely on static question answering with pre-selected evidence, leaving unclear whether LLMs can make reliable clinical decisions from real longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs). To bridge this gap, we introduce ObGynLongBench, a rule-grounded long-context EHR benchmark for obstetric and gynecologic decision-making, comprising 1,500 clinical decision-point cases from 976 real pregnancy EHR histories and traceable rules. Each case is anchored to a patient, a pregnancy-timeline point, and a pre-decision information boundary, enabling Evidence-only, Visit-level EHR, and History-level EHR evaluation. Evaluating 17 LLMs reveals a substantial Evidence-to-EHR Gap: models perform well when evidence is directly provided, but accuracy drops when evidence must be extracted from same-day records or full pre-decision EHR histories. Further analyses identify evidence utilization as a key bottleneck: performance decreases with longer EHR contexts and more complex evidence requirements, and earlier failures often predict later failures within the same patient history. Finally, active-search agents perform best among EHR access strategies, highlighting patient-specific evidence utilization as a central challenge for reliable personalized medical assistants. Resources are available at https://github.com/xiangjun2003/ObgynLongbench.

AI.tldr: ObGynLongBench is a new benchmark that tests how well large language models make obstetric/gynecologic decisions from real, long-term EHRs, showing a big drop in performance when models must find and use evidence in full records instead of being given curated evidence directly.
AI.motivation: Most current medical LLM benchmarks rely on short, static QA with hand-selected evidence, which does not reflect the real clinical setting where models must read and reason over long, messy longitudinal EHRs. It is unclear whether LLMs can reliably support patient-specific decision-making from such records, especially in obstetrics and gynecology, where decisions depend heavily on pregnancy timelines and prior history. The authors aim to create a realistic, rule-grounded benchmark to systematically evaluate and diagnose LLM performance in this setting.
AI.method: The authors construct ObGynLongBench, a long-context EHR benchmark focused on obstetric and gynecologic decisions. They curate 1,500 clinical decision-point cases drawn from 976 real pregnancy EHR histories, each linked to explicit, traceable decision rules. Every case is tied to a specific patient, a time point on the pregnancy timeline, and a pre-decision information boundary so that only prior data are accessible. They define multiple evaluation modes—Evidence-only, Visit-level EHR, and History-level EHR—to vary how much of the underlying record the model must search. They then evaluate 17 LLMs under these settings and also test different EHR access strategies, including active-search agents, to study how models locate and use relevant evidence.
AI.result: Across 17 LLMs, accuracy is high when the key evidence is explicitly provided (Evidence-only mode), but drops markedly when models must locate evidence within same-day visit notes or in the entire pre-decision longitudinal EHR, revealing a pronounced Evidence-to-EHR performance gap. Performance degrades as EHR context length increases and as evidence requirements become more complex, indicating poor scalability of evidence utilization. The authors also observe that failures tend to persist along a patient’s timeline: if a model fails at earlier decision points, it is likely to fail at later ones for the same patient. Among EHR access strategies, active-search agents—systems that iteratively search within the record—achieve the best results, though they still face challenges.
AI.conclusion: ObGynLongBench demonstrates that current LLMs struggle not with medical knowledge in isolation, but with finding and using patient-specific evidence in long, real-world EHRs. The benchmark exposes a significant Evidence-to-EHR gap and shows that evidence utilization, particularly over long contexts and complex requirements, is a central bottleneck for building reliable personalized medical assistants in obstetrics and gynecology. Active-search approaches help but do not fully solve the problem, underscoring the need for improved methods for patient-specific retrieval, reasoning over timelines, and robust decision-making from longitudinal clinical data.

title: World Models Under Asynchronous Sensor Observations
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures. All authors contributed equally
summary: Learned world models typically assume that observations arrive synchronously, an abstraction inherited from simulators that return a complete state vector at each environment step. Physical sensing instead operates at heterogeneous rates, leaving most observation channels stale at any given instant. Interpolating stale channels introduces measurements that were never observed, while downsampling to the slowest sensor discards valid measurements. A natural alternative is to zero-order-hold the most recent reading and provide the known sampling schedule to the model through two features, staleness and time-to-refresh. We test this prediction using transformer world models across three regimes of increasing causal coupling: open-loop rollouts in continuous-control locomotion, closed-loop model-predictive planning in which each learned model serves as the planner dynamics, and a linear latched-actuator system in which refresh events apply a zero-order-held command to the plant. Our findings show that the effectiveness of time-to-refresh depends on the causal role of the sampling schedule, specifically when refresh events affect the system rather than merely report its state. These results establish when sampling schedules provide useful information for predictive world models operating under asynchronous physical observations.

AI.tldr: Paper studies how to handle asynchronous, heterogeneous-rate sensor observations in learned world models and when sampling schedules help prediction.
AI.motivation: Most learned world models assume synchronous observations, but real physical sensors operate at different and asynchronous rates. Common fixes like interpolation or downsampling either fabricate data or throw away valid measurements. The authors want a principled way to use all real data while modeling how sensor timing and refresh events influence dynamics.
AI.method: They propose representing asynchronous sensing via zero-order hold of each sensor’s last value plus two explicit timing features per channel: staleness (time since last refresh) and time-to-refresh (time until next sample). They train transformer-based world models under this scheme and evaluate across three regimes with different causal roles of the sampling schedule: (1) open-loop rollouts in continuous-control locomotion tasks; (2) closed-loop model-predictive control where the learned model is used as the planning dynamics; and (3) a linear system with latched actuators where refresh events change the physical plant input via held commands.
AI.result: Across experiments, adding time-to-refresh is not universally helpful. Its benefit depends on whether the sampling schedule causally influences the underlying system, e.g., when refresh events trigger actuation as in the latched-actuator setup. When the schedule only determines when sensors report but does not affect the dynamics, time-to-refresh provides limited or no advantage beyond staleness and zero-order hold.
AI.conclusion: Sampling schedules carry useful information for predictive world models only when refresh events causally affect the system dynamics, not merely when they control observation timing. Zero-order-holding measurements plus explicit staleness is generally sufficient for asynchronous sensing, while time-to-refresh becomes important in systems where refresh events also modify actuation or other causal mechanisms.

title: The Art of Hierarchical Competing Patterns: Gaussian Process Optimization of Hyphenation
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures, 9 tables. Accepted at EMNLP 2026 (Findings). Code and data: https://github.com/ondrejsojka/pat-gen-opt
summary:
Hyphenation patterns remain a compact and widely deployed solution for word breaking in typesetting systems, text processors, and web rendering engines, but their generation still depends on manually tuned patgen program parameter profiles. We formulate patgen profile selection as a black-box hyperparameter optimization problem and evaluate Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization for this task. The search objective combines a precision-oriented F_{1/7}-score with an explicit trie size-accuracy trade-off using a normalized trie-size penalty.
  We evaluate the method on 17 hyphenated word-list datasets covering 14 languages and multiple scripts. Against two strong hand-tuned profiles regenerated from the same 8/10 training split and evaluated on the same 1/10 held-out test split, the GP-optimized profiles improve F_{1/7} on 16 of 17 datasets and reduce trie size on all 17. The median optimized/baseline trie ratio is 0.407. A dataset-level sign test gives p = 1.37e-4; a separate budget-matched comparison on five representative datasets shows that systematic search is competitive and usually improves over the best hand-tuned profile under the fixed comparison objective. The results show that model-based optimization can make pattern generation more reproducible and less dependent on expert trial-and-error while keeping the accuracy-compactness trade-off explicit.

AI.tldr: The paper uses Bayesian optimization to automatically tune hyphenation pattern generation parameters, outperforming manually tuned profiles in both accuracy and compactness across many languages.
AI.motivation: Hyphenation patterns are crucial for proper word breaking in typesetting and rendering systems. Currently, generating these patterns with the patgen program requires manual, expert-driven tuning of parameter profiles, which is time-consuming, non-reproducible, and difficult to transfer across languages. There is a need for an automatic, principled way to select patgen parameters that balances accuracy and pattern compactness.
AI.method: The authors cast the choice of patgen parameters as a black-box hyperparameter optimization problem. They apply Gaussian-process-based Bayesian optimization to search over patgen profiles. The optimization objective combines a precision-focused F_{1/7} score with a normalized penalty term that reflects the size of the resulting trie, explicitly managing the trade-off between hyphenation accuracy and pattern compactness. They train on 8/10 of each dataset, validate on 1/10, and test on the remaining 1/10, running the Bayesian optimizer over this setup for multiple language datasets.
AI.result: On 17 hyphenated word-list datasets in 14 languages and various scripts, the Gaussian-process-optimized patgen profiles outperform two strong hand-tuned baselines. The optimized profiles improve F_{1/7} on 16 out of 17 datasets and reduce trie size on all 17, with a median optimized-to-baseline trie-size ratio of 0.407. A dataset-level sign test yields p = 1.37e-4, supporting the statistical significance of the improvements. A separate, budget-matched comparison on five representative datasets shows that Bayesian optimization is competitive with and often better than the best manually tuned profiles under the same objective.
AI.conclusion: Model-based, Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization is an effective method for automatically tuning patgen parameter profiles for hyphenation pattern generation. It yields more accurate and substantially more compact pattern tries than expert-crafted profiles, with statistically significant gains across many languages. The approach makes pattern generation more reproducible, reduces dependence on expert trial-and-error, and maintains an explicit, controllable trade-off between accuracy and compactness.

title: Weakly supervised neural network: segmentation of complex structures in X-ray microCT
summary: Segmentation of complex structures in X-ray tomographic data is a fundamental task in biomedical research, but it often requires large amounts of precisely annotated data, making fully supervised approaches costly and difficult to scale. In this study, weakly supervised deep learning is investigated as a strategy to reduce annotation effort while maintaining accurate segmentation. A two-dimensional convolutional neural network based on the nnU-Net framework was adapted to a weak supervision setting using sparse dot-based annotations, complemented by a limited number of fully segmented images. The approach was evaluated on high-resolution microCT slices of rat kidneys, targeting the segmentation of renal glomeruli, which are small, low-contrast anatomical structures. Results indicate that weak supervision provides a meaningful learning signal, enabling reliable localization of glomeruli even in the absence of dense labels. Incorporating a small set of high-quality annotations substantially improves segmentation performance, approaching that of a fully supervised model. These findings highlight the potential of weakly supervised learning as an annotation-efficient strategy for the analysis of complex structures in X-ray tomographic data, and suggest that alternative loss formulations tailored to sparse annotations may further enhance performance.
