AI.tldr: Weakly supervised nnU-Net using sparse dot annotations plus few full masks can accurately segment renal glomeruli in microCT, approaching fully supervised performance while reducing labeling cost.
AI.motivation: Manual dense annotation for segmenting complex structures in high-resolution X-ray tomographic (microCT) biomedical data is expensive and hard to scale, especially for small, low-contrast targets like renal glomeruli. The authors aim to reduce annotation cost while retaining high segmentation quality by exploiting weakly supervised learning that can learn from cheaper, sparse labels.
AI.method: Adapt a 2D convolutional neural network derived from nnU-Net to a weakly supervised regime where most training data have only sparse dot-based annotations for target structures, supplemented by a limited number of fully segmented images. Train and evaluate this model on microCT slices of rat kidneys for glomeruli segmentation, exploring loss functions and training strategies that make use of sparse labels as a learning signal.
AI.result: The weakly supervised model trained primarily on sparse dot annotations was able to reliably localize glomeruli, demonstrating that sparse labels alone provide a useful learning signal. When a small set of densely annotated images was added, segmentation performance significantly improved and came close to that of a fully supervised nnU-Net trained on extensive dense labels.
AI.conclusion: Weakly supervised deep learning with sparse dot-based annotations, augmented with a small number of full masks, can achieve near–fully supervised performance for segmenting small, low-contrast structures in X-ray tomographic data, offering a more annotation-efficient alternative. The study suggests that further gains are likely possible by designing loss functions specifically tailored to sparse supervision.

title: Syntactic Patterns and Stylistic Functions in Narrative Prose: A Rule-Based and Machine-Learning Approach
comment: Submitted as a Discussion Paper to JOHD (Journal of Open Humanities Data), 2026
summary: This paper presents a small-scale quantitative experiment that links syntactic structure to stylistic functions in narrative prose. Starting from a dependency-parsed corpus of 3,300 sentences, we derive sentence-level stylistic labels across five categories --- descriptive, introspective, causal, ideological, and neutral --- using a transparent rule-based procedure that inspects lemmas, universal part-of-speech tags, and syntactic relations. For each sentence we construct a compact representation of its syntactic profile as a sequence of linearised triples combining lemma, POS tag, and dependency relation. These patterns serve as input to standard machine-learning classifiers trained to predict sentence-level style. The best-performing model achieves a macro-F1 of 0.948 under 10-fold cross-validation. The experiment is implemented entirely in Python using open-source tools. Our goal is not to propose a fully fledged stylistic theory, but to offer a reproducible and extensible workflow for exploring how grammatical structure contributes to narrative interpretation.

AI.tldr: They build a syntactic-profile-based classifier to label narrative sentences into five stylistic functions with high accuracy, showing a practical workflow for connecting grammar to style.
AI.motivation: To understand and systematically explore how grammatical structure contributes to different stylistic functions in narrative prose (e.g., description vs introspection), and to provide a reproducible way to study this link rather than a full stylistic theory.
AI.method: They take a dependency-parsed corpus of 3,300 narrative sentences. Using a transparent rule-based procedure over lemmas, universal POS tags, and dependency relations, they assign each sentence one of five stylistic labels: descriptive, introspective, causal, ideological, or neutral. For each sentence, they build a compact representation of its syntactic profile as a linearised sequence of triples (lemma, POS, dependency relation). These sequences are fed into standard machine-learning classifiers trained to predict the sentence’s stylistic category. Performance is evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation.
AI.result: The best classifier, using the syntactic-profile representations, achieves a macro-F1 score of 0.948 across the five stylistic categories under 10-fold cross-validation, indicating very strong predictive performance from grammatical patterns alone.
AI.conclusion: A relatively simple, transparent pipeline—from dependency parsing through rule-based stylistic labelling to syntactic-profile-based classification—can effectively model stylistic functions at the sentence level in narrative prose. While not claiming to be a complete theory of style, the approach demonstrates that grammatical structure carries rich signals about narrative function and offers a reproducible, extensible workflow for future stylistic research.

title: DGCPath: Distribution-Aware Generative Contrastive Framework for Self-supervised Path Representation Learning -- Extended Version
comment: This paper is an extended version of DGCPath, which was published at IJCAI 2026
summary: Due to the proliferation of vehicle trajectory data enabled by advanced sensing technologies, path representation learning has become a pivotal task in intelligent transportation systems. Although existing self-supervised approaches have achieved promising performance, their dependence on deterministic contrastive learning paradigms and handcrafted view augmentation strategies inherently restricts their cross-scenario generalization capabilities. To address these limitations, we present DGCPath, an innovative Distribution-aware Generative Contrastive learning framework for Path representation. This framework establishes a synergistic connection between generative modeling and distributional contrastive learning, enabling the acquisition of robust and transferable feature embeddings. Specifically, our framework incorporates: (1) a diffusion-based view generator that autonomously produces semantically coherent yet diverse trajectory views from Gaussian noise; (2) a variational contrastive mechanism that enforces latent feature alignment at the distribution level, transcending conventional instance-wise consistency; and (3) a novel generative cross-supervision module that reinforces view-level consistency through cross-view reconstruction learning. Comprehensive evaluations on three real-world trajectory datasets demonstrate that DGCPath outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on two distinct downstream tasks, validating its enhanced generalization capability and representation effectiveness.

AI.tldr: Proposes DGCPath, a distribution-aware generative contrastive learning framework that uses diffusion-based view generation, variational contrastive learning, and generative cross-supervision to learn robust, transferable path representations from vehicle trajectories, outperforming prior methods on multiple datasets and tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised trajectory/path representation methods rely on deterministic contrastive learning and manually designed data augmentations, which limit how well learned representations generalize across different scenarios. There is a need for a framework that can automatically generate rich trajectory views and align representations at the distribution level to improve robustness and transferability.
AI.method: The paper introduces DGCPath, which couples generative modeling with distributional contrastive learning. (1) It employs a diffusion-based generator to synthesize diverse, semantically consistent trajectory views from Gaussian noise instead of hand-crafted augmentations. (2) It applies a variational contrastive mechanism that aligns latent features at the distribution level (e.g., via variational inference on latent distributions) rather than just enforcing instance-wise similarity. (3) It adds a generative cross-supervision module that performs cross-view reconstruction, where one view is reconstructed from another, enforcing consistency and richer supervision across generated views.
AI.result: On three real-world vehicle trajectory datasets and two different downstream tasks, DGCPath achieves superior performance compared with state-of-the-art self-supervised and contrastive learning baselines, indicating improved representation quality and better cross-scenario generalization.
AI.conclusion: Integrating diffusion-based generative view creation, distribution-level contrastive learning, and cross-view generative supervision yields more robust and transferable path representations for vehicle trajectories, improving performance across datasets and tasks and suggesting a promising direction for self-supervised learning in intelligent transportation systems.

title: How AI Models Manage Epistemic Authority: A Taxonomy and Comparative Analysis of Responses to User Disagreement
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as sources of advice and information, including in high-stakes settings, yet little is known about how they respond to user disagreement. We study how a model manages its epistemic authority, referring here to its claim to knowledge, competence, or the right to advise, once a user challenges its answer. Building on Conversation Analysis, we introduce a taxonomy of six challenge types and a four-layer framework for analysing each response: whether the original claim is maintained or changed, where authority is located, how the disagreement is socially managed, and what kind of evidential support is offered. We construct a new dataset of 2,310 controlled challenge scenarios and 32,340 corresponding responses from 14 models, and analyse them using our framework with an LLM-as-judge pipeline, providing a vocabulary which future evaluation and benchmark design can build on. We find that models show conflicting behaviour: they validate users in 85% of responses but maintain their original claim in 65%. They explicitly apologise in 33% of responses, yet 59% of those apologies accompany maintenance of the original claim. They transfer authority most often in advice tasks, doing so in 28% of responses and reaching 57% in health advice and 49% in legal advice, compared with 6% in fact and 3% in explanation tasks. Abandonment of the original claim ranges from 0.8% for GPT-5.2 to 40% for DeepSeek 7B, while complete replacement of the original claim is rare overall at 1.5%.

AI.tldr: The paper examines how large language models handle user disagreement and manage their perceived authority when challenged, proposing a framework and dataset to systematically evaluate their responses.
AI.motivation: As large language models are increasingly used for advice and information in high-stakes domains, it is crucial to understand not only the accuracy of their answers but also how they react when users challenge them, since this shapes trust, safety, and appropriate reliance on the models.
AI.method: The authors develop a taxonomy of six types of user challenges and a four-layer analytic framework focusing on claim maintenance vs change, authority location, social management of disagreement, and evidential support. They then construct a dataset of 2,310 controlled challenge scenarios and collect 32,340 responses from 14 LLMs. Using an LLM-as-judge pipeline, they annotate and analyse these responses according to their framework.
AI.result: Models frequently validate users (85% of responses) but still maintain their original claim in most cases (65%). Apologies are common (33% of responses), but a majority of those apologies (59%) co-occur with maintaining the original claim rather than revising it. Models shift authority most often in advice tasks (28% overall, 57% in health and 49% in legal advice) and far less in fact (6%) or explanation (3%) tasks. Rates of abandoning the original claim vary dramatically across models—from as low as 0.8% (GPT-5.2) to as high as 40% (DeepSeek 7B)—while completely replacing the original claim is rare (1.5% overall).
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that LLMs exhibit complex and sometimes inconsistent patterns in managing epistemic authority under challenge: they often offer social alignment (validation and apologies) without substantive revision of their claims, and their willingness to defer authority depends strongly on task type and model. The proposed taxonomy, framework, and dataset provide a systematic basis for future benchmarks and for designing models that handle disagreement and authority in more transparent and appropriate ways.

title: AAS-RAIL: Improving Information Extraction for Asset Administration Shells through Retrieval-Augmented In-Context Learning
summary: The Asset Administration Shell (AAS) is a cornerstone of Industry 4.0 and the Digital Product Passport, providing standardized digital representations of industrial assets. While manufacturers already maintain extensive technical product documentation, generating AAS instances from existing product datasheets remains a labor-intensive task because technical information is extracted from heterogeneous document structures and often involves company-specific terminology and conventions. In this work, we present AAS-RAIL, a retrieval-augmented information extraction (IE) approach that automatically generates Asset Administration Shells from PDF product datasheets using large language models (LLMs). Instead of relying on a fixed set of few-shot examples, the proposed retrieval-augmented in-context learning (RAIL) approach retrieves LLM-generated extraction helpers from similar Asset Administration Shells to provide instance-specific in-context learning (ICL). This enables the model to adapt its extraction behavior to company-specific naming conventions and formatting styles without fine-tuning. Our core contribution is the dynamic selection of company-specific AAS examples for each datasheet, replacing static prompting with an extraction pipeline that adapts to instances and combines semantic retrieval and structured information extraction. The proposed approach is evaluated on a collection of industrial product datasheets using a selection of open- and closed-weight LLMs. Experimental results show that RAIL consistently improves extraction quality over conventional few-shot prompting, yielding relative improvements of 30.4-52.4%. These results demonstrate that our approach provides an effective improvement for company-specific AAS generation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AAS-RAIL, a retrieval-augmented information extraction system that uses large language models to automatically generate Asset Administration Shells from heterogeneous PDF product datasheets, significantly improving extraction accuracy over standard few-shot prompting.
AI.motivation: Creating Asset Administration Shells (AAS) is crucial for Industry 4.0 and Digital Product Passports, but current practice requires manual, error-prone extraction of technical data from heterogeneous, company-specific product datasheets. Existing LLM-based extraction typically relies on fixed few-shot prompts that do not adapt to company-specific terminology, formatting, and document structure, leading to limited performance and scalability. The authors aim to automate and improve AAS generation without costly model fine-tuning while handling diverse, proprietary documentation styles.
AI.method: The authors propose AAS-RAIL, a retrieval-augmented information extraction approach centered on retrieval-augmented in-context learning (RAIL). The system takes PDF product datasheets, parses them, and uses semantic retrieval to find similar existing Asset Administration Shell instances and associated LLM-generated “extraction helpers.” These helpers capture how relevant attributes were previously extracted for similar products or companies. For a new datasheet, RAIL dynamically selects the most relevant AAS examples and helpers and injects them into the LLM prompt to guide extraction, instead of using a static few-shot prompt. The pipeline combines document parsing, semantic similarity search over a library of AAS examples, construction of an instance-specific prompt, and structured information extraction into a new AAS instance, all without fine-tuning the underlying LLM. The approach is tested with multiple open- and closed-weight LLMs.
AI.result: On a dataset of industrial product datasheets, AAS-RAIL is compared against conventional few-shot prompting baselines for generating Asset Administration Shells. Across different LLM backends, RAIL consistently outperforms static few-shot methods, achieving relative improvements in extraction quality of 30.4–52.4%. This indicates more accurate mapping of fields, better handling of company-specific terminology, and more robust extraction from heterogeneous document layouts.
AI.conclusion: AAS-RAIL demonstrates that retrieval-augmented in-context learning, driven by dynamically selected company-specific AAS examples and extraction helpers, can substantially improve automatic generation of Asset Administration Shells from unstructured product datasheets. The method adapts to diverse naming conventions and formatting styles without fine-tuning, making it more scalable and practical for industrial deployment. The authors conclude that RAIL is an effective step toward automated, high-quality, company-specific AAS generation and can be integrated into Industry 4.0 workflows and Digital Product Passport creation.

title: Perspectives on Cross-Lingual Consistency in LLMs for Medical Questions
summary: Should multilingual LLMs answer medical questions consistently across input languages, or adapt responses to cultural cues? Existing multilingual medical benchmarks usually assume that medically correct answers should remain consistent across languages and treat cross-lingual variation as model error. In contrast, cultural adaptation research argues that appropriate medical answers may legitimately differ across contexts. We review the multilingual medical NLP literature through these two perspectives, we identify three gaps: limited stakeholder perspectives (e.g., of medical professionals), a lack of empirical evidence on which approach better serves users, and no benchmarks capable of distinguishing universally correct from culture-specific cases. To address the first gap, we survey 356 participants across three stakeholder groups (medical, NLP, and anthropology professionals) in three countries (Germany, Spain, and the United States). Anthropologists consistently favor adaptation, while medical and NLP respondents remain divided, with notable divergence between U.S. and European medical professionals. LLMs prompted with profession and country personas fail to reproduce this variation, overestimating cross-lingual consistency preference among NLP and medical personas. We conclude that neither consistency nor adaptation can currently be considered clearly preferable, highlighting the need for empirical evidence on which approach better serves users across cultural contexts.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether multilingual medical LLMs should give the same answers across languages or adapt to cultural context, showing that expert stakeholders disagree and that current LLM persona prompting does not capture this variation.
AI.motivation: Multilingual medical LLMs are deployed globally, but it is unclear whether they should enforce cross-lingual consistency in medical advice or culturally adapt their responses. Existing benchmarks usually equate variation with error, while cultural adaptation work suggests context-dependent correctness. There is a lack of stakeholder perspectives, empirical evidence on user benefit, and benchmarks that separate universal from culture-specific medical norms.
AI.method: The authors conceptually contrast two paradigms—cross-lingual consistency vs. cultural adaptation—and review multilingual medical NLP literature under these lenses. To fill the stakeholder gap, they conduct a survey with 356 participants from three expert groups (medical, NLP, anthropology) across three countries (Germany, Spain, United States) to elicit preferences about consistency vs. adaptation in medical responses. They also evaluate multilingual LLMs prompted with profession and country personas to see whether model preferences align with human stakeholders.
AI.result: Anthropologists consistently prefer culturally adaptive medical responses. Medical and NLP stakeholders are split, with U.S. and European medical professionals showing notably different patterns of preference. When LLMs are prompted with expert and country personas, they fail to reproduce these nuanced variations and tend to overestimate the preference for cross-lingual consistency among medical and NLP professionals.
AI.conclusion: There is no clear consensus that either cross-lingual consistency or cultural adaptation is universally preferable for multilingual medical LLMs. Stakeholder opinions diverge across professions and regions, and current LLM persona prompting does not faithfully capture these differences. The field needs empirical studies that directly measure which strategy better serves users in diverse cultural contexts, as well as improved benchmarks that distinguish universally valid medical guidance from culture-specific practices.

title: Human-like moral judgments conceal divergent motive attributions in large language models
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 1 table; Supplementary Information (10 pages) appended
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are used to simulate human participants in psychological research. We asked whether LLMs that reproduce human evaluations of a whistleblower's moral character also reproduce the motive attributions that accompany them. Five LLMs and two human samples (N = 125 and N = 742) evaluated a physician who either remained silent about fraudulent billing or reported it to a hospital, regulator, or newspaper. Models reproduced the human ranking of the physician's moral character but portrayed whistleblowers as more helpful, less self-interested, and less hostile. In four of five models, competitive motives were less strongly associated with moral-character judgments. Model ratings changed little when prompts reproduced the narratives and demographic profiles of both human samples, although this comparison cannot isolate a perspective effect. Thus, agreement in average ratings can conceal differences in attributed motives, relationships among judgments, and sensitivity to context. Validating LLMs as simulated participants therefore requires testing psychologically informative response patterns, not average agreement alone.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether large language models (LLMs) not only match humans’ moral evaluations of a whistleblower but also match the underlying motive attributions, finding that LLMs align on overall moral judgments but systematically differ in inferred motives and in how motives relate to moral character.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as stand-ins for human participants in psychological research, often validated only by comparing average responses on judgments like moral evaluations. However, psychological theories focus on latent processes—such as attributed motives and how they shape judgments—not just mean ratings. The authors want to know whether LLMs that appear human-like on surface moral judgments also reproduce human-like patterns of motive attributions and their links to moral character, which is crucial if LLMs are to be trusted as simulated participants.
AI.method: The authors compared five LLMs with two human samples (N=125 and N=742). All evaluated scenarios involving a physician who discovers fraudulent billing and either stays silent or reports it to different entities (hospital, regulator, or newspaper). Participants and models rated the physician’s moral character and attributed different motives (e.g., helpfulness, self-interest, hostility, competitive motives). The authors examined (a) average ratings, (b) differences between models and humans in motive attributions, (c) correlations between attributed motives and moral-character judgments, and (d) how ratings changed when prompts were tailored to match the narratives and demographic profiles of the human samples.
AI.result: LLMs reproduced humans’ ranking of the physician’s moral character across conditions (e.g., whistleblowing vs. silence) but diverged systematically in motive attributions: they saw whistleblowers as more helpful, less self-interested, and less hostile than human participants did. In four of five models, competitive motives were less strongly tied to moral-character judgments than in humans. Adjusting prompts to mirror human narratives and demographics produced little change in model ratings, though this manipulation could not cleanly isolate perspective-taking effects.
AI.conclusion: Surface agreement between LLMs and humans on average moral evaluations can mask deeper psychological mismatches: LLMs differ from humans in the motives they attribute to actors, in how those motives relate to moral-character judgments, and in their sensitivity to contextual factors. Therefore, validating LLMs as simulated participants for psychological research must go beyond mean-level agreement and assess whether they reproduce theoretically meaningful response patterns and underlying psychological structures.

title: Fine PT-PT Web: A High-Quality 41 Billion Tokens Data Collection of the European Portuguese Web
summary: Curating Web corpora for regional language variants like European Portuguese (PT-PT) is heavily bottlenecked by dialectal overlap (mainly with PT-BR) and data processing scale. This paper presents an efficient pipeline to curate a production-ready PT-PT corpus from the Portuguese Web, spanning 411 TB of raw data from Arquivo.pt. We introduce a novel post-scraping block that removes boilerplate and line duplicates prior to filtering. This early-stage intervention increases final document yield by 19.04% by rescuing valid text that standard heuristic filters prematurely discard. Integrated with rigorous language identification, weighted fuzzy deduplication, and neural quality classification, our pipeline offers a scalable framework and a clean, representative corpus optimized for LLM pre-training.

AI.tldr: Efficient pipeline to curate a large, clean European Portuguese web corpus from massive archival data, improving yield via early boilerplate and duplicate removal plus advanced filtering for LLM pre-training.
AI.motivation: Building high-quality web corpora for specific regional variants like European Portuguese is difficult because web data mixes dialects (especially with Brazilian Portuguese) and operates at huge scale. Existing pipelines often lose good text when using heuristic filters after scraping, and they lack tailored tools to distinguish close dialects and handle near-duplicates and quality noise, which limits the usefulness of such corpora for training large language models.
AI.method: Process 411 TB of raw Portuguese web data from Arquivo.pt through a new pipeline. Introduce a novel post-scraping block that removes boilerplate and line-level duplicates before standard filtering, preventing premature discarding of valid text. Combine this with strong language identification tuned for PT-PT, weighted fuzzy deduplication to remove near-duplicates, and a neural quality classifier to keep only high-quality content. The pipeline is designed to be scalable and production-ready.
AI.result: The early boilerplate and line-duplicate removal step increases the final usable document yield by 19.04% compared to pipelines that apply heuristic filters directly after scraping. The complete pipeline produces a cleaner, more representative corpus of European Portuguese suitable for LLM pre-training, demonstrating scalability on hundreds of terabytes of web data.
AI.conclusion: An optimized pipeline with an early post-scraping cleanup block, rigorous language and dialect identification, fuzzy deduplication, and neural quality filtering can significantly improve both yield and quality of regional web corpora. The resulting European Portuguese corpus is better aligned with the needs of modern LLM pre-training and provides a scalable framework that can be adapted to other regional language variants facing similar overlap and quality challenges.

title: RAFM-SER++: A Lightweight Multimodal Emotion Recognition Framework for Real-Time Behavioral Monitoring in Surveillance Systems
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Advanced Video and Signal-based Surveillance (AVSS 2026). (c) 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses
summary:
Recent multimodal Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) systems achieve high accuracy through interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers, but their computational cost limits deployment in latency-sensitive and resource-constrained surveillance systems. To address this challenge, we propose RAFM_SER++, a lightweight multimodal SER framework featuring an asymmetric Residual Attention Fusion Mechanism (RAFM). Rather than relying on computationally expensive bidirectional interactions, RAFM injects affective speech cues into semantic text representations through a one-directional residual attention pathway. Combined with a BYOL-inspired cross-modal alignment objective and attention-guided pooling, the proposed framework improves multimodal representation learning while maintaining low computational overhead.
  Experiments on the IEMOCAP and ESD benchmarks demonstrate that RAFM_SER++ consistently outperforms the HuBERT-Base baseline and achieves a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off compared with the state-of-the-art MemoCMT. Specifically, RAFM_SER++ reduces trainable parameters by more than 60%, achieves faster inference (79.60 it/s), and attains BACC scores of 81.10% on IEMOCAP and 95.39% on ESD. These results indicate that lightweight asymmetric multimodal fusion is an effective alternative to interaction-heavy cross-modal transformers for real-time surveillance applications.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RAFM_SER++, a lightweight multimodal speech emotion recognition framework that uses asymmetric residual attention fusion from speech to text, plus BYOL-style cross-modal alignment and attention pooling, to achieve better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than heavier cross-modal transformers on IEMOCAP and ESD.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal speech emotion recognition systems often rely on heavy cross-modal transformers with intensive bidirectional interaction between modalities. While accurate, these models are computationally expensive and ill-suited for latency-sensitive and resource-constrained surveillance scenarios that require real-time processing. There is a need for fusion strategies that preserve or improve performance while significantly reducing computational overhead and parameter counts.
AI.method: The authors design RAFM_SER++, a multimodal SER framework centered on an asymmetric Residual Attention Fusion Mechanism (RAFM). Instead of using full bidirectional cross-modal transformers, RAFM performs one-directional residual attention from speech to text, injecting affective acoustic cues into semantic text representations with lower computational cost. The framework also incorporates a BYOL-inspired cross-modal alignment loss to encourage consistent representations across modalities without requiring negative samples, and uses attention-guided pooling to better aggregate temporal information. The entire architecture is optimized to be lightweight in terms of trainable parameters and inference cost while retaining strong discriminative power for emotion recognition.
AI.result: On two standard benchmarks, IEMOCAP and ESD, RAFM_SER++ consistently surpasses a HuBERT-Base multimodal baseline and provides a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off than the state-of-the-art MemoCMT. The model reduces the number of trainable parameters by over 60%, achieves a faster inference speed of 79.60 iterations per second, and reaches balanced accuracy (BACC) scores of 81.10% on IEMOCAP and 95.39% on ESD.
AI.conclusion: RAFM_SER++ shows that asymmetric, lightweight multimodal fusion can effectively replace heavier interaction-rich cross-modal transformers for speech emotion recognition, especially in real-time and resource-limited surveillance contexts. By combining residual attention fusion from speech to text with BYOL-style cross-modal alignment and attention-guided pooling, the framework attains strong emotion recognition performance while significantly lowering computational demands, making it suitable for practical deployment.

title: DeepTable: Structural Attention Biases and Tree Path Encoding for Hierarchical Table Understanding
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in table understanding. However, they typically process table content and headers as linearized token sequences. This representation weakens the two-dimensional and hierarchical structural relationships encoded by multi-level row and column headers. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods incorporate basic row and column information but do not explicitly capture the rich structural dependencies induced by hierarchical table headers. We propose DeepTable, a structure-aware approach for table understanding with LLMs. DeepTable comprises two complementary components. Structural Attention Bias (SAB) introduces learnable biases into the attention logits to explicitly represent whether pairs of table tokens share the same row or column. Tree Path Encoding (TPE) represents each table token using the ancestor paths of its row and column headers, preserving its position within the multi-level table structure. We integrate DeepTable with TableLoRA (He et al., 2025) to inject structural information into parameter-efficient adaptation. Across three LLM backbones, DeepTable consistently improves the corresponding TableLoRA baselines on three table question answering benchmarks, achieving average gains of 7.42 points on HiTab, 3.23 points on WikiTQ, and 2.01 BLEU points on FeTaQA. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed structural biases across different LLM backbones.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes DeepTable, a structure-aware method that better captures 2D and hierarchical table structure in LLMs, significantly improving table QA performance over existing parameter‑efficient approaches like TableLoRA.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based table understanding methods linearize tables into token sequences, which loses important two-dimensional and hierarchical relationships, especially those encoded by multi-level row and column headers. Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods only include shallow row/column indicators and fail to capture richer structural dependencies, limiting accuracy on table question answering tasks. The paper aims to overcome this structural information loss while staying parameter-efficient.
AI.method: The authors introduce DeepTable, composed of two key components designed to inject structure into LLMs without full retraining. (1) Structural Attention Bias (SAB): learnable bias terms added to attention logits to explicitly encode whether pairs of table tokens share the same row or column, guiding the model’s attention based on table topology. (2) Tree Path Encoding (TPE): each table token is augmented with representations of the ancestor paths of its associated row and column headers, preserving its location within multi-level (hierarchical) header trees. DeepTable is integrated with the existing parameter-efficient method TableLoRA so that these structural signals are incorporated during adaptation of LLMs to table tasks.
AI.result: When applied on top of TableLoRA across three different LLM backbones, DeepTable yields consistent gains on three table QA benchmarks. Specifically, it improves average performance by 7.42 points on HiTab, 3.23 points on WikiTQ, and 2.01 BLEU points on FeTaQA compared with TableLoRA baselines, showing that explicitly modeling row/column structure and hierarchical headers leads to better table understanding.
AI.conclusion: DeepTable successfully injects structural awareness into LLM-based table understanding through attention biases and tree-based positional encodings, addressing the limitations of naive linearization. The consistent improvements over TableLoRA on multiple backbones and datasets demonstrate that modeling 2D and hierarchical table structure is both effective and broadly applicable for table question answering in a parameter-efficient way.

title: CIT-CAD: Constraint Intent Tree-based CAD Code Generation and Verification
summary: Natural-language Computer-Aided Design (CAD) code generation aims to turn design intent into executable and editable parametric programs. Large language models (LLMs) make this goal increasingly practical, but useful systems must preserve the construction process behind the rendered geometry. Existing benchmarks and methods mostly focus on how closely the generated CAD model matches the reference geometry, often using metrics such as Intersection over Union (IoU). Such metrics can miss errors in part decomposition, construction hierarchy, Boolean operations, sketch structure, and geometric relations. This gap calls for a representation that makes design intent explicit and lets a system check generated code against that intent. We propose CIT-CAD, a framework that infers a Constraint Intent Tree (CIT) from the input description to represent the intended entities, hierarchy, operations, and relations. The tree has two roles: it guides CAD code generation and defines expected constraints for verification. The framework extracts actual constraints from the generated program, compares them with the expected constraints, and uses mismatches to localize and repair design violations. Experiments show that the framework improves CAD generation performance, with larger gains on more complex multi-entity designs. By turning design intent into an explicit and checkable object, this work is the first attempt to move text-to-CAD generation beyond rendered-geometry matching toward construction-aware synthesis, verification, and repair.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CIT-CAD, a framework that uses an intermediate Constraint Intent Tree representation to capture design intent from natural language and enforce it during text-to-CAD code generation, verification, and repair, going beyond pure geometry-matching metrics.
AI.motivation: Current natural language to CAD generation systems and benchmarks largely rely on rendered geometry similarity metrics (e.g., IoU) to evaluate and guide generation. These overlook critical aspects of parametric CAD such as part decomposition, construction hierarchy, Boolean operations, sketch structure, and geometric constraints, which encode the true design intent and editability of models. There is a need for a representation and framework that makes design intent explicit so systems can generate, check, and correct CAD code accordingly.
AI.method: The authors propose CIT-CAD, which first infers a Constraint Intent Tree (CIT) from the natural-language description. The CIT encodes intended entities, their hierarchy, operations (e.g., Booleans), and geometric and parametric relations. This tree serves as both a guide for generating CAD code and a specification of expected constraints. From the generated CAD program, the framework extracts the realized constraints and compares them with the CIT-derived expected constraints. Detected mismatches are used to localize where the design intent was violated and to trigger targeted repairs of the CAD code.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that incorporating CIT-CAD into the text-to-CAD pipeline improves CAD generation quality compared to baselines that focus mainly on geometry matching, with especially notable gains for complex, multi-entity designs. The verification and repair loop using constraint comparisons yields better alignment with the intended construction process and structure.
AI.conclusion: By introducing the Constraint Intent Tree representation and integrating it into generation, verification, and repair, the paper presents a first step toward construction-aware text-to-CAD systems. It shifts emphasis from matching final rendered geometry to capturing, checking, and enforcing design intent, enabling more faithful, interpretable, and editable CAD code generation from natural language descriptions.

title: Translation Indeterminacy and the Distributional Fallacy
comment: Accepted for publication in Philosophy of Translation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly associated with the distributional hypothesis, according to which (1) semantic meaning is grounded in distributional patterns of linguistic context, and (2) knowledge of cross-linguistic distributional correspondences allows for successful translation. This paper rejects the first claim as a causal inversion: linguistic distributions reflect patterns arising from meaning-making practices rather than constituting their source. At the same time, it accepts the second claim, arguing that translation -human or machine - can succeed without requiring access to meaning or reference. Knowledge of interlingual distributional correspondence and their inferential organization may be sufficient for translation. The paper develops an ecological-enactivist perspective, according to which reference and meaning are grounded in agent-environment interaction and stabilized through action-grounded concepts, forms of world-involving cognition that current LLMs do not possess.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that language models don’t “have” meaning; they exploit patterns in language that reflect human meaning-making, and those patterns can be enough for good translation without genuine understanding.
AI.motivation: Clarify what kind of “meaning” and “understanding” large language models actually have, and whether successful tasks like translation show that they possess semantic competence. The authors respond to widespread assumptions that distributional patterns in text both ground meaning and explain why LLMs work.
AI.method: Conceptual and philosophical analysis: the authors dissect two components of the distributional hypothesis, argue that one is a causal inversion, and then integrate insights from ecological-enactivist theories of cognition to distinguish linguistic pattern mastery from genuine meaning-grounded cognition.
AI.result: They reject the idea that meaning is constituted by linguistic distributions but retain the idea that translation can be done purely from interlingual distributional correspondences. They offer an alternative account: meaning and reference are grounded in embodied agent–environment interactions and “action-grounded concepts,” which current LLMs lack.
AI.conclusion: LLMs do not have meaning or reference in the ecological-enactivist sense; they model and exploit distributional regularities produced by humans who do have such meaning. Successful translation does not show that LLMs understand; rather, it shows that understanding is not strictly necessary for mapping between languages when one has sufficiently rich distributional correspondence knowledge.

title: The Internal Anatomy of Strategic Choice in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models act as strategic agents and models of human choice, yet choosing like a strategic agent does not mean computing like one. We recorded activations from four open-weight models --- dense and mixture-of-experts, including a matched base--instruct pair --- in one-shot play of 144 strict ordinal $2\times2$ games. We followed a prespecified incentive from prompt, through activations, to choice. Dense models mirrored the unadjusted human decline with game complexity. Incentive and choice were detectable in every model, but models differed in whether incentive reached the choice, aligned with it and, where tested, whether strengthening it shifted preference. The base and instruction-tuned Qwen2.5 models chose almost identically at baseline yet differed in whether incentive reached choice. Fixed decision cues were distinguishable internally but changed choices selectively. Similar behaviour can rest on different computation; post-training can reshape the path from represented incentive to decision while leaving behaviour and decodable information largely intact.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how large language models (LLMs) internally represent incentives and make strategic decisions in simple games, showing that similar observable behavior can arise from different internal computational pathways, and that post-training (instruction tuning) can reshape these pathways without much changing choices.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as strategic agents and models of human decision-making, but it is unclear whether their internal computations resemble those of strategic agents or humans, even when their choices do. Understanding how incentives are represented and translated into decisions is important both for using LLMs as models of human behavior and for aligning them as agents.
AI.method: The authors probe four open-weight LLMs (both dense and mixture-of-experts, including a base and instruction-tuned version of Qwen2.5) by having them play 144 one-shot strict ordinal 2×2 games. They record internal activations throughout the forward pass, and trace how information about incentives flows from the prompt, through layers, to the final choice. They examine detectability of incentive and choices in activations, whether and how incentive representations align with final choices, and how strengthening incentives or altering fixed decision cues affects internal representations and behavior.
AI.result: Dense models show a decline in performance with game complexity similar to unadjusted humans. In all models, both incentives and eventual choices are decodable from internal activations, but models differ in whether the incentive signal reaches and aligns with the final decision. The base and instruction-tuned Qwen2.5 exhibit almost identical baseline choices, yet differ markedly in how incentives propagate to choice. Manipulating fixed decision cues changes choices in a targeted way while remaining distinguishable internally. Strengthening incentives only shifts preferences in some models, revealing architectural and training-dependent differences in how incentives are used.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can exhibit similar outward strategic behavior while relying on different internal computational mechanisms. Post-training procedures such as instruction tuning can substantially modify the path from represented incentives to final decisions without notably altering observable choices or the decodability of incentives and choices from activations. This has implications for interpreting LLMs as models of human reasoning and for safety/alignment, since behaviorally similar models may respond differently to incentives at the computational level.

title: From Echo Chambers to Epistemic Monoculture: Large Language Models Present Temporally Contingent Partisan Alignments as Knowledge
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming an interface between citizens and political information. They are often regarded as "a better Google." While this analogy might work for some instances, it is unintuitively problematic for democratic politics. A search engine retrieves human-authored documents, while a language model generates novel text that necessarily embeds invisible framing decisions. Because conveying knowledge involves framing, a system that generates answers cannot serve as a neutral conduit to "all human knowledge." Instead, these systems are becoming a new kind of political intermediary. Mechanistic evidence shows that partisan identity is encoded as a locatable geometric direction inside the Llama 3.1 8B model, and that alignment training masks rather than removes this structure. Building on that evidence, we present steering experiments that exploit a model's training cutoff in 2024. This cutpoint auspiciously falls just before a dramatic realignment in American politics marked by the second Trump administration and the MAHA transformation of health politics, providing us with a natural experiment. We find that the model presents temporally contingent partisan alignments as knowledge, with no mechanism for distinguishing fact from opinion. This reality moves the information environment beyond the echo chamber toward an epistemic monoculture where language models, purporting to summarize "all human knowledge" are, in actuality, simply magnifying the cultural and partisan divides inherent in their training data.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that large language models are not neutral information tools but political intermediaries that embed partisan framings, and it empirically shows how a modern LLM reflects and amplifies temporally contingent partisan divides.
AI.motivation: As LLMs increasingly mediate how citizens access political information, it becomes crucial to understand whether they behave like neutral search engines or whether they embed political biases and framings that can shape democratic discourse.
AI.method: The authors use mechanistic interpretability to identify a geometric direction within Llama 3.1 8B corresponding to partisan identity and examine how alignment training affects this structure. They then run steering experiments that leverage the model’s 2024 training cutoff as a natural experiment, comparing the model’s responses to political issues before and after a major political realignment, to test how partisan alignments are presented as knowledge.
AI.result: They find that partisan identity is encoded in a specific direction in representation space and that alignment training largely masks, rather than eliminates, this structure. Their steering experiments reveal that the model encodes time-specific partisan alignments as if they were neutral knowledge, with no internal mechanism to distinguish fact from opinion in these contexts.
AI.conclusion: LLMs function as political intermediaries rather than neutral conduits to human knowledge. By embedding and amplifying partisan and cultural divides from their training data, they risk creating an epistemic monoculture in which generated answers appear authoritative while actually reproducing contingent political framings.

title: Modus Tollens and Counterfactuals and Counterfactual Reasoning Based on Three Types of Negation
summary: Modus Tollens (MT) is a classical logical inference rule, while counterfactuals are hypothetical statements that are contrary to facts, and counterfactual reasoning is a process of reasoning based on counterfactuals. Negation is an indispensable core concept in them. In this paper, based on the logical systems LCOI&PLCOI with contradictory negation, opposite negation and intermediary negation, we propose three variants of Modus Tollens corresponding to distinct negation types, namely MTC: Modus Tollens based on contradictory negation, MTO: Modus Tollens based on opposite negation, and MTI: Modus Tollens based on intermediary negation. We define the implications within MTC, MTO and MTI, provide the truth value algorithms of MTC, MTO and MTI, and discuss the reducibility of these algorithms. To incorporate these three types of negation into counterfactuals and counterfactual reasoning, we differentiate counterfactuals into two types based on whether they possess logical negation, thereby proposing three counterfactuals and counterfactuals reasoning based on different logical negations. In this paper, we further argue that the three counterfactuals reasoning based on different logical negations have the same inference form as MTC, MTO and MTI, respectively. In other words, they share the same inference structure. As a result, the truth value algorithms for MTC, MTO and MTI can be as the truth value algorithms for the three counterfactuals reasoning based on different logical negations. The algorithms indicates that if the first premise of the reasoning is true, the truth values of the reasoning conclusions are identical to the truth values of the three negative premises in the reasoning premises, respectively. This reflects the consistency and accuracy of the truth value algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Modus Tollens and counterfactual reasoning to a logic with three distinct kinds of negation, defines corresponding inference rules and truth-value algorithms, and shows they share a common inference structure.
AI.motivation: Classical Modus Tollens and standard counterfactual logics assume a single, classical negation, which is insufficient for logics that differentiate kinds of negation (e.g., contradictory, opposite, and intermediary). The authors want to adapt MT and counterfactual reasoning to a richer logical system (LCOI&PLCOI) where negation is more fine‑grained, and to provide precise semantic (truth‑value) algorithms for these inferences.
AI.method: Starting from the logical systems LCOI&PLCOI, which distinguish three forms of negation, the authors: (1) define three variants of Modus Tollens (MTC, MTO, MTI) aligned with each negation type; (2) define the corresponding implication operators in each variant; (3) construct explicit truth‑value algorithms for each inference pattern and analyze when these algorithms can be reduced or simplified; (4) classify counterfactuals according to whether they contain logical negation and then introduce three kinds of counterfactuals and associated reasoning schemes, each tied to one of the three negations; (5) prove that these counterfactual reasoning schemes share the same formal inference form as MTC, MTO, and MTI, thereby allowing the reuse of the MT truth‑value algorithms for counterfactual reasoning.
AI.result: They obtain three formally specified Modus Tollens rules (MTC, MTO, MTI) with their own implication connectives and truth‑value algorithms. They also define three parallel counterfactual reasoning schemes, one for each negation type, and show that these schemes are structurally isomorphic to the corresponding MT variants. Consequently, the same truth‑value algorithms governing MTC, MTO, and MTI can be directly used to compute truth values in the three forms of counterfactual reasoning. The algorithms guarantee that when the first premise is true, the conclusion’s truth value coincides with that of the specific negative premise involved in each reasoning pattern.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Modus Tollens and counterfactual reasoning can be consistently generalized to a logical framework that distinguishes multiple types of negation. The three MT variants and the three corresponding counterfactual reasoning forms share a common inference structure, enabling unified truth‑value algorithms. These algorithms behave coherently: given a true first premise, the truth value of the conclusion matches that of the relevant negative premise, supporting the soundness and internal consistency of the proposed system.

title: LLM Forensics: Where Do Backdoors Hide? Localizing and Controlling Trigger Mechanisms with Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Even though backdoors in LLMs have been a growing concern, their inner workings are still under heavy scrutiny. Trigger-based backdoors are easy to define behaviorally, a rare input that makes the model switch to a chosen response pattern, but the mechanism between triggers and their responses is less clear. We study this mechanism in a controlled, harmless language-switching setting, where fixed trigger sequences make 1B and 8B language models continue English prompts in French or German. For this, we train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) across layers and transformer components, then compare triggered prompts with translation and pretraining controls to identify trigger-relevant feature directions. We show how SAE features separate triggered prompts from controls with near-perfect F1, but features that detect the trigger do not necessarily control the behavior. In intervention tests, attention and MLP features often fire reliably on triggered prompts, making them good detectors, but ablating them rarely suppresses the language switch and activating them rarely induces it. In contrast, residual-stream features can suppress triggered generation when ablated, and some selected features can induce target-language continuations without the trigger. In short, these token-trigger mechanisms decompose into distinct SAE feature directions, with separate features for trigger detection, residual-stream propagation, and later language tracking. This role-level decomposition is the part most likely to transfer to other trigger-based backdoors, even when the payload, layers, or circuit locations differ.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how trigger-based backdoors in language models actually work internally, using a controlled setting where specific token triggers cause models to switch output language. Using sparse autoencoders, it identifies distinct feature directions for detecting triggers, propagating their effect, and tracking the new language, showing that not all features that detect triggers control behavior.
AI.motivation: Backdoors in large language models, where rare triggers cause specific, often malicious behaviors, are a major safety concern, but the mechanisms connecting triggers to behaviors are poorly understood. Existing descriptions are largely behavioral (input–output) rather than mechanistic. The paper aims to open this black box by providing a detailed feature-level understanding of how token triggers cause systematic changes in model behavior, in hopes of building insights that generalize to harmful backdoors.
AI.method: The authors construct a benign backdoor-like setup where special trigger token sequences cause 1B and 8B LLMs to continue English prompts in French or German. They train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) across layers and components (attention, MLP, residual stream) to obtain interpretable features. They then (1) compare activations on triggered prompts vs. translation and pretraining controls to isolate trigger-relevant directions, (2) evaluate how well SAE features separate triggered vs. non-triggered prompts, and (3) perform causal interventions by ablating or activating specific features in different components to see their effect on language switching behavior.
AI.result: SAE features can distinguish triggered prompts from control prompts with near-perfect F1 scores, indicating a clear feature-level signature of the backdoor. However, features that reliably detect the trigger in attention and MLP components generally do not causally control the language switch: ablating them rarely prevents the switch and activating them rarely induces it. In contrast, certain residual-stream features do have strong causal influence: ablating them can suppress the triggered language switch and selected features, when activated, can induce continuations in the target language without the explicit trigger. The mechanisms separate into multiple feature directions with different functional roles.
AI.conclusion: Trigger-based backdoor behavior in LLMs decomposes into distinct, interpretable feature directions within the model, corresponding to trigger detection, propagation through the residual stream, and subsequent tracking of the target language. The features that detect triggers are not necessarily those that control behavior; causal control is more associated with specific residual-stream features. This role-level decomposition suggests a generalizable structure for token-trigger backdoors that may persist even when the backdoor’s specific payload, affected layers, or circuit details differ, offering a promising foundation for mechanistic detection and mitigation of backdoors in LLMs.

title: Quantile-Led Feature Extraction for Multi-Horizon Predictive Maintenance in Industrial Manufacturing Systems
summary: In data-driven predictive maintenance (PdM), feature extraction is usually treated as fixed preprocessing: a descriptor set is chosen once and reused while the downstream model or forecasting horizon changes. This paper isolates the representation-learning stage and presents a quantile-led feature-extraction framework based on a dual-stage MLP-QRNN hierarchy. QRNN1 learns a broad ten-quantile conditional distribution for each sensor channel, while skip-connected QRNN2 refines a retained mid-tail quantile set into compact, channel-resolved, distribution-aware features. A fixed thirteen-pipeline ablation spans 1-hour, 70-hour, and 30-day regimes across 72 machines in 9 industrial facilities, with the downstream temporal classifier held fixed within each regime. Increasing the retained mid-tail set from two to four quantiles improves 30- and 60-minute F1-score, reaching 75.92% and 72.44% with attention enabled. The results also show that representations do not transfer reliably beyond their design horizon unless feature capacity, temporal embedding, activation strategy, and sensor breadth are scaled with the forecasting task. The unmodified short-horizon extractor falls to 42.90% F1 at 70 hours, whereas horizon-conditioned extractors reach 60.38% at 70 hours and 79.97% at 30 days. The framework therefore supports treating PdM feature extraction as a horizon-dependent representational stage rather than fixed preprocessing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a quantile-based neural feature-extraction framework for predictive maintenance that adapts to different prediction horizons instead of using a fixed descriptor set.
AI.motivation: Most data-driven predictive maintenance pipelines treat feature extraction as a static preprocessing step: one handcrafted or learned feature set is reused regardless of the prediction horizon or downstream model. This ignores that degradation signatures and useful temporal patterns can change with the forecasting horizon, leading to suboptimal performance and poor transfer of representations across horizons. The authors aim to study feature extraction as an independent, horizon-sensitive representation-learning stage and understand how quantile-based temporal representations can improve maintenance-event prediction.
AI.method: The authors design a dual-stage hierarchy combining multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and Quantile Recurrent Neural Networks (QRNNs). In the first stage (QRNN1), the model learns a broad 10-quantile conditional distribution per sensor channel to capture rich distributional dynamics over time. In the second stage (QRNN2), with skip connections from QRNN1, the model selects and refines a reduced set of mid-to-tail quantiles into compact, channel-specific, distribution-aware feature vectors. They systematically vary the number of retained quantiles (e.g., 2 vs 4) and construct a fixed set of 13 experimental pipelines spanning three prediction regimes: short (1 hour), medium (70 hours), and long (30 days). Across 72 machines in 9 industrial facilities, they keep the downstream temporal classifier fixed within each regime to isolate the effect of the feature extractor. They also compare horizon-mismatched extractors (trained on one horizon, applied to another) against horizon-conditioned extractors designed for each horizon.
AI.result: Increasing the retained mid-tail quantile set from two to four improves short-horizon performance; with attention enabled, the framework reaches F1-scores of 75.92% and 72.44% for 30- and 60-minute predictions, respectively. However, features learned for short horizons transfer poorly to longer horizons: an extractor trained for short horizons drops to 42.90% F1 when applied at a 70-hour horizon. In contrast, horizon-conditioned extractors, whose capacity and configuration are adapted to each forecasting regime, achieve substantially better performance: 60.38% F1 at 70 hours and 79.97% F1 at 30 days. These results show strong horizon dependence in representational needs for PdM.
AI.conclusion: Feature extraction in predictive maintenance should be treated as a horizon-dependent representation-learning problem, not as a fixed preprocessing step. A dual-stage quantile-based QRNN architecture can provide compact, distribution-aware features that improve event prediction, especially when the number of retained quantiles and the model’s capacity, temporal embedding, and sensor coverage are matched to the forecasting horizon. Representations trained for one horizon do not reliably generalize to others unless the feature extractor is explicitly conditioned and scaled for the target horizon.

title: Replicating a Disjoint-Set Union Experiment over Various Notions of Micro Units to assess Translation Effort
summary: The paper describes a replication experiment to assess "the distribution of editing procedures across micro and macro units as an indicator of the strain of text production". We investigate various pause thresholds to isolate Micro and Macro units and conclude that process-based units might be more suitable entity.

AI.tldr: The paper replicates an experiment on how editing behavior distributes across small (micro) and large (macro) text units to indicate cognitive strain in writing, and finds that defining units based on writing process data (like pauses) may work better than traditional structural units.
AI.motivation: To better understand how writers’ editing behaviors reflect the cognitive strain of text production, and to test whether micro and macro text units defined by pause thresholds are reliable indicators of that strain.
AI.method: The authors conduct a replication experiment where they segment writing into micro and macro units using different pause-duration thresholds, then analyze how editing operations are distributed across those units as a proxy for cognitive strain.
AI.result: They observe that the distribution of editing procedures across units depends strongly on how micro and macro units are defined via pause thresholds, suggesting instability or limitations in this approach.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that units defined directly from process data (process-based units), rather than pre-imposed pause-based micro/macro units, may be more appropriate for analyzing editing behavior and cognitive strain in writing.

title: Scoring Without the Engine: Validating a Deterministic, Manipulation-Resistant Content Score for Generative Engines, End to End
comment: 42 pages, 4 figures. Code and data: https://github.com/TW3-Partners-OS/geo-score-reproducibility & More informations on Citead.com
summary: How do you validate a cheap, deterministic proxy for an oracle that is expensive, rate-limited, and non-stationary? We present a protocol built on adversarial falsification gates (negative control, dose response, bounded amplification, duplication penalty, length neutrality) that define and select the proxy, fitted on a training split and confirmed held-out; around them it bounds what the proxy can never resolve, and re-measures external causal evidence on the current oracle rather than assuming it. We demonstrate it end to end on Generative Engine Optimization, where the proxy is a deterministic content score, and one step fails on that domain exactly as the protocol is built to detect: re-measuring the only published causal anchors (2023 effect sizes) on ten modern engine families shows their levers move citation on none, so the anchors are an expired external check; recalibrating to the near-zero modern vector strips the score of its lever-responsive components. What survives is the gate-enforced response surface. The gates buy a measured property: on a 500-source benchmark of adversarial edits, amplifying the score's calibrated levers gains an attacker at most 6 points, and decreases with dose; single-lever amplification is provably bounded, while the cap and cross-lever sub-additivity are empirical findings consistent with it. On detection, web-spam baselines dominate and out-of-distribution attacks evade the score, so the deployable filter layers it over them. A query-conditioned skyline bounds the score's citation signal (within-query Spearman 0.11), repositioning query-agnostic scores as quality filters rather than citation predictors. A query-leakage bug in our first ranking evaluation and a failed confidence flag are disclosed and corrected; every number reproduces offline from released artifacts at zero marginal API cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes and validates a protocol for building a cheap, deterministic proxy model that approximates an expensive, changing oracle, demonstrated on search-engine-oriented content scores.
AI.motivation: There is a need for inexpensive, deterministic proxies to replace or approximate expensive, rate-limited, and non-stationary oracles (like modern search engines or APIs). Existing proxies are often validated weakly, can overfit to outdated external evidence, and may be vulnerable to adversarial optimization. The authors want a principled way to define, stress-test, and bound what such a proxy can and cannot do, particularly in the context of Generative Engine Optimization (GEO), where people optimize content for search engines using proxy scores.
AI.method: They design a protocol based on a sequence of “adversarial falsification gates” (negative control, dose response, bounded amplification, duplication penalty, length neutrality). These gates serve both to define the proxy, and to attempt to falsify it under adversarial perturbations. The proxy is trained on a split of data and validated on a held-out set. They also explicitly re-measure external causal evidence (e.g., known effect sizes of levers on citation) on the current oracle instead of assuming past results hold. Applied to GEO, the proxy is a deterministic content quality/optimization score. They test dose-response behavior, amplification bounds, and sub-additivity of multiple levers, and examine adversarial edits on a 500-source benchmark. They compare against web-spam baselines and analyze the proxy’s effectiveness as a filter versus a citation predictor using within-query correlation (Spearman). They also disclose and correct evaluation errors (query leakage and a failed confidence flag).
AI.result: In the GEO case, when they re-measure the previously published 2023 causal levers on ten modern engine families, these levers no longer significantly move citation, so earlier anchors are now invalid as external checks. Recalibrating to these near-zero modern effects removes lever-responsive components from the score, leaving a constrained response surface enforced by the gates. On a 500-source adversarial benchmark, attackers can increase the calibrated proxy score by at most 6 points through lever amplification, with gains decreasing as dose increases; single-lever amplification is theoretically bounded, and empirical results suggest a cap and sub-additivity when combining levers. Web-spam baselines perform better for detection, and out-of-distribution attacks bypass the proxy, so the practical deployment is to layer this score on top of spam filters. The query-conditioned skyline shows the proxy’s within-query Spearman correlation with citation is low (0.11), implying the score is better viewed as a quality filter than a citation predictor. All reported numbers reproduce offline from released artifacts without extra API cost.
AI.conclusion: The adversarial falsification gate protocol provides a structured way to build and stress-test a deterministic proxy for a changing oracle, explicitly bounding what the proxy can resolve and validating it under adversarial conditions. In the GEO setting, the method reveals that historical causal anchors have expired on modern engines, and once recalibrated, the remaining score behaves in a controlled, bounded way under adversarial manipulation, though it is weak as a direct citation predictor. The approach supports using such proxies primarily as robust quality filters, layered with stronger detection systems, and emphasizes continuous re-measurement of external evidence and transparent, reproducible evaluation.

title: Bag of Tricks or Bag of Myths? Reducing Modeling Complexity with Task Knowledge in Explainable Suicide Risk Assessment
comment: This work was shaped by the IEEE Big Data Cup, where our team, NIDHI, ranked 3rd overall. NIDHI (Neurosymbolic Intelligent Diagnostics for Holistic Trauma-Informed Care) is an effort from IAIRO.ai . 21 pages, 6 Tables, 4 Figures
summary: Assessing suicide risk from social media text is a small-data, high-stakes setting requiring not only severity prediction but also supporting evidence and clinically relevant risk and protective factors. Yet common NLP techniques, including model scaling, synthetic data, loss reweighting, ensembling, and threshold tuning, are often applied without testing whether their gains hold up under severe class imbalance, coupled outputs, and limited author-level data. We study 1,635 clinician-annotated posts and audit 31 pre-specified techniques from 7 methodological families through roughly 300 controlled experiments on author-disjoint partitions. We found no prior audit of this playbook in this regime. The findings guide a task-grounded system for three outputs: 4-level suicide risk, evidence spans, and 24 clinical risk and protective factors. Only 5 of 31 comparisons produced reliable gains. We reformulate factor prediction as entailment between each post and its codebook definitions, using an architecturally diverse ensemble with class-balanced training and score rescaling. Risk predictions condition a 7-model evidence tagger ensemble; evidence restricts symbolic risk rules; and a difficult risk class is routed separately. The factor predictor remains independent because risk evidence provides no additional factor signal. We also correct a mismatch between validation scores used for threshold fitting and test-time ensemble scores through deployment-consistent calibration, yielding the largest improvement to the factor system. The final system achieves 0.8203 for risk, 0.7953 for evidence, and 0.7045 macro-F1 for factors, with a 0.7781 composite, ranking third among 53 teams. We call the underlying principle task-conditioned technique selection: retain techniques only when task-specific knowledge, structure, or empirical evidence justifies them.

AI.tldr: The paper audits common NLP techniques for suicide risk detection on social media in a realistic small, imbalanced, high-stakes clinical setting, finding that only a few methods yield robust gains and proposing a task-conditioned, multi-output system that ranks highly in shared-task evaluation.
AI.motivation: Suicide risk assessment from social media is clinically important but involves small, highly imbalanced, and high-stakes datasets. Existing NLP work often applies a standard toolbox of techniques (model scaling, synthetic data, ensembling, etc.) without verifying whether these actually help under such constraints or in multi-output settings requiring risk levels, evidence spans, and risk/protective factors. There was also no prior systematic audit of these techniques in this regime, motivating a principled, task-grounded evaluation and system design.
AI.method: The authors compile 1,635 clinician-annotated social media posts labeled with suicide risk levels, evidence spans, and 24 clinical risk/protective factors. They define 31 specific techniques across 7 methodological families (e.g., scaling, data augmentation, reweighting, ensembles, calibration) and test them via about 300 controlled experiments on author-disjoint train/validation/test partitions to avoid leakage. They design a multi-component system: factor prediction is recast as natural language entailment between each post and textual definitions of factors, trained with class-balanced data and architecturally diverse ensembles plus score rescaling. Suicide risk prediction feeds into a 7-model ensemble for evidence tagging; detected evidence constrains symbolic risk rules; a particularly hard risk class is handled via a dedicated routing strategy. They also introduce deployment-consistent calibration to align validation-time scores used for threshold selection with test-time ensemble scores.
AI.result: Across 31 technique comparisons, only 5 show robust, reliable improvements in this small-data, highly imbalanced, multi-output setting, indicating that many standard tricks do not translate into real gains. Reformulating factor prediction as textual entailment with diverse ensembles and calibrated, class-balanced training improves factor macro-F1. Calibrating ensemble outputs in a deployment-consistent way—so that threshold fitting and final inference use comparable score distributions—yields the single largest boost for the factor prediction component. The final end-to-end system attains scores of 0.8203 for suicide risk classification, 0.7953 for evidence span detection, and 0.7045 macro-F1 for factor prediction, with an overall composite score of 0.7781, placing third out of 53 teams in a shared task.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that in small, imbalanced, clinically oriented suicide risk detection from social media, most off-the-shelf NLP techniques provide little or no reliable benefit, and that system design must be grounded in task-specific structure and empirical audits. A multi-output architecture that treats factor prediction as entailment, conditions evidence tagging on risk predictions, uses symbolic rules constrained by evidence, and carefully calibrates ensemble scores performs strongly and robustly. The authors advocate a principle of task-conditioned technique selection: methods should be retained only when justified by domain knowledge, task structure, or solid empirical evidence, rather than by default adoption of the standard NLP playbook.

title: From Simulated Citizens to Simulated Deliberation: Challenges in Representation and Interaction
summary: Multi-agent LLM deliberation has been explored as a scalable way to simulate public deliberation. For such simulations to be informative, persona agents should reflect population opinion patterns and interaction should shape their conclusions. We evaluate whether LLM-based deliberation can meet these two conditions using census-grounded Korean personas debating real policy questions benchmarked against national surveys. Persona agents do not reliably reproduce population opinion patterns: responses are often far more concentrated and frequently reverse demographic differences in the human data. Deliberations nonetheless produce reasoned, reciprocal, and varied arguments alongside substantial stance movement. Yet much of this movement does not require peer exchange: sealed-monologue agents change position at similar rates and reach nearly the same final balance as full debates, while groups initialized with very different positions often converge to similar endpoints. Anchoring population-informed starting positions, meanwhile, sharply suppresses updating. Thus, population representation, argument generation, and interaction-driven opinion change do not necessarily go together. The simulations readily surface arguments on both sides, though whether they capture the diversity of human perspectives remains untested, leaving open a promising role for argument surfacing even as population simulation requires further validation.
