AI.result: They find that highly capable LLMs are well-described by latent variables interpretable as beliefs: a single inferred belief dimension predicts their responses to new prompts in a structured and interpretable way. The strength and usefulness of this belief-based prediction increases with model capability, indicating that more advanced models exhibit more coherent, belief-like internal structure. They also obtain empirical evidence that their methods can be used to assess belief measurement, rule/payoff compliance, and intra-run evolution of beliefs during reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The study supports the view that beliefs are a useful abstraction for describing the behavior of capable LLMs, in the sense that a latent belief variable inferred from behavior can predict future outputs. This strengthens the case for using belief-like constructs in alignment and safety research, and the proposed methodology offers concrete tools to measure and analyze LLM beliefs, decision-rule compliance, and belief dynamics over the course of reasoning.

title: EviSI: An Evaluation Agent for Simultaneous Interpreting
summary: Simultaneous speech-to-speech translation requires understanding, translation and spoken delivery while the source stream continues. To support timely delivery and limit accumulated delay, systems adopt reformulation and summarization, which can preserve meaning while departing from written references. BLEU and COMET may not reliably distinguish such variation from semantic loss. We introduce EviSI, a large language model evaluation agent adapting the error analysis and penalty principles of Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM). It constructs shared source evidence, assesses semantic fidelity and oral expression, reconciles overlapping errors and scores deterministically. EviSI recovers the aggregate human system ranking for English to Chinese. Mean Kendall agreement with human system rankings within corpora reaches 0.707 for English to Chinese and 0.467 for Chinese to English, exceeding evaluated baselines. An extension across five directions shows positive concordance with COMET without human ratings. Individual output agreement with humans remains mixed.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces EviSI, an LLM-based evaluation agent for simultaneous speech-to-speech translation that better captures semantic fidelity and oral expression than standard metrics like BLEU and COMET, achieving higher correlation with human system rankings.
AI.motivation: Conventional MT evaluation metrics such as BLEU and COMET struggle with simultaneous speech-to-speech translation outputs, which often use reformulation and summarization to reduce delay. These outputs can diverge from written references while preserving meaning, causing conventional metrics to conflate legitimate variation with semantic errors. There is a need for an evaluation method that can accurately assess semantic fidelity and spoken quality in this setting and align more closely with human judgments.
AI.method: The authors design EviSI, a large language model-based evaluation agent inspired by Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM). EviSI builds shared source-side evidence, analyzes translation outputs for semantic fidelity and oral expression, applies MQM-style error categories and penalties, reconciles overlapping errors to avoid double counting, and produces deterministic scores. They then benchmark EviSI against BLEU, COMET, and other baselines by measuring how well each metric’s system-level scores correlate with human rankings across multiple language directions and corpora.
AI.result: EviSI successfully recovers the aggregate human ranking of systems for English→Chinese simultaneous speech-to-speech translation. Across corpora, its mean Kendall correlation with human system rankings reaches 0.707 for English→Chinese and 0.467 for Chinese→English, outperforming all evaluated baselines. In experiments extended to five translation directions without human labels, EviSI’s scores show positive concordance with COMET, suggesting compatibility with existing metrics. However, at the individual sentence/output level, agreement between EviSI and human judgments is still inconsistent.
AI.conclusion: EviSI provides a more human-aligned, MQM-inspired evaluation for simultaneous speech-to-speech translation than traditional automatic metrics, particularly at the system level and for English→Chinese. Its design explicitly targets semantic fidelity and oral expression and handles legitimate reformulations and summaries better than BLEU and COMET. While it improves system ranking correlation with human judgments, per-output agreement remains mixed, highlighting room for further refinement of LLM-based evaluators.

title: CausalVerify: An Execution-Grounded Benchmark for LLM Causal Inference Workflows
comment: 22 pages, 9 figures, 12 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/causalverify/causalverify
summary: Existing causal-inference benchmarks for LLMs mostly score method descriptions or whether generated code runs, not whether the executed workflow recovers the target causal estimate. CausalVerify studies this verification problem for structured econometric causal-estimation workflows by separating realistic interpretation from verifiable computation. It pairs 259 published economics papers (reconstructed research question, data description, institutional context) with 100 fixed-seed synthetic scenarios that realise CSV datasets for difference-in-differences, event study, instrumental variables, and regression discontinuity designs. Experiment A (real-paper text agreement) scores method-family and direction agreement against four-LLM consensus labels. Experiment B (synthetic execution) runs model-written R code and checks whether the extracted treatment-effect estimate matches a canonical estimator on the same realised dataset; this execution-grounded correctness layer is L2b+, distinct from L2b, which records only whether the code executes. A calibration arm asks whether self-reported confidence separates correct from incorrect workflows. On Experiment B, seven LLMs reach L2b+ pass rates of 10% to 88% at the default 50% tolerance, and 66 of the 426 workflows that execute (15.5%) return a wrong estimate. Execution ranking (L2b) agrees with L2b+ far better than text-direction scoring (L4): Kendall $τ=0.81$ and Spearman $ρ=0.93$, versus Kendall $τ$ between $-0.20$ and $0.10$ for L4. Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct shows the same qualitative gap, and reported confidence does not reliably separate correct from incorrect workflows. The claims are confined to standardized single-shot workflows in these four design families under the evaluated R backend and model panel; the benchmark does not measure general causal-inference ability. Code, data, cached outputs, and a datasheet are released.

AI.tldr: CausalVerify is a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM-generated econometric workflows actually recover the correct causal effect, not just whether their code runs or their method descriptions sound right.
AI.motivation: Most current causal-inference benchmarks for LLMs focus on surface-level criteria: matching textual method descriptions or checking if generated code executes. They rarely verify whether the full workflow—interpretation of a causal question, choice of estimator, and coding—actually recovers the correct treatment-effect estimate. This creates a gap between apparent and real causal-reasoning ability. The authors want a benchmark that directly tests execution-grounded correctness of causal estimators for common econometric designs.
AI.method: The authors construct CausalVerify by pairing 259 real economics papers (with reconstructed research questions, data descriptions, and institutional contexts) with 100 fixed-seed synthetic scenarios that generate CSV datasets for four standard causal designs: difference-in-differences, event studies, instrumental variables, and regression discontinuity. They design two main experiments: (A) a text-based agreement task where LLMs must identify the method family and directionality from paper-like text, scored against a four-LLM consensus; (B) a synthetic execution task where models write R code to estimate a treatment effect on provided synthetic datasets. For Experiment B, they introduce L2b+ scoring, which checks whether the extracted treatment-effect estimate matches a canonical estimator on the same data, contrasting this with L2b, which only checks whether the code runs. They also add a calibration component where models report confidence, to see if confidence correlates with correctness. Multiple LLMs are evaluated under standardized single-shot conditions using an R backend.
AI.result: In the execution-based Experiment B, seven LLMs achieve L2b+ pass rates between 10% and 88% when a 50% tolerance is allowed between the model’s estimate and the canonical estimator. Among the 426 workflows where the code executes, 66 (15.5%) still produce incorrect estimates, illustrating that mere successful execution (L2b) overstates model reliability. Rankings based on execution success (L2b) correlate strongly with rankings based on correct estimation (L2b+), with Kendall τ=0.81 and Spearman ρ=0.93. In contrast, rankings derived from text-only direction scoring (L4) correlate poorly with L2b+, with Kendall τ between -0.20 and 0.10. Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct exhibits this same pattern of divergence between text-based and execution-based performance. Self-reported confidence fails to separate correct from incorrect workflows in a reliable way.
AI.conclusion: CausalVerify demonstrates that evaluating LLMs on causal inference requires checking whether end-to-end econometric workflows recover the correct treatment effect, not just whether the description is plausible or the code runs. The new L2b+ execution-grounded metric reveals nontrivial rates of wrong estimates even when code executes and shows that text-only metrics can be misleading about true causal performance. Execution-based rankings align well with each other but not with text-based direction scores, and confidence calibration is weak. The benchmark is carefully scoped: it tests standardized single-shot workflows for four common causal designs under a specific R backend and model set, and should not be interpreted as a general measure of overall causal-inference ability. The authors release code, data, outputs, and a datasheet to support further research and extension of this benchmark.

title: NeoHorse-1: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement via Agentic Post-Training with Routing Harness
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires a concrete mechanism through which an AI system observes its capabilities and converts that evidence into the next round of learning. We present NeoHorse-1, a family of agent-native models developed to explore this path through agentic post-training. Our system combines a heterogeneous model pool with intelligent routing, recording the predicted capability demand, selected service tier, and subsequent interaction for each user turn. These records are converted into training examples that preserve interleaved reasoning, tool calls, and harness context, and are admitted through structural validation, six-dimensional semantic evaluation, and subscene-level labeling. Routing signals organize supervised fine-tuning into a three-stage curriculum and extend to routing-guided on-policy distillation, where a teacher supervises student-generated responses under the same progression. Capability-guided allocation then converts evaluation feedback into the next training mixture, closing an evaluation-selection-update loop in which what the system learns to do shapes what it learns from next. Across eleven benchmarks covering harness-based agents, tool use, coding, and instruction following, post-training raises the macro-average from 58.94 to 64.87 at 4B and from 65.60 to 69.04 at 9B, substantially narrowing the aggregate gap between the post-trained 4B model and the 9B base model. NeoHorse-1 provides an initial prototype of this feedback-driven process and a path toward harness-mediated RSI across successive iterations.

AI.tldr: NeoHorse-1 is a family of agent-native models that use recorded routing and evaluation signals from real agent interactions to drive a closed-loop post-training process, improving capabilities and prototyping a path to recursive self-improvement.
AI.motivation: To make recursive self-improvement concrete, the authors need a mechanism for an AI system to observe its own capabilities in realistic agentic use, transform those observations into high-quality training data, and then update itself in a way that systematically improves future behavior. Existing post-training and evaluation pipelines are typically offline, loosely coupled, or not agent-centered, limiting their ability to support continuous, feedback-driven improvement in harness-based agents.
AI.method: They build NeoHorse-1, a system where a heterogeneous pool of models is fronted by an intelligent router that predicts capability demands and selects a "service tier" (which model to use) for each user turn. For every interaction they log the routing decision, harness context, reasoning traces, and tool calls. These logs are converted into structurally validated training examples, filtered and annotated via six-dimensional semantic evaluation and fine-grained subscene labeling. Routing signals and capability labels define a three-stage supervised fine-tuning curriculum and also guide on-policy distillation, where a stronger teacher supervises a student under the same staged progression. Finally, they perform capability-guided allocation, using evaluation feedback to choose the next training mixture, thereby closing an evaluation-selection-update loop that links what the system currently does well or poorly to what data it learns from next.
AI.result: On eleven benchmarks spanning harness-based agents, tool use, coding, and instruction following, the post-training pipeline improves macro-average performance from 58.94 to 64.87 for a 4B model and from 65.60 to 69.04 for a 9B model. The post-trained 4B model approaches the capability of the 9B base model, reducing the performance gap and demonstrating that the feedback-driven, routing- and evaluation-informed pipeline yields substantial gains, especially for smaller models.
AI.conclusion: NeoHorse-1 demonstrates a concrete, prototype implementation of a feedback-driven, agent-native post-training loop that links routing, evaluation, and training in a closed cycle. This pipeline both improves benchmark performance and suggests a practical route toward harness-mediated recursive self-improvement, where each iteration’s learned behaviors determine the data and training focus of the next iteration.

title: Support Topology and Gradient Mixing in Sinkhorn Layers
summary: Sparse Sinkhorn layers use a fixed support graph to restrict transport between tokens. How does this graph control gradient propagation through the scaling iterations. We develop a fixed-support calculus showing that each row-column cycle induces a row-stochastic operator on column-potential perturbations modulo constants. Its transpose propagates zero-mass reverse-mode cotangents. The finite-cycle operator uses two distinct half-step transport plans; at a balanced fixed point it reduces to a two-step walk determined by a single plan. We derive the accompanying score and marginal source terms and use Dobrushin contraction and minorization to bound homogeneous and source-driven tail cotangents. Our main result characterizes when support and marginals guarantee one-step contraction uniformly over finite scores: every feasible face of the transportation polytope must have pairwise two-hop column overlap. Otherwise, suitable score directions make the contraction coefficient arbitrarily close to one. We extend this analysis to ordered support schedules and derive certificates for partition heat-bath layers, coordinate sweeps, forced shared mass, and register-augmented supports. These results provide mathematical criteria for support design in differentiable transport layers, with guarantees restricted to the fixed-support quotient-gradient component.

AI.tldr: Analyzes how the fixed support graph in sparse Sinkhorn layers governs gradient propagation, providing contraction conditions and design criteria for differentiable transport layers.
AI.motivation: Sparse Sinkhorn layers restrict transport between tokens using a fixed support graph, but how this structural sparsity affects gradient flow through iterative scaling is not well understood. The paper aims to build a precise mathematical theory of gradient propagation under fixed supports to guide the design of stable and efficient differentiable transport layers.
AI.method: Develop a ‘fixed-support calculus’ for Sinkhorn iterations. Model perturbations of column potentials and reverse-mode cotangents within the subspace modulo constants. Show that each row-column cycle in the support graph defines a row-stochastic linear operator on these perturbations and that its transpose governs reverse-mode gradient propagation. Analyze the resulting finite-cycle operators, especially at balanced fixed points where they simplify to two-step walks. Use Dobrushin contraction coefficients and minorization arguments to bound both homogeneous and source-driven gradient tails, and derive sharp conditions under which one-step contraction holds uniformly over all finite score tensors. Extend the framework to time-varying (ordered) supports and specialized support schedules such as partition heat-bath, coordinate sweeps, forced shared mass, and register-augmented supports.
AI.result: Show that the support graph structure tightly controls gradient contraction. At each fixed support, gradient propagation in the quotient space is governed by a row-stochastic operator derived from cycles in the support. The key structural condition for uniform one-step contraction over all finite scores is that every feasible face of the transportation polytope exhibits pairwise two-hop overlap between its columns. If this fails, there exist score directions whose associated gradient operator can have contraction coefficient arbitrarily close to one, implying very slow decay of gradients. The analysis is generalized to ordered support schedules and yields explicit contraction certificates for several practical structured-support schemes used in differentiable transport architectures.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous characterization of how fixed support patterns in sparse Sinkhorn layers regulate gradient flow, identifying precise graph-theoretic and polyhedral conditions under which gradients contract reliably. It offers mathematically grounded design rules for constructing support graphs and update schedules that yield well-behaved gradient propagation, while clarifying that guarantees apply only to the quotient component of gradients associated with the fixed support. These results can guide the principled design of differentiable transport layers in modern machine learning models.

title: What Eviction Destroys: A Restore-Counterfactual Audit of Forgetting in Agent Memory
summary: Agent memory systems must discard stored information when their history exceeds a fixed token budget. Existing budget-accuracy frontiers quantify the resulting loss in accuracy, but do not distinguish irreversible losses caused by eviction from recoverable retrieval failures. We introduce the restore counterfactual, a per-question paired intervention that reinstates the question's gold evidence in the read-time context and reruns the same reader. Combining the change in correctness with whether the evidence was retained after eviction classifies each oracle-answerable error as recoverable, irreversible, or residual; in the residual case, the answer remains incorrect after restoration. We evaluate FIFO, random, redundancy-aware, and LLM-importance eviction on LongMemEval-S at three budgets and under two retrieval regimes, using GPT-4o-mini as the primary reader and judge and GPT-5.4-mini as a robustness reader. Under top-k retrieval at an 80k-token budget, the irreversible share among errors corrected by restoration is 0.67-0.73 for FIFO, random, and redundancy-aware eviction, compared with 0.60 for LLM-importance. At 8k tokens, it reaches 1.00 for all four policies. Recoverable errors occur under top-k retrieval at 80k tokens but are absent under forced-gold injection by construction, so budget-accuracy results are not directly comparable unless the retrieval regime is reported. An exploratory matched-accuracy analysis detects no difference in irreversible rate among accuracy-matched policy pairs at a resolution of 1.2-6 percentage points. The same analysis detects the deliberately destructive control. To our knowledge, this is the first per-item, per-question restore-counterfactual audit of eviction for external agent-memory stores on a standard conversational benchmark.

AI.tldr: They propose a new way to audit what kinds of errors come from evicting memory vs. retrieval failures in long-context agent systems, using a restore-counterfactual method that re-injects gold evidence to classify errors as recoverable, irreversible, or residual.
AI.motivation: Current evaluations of long-context agent memory only measure how accuracy drops as the memory token budget shrinks, but they do not tell us whether accuracy loss is fundamentally irreversible (information was evicted and can’t be recovered) or just due to retrieval/usage issues, which matters for designing better memory and retrieval policies.
AI.method: They define a restore counterfactual procedure: for each question, they artificially restore the exact gold evidence into the model’s context at answer time and rerun the same reader model. By comparing correctness before vs. after restoration and checking whether the evidence had actually been retained in memory, they classify each oracle-answerable error as recoverable, irreversible, or residual. They then apply this to different eviction strategies (FIFO, random, redundancy-aware, LLM-importance) on the LongMemEval-S benchmark at multiple token budgets (8k–80k) and under two retrieval regimes (top-k retrieval vs. forced-gold injection), using GPT-4o-mini as the main reader/judge and GPT-5.4-mini as a secondary reader for robustness checks. They also run matched-accuracy analyses to compare policies at similar overall accuracy and include a deliberately destructive control to validate the sensitivity of their audit.
AI.result: Using top-k retrieval at an 80k-token budget, they find most corrected errors are irreversible (0.67–0.73 share for FIFO, random, redundancy-aware vs. 0.60 for LLM-importance), and at a tight 8k budget nearly all such errors are irreversible (1.00 for all policies). Recoverable errors appear under top-k retrieval at 80k but, by design, not under forced-gold injection, showing that budget-accuracy numbers depend critically on the retrieval regime. In matched-accuracy comparisons, they detect no statistically significant differences in irreversible-error rates between accuracy-matched eviction policies within a modest resolution (1.2–6 percentage points), while the framework does detect the purposely destructive baseline, indicating the method’s discriminative power.
AI.conclusion: The restore counterfactual provides a fine-grained, per-question audit of how memory eviction policies affect different kinds of errors in long-context agent systems, distinguishing irreversible losses from recoverable retrieval problems and residual model limitations. Their experiments suggest that, within typical accuracy ranges, standard eviction policies have similar proportions of irreversible errors at given accuracy levels, but retrieval regime and budget strongly shape whether errors are fundamentally due to lost information or to retriever/reader behavior. This is, to their claim, the first such detailed restore-counterfactual study on a standard conversational long-memory benchmark.

title: From Event Logs to Governed Action: A BlueSky Agenda for Agentic Process Mining
summary: Process mining has long turned event logs into process knowledge: discovered models, conformance evidence, bottleneck diagnoses, and runtime predictions. Agentic AI changes the target. Process-aware agents will not only ask what happened. They will ask whether a proposed action should be taken, given the available evidence, privacy budget, organizational authority, and downstream risk. This BlueSky paper proposes event-to-action process mining: a process-mining agenda for transforming heterogeneous operational event data into governed action. The goal is not another dashboard, a generic enterprise simulator, or a language interface over logs. We argue that the community needs four mineable artifacts: event-object representations, action evidence packages, governance contracts, and benchmarks where act, defer, ask, and refuse are all valid outputs. This agenda is timely because agentic business process management (BPM), LLM-assisted process mining, object-centric event standards, causal process monitoring, and privacy-preserving learning are maturing separately. Bringing them together defines a data-mining target inside process mining: mining logged organizational behavior for accountable action, not only retrospective insight.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new agenda called event-to-action process mining, shifting process mining from explaining past events to guiding whether concrete actions should be taken by process-aware agents, under constraints like evidence, privacy, authority, and risk.
AI.motivation: Traditional process mining turns event logs into retrospective insights such as discovered process models, conformance checks, bottleneck analysis, and predictions. However, with the emergence of agentic AI and process-aware agents, organizations need systems that do not just analyze what happened but can decide what to do next in a governed, accountable manner. Existing strands—agentic BPM, LLM-assisted mining, object-centric events, causal monitoring, and privacy-preserving learning—are maturing in isolation. There is a gap in unifying them toward actionable, accountable decision-making based on logged behavior.
AI.method: As a BlueSky/vision paper, the method is conceptual rather than algorithmic. The authors propose an agenda called event-to-action process mining, defining a new target for process mining and specifying four key artifacts to be mined: (1) event-object representations that capture heterogeneous operational data in a structured, object-centric way; (2) action evidence packages that bundle the relevant data, reasoning, and justification for a specific proposed action; (3) governance contracts that encode constraints such as privacy budgets, organizational authority, and acceptable risk; and (4) benchmarks and evaluation setups where different agent outputs (act, defer, ask for more information, or refuse) are all treated as valid, measurable outcomes.
AI.result: The paper’s result is a structured research agenda and conceptual framework for event-to-action process mining. It articulates the four mineable artifacts, positions the agenda relative to current developments (agentic BPM, LLM-assisted process mining, object-centric standards, causal monitoring, privacy-preserving learning), and reframes the goal of process mining from retrospective insight to accountable decision support for autonomous or semi-autonomous agents.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that process mining should evolve to support governed, accountable action decisions, not only explain past behavior. By centering on event-to-action process mining and its four proposed artifacts, the community can leverage recent advances across several subfields to build process-aware agents that decide when to act, defer, seek clarification, or refuse, under explicit governance constraints. This integration defines a new data-mining target: mining organizational behavior logs to produce justifiable, risk-aware actions rather than only descriptive analytics.

title: Tracing Stereotypes from Representation to Output in Multilingual LLMs
comment: 18 pages total (9 pages main text), 13 figures. Accepted to EMNLP 2026
summary: Multilingual LLMs show stereotype-related behavior that varies across languages, but behavioral scores do not show where the relevant information is represented or how it affects the output. To investigate these internal mechanisms, we compare linear probing, attribution patching, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and feature ablation in Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2-9B. Probe performance peaks substantially earlier than attribution in all three models, with a separation of 36-53% of model depth. Retained Llama-Scope features often match the social category on which they were selected and form recurring semantic families, but their lexical alignment and ablation effects vary across SAE suites. Only 6-18% of evaluated residual-stream features have language-agnostic effects under our criterion, and none are category-agnostic. Language-agnostic features have larger mean ablation effects in Llama-Scope, but this pattern does not repeat in the other SAE suites. Decodability, output influence, and cross-lingual ablation effects therefore need to be measured separately.

AI.tldr: The paper studies where and how multilingual large language models internally represent stereotypes, by comparing several interpretability methods and showing that decodability, internal representation, and behavioral influence diverge across depths, languages, and feature sets.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LLMs behave differently with respect to stereotypes across languages, but current behavioral metrics do not reveal how or where this information is encoded in the models, or which internal features actually drive outputs. Understanding these mechanisms is important for diagnosing and mitigating harmful bias and for evaluating interpretability methods in multilingual settings.
AI.method: The authors empirically compare four interpretability techniques—linear probing, attribution patching, sparse autoencoders, and feature ablation—on three multilingual LLMs: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma-2-9B. They trace stereotype-related information layer-by-layer, examine when probes and attribution peak, analyze SAE features from Llama-Scope for semantic structure and alignment to social categories, and quantify how ablating individual residual-stream features affects outputs across languages and categories.
AI.result: They find that linear probes reach peak performance substantially earlier in the network than attribution scores, with a depth separation of 36–53% in all three models. In Llama-Scope, many retained SAE features correspond well to specific social categories and cluster into recurring semantic families, but their lexical alignment and ablation impact differ across SAE suites. Only 6–18% of residual-stream features show language-agnostic effects under the paper’s criterion, and none are both language- and category-agnostic. Language-agnostic features in Llama-Scope exhibit larger average ablation effects, but this does not generalize to other SAE suites.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that stereotype-related information in multilingual LLMs is distributed and structured in ways that are not captured by any single interpretability signal. Where information is decodable (via probes), where attribution methods assign importance, and which features actually influence outputs—especially across languages—can diverge substantially. Therefore, decodability, output influence, and cross-lingual effects must be evaluated as distinct properties when analyzing and mitigating stereotypical behavior in multilingual LLMs.

title: When Can LLM Digital Twins Reduce Human Measurement? From Behavioral Fidelity to Statistical Substitutability
summary: LLM-based digital twins promise to reduce repeated human data collection by generating person- specific responses, yet existing evaluations provide little evidence about whether they can reduce human measurement while preserving valid inference. To address this, we introduce statistical substitutability, an inferential criterion that evaluates the extent to which twin predictions can reduce human measurement for a particular estimand while preserving valid inference. We develop a framework, grounded in mixed-subject and prediction-powered inference, that evaluates statistical substitutability along four dimensions: aggregate fidelity, paired respondent-level signal, finite-sample human-label recovery, and stability across populations. Across two empirical evaluations spanning behavioral experiments, multiple models, and alternative respondent representations, we find that digital twins can reproduce average human effects while providing little information about which individuals differ from those averages. Newer models and richer respondent information improve some dimensions of performance but do not reliably translate into human-data savings. Human calibration can reduce aggregate prediction error, yet limited labeled samples often fail to produce stable precision gains. Importantly, these findings demonstrate that behavioral fidelity is neither necessary nor sufficient for statistical substitutability. More broadly, they suggest that AI-generated evidence should be evaluated based on its ability to support valid scientific inference rather than its ability to reproduce human outcomes alone. Digital twins should therefore be judged for confirmatory use by whether they reduce uncertainty about human quantities, not merely by whether they reproduce human means, distributions, or effects.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and empirically tests a statistical criterion—statistical substitutability—for judging when LLM-based "digital twins" can replace some human data collection while still allowing valid statistical inference.
AI.motivation:
LLM-based digital twins are being proposed as a way to cheaply simulate human responses and reduce costly human data collection. However, existing evaluations mostly check whether models match average human behavior, not whether model-generated data can actually stand in for human data in statistical analyses without breaking inference.
The authors are motivated by the gap between behavioral fidelity (matching means, distributions, or treatment effects) and the stronger requirement that model predictions allow researchers to draw correct conclusions about population quantities and heterogeneity while using fewer human measurements.
AI.method:
The authors define "statistical substitutability" as an inferential criterion and build a framework rooted in mixed-subject designs and prediction-powered inference. They operationalize substitutability along four measurable dimensions: (1) aggregate fidelity—how well twins match average human effects; (2) paired respondent-level signal—how well predictions for a specific individual track that individual's true responses; (3) finite-sample human-label recovery—how well models help recover human effects when human labels are scarce; and (4) stability across populations—how robust performance is when applied to different populations.
They then conduct two empirical evaluations using behavioral experiments, multiple LLMs, and various ways of encoding respondents, and test effects of model improvements and human calibration (fine-tuning or prompting with labeled data).
AI.result:
Empirically, digital twins can reproduce average human effects reasonably well, satisfying aggregate fidelity, but they perform poorly at capturing which individuals deviate from those averages, indicating weak respondent-level signal. Improvements in model size or respondent representations yield some gains on certain dimensions but do not consistently reduce the amount of human data needed in practice. Human calibration can decrease aggregate prediction error, but when labeled human data are limited, it often fails to produce stable gains in precision or reliable uncertainty reduction.
Behavioral fidelity (matching observed means/effects) does not reliably align with the ability to substitute for human measurements in inferential tasks.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that current LLM-based digital twins are limited as substitutes for human data in many inferential contexts: they can mimic average effects but do not reliably support valid inference about individual-level variation or reduce the need for human data. Behavioral fidelity is neither a necessary nor sufficient condition for statistical substitutability. The authors argue that AI-generated evidence should be evaluated on its capacity to enable valid statistical inference and to reduce uncertainty about true human quantities, not just on its ability to reproduce human outcomes or distributions. As a result, digital twins should be judged, especially in confirmatory scientific use, by whether they measurably reduce uncertainty about target estimands when combined with finite human data.

title: SentryLine: Evidence-Grounded Question Answering over Evolving Documents in Oncology Care
summary: Oncology care operates at constant pressure of absorbing rapidly evolving evidence base in biomedicine. The American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) addresses this through living guidelines, but the format introduces a new burden: any recommendation can change at any point, across multiple versioned documents. We present SENTRYLINE, a living guideline-aware clinical question answering system. SENTRYLINE retrieves guideline passages through a vectorless hierarchical RAG pipeline and returns a role-specific answer with inline citations, factual and temporal verification reports, and drift detection notes that surface when a guideline has been updated. We construct ASCOBENCH, a benchmark of 405 three-turn conversations across four question categories with gold answers from expert annotators(clinicians), and use test set to evaluate SENTRYLINE against five baselines under an LLM-as-judge framework. Experiments across three generation backbones show consistent improvements over four retrieval baselines and ASCO's guideline assistant, with particularly strong gains on Reasoning and Role-Specific questions where multi-hop synthesis and register adaptation are required

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SENTRYLINE, a clinical question-answering system tailored to ASCO living oncology guidelines, and ASCOBENCH, a benchmark to evaluate such systems, showing that SENTRYLINE outperforms existing baselines, especially on reasoning- and role-specific queries.
AI.motivation: Oncology guidelines from ASCO are now `living`—continuously updated rather than periodically revised. This improves clinical relevance but creates cognitive and operational burden: any recommendation may change at any time, across multiple versions and documents. Traditional QA and search tools are not designed to track, verify, and explain such evolving guidance. The authors aim to build a system that can reliably answer clinical questions from living guidelines, surface evidence and temporal validity, and detect guideline drift, while also rigorously evaluating such systems with an appropriate benchmark.
AI.method: The authors design SENTRYLINE, a living-guideline–aware clinical QA system. Instead of dense vector retrieval, they use a vectorless hierarchical RAG pipeline tailored to guideline structure to retrieve relevant passages. The system generates role-specific answers (e.g., for different clinical roles) and includes inline citations, factual and temporal verification reports, and `drift detection` notes to flag when guidelines have been updated. To evaluate such systems, they construct ASCOBENCH: 405 three-turn conversations across four question categories, each with gold answers produced by clinician annotators. They then evaluate SENTRYLINE against five retrieval and QA baselines and ASCO’s own guideline assistant under an LLM-as-judge evaluation framework, and test across three different LLM generation backbones.
AI.result: Across the ASCOBENCH test set, SENTRYLINE consistently outperforms four retrieval baselines and ASCO’s guideline assistant. The performance gains hold across three different LLM generation backbones, indicating robustness of the approach. Improvements are most pronounced for `Reasoning` and `Role-Specific` questions, where multi-hop reasoning over the guideline text and adaptation of tone/detail to the user’s role are critical.
AI.conclusion: A guideline-structure–aware, vectorless hierarchical RAG approach can substantially improve clinical QA over living oncology guidelines compared to existing tools, especially for complex reasoning and role-tailored questions. The inclusion of inline citations, temporal and factual verification, and drift detection is effective for handling continuously updated guidance. ASCOBENCH provides a new benchmark for evaluating such systems and could facilitate future research on reliable, up-to-date clinical QA in dynamic guideline environments.

title: Mini-Batch Risk-Averse Deep Q-Learning: A Robot Navigation Case Study
summary:
We study the control of Markov decision processes in which the quality of a policy is evaluated by a dynamic, time-consistent Markov risk measure rather than by an expected discounted cost. The main obstacle to combining such measures with reinforcement learning is that a transition risk mapping depends on the transition kernel in a nonlinear way, and therefore cannot be estimated from a single observed transition. We remove this obstacle by employing mini-batch transition risk mappings: the mapping is applied to the empirical measure of $N$ independent next-state samples, and the result is averaged. The resulting mapping is again coherent. However, as an expected value of a function of $N$ next-state values, it admits an unbiased one-sample estimator.
  We embed this mapping into a double deep Q-network, analyze the two sources of estimation bias that arise, and obtain a risk-averse Q-learning method applicable to state spaces far beyond the reach of tabular schemes. The method is applied to an underwater robot navigation problem, in which a vehicle must visit collection points, gather stochastic information payloads, and deliver them at transmission points, while exposed at each step to the risk of destruction. A hierarchical decomposition delegates path execution to an exact graph search and confines learning to the high-level ``collect or transmit'' decision. A low-dimensional feature map, invariant under the symmetries of the problem, replaces the raw state--configuration encoding. In experiments on $300$ held-out environments, the resulting policies transfer to instance sizes never seen in training, and already $N=2$ reduces the upper semideviation of the outcome distribution while simultaneously improving its mean whenever the simulator is misspecified---an empirical counterpart of the duality between coherent risk measures and distributional robustness.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a practical deep Q-learning method for Markov decision processes where performance is measured by dynamic coherent risk (rather than expectation), by introducing mini-batch transition risk mappings that are both coherent and admit unbiased single-sample estimators, enabling scalable risk-averse control and demonstrating strong transfer in an underwater robot navigation task.
AI.motivation: Standard reinforcement learning optimizes expected return and struggles to incorporate dynamic, time-consistent risk measures, which are crucial in safety-critical or highly uncertain domains. For coherent Markov risk measures, the transition risk mapping depends nonlinearly on the transition kernel, so it cannot be reliably estimated from single transitions, blocking straightforward integration with sample-based RL. The authors aim to overcome this incompatibility so that powerful deep RL methods can be used for risk-averse control in large/state complex spaces.
AI.method: They introduce mini-batch transition risk mappings: instead of applying the risk mapping to the true transition kernel, it is applied to an empirical distribution formed from N i.i.d. next-state samples, and the result is averaged. This construction preserves coherence of the risk measure yet, because it becomes an expectation of a function of N samples, it allows an unbiased estimator based on one multi-sample observation. They then embed this construction into a double deep Q-network architecture, analyze the additional estimation biases introduced (both from function approximation and from the mini-batch risk mapping), and propose a risk-averse Q-learning algorithm suitable for high-dimensional state spaces. Further, they use a hierarchical decomposition for an underwater navigation task, performing exact graph search for low-level path planning and learning only the high-level collect/transmit decision, along with a symmetry-invariant low-dimensional feature representation.
AI.result: The resulting algorithm yields coherent, dynamically consistent risk-averse policies and is scalable via deep function approximation. In extensive experiments on 300 held-out underwater robot navigation environments, learned policies generalize to problem instances larger than those seen in training. Even with very small batch size (N=2), the approach significantly reduces upper semideviation (a measure of tail risk) while simultaneously improving the mean performance whenever the simulator model is misspecified, illustrating empirically that coherent risk optimization can act as a form of distributional robustness.
AI.conclusion: Mini-batch transition risk mappings resolve the incompatibility between dynamic coherent risk measures and sample-based reinforcement learning, making it possible to design scalable, deep risk-averse Q-learning algorithms. The proposed method achieves both improved average performance and reduced downside risk, and exhibits strong transfer to larger unseen instances, especially under model misspecification, supporting the view that coherent risk measures naturally embody distributional robustness in practical control problems.

title: Reading a Legal Question Word by Word: Embedding Trajectories of 2,144 Vietnamese Legal Headlines
summary: A dense retriever encodes a question as one vector, but the question arrives one word at a time. We read 2,144 held-out headlines from Thu Vien Phap Luat (Vietnamese legal library) word by word with Nemotron-3-Embed 8B/1B and Qwen3-Embedding 8B/0.6B, encoding 65,444 prefixes against 20,034 articles, plus every prefix of 3,438 sub-questions from 1,112 multi-question headlines and of 168 answers. (i) The gold article becomes rank 1 after a median of 6-7 content words in every encoder, before the interrogative frame is read, and stays there to the end in 78-85% of cases. (ii) In a multi-question headline the lock is inside the first sub-question 94-98% of the time; the second leaves rank unchanged in 89-95%; encoded alone, the second reaches rank 1 in 42-58% vs 91-96% for the first, at the same lock word (95-97% identical). (iii) Numbers, dates and instrument identifiers move the embedding twice as far as content words and four times as far as interrogative words; 72-78% of steps move toward the gold article, and the closing interrogative frame moves against that direction in 95-99% of headlines. (iv) Rank/cosine clustering yields six archetypes (instant, typical, unstable, late, never-locking) that differ by legal area and form (chi-squared p < 1e-8): real-estate and litigation headlines never lock on a number; environmental and accounting headlines do so a third of the time. (v) An answer read word by word retrieves its article after 8-16 words and addresses the sub-questions in order asked in 83-89% of cases. (vi) A word's step keeps a consistent direction across headlines (cosine 0.25-0.33; 0.44-0.60 for numbers); a preceding question rotates that step by about 60 degrees and a greeting by about 30 degrees; steps shrink as i^{-0.8}; and a two-question headline is within 12-17 degrees of a linear mix of its two questions. We call this a context-modulated additive walk.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how dense retrievers’ embeddings evolve as a question is read word by word, using Vietnamese legal search, and finds that retrieval ‘locks’ onto the right article early based on content tokens, while later interrogative framing often moves the embedding away; token types, legal domains, and discourse context systematically shape the embedding trajectory, which behaves like a context-modulated additive walk.
AI.motivation: Standard dense retrievers encode an entire question into a single vector, but in real interaction, questions are produced and processed incrementally, word by word. It is unclear when during this incremental process the model effectively identifies the target document, how different token types (content, numbers, interrogatives) contribute, and how question structure and context affect retrieval. Understanding this can inform better retriever design, prompt engineering, and diagnosis of retrieval failures, especially for complex, multi-question legal queries.
AI.method: The authors use several large embedding models (Nemotron-3-Embed 8B/1B and Qwen3-Embedding 8B/0.6B) on a Vietnamese legal corpus (20,034 articles) and 2,144 held-out legal headlines from Thu Vien Phap Luat. They read each headline word by word, computing embeddings for every prefix (65,444 prefixes). They also generate prefixes for sub-questions in multi-question headlines (3,438 sub-questions from 1,112 headlines) and for 168 answers. For each prefix, they compute the ranking of the gold article and analyze rank trajectories, cosine distances, and step vectors between successive prefixes. They quantify how different word types affect movement in embedding space, when the gold article first becomes rank 1 (“locks”), and how stable that lock is. They cluster rank/cosine trajectories to identify archetypal behaviors and analyze correlations with legal domains. They also study how prior context (previous questions, greetings) rotates and scales token steps, modeling embeddings as a context-modulated additive walk.
AI.result: (i) The correct (gold) article usually becomes top-1 after only 6–7 content words, before the interrogative framing is finished, and stays top in roughly 80% of cases across encoders. (ii) In multi-question headlines, the crucial ‘lock’ almost always (94–98%) occurs within the first sub-question; the second sub-question rarely changes rank (89–95% unchanged) and, when encoded in isolation, is much worse at reaching rank 1 (42–58%) than the first (91–96%), even at equivalent lock words. (iii) Numbers, dates, and identifiers move embeddings much more than ordinary content or interrogative words: about 2x the distance of content words and 4x interrogatives. A majority of steps (72–78%) move toward the gold article, but the final interrogative frame typically moves against that direction in 95–99% of cases. (iv) Clustering rank and cosine trajectories yields six retrieval archetypes (instant, typical, unstable, late, never-locking). Their distribution depends strongly on legal domain and headline form (significant chi-squared, p<1e−8). For example, real-estate and litigation headlines never lock on a number, while environmental and accounting headlines do so roughly one-third of the time. (v) When reading answers word by word, the correct article is usually retrieved after 8–16 words, and the answer tends to address sub-questions in the order they were asked in 83–89% of cases. (vi) Individual word steps have relatively stable directions across headlines (cosine 0.25–0.33, higher 0.44–0.60 for numbers). Prior context systematically rotates and scales these steps: a preceding question rotates them by ~60 degrees, a greeting by ~30 degrees, and step sizes shrink with prefix length as i^{-0.8}. For two-question headlines, the full embedding lies within 12–17 degrees of a linear mixture of the embeddings of the two separate questions, supporting an approximately additive composition view.
AI.conclusion: Dense retrievers on legal text appear to identify the target article very early in a question, mainly from the first sub-question and key content tokens such as numbers and identifiers. Later interrogative framing often pulls the embedding away from the optimal direction. The evolution of embeddings as words are added can be modeled as a context-modulated additive walk: each word contributes a relatively stable step in embedding space whose direction and magnitude are systematically influenced by prior context. Retrieval behavior varies by legal domain and headline form and can be grouped into distinct archetypes. These findings suggest that early, content-heavy cues dominate retrieval, that extraneous interrogative or politeness framing can harm ranking, and that embedding trajectories offer a useful lens for understanding and improving dense retrieval systems, especially in legal search and multi-question scenarios.

title: Sparks of In Silico Cognitive Science: Theories from Simulated Data Can Generalize to Humans
summary: Behavioral foundation models have been proposed as stand-ins for human participants across settings, but it is unclear whether theories discovered on them generalize to humans or merely characterize the simulator. We ran the Automated Cognitive Scientist (\textsc{AutoCog}), a closed-loop discovery system in which LLM agents design theory-discriminating experiments, collect responses, arbitrate between competing theories, and synthesize successors, entirely on behavior simulated by Centaur, a foundation model of human behavior. In a multi-attribute decision-making setting, the theories \textsc{AutoCog} found on Centaur generalized to human data: they outperformed canonical theories on ten held-out experiments and were rivaled only by theories found by running the same loop on people. We argue that this succeeds despite the simulator's inevitable imperfections because a discovery loop that arbitrates between competing theories demands less of its simulator than estimation does. The simulator only needs to capture the regularities that distinguish the theories, and not necessarily reproduce behavior precisely. Imperfect simulators can therefore widen the search over theories, with human data then testing whether the surfaced theories generalize.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether theories discovered using a behavioral foundation model (Centaur) and an automated theory-discovery loop (AutoCog) actually generalize to real human behavior, finding that they largely do in a decision-making domain.
AI.motivation: Behavioral foundation models are being proposed as scalable substitutes for human participants, but it is unknown whether theories derived from simulations on these models describe humans or only the simulator. The authors want to know if these models can safely be used to explore and refine cognitive theories before testing them on real people.
AI.method: They deploy AutoCog, an automated cognitive scientist system using LLM agents to design theory-discriminating experiments, collect responses, compare competing theories, and synthesize improved successors. Crucially, they run this entire closed-loop discovery process on Centaur, a behavioral foundation model, in a multi-attribute decision-making task, and then evaluate the resulting theories on held-out human experiments, comparing them to canonical theories and to theories evolved directly on human data.
AI.result: Theories discovered by running AutoCog on Centaur generalized well to humans: they outperformed standard canonical decision-making theories on ten held-out human experiments and were only matched by theories discovered by running AutoCog on actual human participants rather than the simulator.
AI.conclusion: Even though behavioral simulators like Centaur are imperfect, they can still be useful engines for theory discovery because a theory-comparison loop only requires that the simulator reliably capture the regularities that distinguish competing theories, not that it precisely match human behavior. Such imperfect simulators can broaden the search over possible theories, with final validation and generalization checks carried out using human data.

title: Structural Jailbreaks Generalize but Do Not Compound: A cross-provider and multilingual study of Involuntary In-Context Learning
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Pilot study. Includes a cross-family judge-agreement check (kappa=0.86) and output-language verification
summary: Aligned language models fail under two independent pressures: the structural jailbreak class recently formalized as Involuntary In-Context Learning (IICL), which reframes a harmful request as the final missing cell of a data-labeling task completed by pattern rather than judged as content; and the erosion of safety alignment outside English. A natural hypothesis is that these compound. We test it directly. Using a deterministic IICL operator and a StrongREJECT-style rubric judge, we red-team two Google Gemini models on two benchmarks, a 30 general-harm behaviours from HarmBench and 30 financial-abuse behaviours from FinProof, each under a single-shot baseline and under IICL in four languages (English, Spanish, Hindi, Arabic). First, IICL generalizes to a second provider and is worse in finance: it lifts attack success from <=6.7% to 80-90% on HarmBench and 97-100% on FinProof, an order of magnitude above the <=24% its introducing study reported on OpenAI's GPT-5.4. Second, against the hypothesis, forcing the IICL output into a non-English language does not stack the two weaknesses, it attenuates the attack. Eleven of twelve non-English conditions score below their English baseline (sign test, p~0.003), the lone exception a ceiling tie near 100%; on the stronger model's financial set Arabic collapses from 100% to 33%. We attribute this to a relevance curse: once structure has unlocked compliance, the models produce lower-quality harmful content in lower-resource languages, which a substance-grading judge scores as partial. The pattern replicates under an independent non-Google judge (Cohen's kappa=0.86, 377 paired verdicts), and 76.6% of non-English responses were verified in-language. Jailbreak vulnerabilities are therefore not additive; the dominant residual risk is the English structural attack, most acute for financial abuse, not a multilingual one.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a known structural jailbreak method (Involuntary In-Context Learning, IICL) makes safety-aligned language models highly vulnerable, especially for financial-abuse prompts, but that forcing responses into non-English languages actually weakens, rather than strengthens, this attack.
AI.motivation: Safety-aligned language models are known to be vulnerable to two separate issues: (1) structural jailbreaks like IICL, which trick the model into treating harmful content as part of a data-labeling pattern-completion task, and (2) weaker safety behavior and oversight in non-English languages. A natural concern is that these two weaknesses might combine, producing especially dangerous multilingual jailbreaks. The authors want to test whether this compounding actually happens in practice and to quantify the real residual risk profile across tasks and languages.
AI.method: The authors apply a deterministic IICL attack operator to prompts drawn from two benchmarks: 30 general-harm behaviors from HarmBench and 30 financial-abuse behaviors from FinProof. They evaluate two Google Gemini models under single-shot baseline prompts and under IICL-augmented prompts, in four target languages (English, Spanish, Hindi, Arabic). They use a StrongREJECT-style rubric-based judge model to grade whether the model’s response constitutes successful harmful behavior. They then compare success rates across models, tasks, and languages, and cross-check with an independent, non-Google judge to measure agreement (Cohen’s kappa) and ensure responses are actually produced in the claimed language.
AI.result: IICL substantially increases attack success rates on Google Gemini models, generalizing prior findings from a different provider and being even more severe in financial settings. Success rates rise from at most 6.7% to 80–90% on the general-harm HarmBench tasks and to 97–100% on FinProof financial-abuse tasks, well above previously reported figures on another model family. Contrary to the compounding-weakness hypothesis, forcing IICL outputs into non-English languages attenuates the attack instead of strengthening it: in 11 of 12 non-English configurations, success is lower than the English baseline, with the only exception being a near-100% ceiling tie. In one striking case, for the stronger model on financial tasks in Arabic, success drops from 100% to 33%. The replication with an independent judge yields high agreement (Cohen’s kappa = 0.86), and most non-English responses are verified to actually be in the target language.
AI.conclusion: Structural jailbreaks via IICL pose a major residual safety risk for aligned language models, especially in high-stakes financial-abuse scenarios, and this vulnerability can be extremely severe even for leading commercial systems. However, the feared compounding of structural jailbreaks with multilingual safety weaknesses does not materialize: non-English responses under IICL tend to be of lower substantive quality and are often graded as only partially harmful, leading to reduced measured attack success. The dominant risk surface is therefore the English-language structural jailbreak, not a multilingual one, and mitigation efforts should prioritize shoring up defenses against such pattern-based attacks, particularly in financial domains.

title: From Version Conflicts to Decision Conflicts: Selective Revalidation for Long-Running AI Agents
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Supplemental artifact available at https://github.com/ezreal13/atr-decision-validation/tree/89c32fa475f5216db4c9d76a1eddde79e874073b
summary: Long-running AI agents may read state, reason, wait for tools or human approval, and perform an external action much later. The state that justified the action can change in the meantime. For example, after an agent proposes an 80 GBP refund under a limit of 100, a customer-name change affects only presentation metadata, a new limit of 90 still permits the refund, a limit of 50 invalidates it, and a refund issued by another worker must prevent a duplicate. Standard optimistic concurrency control and version checks can detect that previously read state has changed, but by themselves do not determine whether that change invalidates the pending action's justification. We call any detected version change a version conflict; when that change invalidates the action's justification, it is also a decision conflict. ATR records the explicit, executable conditions that justify a pending action and rechecks only the conditions affected by a change before releasing the external operation. It can retain the action, refresh non-decisive metadata, require replanning, or block execution; a target-side transaction or compare-and-set binds checked state to commit. Across 210,000 controlled executions over 15 mutation cases, ATR matched every developer-specified outcome with no false allows or blocks. In ten durable SQLite checkpoint/resume cells, it evaluated 0.6 conditions per change versus 6.0 for FullScan. At 4,093 recorded reads, ATR took 9.3 microseconds versus 2595.9 microseconds for FullScan. These deterministic results establish controlled feasibility, not production generality or automatic extraction of the required conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ATR, a system for safely executing delayed actions by re-checking only the specific conditions that justify the action when underlying state changes.
AI.motivation: Long-running AI agents often decide on actions based on environment state that may change before the action is actually executed. Simple version checks can detect that something changed, but they cannot say whether the change truly invalidates the original decision. This gap leads either to unsafe actions (if changes are ignored) or to overly conservative blocking or recomputation (if any change cancels the action). The paper seeks a principled way to distinguish harmless from decision-critical state changes for delayed actions.
AI.method: The authors define two concepts: version conflicts (any detected change in previously read state) and decision conflicts (changes that truly invalidate the action’s justification). They propose ATR, which records explicit, executable decision conditions at planning time for each pending action. When state changes are detected before action execution, ATR selectively re-evaluates only the conditions that depend on the changed data. Based on the results, ATR can: keep the action as-is, update non-critical metadata, force replanning, or block the action. They use a target-side transaction or compare-and-set to atomically bind the verified state to the final commit. The evaluation runs controlled experiments with many mutation cases and compares ATR against a naive FullScan approach that re-checks all reads.
AI.result: In 210,000 controlled executions across 15 mutation cases, ATR’s behavior always matched developer-specified intended outcomes, with no incorrect allowances or blocks. In experiments on ten durable SQLite checkpoint/resume cells, ATR needed on average 0.6 condition evaluations per change compared to 6.0 for FullScan, and with 4,093 recorded reads it achieved 9.3 microseconds latency versus 2595.9 microseconds for FullScan, demonstrating large efficiency gains and deterministic behavior.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that ATR can reliably distinguish between mere version conflicts and true decision conflicts for delayed actions, and can do so much more efficiently than re-checking all past reads. This establishes that the approach is technically feasible and deterministic in controlled settings, though the authors caution that this does not yet demonstrate general applicability in production systems or automatic derivation of the required decision conditions.

title: Compositional Multilingual and Behavioral Attribute Steering
summary: This study examines the compositionality of steering vectors for language and behavioral control in large language models. Focusing on language, jailbreak, and conciseness, we investigate whether additive, training-free composition of attribute steering vectors can preserve the intended steering effect of each attribute, across four instruction-tuned models from two model families and two size scales. We find that single-attribute steering is reliable for all three attributes, but only within an appropriate combination of intervention layer and steering strength, with abstract behaviors (jailbreak, conciseness) favoring middle layers and language favoring earlier layers. We show that additive composition of two attribute vectors succeeds in steering both attributes simultaneously when each is injected at its own best-performing layer, and that this partially extends to three simultaneously composed attributes, addressing an inconsistency left open by prior work on training-free composition. We further analyze the geometric properties of these steering vectors, finding that they are approximately orthogonal in the residual stream, consistent with their compositional behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether steering vectors for different attributes in large language models can be combined additively to control multiple behaviors at once, without extra training.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows that single steering vectors can control attributes like style or safety in LLMs, but it is unclear if these vectors can be combined in a simple, training-free way while preserving each attribute’s effect. This paper aims to clarify when and how such compositional control works, addressing gaps and inconsistencies in earlier findings on vector composition.
AI.method: The authors construct steering vectors for three attributes—language (e.g., output language), jailbreak (safety-violating behavior), and conciseness—and inject them into different layers of four instruction-tuned models spanning two families and two sizes. They systematically vary the intervention layer and steering strength, test single-attribute steering, and then evaluate additive composition of two and three attribute vectors, measuring how well each target behavior is expressed. They also study the geometry of the steering vectors, particularly their mutual orientations in residual stream space.
AI.result: Single-attribute steering works reliably for all three attributes, but only when the steering vector is applied at suitable layers and with appropriate strengths: abstract behavioral attributes like jailbreak and conciseness work best in middle layers, while language control works best in earlier layers. When composing two steering vectors additively, the model can simultaneously express both target attributes if each vector is injected at its own optimal layer. This effect partially extends to three-attribute compositions. Geometric analysis reveals that the steering vectors are approximately orthogonal in the residual stream, consistent with their ability to compose without strongly interfering with each other.
AI.conclusion: Attribute steering in LLMs is layer- and strength-dependent, with different types of behaviors favoring different intervention depths. Simple additive, training-free composition of steering vectors can successfully control multiple attributes at once, particularly when each vector is applied at its best-performing layer, and this scales to three attributes to a limited degree. The near-orthogonality of steering vectors in representation space provides a geometric explanation for why such compositionality can work, offering guidance for designing practical multi-attribute control schemes for LLMs.

title: A Layered Analysis of Disagreement And Answer Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
summary: Multi-agent debate, in which several LLMs exchange arguments before answering, is widely assumed to improve answer quality by surfacing genuine disagreement. That mechanism is rarely checked. We introduce four measurements: (A) the agreement a debater reports; (B) whether its reply text actually pushes back; (C) whether the position persists once the eliciting instruction is removed; and (D) for open-weight models, the stance response in the debater's own token log-probabilities. We evaluate three-model committees debating open-ended GlobalOpinionQA across 750 debates under three tones: friendly (seek common ground), neutral, and hostile (stress-test every position). (A) Tone strongly reshapes reported agreement: full agreement differs by 50.4 percentage points between the friendly and hostile endpoints. (B) A judge that reads only the reply text, never the self-report or the condition, recovers the same pattern. (C) The dissent appears partly tied to the instruction that elicited it: labels revert toward agreement 23.1 points more often after deleting the hostile instruction than under a matched re-ask that keeps it; question-weighted inference is inconclusive on first-round turns alone (p=0.0625), significant pooling all rounds (p=0.016), and only 11/28 first-round reversions also appear in the reply text. (D) Opposing arguments weaken a debater's stance margin more consistently than they shift its direction. For final answers we detect no quality gain: a bias-checked jury returns 299/299 ties (ruling out only large differences), accuracy on a verifiable control task is unchanged, and a jury without the bias check had declared debate the winner 66% of the time -- an artifact of reading order. Taken together, LLM debate readily changes what agents say, but we find much weaker evidence that it changes what they persistently endorse or improves the quality of the final answer.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether multi-agent LLM debate actually improves answer quality or reflects genuine disagreement, and finds that while debate changes what models say, it has little evidence of changing underlying stances or improving final answers.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent debate with multiple LLMs is popular and assumed to enhance reliability by surfacing and resolving disagreements, but this assumption is rarely empirically examined. The authors are motivated to rigorously test whether debate alters models’ underlying beliefs or just their surface-level outputs, and whether it truly improves answer quality.
AI.method: They define four measures: (A) explicit self-reported agreement among debaters; (B) whether the textual reply actually disagrees or pushes back; (C) whether expressed stances persist after removing the debate-eliciting instruction; and (D) for open-weight models, whether internal token log-probabilities show a changed stance. They run 750 three-model debates on open-ended GlobalOpinionQA questions under three tones (friendly, neutral, hostile) and analyze agreement patterns, reversions when instructions are removed, stance margins from log-probs, and down-stream answer quality judged by juries with and without bias controls and by accuracy on a verifiable control task.
AI.result: (A) Reported agreement varies greatly with tone, with a 50.4 percentage point difference in full agreement between friendly and hostile conditions. (B) A blind judge looking only at the reply texts recovers the same tone-dependent disagreement pattern. (C) Many disagreements appear instruction-dependent: when hostile instructions are removed, labels revert toward agreement 23.1 percentage points more often than in re-asks that retain hostility; statistical tests are marginal on first rounds but significant when pooling all rounds, and only a minority of label reversions are reflected in the reply text. (D) Opposing arguments tend to reduce stance confidence (margin) rather than flip stance direction in token log-probabilities. For final answers, a bias-controlled jury finds 299/299 ties between debate and non-debate answers, accuracy on a verifiable task is unchanged, and an uncontrolled jury’s earlier preference for debated answers (66%) is attributable to reading-order bias.
AI.conclusion: LLM debate is highly effective at changing expressed agreement and the surface form of answers but offers much weaker evidence of changing underlying or persistent stances, and it does not show clear improvements in final answer quality. Much of the apparent benefit of debate may be an artifact of instructions and presentation, not a genuine epistemic gain.

title: Detecting Authorship in Political Texts with Inductive Stylometry
comment: 34 pages, 17 figures, 3 tables. Includes appendices A-D (validation materials and discriminant validity checks). Under review
summary: Political texts are rarely authored by the nominal speaker alone. Tweets, speeches, reports, and official statements are drafted, edited, or harmonized by staff, yet political science has paid limited attention to the stylistic traces these hidden authors leave behind. This paper develops and stress-tests an inductive stylometric approach for recovering latent authorship structure in political communication, combining character 3-gram features with UMAP dimensionality reduction, and Burrows' Delta. We apply the approach to six corpora that vary in length (from tweets to long documents), in mode (written and oral), and in language (English and Hungarian). The approach recovers near-disjoint analyst fingerprints in formal legal prose in both languages, sorts a politician's tweets into validated subsets while uncovering additional insights, and distinguishes scripted from improvised speech. It fails, however, to resolve individual speechwriters within scripted corpora. Frequency-based stylometry is thus a powerful tool that, depending on authorial signal strength and institutional editing, can uncover authorship traces relevant to legislative studies, political communication, and policy research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and tests a stylometric method to uncover hidden authorship patterns in political texts, showing when it works well and where it fails.
AI.motivation: Political communication is usually attributed to a single public figure, but in reality texts are heavily shaped by staffers, analysts, and speechwriters. Political science rarely accounts for these hidden contributors, leaving a gap in understanding who actually crafts political messages and how institutional processes shape them. The authors aim to develop a systematic way to detect and study latent authorship structures in such texts.
AI.method: They propose an inductive stylometric approach based on frequency features. Specifically, they use character 3-grams to capture stylistic patterns, apply UMAP for dimensionality reduction to visualize and structure the text space, and use Burrows' Delta as a distance metric for stylometric comparison. They then stress-test this pipeline on six diverse corpora that vary in text length (from tweets to lengthy documents), modality (written vs. oral), and language (English and Hungarian).
AI.result: The method successfully identifies almost non-overlapping stylistic fingerprints of analysts in formal legal texts in both English and Hungarian, correctly partitions a politician’s tweet corpus into validated subsets while revealing further patterns, and can distinguish scripted from improvised speech. However, it does not perform well at separating individual speechwriters within fully scripted speech corpora, indicating limits when authorial signals are weak or heavily blended by institutional editing.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-based stylometry using character 3-grams, UMAP, and Burrows' Delta can be a strong tool for uncovering hidden authorship structures in political communication, but its effectiveness depends on the strength and distinctness of authorial signals and the degree of institutional editing. When these conditions are favorable, it can generate insights valuable to legislative studies, political communication research, and policy analysis; when they are not, its resolution at the individual author level is limited.

title: Eliciting Self-Verification in Multimodal Reasoning Agents with Reinforcement Learning
comment: To appear in ECCV 2026. 11 main pages. 7 figures
summary: Reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools such as web search to answer complex queries. Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning algorithms such as GRPO have improved long-form reasoning in text-only language models, particularly for coding and mathematics. Reliable tool use in multimodal agents, however, remains challenging because models must interpret text and images while integrating noisy retrieved evidence, often under sparse outcome-level supervision without explicit verification signals. We present Self-Verification via Reinforcement Learning (SVRL), an RL-only finetuning framework that trains multimodal agents to verify and filter retrieved evidence within their own reasoning traces, reducing reliance on external verifiers at inference time.
