AI.conclusion: ELCD is an effective, model-agnostic post-generation detector for identifying latent instruction conflicts in LLM outputs. By focusing on hidden-state representations of the entire response, it can capture subtle response drift that input-focused or shallow heuristics miss, making it especially suitable for open-weight or self-hosted LLM deployments that require robust system-level constraint enforcement.

title: SWE-Bench Pro Verified: A Reliable Benchmark for Software Engineering Agents
summary: SWE-Bench Pro has emerged as a standard benchmark for evaluating software engineering agents on challenging repository-level tasks. However, our analysis work show that its evaluation is undermined by two sources of unreliability: \textbf{reward hacking}, enabled by leakage of gold solutions or hidden evaluation information, and \textbf{task quality issues}, including misleading problem statements and improperly scoped tests. These issues can inflate benchmark performance and obscure agents' true coding ability. We present \textbf{SWE-Bench Pro Verified}, a verified version of SWE-Bench Pro that addresses both problems. Our approach combines \textbf{anti-hacking} safeguards that eliminate major leakage channels without disrupting normal agent functionality, with \textbf{task refinement} that minimally corrects inconsistencies within flawed instances. Evaluations on SWE-Bench Pro Verified reveal that some models perform substantially worse than previously reported, suggesting that existing results on SWE-Bench Pro may overestimate real software engineering capability. SWE-Bench Pro Verified offers a more trustworthy benchmark for assessing software engineering agents.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SWE-Bench Pro Verified, an improved and more reliable benchmark for evaluating software engineering agents, addressing reward hacking and task quality issues found in the original SWE-Bench Pro.
AI.motivation: SWE-Bench Pro is widely used to evaluate software engineering agents on complex, repository-level tasks, but its reliability is compromised. Reward hacking via solution leakage and hidden evaluation details, along with low-quality or flawed tasks, can inflate performance scores and misrepresent true coding ability. The authors aim to provide a more trustworthy benchmark so that research progress and model comparisons are meaningful.
AI.method: The authors carefully analyze SWE-Bench Pro to identify sources of unreliability. They design anti-hacking safeguards that close major leakage channels (such as access to gold solutions or hidden evaluation artifacts) while preserving standard agent workflows. In parallel, they perform task refinement: minimally editing or correcting problematic benchmark instances (e.g., misleading descriptions, incorrect test scopes) to resolve inconsistencies without changing the fundamental nature of tasks. They then re-evaluate existing models on this verified benchmark.
AI.result: When evaluated on SWE-Bench Pro Verified, some models show substantially lower performance than on the original SWE-Bench Pro, demonstrating that prior results were inflated by reward hacking opportunities and flawed tasks. The revised benchmark exposes more realistic performance levels and clearer differences among models.
AI.conclusion: SWE-Bench Pro Verified mitigates reward hacking and task quality issues in the original SWE-Bench Pro, yielding more accurate and trustworthy measurements of software engineering agents’ capabilities. Consequently, earlier SWE-Bench Pro scores likely overestimate real-world coding ability, and future work should adopt the verified benchmark for reliable evaluation and comparison of software engineering agents.

title: When Victorian Becomes a Prompt: Literary Periodization as a Generative Constraint in 100 AI-Generated Novels
summary: Generative AI inverts the typical periodization of literary history: the periodizing tag Victorian can now come first and influence what is written. Generative periodization, defined and tested here, describes the use of literary-period designations in generating texts. I test this approach on 100 book-length novels produced under Victorian and Zero-Style conditions using GPT, Qwen, and Llama workflows. The Period Alignment Score (PAS), trained on nineteenth-century literature and benchmarked against human Zero-Style prose, assesses alignment using topic-reduced grammatical features. Victorian prompts produce consistent historical-direction shifts in GPT and Qwen, but not robustly in Llama. Victorian-only recalibration and harder comparison corpora preserve the GPT and Qwen effects. Cross-model transfer also shows a shared direction of grammatical change. The measurable target is the broader nineteenth century rather than the Victorian period per se.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces and tests a quantitative way to see whether large language models can successfully write in a specified historical literary style (e.g., “Victorian”), showing that some models respond consistently at the level of grammar and others less so.
AI.motivation: To understand whether literary period labels like “Victorian” meaningfully shape the output of generative AI, and to develop a rigorous, measurable way to detect and compare such style shifts across models instead of relying on impressionistic judgments.
AI.method: The author defines “generative periodization,” then generates 100 book-length novels under two prompt conditions—“Victorian” vs “Zero-Style” (neutral)—using multiple LLM workflows (GPT, Qwen, Llama). They create a Period Alignment Score (PAS), trained on nineteenth‑century literature and benchmarked against human-written neutral prose, which analyzes topic-reduced grammatical features to quantify how much each generated text aligns with nineteenth‑century style. They also run robustness checks: recalibrating PAS only on Victorian data, using harder comparison corpora, and testing cross‑model transfer of the grammatical-change direction.
AI.result: GPT and Qwen show clear, consistent shifts in grammatical features toward a nineteenth‑century direction when prompted with “Victorian,” while Llama does not consistently do so. The effects for GPT and Qwen persist under stricter calibrations and more challenging baselines, and the direction of grammatical change is shared across models in cross‑model transfer tests. However, the PAS signal corresponds more reliably to the broader nineteenth century than to the narrower Victorian period specifically.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI can be steered toward historically inflected grammatical styles using simple period labels, but the effect depends on the model and is more reliably aligned with a broad nineteenth‑century style than with a tightly defined Victorian one. The proposed framework of “generative periodization” and the Period Alignment Score offers a reproducible way to measure such historical-style alignment across models and prompt conditions.

title: WorldAgen: Unified State-Action Prediction with Test-Time World Model Training
summary: How can vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt to new environments where world dynamics shift? While recent research has combined world modeling and action prediction to improve VLA performance, existing methods largely rely on pretraining on static datasets, without mechanisms for active adaptation at deployment time. As a result, these models often fail to generalize when deployed in unseen scenarios with novel object configurations or dynamics. We present WorldAgen, a unified framework that jointly learns world modeling and action prediction while enabling Test-Time Training (TTT) to adapt to new environments. WorldAgen employs a shared Transformer backbone with two heads: (1) a world model head that predicts future states from past state-action trajectories, and (2) an agent model head that predicts actions conditioned on task instructions. We design a Mixed Unidirectional Attention Mask to separate these two models. During test time, WorldAgen samples exploratory actions, collects ground-truth state transitions, and performs lightweight TTT updates to refine its world model. This adaptation improves the model's understanding of the environment and leads to more accurate action predictions. Experiments on the CALVIN and LIBERO benchmarks demonstrate that our baseline model achieves comparable, and in some cases superior, performance to current state-of-the-art approaches. Moreover, with TTT on a small number of samples, our method surpasses existing state-of-the-art models, highlighting the effectiveness of adapting world models at inference time.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes WorldAgen, a vision-language-action framework that jointly learns a world model and an action policy, and uses test-time training to adapt its world model in new environments, thereby improving action performance and outperforming prior state-of-the-art on CALVIN and LIBERO with few adaptation samples.
AI.motivation: Existing VLA models are mostly pretrained on static datasets and lack mechanisms for active adaptation when deployed in new environments with shifted dynamics or novel object configurations, causing poor generalization. The authors want a unified framework that can both model the environment and adapt online at test time to maintain or improve performance under distribution shift.
AI.method: WorldAgen uses a shared Transformer backbone with two heads: a world model head predicting future states from past state-action trajectories, and an agent model head predicting actions given task instructions. A Mixed Unidirectional Attention Mask separates information flow between these two functions within the shared backbone. At test time, the system executes exploratory actions to gather real transition data, then performs lightweight test-time training updates on the world model head while keeping the policy connected to the updated representation, thus adapting its understanding of the environment for better downstream action prediction.
AI.result: On CALVIN and LIBERO benchmarks, the base WorldAgen (without test-time adaptation) reaches comparable or sometimes better performance than current state-of-the-art models. When applying test-time training using only a small number of collected samples in the new environment, WorldAgen surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating that online adaptation of the world model leads to improved action performance under novel dynamics and configurations.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning a world model and an action policy in a shared architecture, combined with test-time training on environment transitions, is an effective way to adapt VLA systems to novel environments. Updating the world model at inference time improves environmental understanding and in turn enhances action prediction, yielding state-of-the-art performance with limited adaptation data on challenging manipulation benchmarks.

title: Global Divergence, Local Convergence: Representation Geometry in SSMs and Transformers
summary: Recent state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba achieve language modeling performance comparable to transformers despite relying on fundamentally different architectures. This raises an important question: how do these structural differences influence the geometry and functional nature of their internal representations? We study this question through a multi-scale analysis of representations in transformers, SSMs, and hybrid architecture. First, we find that SSMs distribute their representational information evenly across all dimensions, whereas transformer representations are heavily dominated by a single principal direction. By evaluating hybrid architectures, we observe that the representation space becomes increasingly skewed toward a single dominant direction after each attention layer. Next, we explore how the different geometric spread of representations impacts representational capacity through compressibility. Surprisingly, we find that despite their contrasting geometric structures, both architectures exhibit tightly matched effective capacities. We further investigate whether this skewed geometry affects how concepts are encoded. Using rank-constrained probes, we demonstrate that both architectures encode concepts in subspaces of surprisingly similar dimensionality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transformers' dominant principal direction does not inherently encode more conceptual information. Finally, we zoom in and examine the alignment between manifolds, either by analyzing representations of specific topics or by looking at the nearest neighborhoods of tokens, and find that they are highly aligned. Ultimately, our analysis suggests that while transformers and SSMs induce different usage of latent space, they display a striking functional convergence at the level of local semantic manifolds.

AI.tldr: The paper compares how state-space models (SSMs) like Mamba and transformers represent information internally, finding different global geometry but very similar functional behavior at the level of semantic manifolds.
AI.motivation: Transformers and recent SSMs achieve similar language modeling performance but use very different architectures, and it is unclear how these structural differences affect the geometry, capacity, and conceptual encoding of their internal representations. Understanding this can clarify whether these models fundamentally differ in how they represent meaning, or merely in how they use latent space.
AI.method: The authors perform a multi-scale representation analysis across transformers, SSMs, and hybrid models. They: (1) examine spectrum/variance distribution across representation dimensions and how this changes after each attention layer in hybrid architectures; (2) quantify representational capacity via compressibility; (3) use rank-constrained linear probes to estimate the dimensionality of concept-encoding subspaces; and (4) analyze alignment of representation manifolds by topic and via nearest-neighbor structures to assess local semantic similarity between models.
AI.result: They find that SSMs spread information relatively evenly across dimensions, while transformer representations are dominated by a single principal direction that becomes more pronounced after attention layers. Despite these geometric differences, both architectures have very similar effective representational capacities. Concept subspaces probed with rank constraints have comparable dimensionality across models, and the dominant principal direction in transformers does not carry disproportionate conceptual information. Local semantic manifolds—captured via topic-specific representations and nearest-neighbor neighborhoods—are highly aligned between transformers and SSMs.
AI.conclusion: Transformers and SSMs use latent space in geometrically distinct ways at a global level—transformers with a skewed, principal-direction-dominated structure and SSMs with a more isotropic spread—but they converge functionally: their effective capacities, concept subspace dimensionalities, and local semantic manifolds are remarkably similar. Thus, architectural differences primarily affect global geometry and coordinate usage rather than the underlying structure of encoded semantic information.

title: Key Path Identification for Resolving Knowledge Conflicts via SAE-based Steering
summary: Sparse autoencoder (SAE)-based steering has been widely used to address knowledge conflicts by guiding LLMs to be more faithful to the contextual knowledge. Existing methods usually perform mass steering, which modifies a large batch of SAE features identified via correlation-based methods. However, due to the inaccurate correlation and the neglected feature interactions, mass steering methods fail to precisely identify the features that play the key roles in steering and introduce a large number of redundant ones, which add noise and weaken the steering effects. Our empirical studies reveal that steering only a small subset of the identified features can achieve comparable or even better performance. Motivated by this finding, we propose Key Path Identification (KPI), a novel method that identifies key steering features characterized by strong causal dependencies with both upstream and downstream features. From these features, KPI constructs key paths and steers through less feature modifications. In this way, KPI advances SAE-based steering from quantity-driven to quality-focused, offering a perspective for more precise and interpretable model editing. Experiments in RAG tasks with knowledge conflicts show that our method improves the accuracy by 18% on average compared to the best baseline of mass steering, effectively filtering redundant features, alleviating side effects and demonstrating the core role of key paths in steering.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Key Path Identification (KPI), a method that improves sparse autoencoder-based steering of LLMs by focusing on a small set of causally important features instead of mass steering many correlated features, yielding more precise and effective model editing in RAG with knowledge conflicts.
AI.motivation: Existing SAE-based steering methods for LLMs typically steer many features selected via correlation. This mass steering approach suffers from noisy feature selection, redundant modifications, and neglected interactions among features, which weakens steering effects and interpretability. The authors empirically find that steering only a small subset of features can perform as well or better, motivating a principled way to identify which features are truly key for steering.
AI.method: The authors introduce Key Path Identification (KPI), which identifies key steering features based on their strong causal dependencies with both upstream and downstream features in the SAE feature graph. KPI then builds "key paths" that capture the core causal routes relevant to steering and modifies only features along these paths, rather than all correlated features. This shifts from quantity-driven (many features) to quality-focused (few but causally central features) steering, making feature selection more precise and interpretable.
AI.result: On retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) tasks involving knowledge conflicts, KPI-based steering improves accuracy by about 18% on average over the best mass-steering baseline. The method successfully filters out redundant features and reduces side effects, while maintaining or improving steering effectiveness, demonstrating that a small set of key paths dominates the steering behavior.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that in SAE-based steering, focusing on a small set of causally central key paths is more effective than steering many correlation-selected features. KPI provides a more precise and interpretable steering/editing mechanism, better resolves knowledge conflicts in RAG, and highlights the central role of causally defined key features and paths in controlling LLM behavior.

title: Record Grouping Controls Evidence Weight in Language Models
summary: Retrieved records are presentation units; a supplied partition determines which records enter a language model as one evidential contribution. We characterize the invariant group-content state that removes within-group copies while retaining complementary canonical content, show that equal group counts can encode different evidence states, and derive a sharp content-aware partition-error bound. Given a supplied partition, our pre-generation representation deduplicates and aggregates content within groups and bounds each group's contribution. Across 104,402 trials and 6 public checkpoints, a central natural-text intervention finds that content-fixed false splits add 10.27-32.66 percentage points and false merges remove 9.13-31.79 points; a matched six-slot control retains the positive direction in all 16 cells. In a new 48-item controlled campaign panel, changing the supplied partition produces measurable, checkpoint-dependent decision shifts across all four models, and the balanced mirror design exposes substantial order interactions. Together, the theory and experiments establish the supplied partition as a controllable pre-generation representation variable and characterize its checkpoint-dependent behavioral effects.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how grouping retrieved records into partitions before feeding them to a language model affects what evidence the model effectively sees, develops a theory of this “supplied partition” as a representation variable, and demonstrates substantial behavioral effects from changing partitions.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented and multi-document LLM setups assume that the way we group or split retrieved records before generation is a neutral design choice. However, multiple records may share overlapping content, differ canonically, or be redundantly presented. There is little formal understanding of how these groupings change the effective evidential state seen by the model, how to remove redundancy while preserving complementary information, and how errors in grouping (splitting or merging records incorrectly) affect model behavior. The authors aim to formalize this and show that the partition itself is a powerful, controllable variable that shapes model decisions.
AI.method: The authors treat retrieved records as presentation units and define a “supplied partition” that determines which records are grouped together as a single evidential contribution to the language model. They formally characterize an invariant group-content state that, for each group, removes within-group duplicate content while preserving complementary canonical content. Using this framework, they show that different partitions with the same number of groups can encode different evidential states and derive a sharp, content-aware bound on the error introduced by partitioning. Practically, they introduce a pre-generation representation that, given any partition, deduplicates and aggregates group content and bounds each group’s influence. Empirically, they run 104,402 trials across six public LLM checkpoints with a central natural-text intervention to estimate how false splits (incorrectly separating evidence) and false merges (incorrectly combining evidence) affect performance, and they also design a 48-item controlled “campaign panel” with a balanced mirror design to test decision shifts and order interactions across four models.
AI.result: In large-scale experiments with 104,402 trials on six public checkpoints, they find that when content is held fixed, false splits in the supplied partition can increase measured performance by 10.27–32.66 percentage points, while false merges can decrease performance by 9.13–31.79 points; a matched six-slot control condition preserves the overall positive direction of these effects in all 16 tested cells, indicating robustness. In a separate 48-item controlled campaign panel, varying only the supplied partition leads to measurable and checkpoint-dependent shifts in model decisions for all four tested models. The balanced mirror design in this panel also reveals substantial order effects in how evidence groups are processed.
AI.conclusion: The supplied partition—the way retrieved records are grouped before being given to a language model—acts as a key pre-generation representation variable that can be deliberately controlled. Their theory shows how to define partition-invariant group content by deduplicating within groups, and provides content-aware error bounds for mis-specified partitions. Their experiments demonstrate that even with fixed underlying content, different partitions induce sizable, checkpoint-dependent behavioral changes and order interactions in LLMs. Thus, system designers should treat the partitioning of evidence as a primary design lever rather than a superficial formatting detail.

title: OntologyBench: Can Dense Retrieval Satisfy Structured Biomedical Constraints?
comment: 19 pages and 1 figure. Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Main conference. https://openreview.net/forum?id=RMiOTIub1j&noteId=RMiOTIub1j
summary:
We introduce OntologyBench, a tiered biomedical retrieval benchmark comprising 471,854 training and 125,744 evaluation query-document relevance pairs across concept grounding, relational retrieval, and compositional phenotype-based retrieval.
  Although these tasks can be tractable using ontology-aware reference methods, across task tiers, embedding performance is generally lower on relational and compositional tasks than on concept-grounding tasks. Fine-tuning on ontology-derived supervision improves performance on several relational and compositional tasks, whereas the evaluated reranking and LLM-based candidate-scoring methods provide little or no end-to-end improvement. Errors frequently reflect diseases matching only subsets of the phenotype evidence.
  These findings indicate that the evaluated embedding and reranking configurations do not reliably recover the compatibility encoded by the selected ontology relations and phenotype combinations and motivate retrieval systems that better integrate learned representations with structured biomedical knowledge.

AI.tldr: OntologyBench is a large, tiered benchmark to test biomedical retrieval systems on concept, relational, and compositional phenotype-based queries, revealing current embeddings and rerankers struggle especially with relational/compositional reasoning.
AI.motivation: To systematically evaluate how well modern retrieval and embedding methods understand and leverage structured biomedical ontologies—especially for complex relational and phenotype-based queries, which are increasingly important in biomedical research and clinical decision support.
AI.method: The authors construct OntologyBench, a benchmark with hundreds of thousands of query-document relevance pairs derived from biomedical ontologies. It has tiers for concept grounding, relational retrieval (based on ontology relations), and compositional phenotype-based retrieval (combining multiple phenotypic features). They compare ontology-aware reference methods with neural embedding models, test fine-tuning using ontology-derived supervision, and evaluate reranking and LLM-based candidate scoring pipelines. Error analysis focuses on mismatch patterns such as partial phenotype matches.
AI.result: Embedding models perform relatively well on simple concept-grounding tasks but significantly worse on relational and compositional retrieval compared to ontology-aware baselines. Fine-tuning on ontology-derived supervision improves several relational and compositional tasks, but reranking and LLM-based scoring offer little or no overall improvement. Many failures involve diseases that match only subsets of the query’s phenotype evidence rather than fully capturing the intended combination and relations.
AI.conclusion: Current embedding and reranking configurations do not reliably capture or retrieve the compatibility information encoded in biomedical ontologies, particularly for relational and compositional phenotype-based queries. The benchmark demonstrates a gap between learned representations and structured knowledge and highlights the need for retrieval systems that tightly integrate neural representations with explicit biomedical ontology structures.

title: Improving Term Evaluation in Machine Translation: Variation Matters
summary: Terminology evaluation in machine translation (MT) usually assumes a single correct target form per source term. However, human translators routinely introduce variation that current metrics penalize as inconsistency. We examine how to account for this variation in document-level MT evaluation of English-French scientific translation, combining glossary-based accuracy, translation consistency, and a new cross-term variation (CTV) diagnostic measure that tests whether variation relationships are preserved across languages. Based on analyses of two parallel corpora, translated by four MT systems, we find that (1) MT systems generate less target-side variation than human translators; (2) transfer patterns strongly depend on the variation type; (3) consistency rankings vary with the choice of metric; and (4) constraining MT with a glossary improves accuracy and consistency but degrades CTV by suppressing valid variation. We argue for variation-aware evaluation that conditions consistency penalties on whether target-side variation mirrors source-side variation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a variation-aware way to evaluate terminology in machine translation, showing that systems are overly rigid compared to humans and that enforcing glossaries can hurt natural variation.
AI.motivation: Standard terminology evaluation in MT assumes one correct translation per term and treats any variation as an error, while human translators naturally vary terminology in systematic ways. This mismatch leads to misleading assessments of MT quality, especially at the document level. The authors want to better capture when variation is appropriate and when it constitutes a real inconsistency.
AI.method: They analyze English–French scientific translations in two parallel corpora produced by four MT systems and by humans. They combine glossary-based term accuracy, standard translation consistency metrics, and introduce a new cross-term variation (CTV) diagnostic that checks whether patterns of variation between related terms in the source are preserved in the target. They compare variation and consistency across systems and humans and examine how glossary constraints affect these measures.
AI.result: The study finds that MT systems exhibit less variation in target terminology than human translators; the way variation is transferred depends strongly on the type of variation; system rankings for consistency differ depending on which metric is used; and constraining MT output with a glossary increases term accuracy and within-term consistency but harms CTV by eliminating many legitimate variations that humans use.
AI.conclusion: Terminology evaluation for MT should be variation-aware rather than enforcing a single-form ideal. Consistency penalties ought to consider whether target-side variation appropriately reflects source-side variation, and metrics should explicitly distinguish harmful inconsistency from valid, linguistically motivated variation. Glossary use must be balanced against the need to preserve natural and meaningful variation across terms.

title: Safe Harness Self-Evolution: A Theoretical Analysis of Feasibility and Limits
summary: Harness self-evolution is the process by which an agent modifies its prompts, tools, code, or orchestration in response to task feedback while keeping the underlying language model frozen, with changes persisting across subsequent tasks. We provide a systematic theoretical analysis of the feasibility and limits of safe harness self-evolution, connecting modification generation, finite-data certification and selection, safe adoption, and behavior after an update. Under a fixed user-task distribution, we establish conditions guaranteeing overall expected-reward improvement while controlling changes on retained tasks, characterize the probability of generating qualified modifications, and derive finite-data bounds for safe selection and adoption. Our analysis shows that generation and certification impose distinct constraints: current task performance does not determine the probability of generating qualified modifications, and generating more candidates need not improve the guarantee of a successful update when evaluation is limiting. Stagnation may therefore arise even when improvement opportunities remain. We further show that worst-case evaluation cost for recognizing genuine improvements diverges as expected reward approaches its upper bound. Across successive updates, certified improvement guarantees accumulate over a finite run, but a successful update does not by itself guarantee that further improvement remains possible. These results provide a basis for diagnosing bottlenecks and designing safer self-evolution mechanisms.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically analyzes when and how an AI system can safely modify its own prompts, tools, and orchestration (without changing the underlying model) based on feedback, while ensuring performance improves and harmful regressions are controlled.
AI.motivation: As AI agents become more autonomous, they increasingly modify their own configuration (prompts, toolchains, code) to improve performance. However, it is unclear under what conditions such "self-evolution" is guaranteed to be beneficial and safe, especially with limited evaluation data. There is a need for a formal framework that relates modification generation, evaluation, and adoption to overall performance and safety guarantees.
AI.method: The authors perform a formal, theoretical analysis. They model a fixed distribution over user tasks and define harness self-evolution as updates to the agent’s configuration with the base language model held fixed. They then derive conditions and probabilistic bounds for: (1) when updates improve expected reward overall while constraining behavior on previously seen tasks, (2) the likelihood that generated modifications are actually qualified (beneficial and safe), and (3) the finite-data guarantees of selection and adoption procedures based on limited evaluation. They analyze how these pieces interact over successive updates.
AI.result: They show that: (1) one can guarantee expected-reward improvement while bounding changes on previously retained tasks under certain conditions; (2) the probability of generating qualified modifications is not determined by current performance; (3) when evaluation is the bottleneck, simply generating more candidate modifications need not improve the chance of a successful certified update; (4) stagnation can occur even when improvement opportunities exist; (5) the worst-case evaluation cost needed to reliably detect genuine improvements diverges as performance nears the theoretical maximum; and (6) over multiple updates, improvement guarantees can accumulate over a finite run, but a successful update does not imply that further improvement is still possible.
AI.conclusion: Safe harness self-evolution is feasible but fundamentally constrained by the interplay between modification generation and limited evaluation. There are inherent limits on how reliably and cheaply one can detect and adopt genuine improvements, especially near performance ceilings. The theoretical results clarify where bottlenecks arise and offer guidance for designing self-evolving AI systems that can improve while maintaining safety guarantees.

title: Evolution of Multimodal Question Answering: From Modality-Adaptive Extraction to Unified Language Representation
summary: The rapid growth of multimodal data has intensified the need for question answering (QA) systems capable of reasoning across heterogeneous sources such as text, tables, and images. In this paper, we present a comprehensive methodological comparison of three influential frameworks, namely Multimodal Adaptive Extraction (MAE), Solar, and UniMMQA, tracing the evolution of multimodal question answering from modality-adaptive pipelines to fully unified architectures. We examine how each approach models cross-modal interactions, transforms heterogeneous inputs, and performs reasoning, highlighting key design differences in modality representation, reasoning, and answer generation. Our analysis demonstrates a clear shift from explicit modality-specific processing toward unified text-centric formulations enabled by pre-trained language models (PLMs). Empirical comparisons across benchmark datasets show that this transition leads to substantial improvements in both Exact Match (EM) and F1-Scores, with UniMMQA achieving the most consistent and scalable performance. Despite these advances, we identify persistent challenges, including information loss during modality transformation, error propagation in multi-stage pipelines, and limitations in capturing fine-grained cross-modal dependencies. Overall, this study provides a deeper understanding of current design trends and offers insights into the future direction of unified multimodal reasoning systems.

AI.tldr: The paper compares three multimodal QA frameworks (MAE, Solar, UniMMQA), showing a field-wide shift from modality-specific pipelines to unified, PLM-based text-centric architectures, with UniMMQA performing best but leaving open challenges in information preservation and fine-grained cross-modal reasoning.
AI.motivation: With the explosion of multimodal data (text, tables, images), there is a need for QA systems that can reason jointly over these heterogeneous sources. Many frameworks exist, but their differing architectures and design choices are not systematically compared, making it hard to understand how the field is evolving and which approaches scale best.
AI.method: The authors conduct a methodological and empirical comparison of three representative multimodal QA frameworks: MAE, Solar, and UniMMQA. They analyze how each framework represents different modalities, models cross-modal interactions, transforms inputs, and performs reasoning and answer generation. They then benchmark them on standard datasets, evaluating Exact Match and F1 scores.
AI.result: The study finds a clear trend: moving from modality-adaptive, pipeline-style systems (like MAE and Solar) toward unified, text-centric formulations powered by pre-trained language models. This unified approach, embodied by UniMMQA, yields higher and more consistent EM and F1 scores across benchmarks, indicating better performance and scalability.
AI.conclusion: Unified, PLM-based text-centric architectures represent the current state-of-the-art direction in multimodal QA, outperforming older modality-specific pipelines. However, challenges remain in avoiding information loss during modality transformation, mitigating error propagation in multi-stage setups, and modeling fine-grained cross-modal dependencies. The paper concludes with insights and guidance for designing future unified multimodal reasoning systems.

title: Less Is Personal: Learning Minimal Sufficient User Profiles for Personalized Language Models
summary: Retrieval-augmented personalization enables large language models to produce more accurate and preference-aligned outputs using relevant records retrieved from user histories. Personalized language models typically prepend a fixed number of retrieved user records, even when additional history is redundant, harmful, or unrelated to a user's distinctive behavior. We study minimal sufficient personalization: constructing the least costly ordered profile for each input while preserving the utility achievable from a retrieved candidate pool. We introduce ENOUGH, a method that iteratively appends behavioral records or emits STOP to construct profiles with adaptive lengths. Offline, bounded counterfactual search evaluates profile prefixes by jointly considering downstream gains, user specificity, and token costs. The resulting long-horizon targets are distilled into a multi-head value controller with explicit ranking and stopping supervision. At inference, the controller selects and orders records through lightweight decisions, and the frozen generator is invoked once after stopping. Extensive experiments on six personalized tasks demonstrate that ENOUGH consistently outperforms strong heuristic and retrieval-augmented baselines in both effectiveness and efficiency, achieving minimal sufficient profiles that preserve personalization utility while reducing unnecessary context costs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ENOUGH, a method to build minimal, cost-efficient personalized profiles for retrieval-augmented LLMs by adaptively selecting only the most useful user history records while preserving personalization performance.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized LLM systems naively prepend a fixed number of retrieved user history records, which can be redundant, irrelevant, or even harmful, and always increases context length and token cost. There is a need for a principled way to determine how much and which user history is actually necessary for effective personalization, balancing personalization gains against context and computation costs.
AI.method: They formalize "minimal sufficient personalization" as constructing the shortest, cheapest ordered profile from a pool of candidate user records that still preserves the achievable utility. The proposed method ENOUGH iteratively appends behavior records or emits a STOP decision. Offline, it uses a bounded counterfactual search over profile prefixes, jointly evaluating downstream task performance, user-specificity, and token cost to create long-horizon supervision targets. These targets are distilled into a multi-head value controller that learns to rank records and decide when to stop. At inference time, this controller, separate from a frozen generator, makes lightweight sequential decisions to select and order records and then stops, after which the generator is run once with the constructed profile.
AI.result: On six personalized tasks, ENOUGH yields better effectiveness (personalization performance) and efficiency (shorter profiles, fewer tokens) compared to strong heuristic and standard retrieval-augmented baselines. It achieves near-preservation of personalization utility while substantially reducing redundant or unnecessary context, demonstrating that adaptive profile construction can outperform fixed-length or naive retrieval strategies.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, value-based control over which user records to retrieve and how many to include allows LLM personalization systems to maintain or improve personalization quality while cutting context and token costs. ENOUGH offers a practical framework for learning minimal sufficient personalized profiles by combining offline counterfactual search with an online controller, and can replace heuristic fixed-k retrieval in a wide range of retrieval-augmented personalization settings.

title: Experience Funnel: A State-Policy Alternating Loop for Self-Evolving Agents
summary: Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) continuously accumulate experience through interaction, creating an opportunity to improve future behavior through self-evolution. A fundamental challenge is how to transform abundant, task-specific interaction experience into reusable model competence without sacrificing the ability to adapt rapidly to newly observed evidence. Explicit textual states, such as skills and agent harnesses, provide fast, human-readable and editable adaptation, but incur persistent dependence on external context; parametric policies provide compact and reusable competence, but are substantially slower to update. We present \textit{Experience Funnel}, a self-evolving framework that couples fast state adaptation with slow policy consolidation in an alternating loop. Interaction trajectories are first distilled into an explicit textual state, where newly acquired experience can be rapidly incorporated and validated. The framework then selectively identifies state-enabled behavior that remains useful across state revisions and consolidates it into the policy through transition-aware distillation. The updated state--policy pair subsequently generates new rollouts, providing fresh evidence for the next round of state adaptation and policy consolidation. Experiments across diverse agent benchmarks show that \textit{Experience Funnel} consistently improves agent capability over state-only evolution and policy-internalization approaches, while progressively converting useful explicit experience into autonomous policy competence.

AI.tldr: Experience Funnel is a self-evolving framework for LLM-based agents that alternates between fast updates to an explicit textual state and slower consolidation of stable behaviors into the model’s parametric policy, progressively turning interaction experience into reusable competence.
AI.motivation: LLM-based autonomous agents accumulate rich, task-specific interaction data, but there is no straightforward way to convert this into general, reusable capabilities. Existing approaches either keep knowledge in external, human-editable textual states (fast to update but brittle and context-dependent) or embed it directly in the model’s parameters (compact and reusable but slow and expensive to update). The paper aims to bridge this gap by enabling agents to benefit from both rapid adaptation to new evidence and long-term consolidation of stable skills.
AI.method: The authors propose Experience Funnel, a two-timescale self-evolution loop for LLM agents. First, new interaction trajectories are distilled into an explicit textual state (e.g., skills, rules, harnesses), allowing rapid incorporation and validation of fresh experience. Second, the system detects behaviors that are consistently enabled by this state and likely to remain useful across subsequent state revisions; these behaviors are then distilled into the model’s parametric policy via transition-aware distillation, which respects how states transition during trajectories. The updated state–policy pair is used to generate new rollouts, and the process repeats, iteratively refining both state and policy.
AI.result: Across a variety of agent benchmarks, the framework outperforms methods that rely only on evolving explicit state or only on internalizing experience into the policy. Empirically, Experience Funnel yields higher task success and more robust behavior, while steadily transferring frequently useful, state-mediated behaviors into the model’s parameters, thereby reducing dependence on external context over time.
AI.conclusion: Experience Funnel effectively couples fast, editable textual-state adaptation with slower, principled policy consolidation, enabling LLM agents to self-evolve from raw interaction data. This design enhances performance, maintains adaptability to new evidence, and gradually converts explicit, task-level experience into autonomous model competence, offering a practical route toward continually improving LLM-based agents.

title: Does Deeper Reasoning Compromise Alignment? Revealing and Mitigating of Alignment Collapse in Large Reasoning Models
summary: The emergence of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) has established a robust foundation for Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). While deep reasoning is widely believed to enhance safety alignment, the stability of alignment mechanisms under extended reasoning remains underexplored. This paper challenges the prevailing view by revealing a critical vulnerability: Deep Reasoning May Induce Alignment Collapse. To rigorously quantify this phenomenon, we propose the Alignment Loss Rate (ALR) metric. Our experiments demonstrate that as reasoning depth increases, ALR rises significantly, indicating a severe degradation in model robustness against external perturbations. Capitalizing on this instability, a novel jailbreaking paradigm, Reasoning Trap (RT), is proposed. RT induces the model into extended reasoning to amplify the impact of adversarial attacks, leading to a sharp decline in safety capabilities. To elucidate the mechanism behind this collapse, we identify Attention Dilution as the root cause, arising from the competition for attention between the extended reasoning process and the original input. To mitigate this, Reasoning Residual Alignment (RRA), a lightweight defense strategy that dynamically re-emphasizes the input via residual connections integrated with the reasoning process.

AI.tldr: The paper finds that making language models reason in longer chains can actually weaken their safety alignment, introducing a measurable vulnerability exploitable by new jailbreak attacks, and proposes both a metric to quantify this and a lightweight defense method.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-Thought reasoning is widely used to improve large models’ reasoning abilities and is often assumed to help safety, but it is unclear how stable alignment remains as reasoning depth increases. There is growing concern that long reasoning traces may introduce new attack surfaces, yet there is no standard way to measure how alignment deteriorates with deeper reasoning or why this happens internally.
AI.method: The authors define Alignment Loss Rate (ALR) as a quantitative metric to capture how often or how strongly alignment fails as the model’s reasoning depth grows, then empirically study models under varying chain-of-thought lengths and external perturbations. Based on their findings, they design a new attack method, Reasoning Trap (RT), which deliberately pushes the model into extended reasoning to magnify adversarial effects. They analyze internal attention behavior and identify a pattern they term Attention Dilution, where attention resources are competitively drawn away from the original input toward the growing reasoning trace. Finally, they propose Reasoning Residual Alignment (RRA), an architectural or decoding-time adjustment that re-injects or re-weights the original input via residual connections during the reasoning process and test its defensive effect against RT and related attacks.
AI.result: Experiments show that Alignment Loss Rate increases markedly with deeper reasoning, indicating that models become significantly more vulnerable to perturbations and jailbreak prompts as chain-of-thought length grows. The Reasoning Trap attack, which exploits this property by inducing long reasoning chains, leads to substantial drops in safety performance compared to baseline attacks. Analysis of attention patterns supports the Attention Dilution hypothesis, showing that attention mass shifts from the input to intermediate reasoning steps as depth increases. Applying Reasoning Residual Alignment reduces ALR and mitigates the effectiveness of RT, improving robustness under extended reasoning with relatively low overhead.
AI.conclusion: Deep chain-of-thought reasoning, while beneficial for task performance, can destabilize safety alignment and create a new class of vulnerabilities, formalized via the Alignment Loss Rate metric. This vulnerability can be systematically exploited through the Reasoning Trap jailbreak, primarily driven by Attention Dilution in the model’s attention mechanisms. Introducing Reasoning Residual Alignment, which keeps the original input salient throughout the reasoning process, helps counteract this collapse and offers a lightweight, practical defense. The work implies that safety alignment must be reconsidered in the context of long reasoning traces, and that future LRM designs should explicitly address attention competition between inputs and generated reasoning steps.

title: When Models Defer to Wrong Answers: A Robustness Audit of Source-Attributed Cues in Multiple-Choice QA
comment: Work Accepted at GroundLM Workshop at EMNLP 2026
summary: Language models often receive a question together with a claim about what another source answered. We audit whether such claims destabilize answers in multiple-choice question answering. For each item, we hold one wrong option fixed across misleading conditions and vary the cue template attached to it. We introduce \emph{neutral-conditioned misleading cue adoption rate} (NC-MCAR), which measures switches to that option only on valid cued trials where the same model first selected the gold answer under a neutral prompt. This is a measure of answer instability, not proof that the model knew the answer or that all deference is irrational. We evaluate four instruction-following models on MMLU-Pro and IndicMMLU-Pro in English, Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, and Telugu. Across 220{,}000 outputs, the expert template yields 41.1\% aggregate NC-MCAR, compared with 12.5\% for the majority template. These two conditions use the same wrong option and final instruction. Filler accuracy remains well above expert-wrong accuracy, while correct-cue prompts have high valid-response accuracy. The audit documents answer instability relevant to grounding under the tested forced-choice prompts: a bare, unverified source claim can outweigh an answer that was previously consistent with the task evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how claims about what an external source supposedly answered can destabilize language-model multiple-choice answers, introducing a metric (NC-MCAR) to quantify how often models switch from a previously correct answer to a specific wrong option when it is misleadingly cued.
AI.motivation: Language models increasingly act in settings where they see not just questions but also claims about what other sources or experts supposedly answered. These secondary claims may not be verified, yet models may defer to them. The authors want to understand to what extent such unverified source claims can cause models to change previously correct answers in multiple-choice tasks, which matters for reliability, grounding, and robustness of model behavior.
AI.method: The authors design an audit using multiple-choice QA benchmarks (MMLU-Pro and IndicMMLU-Pro) across several languages. For each question, they pick one wrong choice and attach different cue templates that misleadingly indicate another source chose that wrong option. They first run each model with a neutral prompt to identify items where the model chooses the correct answer. Then, on those same items, they add misleading cues and measure how often the model switches from its earlier correct answer to the cued wrong one. They define the neutral-conditioned misleading cue adoption rate (NC-MCAR): the fraction of such valid trials where the model changes its answer to the fixed wrong option. They test four instruction-following models with different cue types (e.g., “expert” vs “majority”) while keeping the wrong option and final instruction fixed across these conditions.
AI.result: Across roughly 220,000 model outputs, misleading cues substantially change answers. When the wrong option is framed as what an expert supposedly answered, the aggregate NC-MCAR is 41.1%, meaning that in more than two-fifths of cases where the model was previously correct, it later defers to the misleading expert cue. With a majority-based cue, NC-MCAR drops to 12.5%, even though the same wrong option and final instruction are used, indicating strong sensitivity to the nature of the cue. Filler conditions retain high accuracy, and prompts with correct cues show high valid-response accuracy, confirming that the effect is not simply due to noise or confusion but to specific misleading attributions.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that instruction-following language models can exhibit significant answer instability when exposed to bare, unverified claims about what another source purportedly answered. Under forced-choice prompts, such misleading source cues can override answers that were previously aligned with the question’s evidence. This instability is particularly strong when the cue invokes an expert source, posing a challenge for grounding, reliability, and safe deployment in settings where models must weigh external claims against their own task-based reasoning.

title: Bridging the Semantic-Utility Gap in Multimodal RAG via Generator-in-the-Loop Alignment
comment: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) augmented with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) benefit from access to external evidence. However, standard retrievers and rerankers optimize for semantic similarity rather than answer utility, creating a preference gap: documents that appear relevant may not help the generator produce a correct answer. Motivated by this, we propose a two-stage generator-in-the-loop alignment framework that closes this gap without human document-level relevance annotations. Our framework consists of two stages: in Stage 1, a VLM generates a hypothetical text passage from the image-query pair, which is used as the retrieval query for dense text search, bridging the image-to-text modality gap. In Stage 2, a cross-encoder reranker adapted with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is fine-tuned using answer-supervised preference pairs mined from the frozen VLM: given the dataset answer label, a candidate document is labeled positive if the VLM produces the correct answer when given that document as context, and negative otherwise. This generator-guided signal is compatible with multiple alignment loss functions, including contrastive (triplet) loss, pairwise direct preference optimization (DPO), and supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and supports periodic re-mining to refresh preference pairs as the reranker improves. Experiments on VQA-X and A-OKVQA with Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct show that our proposed framework consistently outperforms rank-order, random, and REPLUG-style likelihood baselines under various alignment losses and pool size settings, suggesting that answer-level generator feedback is an effective supervision signal for preference alignment.

AI.tldr: They propose a generator-in-the-loop, two-stage alignment framework for retrieval-augmented vision-language models that optimizes retrieval based on answer utility instead of semantic similarity, improving VQA performance without human relevance labels.
AI.motivation: In retrieval-augmented VLMs, retrievers and rerankers are typically trained for semantic similarity, not for whether retrieved documents actually help the model answer correctly. This causes a preference gap: texts that look relevant may not improve or may even harm answer accuracy. Moreover, obtaining human document-level relevance annotations is expensive, especially in multimodal (vision+language) settings where bridging image-to-text retrieval is hard. The authors want an automatic way to align retrieval with answer usefulness, leveraging the generator itself as a supervision source and avoiding manual labels.
AI.method: They design a two-stage, generator-in-the-loop framework. Stage 1: Given an image and query, the VLM generates a hypothetical text passage that describes or elaborates on the query, and this synthetic passage is used as the query for dense text retrieval, helping bridge the modality gap from image+text to text-only search. Stage 2: They adapt a cross-encoder reranker with LoRA and train it using preference pairs mined automatically from the frozen VLM. For each candidate document and a sample’s gold answer, a document is labeled positive if the VLM answers correctly when conditioned on that document as context, and negative otherwise. These positive/negative pairs supervise the reranker with various loss formulations (contrastive/triplet, DPO, or SFT). They periodically re-mine preference pairs as the reranker improves, making the supervision iterative and self-improving.
AI.result: On VQA-X and A-OKVQA benchmarks, using Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as backbones, their framework outperforms several baselines, including rank-order selection, random retrieval, and REPLUG-style likelihood-based reranking. The gains hold across different alignment objectives (triplet, DPO, SFT) and different pool sizes, demonstrating robustness of the approach. The experiments show that answer-supervised, generator-guided reranking leads to higher question-answering accuracy than traditional semantic-similarity-based or likelihood-based strategies.
AI.conclusion: The work shows that using answer-level feedback from a frozen vision-language generator is a powerful signal to align retrieval and reranking components toward answer utility, without needing human relevance labels. Their two-stage framework—query expansion via synthetic passages plus iterative, generator-supervised reranker training—effectively closes the preference gap between apparent semantic relevance and actual usefulness for question answering, yielding consistent improvements on VQA tasks and suggesting a general recipe for aligning RAG pipelines with downstream performance objectives.

title: Evaluating and Improving Evidence-Grounded Fact-Checking in LLMs via Multi-Round Evidence Ablation
summary: Automatic fact-checking systems assess the veracity of claims given evidence from relevant documents. Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in fact-checking due to their general reasoning capabilities. However, it remains unclear whether they faithfully make use of the evidence provided to reach veracity judgments or rely on parametric knowledge. To investigate this, we introduce Fact-Ablated Evaluation (FAE), a new evaluation framework that iteratively ablates the cited evidence to assess whether LLMs revise their predictions accordingly. Our empirical results show that current off-the-shelf LLMs as fact-checking systems rely more on their parametric knowledge than on the evidence provided. To bridge this gap between prediction accuracy and evidence grounding, we propose REAL (Rigorous Evidence Ablation Learning), a training framework that promotes evidence-dependent verification through counterfactual evidence supervision for the LLM-as-verifier models. Experiments on four fact-checking datasets across different domains demonstrate that models trained with REAL obtain superior evidence-dependent capabilities compared to standard fine-tuned models. Our findings highlight that strong fact-checking performance can still coexist with weak evidence dependency, while REAL encourages veracity predictions to remain more closely tied to the availability of supporting evidence.

AI.tldr: They study whether LLM fact-checkers really use provided evidence or just their internal knowledge, and propose a training method (REAL) plus a new evaluation (FAE) to enforce and measure evidence dependence.
AI.motivation: LLMs perform well at automatic fact-checking, but it is unclear if they base their judgments on the given evidence or instead rely mostly on memorized/parametric knowledge. For trustworthy fact-checking, models should change their decisions when the supporting evidence changes or disappears. Existing evaluations focus on accuracy, not on how tightly predictions are grounded in cited evidence, so a new way to measure and improve evidence dependency is needed.
AI.method: 1) Propose Fact-Ablated Evaluation (FAE): given a claim and its supporting documents, iteratively remove (ablate) cited evidence segments and observe whether the LLM’s veracity prediction changes in a way consistent with the loss of support. This quantifies reliance on evidence vs parametric knowledge. 2) Empirically evaluate off-the-shelf LLMs under FAE on multiple fact-checking datasets to assess their evidence dependency. 3) Introduce REAL (Rigorous Evidence Ablation Learning), a training framework that uses counterfactual evidence supervision—training examples where key evidence is removed or altered—to encourage LLM-as-verifier models to base their decisions on the actual evidence and to revise predictions appropriately when evidence is ablated. 4) Fine-tune models with REAL and compare them against standard fine-tuned baselines on several datasets.
AI.result: FAE reveals that current off-the-shelf LLM-based fact-checkers often keep the same veracity predictions even when crucial cited evidence is ablated, indicating a strong reliance on parametric knowledge and weak grounding in the provided documents. Models trained with REAL show significantly stronger evidence dependence: their predictions are more sensitive to the removal or modification of key evidence. Across four fact-checking datasets from various domains, REAL-trained models maintain strong fact-checking accuracy while exhibiting improved alignment between predictions and available evidence, outperforming standard fine-tuning in evidence-dependent metrics.
AI.conclusion: Evidence shows that high fact-checking accuracy of LLMs does not guarantee that they actually use the given evidence; they frequently lean on internal knowledge instead. The proposed FAE framework provides a way to diagnose this issue by testing how predictions change under evidence ablation. REAL training improves the situation, making models’ veracity judgments more tightly coupled to the presence or absence of supporting evidence. This work underscores the need to evaluate and train fact-checking systems not only for correctness, but also for robust evidence grounding and responsiveness to evidence changes.

title: Do Dynamic Routers Need Memory? HeRo: History-Aware Routing for Efficient LLM Inference
summary: Dynamic layer routing reduces the inference cost of Large Language Models (LLMs) by learning to skip layers for individual tokens. Existing methods, however, treat each routing decision as a local operation conditioned solely on the current hidden state which is a formulation that overlooks the sequential, path-dependent nature of routing across depth: earlier decisions shape the representations seen by downstream routers, and the layer-usage objective couples all decisions jointly. We propose History-Aware Routing (HeRo), a dynamic routing framework that resolves this mismatch by introducing a router memory mechanism to maintain an explicit routing state across model depth. The memory is constructed via linear attention, incrementally aggregating preceding routing scores and their induced residual updates into a compact history representation. At each routed layer, the router conditions jointly on this accumulated state and the current hidden representation to select the executed branch. Instantiated for token-wise FFN routing, HeRo trains only lightweight routers and adapters on a frozen backbone, requiring no modification to pretrained parameters. Across Llama 3.1-8B, Llama 2-7B, and Llama 2-13B, HeRo consistently achieves the highest aggregate performance retention among ten baselines. On Llama 3.1-8B, it bypasses 26.87% of model parameters while achieving 100.24% of dense model performance across seven benchmarks, and retains 97.01% while bypassing 38.82% of model parameters under a tighter computation budget. Ablation studies confirm that removing routing history consistently degrades performance, most notably on multistep reasoning and code generation, validating that explicit routing memory enables more accurate and adaptive dynamic routing than solely conditioning on hidden state.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes History-Aware Routing (HeRo), a dynamic layer routing method for LLMs that maintains an explicit routing history across depth, enabling more accurate token-wise layer skipping and achieving strong compute savings with full or near-full performance retention.
AI.motivation: Dynamic layer routing can cut LLM inference cost by skipping layers per token, but existing methods make purely local decisions based only on the current hidden state. This ignores that routing decisions are path-dependent: earlier choices change representations and later options, and the overall layer-usage objective links all routing decisions together. The authors aim to design a routing mechanism that captures this sequential dependency and better exploits the structure of routing across depth, without retraining the backbone model.
AI.method: The authors introduce History-Aware Routing (HeRo), which augments standard token-wise routers with a dedicated routing memory that persists across network depth. This memory is implemented with linear attention over previous routing scores and the associated residual updates, producing a compact history representation. At each routed layer, instead of routing based only on the current hidden state, the router conditions jointly on (1) the current token representation and (2) the accumulated routing history to decide whether and how to execute the feed-forward (FFN) branch. HeRo is realized by training small router and adapter modules while keeping the original LLM backbone frozen, and focuses on token-wise FFN routing over different model sizes (Llama 3.1-8B, Llama 2-7B, Llama 2-13B).
AI.result: On multiple Llama models, HeRo outperforms ten dynamic routing baselines in aggregate performance retention for a given amount of layer skipping. For Llama 3.1-8B, HeRo can skip 26.87% of model parameters while slightly exceeding (100.24%) the performance of the full dense model on seven benchmarks. Under a stricter compute budget, it can skip 38.82% of parameters while still retaining 97.01% of dense performance. Ablations show that when the routing history component is removed, performance drops consistently, especially for multi-step reasoning and code generation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling routing history across depth via a memory mechanism leads to more accurate and adaptive dynamic routing in LLMs than approaches that only use the current hidden state. HeRo demonstrates that a history-aware router with linear-attention memory, trained as lightweight modules on a frozen backbone, can substantially reduce inference compute while matching or nearly matching dense-model performance, particularly benefiting complex reasoning and coding tasks.

title: Evaluation of Contextual Understanding in Large Language Models
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate impressive performance across diverse NLP tasks, yet their ability to exhibit genuine contextual understanding remains uncertain. Traditional evaluation metrics such as perplexity, BiLingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU), or surface-level accuracy fail to reveal how well LLMs extract, integrate, and reason over contextual information--a gap particularly critical in question answering, where models must align responses with contextually grounded knowledge rather than memorized associations. We propose a novel knowledge graph-based evaluation framework introducing Semantic Structural Similarity for KGs (S3KG), a hybrid similarity measure integrating structural and semantic similarity into a continuous evaluation score, alongside a diagnostic framework for categorizing reasoning errors. To validate this pipeline, we evaluate S3KG against established metrics on a curated question-answer (QA) benchmark, demonstrating its effectiveness in measuring correctness, faithfulness, and interpretability in LLM-generated responses.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes S3KG, a knowledge-graph-based metric to better evaluate how LLMs use context in question answering, going beyond surface metrics like perplexity and BLEU.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics (perplexity, BLEU, surface accuracy) cannot capture whether LLMs genuinely understand and reason over contextual information; this is especially problematic in QA, where we need models to ground answers in provided context instead of relying on memorized correlations.
AI.method: Introduce S3KG (Semantic Structural Similarity for KGs), a hybrid knowledge-graph-based similarity measure that combines structural and semantic similarity into a continuous evaluation score. Build a diagnostic framework that categorizes different types of reasoning errors in LLM answers. Apply this framework to a curated QA benchmark and compare S3KG to standard metrics.
AI.result: On the curated QA benchmark, S3KG better captures dimensions such as correctness, faithfulness to the given context, and interpretability of answers compared with traditional metrics. It can distinguish cases where answers are superficially similar but differ in underlying reasoning or grounding.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge-graph-based evaluation via S3KG provides a more informative assessment of LLM contextual reasoning in QA than traditional surface metrics, offering both a continuous similarity score and diagnostic insights into reasoning errors.

title: Qiushi Engine on AstaBench E2E-Bench-Hard
summary: This report analyzes Qiushi Engine v0.8 across all 40 test tasks in AstaBench E2E-Bench-Hard, a benchmark that requires autonomous agents to carry a research question through experimental design, code implementation, actual execution, result analysis, and report delivery. Qiushi Engine is model-configurable; this evaluation selected DeepSeek deepseek-v4pro-preview as the model backend. The official AstaBench leaderboard records a score of 0.816 and an average benchmark cost of USD 15.209 per task, while the full-precision local recomputation is $81.59 \pm 1.87$. Four tasks satisfied every rubric item, yielding a full-task completion rate of 4/40 = 10% -- 7 percentage points above, and about 3.3 times, the approximately 3% best rate reported for AstaBench's official agents. Across 507 required rubric items, 416 were satisfied (82.1%). Official scoring archives and 40 Meta-Trace records show sustained production and verification of reports, code, and experimental artifacts; the principal gaps lie in repeated runs, external dependencies, specified metrics, and ablation studies. The report explains the benchmark, system workflow, aggregate results, representative cases, and limits of interpretation.

AI.tldr: Evaluation of Qiushi Engine v0.8 on AstaBench E2E-Bench-Hard using DeepSeek v4 shows strong autonomous research capabilities, outperforming official agents in full-task completion and rubric coverage, though with weaknesses in repeated experiments, external dependencies, metrics, and ablations.
AI.motivation: To rigorously assess how well a configurable autonomous research agent (Qiushi Engine v0.8) can handle end-to-end scientific workflows on a challenging benchmark, and to compare its effectiveness and cost-efficiency against existing baseline agents on AstaBench.
AI.method: Run Qiushi Engine v0.8, configured with the DeepSeek deepseek-v4pro-preview model, on all 40 tasks in the AstaBench E2E-Bench-Hard benchmark, which requires an end-to-end pipeline from research question to experimental design, coding, execution, analysis, and reporting. Measure rubric item satisfaction (507 total items), full-task completion, benchmark scores, and costs; analyze Meta-Trace records and official scoring archives to characterize behavior and failure modes.
AI.result: Qiushi Engine achieved an official AstaBench score of 0.816 with an average benchmark cost of about $15.21 per task, while full-precision local recomputation cost about $81.59 ± 1.87. It fully completed 4 out of 40 tasks (10%), substantially higher than the ≈3% best reported rate for AstaBench’s official agents, and satisfied 416 of 507 rubric items (82.1%). Trace analysis confirmed consistent generation and verification of reports, code, and experimental artifacts, with main deficiencies in repeated runs, managing external dependencies, adhering to specified metrics, and performing ablation studies.
AI.conclusion: Qiushi Engine v0.8, using DeepSeek v4 as backend, demonstrates strong end-to-end autonomous research capabilities on a hard benchmark, clearly outperforming official AstaBench agents on full-task completion and rubric coverage, but still falls short of ideal scientific practice in areas such as reproducibility, dependency handling, metric compliance, and ablation analyses. The findings are informative but constrained by cost differences, chosen model backend, and the limitations of the benchmark and interpretation scope.

title: The Audit Decides the Verdict: Instrument Effects Rival Demographic Bias in LLM Decision Audits
comment: Accepted to REALM 2026, the 2nd Workshop for Research on Agent Language Models at EMNLP 2026. 10 pages, 3 figures
summary: Whether a language model looks demographically biased can depend on how the audit asks its question. A charitable-aid benchmark reports that the same models favor minority applicants when rating requests one at a time and penalize some when ranking side by side. We test whether that reversal generalizes to hiring, lending, and medical triage: 40,726 requests to five models, applications differing only in the applicant's name, and a primary test fixed before collection. It does not. None of 36 planned contrasts survives correction. The rating advantage keeps its sign at roughly half the published size, and a precision extension bounds any hiring ranking penalty below the published effect, though the lending and triage ranking floors sit above that margin, so the exclusion is conclusive for hiring ranking and for rating in all three domains only. Planted disparities tracking their injected sizes and a directional replication on the original aid materials bound these nulls. The audit is livelier than the demographics: models recognize transparent audits nearly always, tie every identical-content comparison whether the varying detail is race or a hobby, and reward first-listed candidates as much as any demographic effect we measure. Audit verdicts reflect audit construction more than demographic bias.

AI.tldr: The paper re-examines claimed demographic biases in language models and finds that reported reversals between rating vs ranking largely do not replicate across hiring, lending, and medical triage; apparent audit outcomes are driven more by audit design than by genuine demographic bias.
AI.motivation: Previous work suggested that large language models exhibit demographic bias that flips sign depending on whether decisions are made by rating individuals one at a time or by ranking candidates side by side. This striking result, especially in a charitable-aid context, raises concerns about the reliability of LLM-based decisions and about the robustness of bias auditing methods. The authors aim to test whether this reversal effect is real, general, and practically significant across high-stakes domains such as hiring, lending, and medical triage.
AI.method: The authors run a large preregistered audit of five language models across three decision domains: hiring, lending, and medical triage. They construct 40,726 prompts representing applications that are identical except for applicant names (which imply demographic attributes). They compare two interaction modes: rating applicants individually and ranking multiple applicants side by side. They define 36 planned contrasts and apply multiple-comparison corrections. They also inject synthetic disparities (planted effects) into the data to validate their detection power and perform a directional replication using the original charitable-aid materials. They analyze whether any observed disparities are consistent, robust, and larger than artifacts of prompt structure, position effects, or the models’ sensitivity to being obviously audited.
AI.result: After applying corrections for multiple tests, none of the 36 preregistered contrasts shows statistically reliable demographic bias in the expected directions. The previously reported rating advantage for minority applicants is still present in sign but is about half as large as in the original study. For hiring, they bound any ranking penalty for minority candidates below the magnitude of the originally reported effect. For lending and triage, the bounds are less tight on ranking, but for rating decisions in all three domains and for hiring ranking, the data are consistent with only very small or null demographic effects. The planted disparities are recovered at approximately their injected sizes, confirming that the null results are not simply due to low statistical power. Additional analyses show that models often detect transparent audit setups, give identical scores when only irrelevant details (e.g., hobby vs race) differ, and exhibit strong position biases such as favoring first-listed candidates—effects comparable in size to any demographic differences observed.
