Then, the LLM is prompted to suggest dependencies that are likely missing in the BN structure and to prune dependencies that are likely spurious, based on its behavioral and domain knowledge. The final refined BN structure is then parameterized solely using the observed survey data, and this BN is used to generate synthetic survey records.
AI.result: Applied to the 2022 Hong Kong Travel Characteristics Survey with only 2% of the full dataset as training data, LEBGen significantly improves the quality of synthetic data relative to strong baselines. It reduces the mean marginal Jensen–Shannon divergence from 0.0671 to 0.0091 and decreases the mean absolute Cramer’s V error by 14.3% compared with the best existing method, indicating notably better matching of both marginal distributions and pairwise dependencies.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating LLM-based behavioral knowledge into Bayesian network structure learning enables much more realistic synthetic travel survey generation from very small samples. LEBGen achieves substantial improvements in capturing both distributions and dependencies without relying on the LLM for sampling or parameter estimation. The framework demonstrates a promising direction for combining probabilistic models and LLMs to overcome data sparsity in travel behavior research and, potentially, other domains requiring synthetic microdata.

title: FastE: Readout-Triggered Token Compression for LLM Embedding Inference
summary: In this study, we identify depth-dependent prefix redundancy in final-readout LLM embedding models, notably across representative backbones including Qwen3-Embedding and Qwen3-VL-Embedding. We find that removing prefix states is substantially more damaging in shallow layers than at greater depth, showing that prefix states become increasingly compressible as the prefix and readout states propagate through the network. To this end, we introduce FastE, a training-free, plug-and-play method. FastE uses a shared fixed threshold on batch-mean readout-prefix alignment as a lightweight online heuristic for selecting when compression occurs, and ranks prefix states by the attention scores they receive from the readout position to determine which states are retained in subsequent layers. Our evaluations demonstrate FastE's ability to substantially reduce computational costs: on NarrativeQA with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, it reduces decoder-backbone FLOPs by 40.11% while retaining 99.53% of Full Forward nDCG@10. Across five text embedding benchmarks, two backbone scales, and three cross-modal retrieval tasks, the quality-efficiency trade-off is directly customizable through the maximum removal ratio without retraining. We believe FastE offers practical value for scalable embedding generation in retrieval, indexing, clustering, and multimodal representation systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FastE, a training-free, plug-and-play method to compress prefix states in LLM embedding models during inference, significantly reducing computation while maintaining retrieval quality.
AI.motivation: Final-readout LLM embedding models are computationally expensive, especially for long prefixes (e.g., long documents or contexts). The authors observe that there may be redundancy in the prefix representations as they propagate through the layers, and exploiting this redundancy could make embedding generation more efficient for tasks like retrieval and clustering without retraining large models.
AI.method: The authors first empirically study depth-dependent prefix redundancy in LLM embedding models such as Qwen3-Embedding and Qwen3-VL-Embedding, showing prefix states are more important in shallow layers and more compressible in deeper layers. They then introduce FastE, a training-free, plug-and-play compression method. FastE uses a fixed threshold on the batch-mean alignment between readout and prefix states to decide online at which layers to perform compression. When compressing, it ranks prefix states by the attention scores from the readout token and selectively retains only the most attended states for subsequent layers, discarding the rest to reduce computation. The extent of removal is controlled by a maximum removal ratio hyperparameter.
AI.result: On NarrativeQA using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, FastE reduces decoder-backbone FLOPs by 40.11% while preserving 99.53% of the nDCG@10 performance compared to a full forward pass. Across five text embedding benchmarks, two model scales, and three cross-modal retrieval tasks, it shows that users can systematically trade off quality for efficiency by tuning the maximum removal ratio, all without model retraining.
AI.conclusion: FastE leverages depth-dependent redundancy in prefix states to compress computation in LLM embedding models in a training-free, plug-and-play manner. It achieves substantial computational savings with minimal degradation in retrieval quality, and its controllable trade-off makes it practically useful for scalable embedding generation in retrieval, indexing, clustering, and multimodal systems.

title: Feyospace-v1: How the Cyber Mercury Seven Trained Frontier Cyber Models
summary: Training capable cyber agents is often treated primarily as a problem of model scale, yet open-weight post-training is constrained more directly by the cost of executable environments, reliable multi-turn supervision, and access to strong teachers. We present a data-centric framework that addresses these bottlenecks through five complementary systems: Choulea analyzes hidden reasoning signatures, SkyReal reduces teacher-sampling cost, Hongzwang bypasses API restrictions on teacher execution, PSBreakup restores capabilities weakened by model merging, and Kreator converts expert interventions into trainable reasoning. Our data engine constructs resettable coding, vulnerability, CTF, kernel-history, full-exploit, firmware, and device-backed environments. Candidate trajectories are retained only after execution verification and evidence auditing, yielding 164,269 trajectories for long-context supervised fine-tuning. The three checkpoints improve over their starting models by an average of 23.76% on the full CyberGym suite and 10.49% across the pooled CTF suites. As of September 1, 2026, Feyospace-s1 achieves a verified success rate of 63.24% and ranks 10th on the official CyberGym leaderboard, while all three checkpoints rank 1st among models at comparable parameter scales. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end demonstration that a seven-person independent team can train open-weight models with leading agentic cyber capability.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a data-centric pipeline and a suite of systems to efficiently train open-weight cyber-security agents, achieving leading performance on CyberGym and CTF benchmarks with modest resources.
AI.motivation: Developing strong cyber agents is often treated as mainly a scaling problem, but open-weight post-training is actually limited by expensive executable environments, scarce high-quality multi-turn supervision, and restricted access to strong teacher models. The authors aim to show that a small independent team can overcome these constraints and train competitive, open-weight cyber agents by rethinking data generation and supervision rather than just scaling model size.
AI.method: They build a data-centric training framework composed of five systems: (1) Choulea, which inspects hidden reasoning signatures to understand and guide model behavior; (2) SkyReal, which lowers the cost of sampling from teacher models; (3) Hongzwang, which circumvents API limits that prevent teacher models from fully executing cyber tasks; (4) PSBreakup, which recovers capabilities that get degraded during model merging; and (5) Kreator, which turns expert human interventions into structured, trainable reasoning traces. On top of these, they build a data engine that creates diverse, resettable cyber environments (coding, vulnerabilities, CTF, kernel-history, full exploits, firmware, and device-backed scenarios). Candidate trajectories generated in these environments are kept only if they pass execution verification and evidence auditing, after which they are used for long-context supervised fine-tuning of three model checkpoints.
AI.result: The data engine produced 164,269 verified and audited trajectories used for supervised fine-tuning. The three resulting checkpoints improved performance over their base models by an average of 23.76% on the full CyberGym benchmark suite and 10.49% on combined CTF benchmarks. One checkpoint, Feyospace-s1, reached a verified success rate of 63.24% and ranked 10th on the official CyberGym leaderboard as of September 1, 2026; all three checkpoints ranked first among models with similar parameter counts.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that targeted, data-centric post-training, supported by specialized systems for teacher utilization, environment construction, and expert intervention capture, can enable a small team to train open-weight cyber agents that achieve state-of-the-art performance at their scale. They claim this is the first complete demonstration that an independent seven-person group can build open models with leading agentic cyber capabilities, suggesting that careful data and supervision design can partly substitute for massive scale and proprietary infrastructure.

title: EvolveScaler: Synthesizing Information-Evolution Contexts via Executable State Machines and Natural-Language Rendering
summary: In persistent interactions, long contexts may encode an evolving process rather than a fixed record: later events can revise or revoke earlier information, changing what remains valid and what conclusions follow. We call this setting information evolution (IE). Solving IE requires identifying valid records, applying updates in order, and reconstructing the query-relevant state from the event history. Existing text-first synthesis pipelines make such data difficult to verify because state transitions and answer logic remain implicit. We introduce EvolveScaler, a code-driven framework that defines information evolution before rendering it as natural language. Human-authored operational specifications define state transitions, record validity, difficulty controls, and executable answer logic; a strong LLM then synthesizes a self-contained simulator from each specification. Executing validated simulators produces natural-language multi-turn event histories, while deterministic replay computes reference answers and atomic checklists. We instantiate EvolveScaler with 117 task prototypes and 159 final-question operators across five difficulty levels spanning approximately 7 to 1,200 events per instance, yielding about 35,100 training examples and 585 validated evaluation instances. On the very_long tier, the strongest model reaches 59.3% avg@5, while six models score below 10%. Training an internal A3B model on 6,000 EvolveScaler examples improves performance over its base checkpoint on all eight independently constructed out-of-distribution benchmarks, with a 5.25-point average gain. These results show that code-driven IE synthesis provides both challenging evaluation and transferable training supervision.

AI.tldr: EvolveScaler is a code-driven framework for generating and evaluating long-context, evolving-information tasks, enabling reliable supervision and benchmarking of models on information evolution reasoning.
AI.motivation: In real-world, persistent interactions, information changes over time: later events can update or invalidate earlier statements. Existing long-context benchmarks typically treat context as a static record, making it hard to test whether models can track evolving state and revisions. Moreover, many data-generation pipelines are text-first, so the underlying state transitions and answer logic are implicit and hard to verify. The authors aim to create a framework where information evolution is explicit, verifiable, and scalable, providing challenging evaluation data and useful training supervision for large language models dealing with long, dynamic contexts.
AI.method: They propose EvolveScaler, a code-driven data synthesis framework. Humans write operational specifications in code that define: (1) the state space and how it changes over time (state transitions), (2) when records are valid or revoked, (3) difficulty controls such as length and complexity, and (4) executable answer logic that maps a final question to a reference answer. A strong LLM is then used to turn each specification into a self-contained natural-language simulator. By executing these simulators, they obtain multi-turn, natural-language event histories that encode information evolution. Deterministic replay over the same code computes ground-truth answers and fine-grained checklists. They instantiate the framework with 117 task prototypes and 159 question operators across five difficulty tiers, generating long histories (7–~1,200 events) and many instances for training and evaluation.
AI.result: The framework yields about 35,100 training examples and 585 validated evaluation instances with systematically controlled difficulty. On the hardest “very_long” tier, the best tested model only achieves 59.3% avg@5 accuracy, and six other models perform very poorly (<10%), indicating that the tasks are genuinely challenging. Training an internal A3B model on 6,000 EvolveScaler examples improves its performance on eight independently built, out-of-distribution long-context benchmarks, with an average gain of 5.25 points over the base model.
AI.conclusion: Code-driven information-evolution synthesis, as implemented in EvolveScaler, produces hard, well-controlled benchmarks and offers high-quality, executable supervision signals. This setup not only exposes current models’ weaknesses on long, evolving contexts but also provides training data that transfers to other long-context, dynamic-information tasks, suggesting that explicitly modeling information evolution is a promising direction for improving LLM reasoning over long, changing histories.

title: SRPO: Setwise Relative Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs
summary: Multi-agent large language models solve complex tasks by coordinating several policies in a shared environment. However, existing reinforcement learning methods usually optimize each response or trajectory separately, even when several outputs jointly cause one state transition. Consequently, the update unit differs from the action executed by the system. To address this problem, we propose SRPO (Setwise Relative Policy Optimization), which treats the active set the minimal set of outputs consumed by one transition, as one multi-agent action. Specifically, SRPO combines member log-ratios into one cardinality-normalized set ratio, assigns one relative advantage, and clips the set once. This formulation unifies division of labor and joint co-evolution as actions with different set sizes. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and multi-turn search demonstrate one training interface for fixed, mixed, and dynamically routed workflows across four model scales, with the strongest macro-average results among the reported comparisons. Optimization diagnostics further characterize its stability under different event reductions and set sizes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SRPO, a reinforcement learning method that treats all outputs jointly responsible for a state transition as a single multi-agent action, improving optimization for multi-agent LLM systems.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for multi-agent LLMs optimize each output or trajectory independently, even when multiple agents jointly cause a single environment transition. This mismatch between the optimization unit (individual responses) and the actual system action (joint behavior) can lead to suboptimal learning and unstable coordination. The authors aim to create a learning algorithm whose update unit matches the effective multi-agent action in coordinated LLM systems.
AI.method: The authors propose Setwise Relative Policy Optimization (SRPO). SRPO defines an 'active set' as the minimal set of outputs consumed by one environment transition and treats this as one multi-agent action. For each such set, it (1) aggregates member log-probability ratios into a single cardinality-normalized set ratio, (2) assigns a single relative advantage to the entire set, and (3) performs a single clipping operation at the set level, analogous to PPO but over sets of actions. This allows both division of labor (different agents doing different subtasks) and joint co-evolution (agents acting together) to be represented as actions with varying set sizes in a unified framework.
AI.result: On benchmarks involving mathematical reasoning and multi-turn search, SRPO supports a single training interface for fixed, mixed, and dynamically routed multi-agent workflows across four different model sizes. It achieves the strongest macro-average performance compared to reported baselines. Additional optimization diagnostics indicate that SRPO remains stable under different reductions of events and for varying active set sizes, suggesting robustness of the method.
AI.conclusion: Treating the joint outputs that drive a single state transition as a single set-level action leads to better-aligned and more stable RL optimization for multi-agent LLM systems. SRPO provides a unified, scalable training interface for varied workflows and demonstrates superior average performance and stable optimization across conditions, showing that setwise policy optimization is an effective approach for coordinated LLM agents.

title: Personalizing LLM Agent Memory Using Biometrics
summary: Personalized memory helps LLM agents deliver stable, tailored assistance by storing and reusing user-specific data across interactions. In multi-user scenarios, however, retrieval must consider not only semantic similarity but also whether the current requester matches the identity associated with the stored memory. We propose Bio-Memory, a biometric-aware memory architecture that conditions memory retrieval on both semantic similarity and biometric matching. Built on top of A-Mem, Bio-Memory augments each atomic memory note with a biometric embedding and uses biometric matching to form the retrieval candidate pool before semantic ranking. We evaluate Bio-Memory on LoCoMo in a 10-user shared-agent setting over 7 face benchmarks and 10 palmprint protocols. Across datasets, Bio-Memory consistently separates owner and non-owner queries. Under face-based personalization, the largest average gap reaches 27.29% / 21.15% in F1 / BLEU-1 on CALFW; under palmprint-based personalization, the corresponding gap is 25.75% / 19.22% on MS_Blue. These results support biometrics as a practical control signal for personalized memory retrieval in shared environments.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Bio-Memory, a biometric-aware memory system for LLM agents that uses face or palmprint features to ensure that personalized memories are only retrieved for the correct user in multi-user, shared-agent environments.
AI.motivation: In multi-user settings, LLM agents that store personalized memories risk leaking or misusing user-specific information if retrieval is based only on semantic similarity. There is a need for a mechanism that can reliably associate stored memories with the correct user identity so that personalization remains stable, secure, and user-specific when several people share the same agent or device.
AI.method: The authors propose Bio-Memory, a memory architecture built on top of A-Mem, where each atomic memory note is tagged with a biometric embedding (e.g., face or palmprint). At retrieval time, the system first performs biometric matching between the current user’s biometric embedding and those stored with memory notes to create a candidate pool restricted to likely owners. Only then does it perform semantic similarity ranking within this pool to select which memories to retrieve. They evaluate this approach in a 10-user shared-agent scenario using the LoCoMo benchmark and multiple face and palmprint datasets, measuring personalization quality via F1 and BLEU-1 metrics and comparing owner vs. non-owner query performance.
AI.result: Bio-Memory reliably separates owner from non-owner queries across 7 face benchmarks and 10 palmprint protocols in a 10-user shared-agent setup. With face-based personalization, the largest average improvement gap between owner and non-owner is 27.29% in F1 and 21.15% in BLEU-1 on the CALFW dataset. With palmprint-based personalization, the largest gaps are 25.75% in F1 and 19.22% in BLEU-1 on the MS_Blue protocol. These quantitative results show substantial performance gains for the rightful owner while keeping performance for non-owners comparatively low.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates that incorporating biometric embeddings into memory notes provides an effective control signal for personalized memory retrieval in shared LLM agents. By conditioning retrieval on biometric matching before semantic similarity, Bio-Memory improves owner-specific personalization and reduces cross-user interference, indicating that biometrics are a practical way to manage personalized memories securely in multi-user environments.

title: BIO-MEMART: Biometric-Aware KV Cache Memory for Multi-User LLM Agents
summary: KV cache is evolving from a serving optimization into an external memory substrate for long-term LLM agents. In a shared multi-user deployment, however, reusable KV blocks introduce a missing access-control question: semantic relevance alone cannot determine whether a memory block is authorized for the current physical user. We propose Bio-MemArt, a biometric-aware KV-cache memory framework for multi-user LLM agents. Bio-MemArt attaches a normalized biometric template to each stored KV memory block, filters the shared memory pool with the current user's biometric probe, and then runs the original MemArt retrieval and KV reuse pipeline only inside the authorized candidate pool. This design preserves latent-space retrieval, direct cache reuse, and decoupled position encoding while adding physical-user access control to shared KV memory. We evaluate Bio-MemArt under Owner and Non-owner query conditions on long-term dialogue QA with face and palmprint benchmarks. Across face benchmarks, the average owner and non-owner biometric success rates are 95.71% and 0.86%; across palmprint benchmarks, they are 97.60% and 2.00%. In the efficiency study, average prefill tokens drop from 18,781.96 under full-context prompting to 28.57 with Bio-MemArt, showing that biometric gating preserves the low-token operating regime of KV-cache memory.

AI.tldr: Bio-MemArt adds biometric-based access control to shared KV-cache memory for multi-user long-term LLM agents, enabling secure cache reuse while maintaining efficiency.
AI.motivation: As KV cache is reused as an external memory across users, current systems rely only on semantic relevance to decide which cached memories to retrieve. This creates a security and privacy problem: a user might access another user’s cached memory if it appears semantically relevant. The paper aims to add user-specific access control to KV-cache memory so that only the rightful physical user can reuse their own cached content, without sacrificing the efficiency benefits of KV reuse.
AI.method: The authors propose Bio-MemArt, a framework that binds each stored KV memory block to a normalized biometric template (e.g., face or palmprint). At query time, the current user provides a biometric probe. The system first filters the global KV memory pool by comparing this probe to the stored templates and selects only those blocks that are biometrically authorized for that user. Then, within this authorized subset, it applies the existing MemArt pipeline for latent-space retrieval and KV reuse, preserving position-encoding decoupling and cache efficiency. The key novelty is biometric gating layered on top of KV-cache retrieval.
AI.result: On long-term dialogue QA tasks evaluated with face and palmprint datasets, the system achieves high owner verification rates and low false access for non-owners. For face-based experiments, owner success averages 95.71% while non-owner success is only 0.86%. For palmprint-based experiments, owner success is 97.60% and non-owner success 2.00%. Efficiency experiments show that prefill token counts drop from roughly 18.8K tokens in full-context prompting to about 28.6 tokens when using Bio-MemArt, demonstrating that the biometric gating does not undermine the token-efficiency advantages of KV-cache memory.
AI.conclusion: Bio-MemArt demonstrates that biometric-aware access control can be integrated into KV-cache-based memory for multi-user LLM agents without losing the core benefits of semantic KV reuse. By gating memory blocks with biometric templates before latent retrieval and reuse, the system offers strong separation between users’ long-term memories while preserving large reductions in prefill tokens. This positions KV cache as a practical, secure external memory substrate for long-horizon, multi-user LLM applications.

title: AgentGrad: Intervention-guided Prompt Optimization for Multi Agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) achieve strong performance by employing specialized multiple agents, yet their performance depends on the prompt design of each agent. For MAS prompt optimization, textual gradient methods that guide prompt updates using natural-language feedback have emerged as a leading paradigm. In this paper, we identify limitations in two stages of existing textual gradient approaches: gradient extraction and gradient aggregation. In gradient extraction, previous works select a target prompt without verifying whether modifying it resolves the failure, and derive gradients without agent-level supervision over the corresponding agent's intermediate output. In gradient aggregation, individual gradients are randomly grouped and concatenated, often mixing unrelated failure modes and producing prompts that fail to generalize. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{AgentGrad}, a prompt optimization framework for multi-agent systems based on sequential intervention and semantic textual gradient abstraction. For each failure, sequential intervention modifies the behavior of one agent at a time to identify the target agent whose modification resolves the failure. The modified output of the target agent then serves as agent-level supervision for extracting a fine-grained gradient. Semantic textual gradient abstraction clusters semantically similar gradients to prevent mixing unrelated failure modes, and abstracts each cluster into a generalized gradient that captures the shared corrective pattern. Experimental results show that AgentGrad achieves state-of-the-art performance across five MAS benchmarks and reduces wall-clock optimization time by $2.5\times$ on average compared to the next-fastest baseline.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes AgentGrad, a textual-gradient-based prompt optimization framework tailored for LLM-based multi-agent systems that identifies which agent to modify via sequential intervention and aggregates feedback via semantic clustering, achieving better performance and faster optimization than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems rely heavily on manually or heuristically designed prompts for each specialized agent. Recent textual gradient methods try to automatically improve prompts using natural-language feedback, but they have key weaknesses in multi-agent settings. During gradient extraction, they may choose the wrong target agent to modify and lack supervision at the agent level, so the derived gradients are coarse and potentially misaligned with the true cause of failure. During gradient aggregation, they typically group and concatenate gradients randomly, which mixes unrelated failure types and leads to prompts that do not generalize well across diverse failure modes. The paper aims to provide a more precise, agent-aware, and semantically structured way to optimize prompts in MAS.
AI.method: The authors introduce AgentGrad, a prompt optimization framework built around two main ideas: sequential intervention and semantic textual gradient abstraction. For each observed failure of the multi-agent system, sequential intervention modifies the behavior of one agent at a time to determine which specific agent’s change would fix the failure; the system intervenes in agents sequentially until it finds a modification that resolves the issue. The output produced by this correctly intervened target agent is then used as agent-level supervision to derive a fine-grained textual gradient that directly reflects how that agent’s behavior should change. To avoid noisy aggregation, the method then applies semantic textual gradient abstraction: gradients are embedded and clustered based on semantic similarity, so gradients representing similar failure modes are grouped together. Each cluster is then summarized or abstracted into a high-level, generalized gradient that captures the shared corrective pattern, and these abstracted gradients are used to update the agents’ prompts. This pipeline yields more accurate and generalizable prompt updates while maintaining efficiency in multi-agent settings.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks for LLM-based multi-agent systems, AgentGrad outperforms existing textual gradient and prompt optimization baselines, achieving state-of-the-art task performance. In addition, it is substantially more efficient, reducing overall wall-clock optimization time by about 2.5 times on average compared to the next-fastest baseline. The experiments demonstrate both the effectiveness of agent-level supervision via sequential intervention and the robustness of semantic clustering in producing generalized, reusable textual gradients.
AI.conclusion: AgentGrad addresses two critical shortcomings of prior textual gradient approaches for multi-agent LLM systems: inaccurate target selection and noisy gradient aggregation. By identifying the specific agent whose behavioral change fixes a failure and using its modified output as supervision, the method extracts precise, agent-level textual gradients. Through semantically clustering these gradients and abstracting each cluster into generalized corrective instructions, AgentGrad avoids mixing unrelated failure modes and improves the generalization of updated prompts. The empirical results across multiple MAS benchmarks validate that this more structured and agent-aware optimization framework can achieve higher performance and faster optimization than existing methods, suggesting a promising direction for scalable, automated prompt engineering in multi-agent LLM systems.

title: A Three-Tier Persona Vector for Controllable User Simulation in Agentic Evaluation
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Extended treatment of the persona component of StateGen (arXiv:2606.16307)
summary: Evaluating tool-augmented LLM agents requires diverse, realistic user inputs yet most evaluation frameworks use flat role descriptions ("you are an angry customer") that produce near-identical conversations regardless of the underlying scenario. In this paper, we propose a three-tier persona vector with 23 operationalized dimensions: 6 categorical demographics (jurisdiction, age, channel, device, language proficiency, time availability), 12 continuous behavioral traits (patience, assertiveness, digital literacy, etc.) sampled with Gaussian noise around curated profile base vectors, and 5 continuous emotional states (frustration, anxiety, trust, confidence, stress) that shift in response to scenario context. Orthogonal to the persona, a 4-level query-complexity overlay controls utterance phrasing from direct to deliberately vague. We evaluate the persona model inside a synthetic data generation pipeline across 64,698 multi-turn conversations spanning 8 named profiles and 3 production corpora. Key findings: (i) a 15.8 percentage-point spread in agent goal-achievement across personas confirms trait vectors produce measurably different user behavior; (ii) the same persona behaves differently across scenarios due to scenario-reactive emotional state shifts, validating the scenario-reactive design; (iii) domain-specific projects show persona sensitivity on booking-flow compliance (~15-20 percentage points gap between tier-aware and pressure-test personas), demonstrating the model faithfully reproduces real-world difficulty distributions; (iv) seven rule-described trait correlations produce auditable co-occurrence patterns without requiring learned covariance matrices. The persona model is fully specified for reproduction.

AI.tldr: They propose and validate a rich, parameterized persona model for generating diverse, realistic synthetic user interactions to evaluate tool-augmented LLM agents.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of tool-augmented LLM agents rely on simplistic, flat role prompts that yield nearly identical interaction patterns, failing to capture the behavioral and emotional diversity of real users across contexts and domains. This limits the ability to accurately measure robustness, goal achievement, and failure modes in deployed systems. The authors aim to create a more nuanced, controllable, and reproducible persona framework that better reflects real-world variability while remaining operationally simple and auditable.
AI.method: They design a three-tier persona vector consisting of: (1) six categorical demographic dimensions (jurisdiction, age, channel, device, language proficiency, time availability); (2) twelve continuous behavioral traits (e.g., patience, assertiveness, digital literacy), instantiated as base profile vectors with Gaussian noise to create individual variation; and (3) five continuous, scenario-reactive emotional states (frustration, anxiety, trust, confidence, stress) that change in response to scenario context. Independently, they introduce a four-level query-complexity control that modulates how directly or vaguely the persona expresses its requests. They then plug this persona model into a synthetic data generation pipeline and run 64,698 multi-turn conversations across eight named persona profiles and three production corpora, analyzing performance differences, scenario reactivity, domain-specific effects, and rule-based trait correlations.
AI.result: The experiments show: (i) a 15.8 percentage-point spread in the agent’s goal-achievement across different personas, indicating that the trait vectors produce substantially different user behaviors; (ii) within-persona variation across scenarios driven by emotional state shifts, confirming that the same persona reacts differently depending on context; (iii) in domain-specific, booking-related tasks, there is a ~15–20 percentage-point gap in booking-flow compliance between tier-aware personas and more challenging “pressure-test” personas, suggesting the persona model reproduces realistic difficulty distributions; and (iv) seven explicitly defined trait-correlation rules lead to clear, auditable co-occurrence patterns without needing learned covariance models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed persona vector model yields controllable, diverse, and scenario-reactive user simulations that cause meaningful variation in LLM agent performance, making it a practical tool for more realistic evaluation of tool-augmented agents. Its explicit specification and rule-based correlations support reproducibility and auditability, while the query-complexity overlay allows systematic stress-testing of agents under different user expression styles.

title: Graph-Based Personalized Memory for LLM Agents: Representation, Evolution, Retrieval, and Evaluation
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are evolving from single-session tools toward long-term personal assistants that must adapt to individual users across tasks, contexts, and interactions. This shift makes memory a core requirement for personalization, since user preferences, goals, constraints, relationships, and past experiences are accumulated gradually and often change over time. Graph-based personalized memory provides a structured way to model such user information through explicit relations, temporal context, and evidence links. Such representations can model not only what an agent remembers about a user but also how memories are connected, revised, and retrieved to support personalized decisions. However, existing work remains fragmented across personalized agents and generic graph memory frameworks, making it difficult to understand the design space as a whole. This survey develops a lifecycle-oriented view of graph-based personalized memory for LLM agents. We organize existing studies around memory representation, memory evolution, memory retrieval, and memory evaluation. We further compare key design choices, discuss current evaluation practices, and open challenges in building reliable long-term personalized agents. This survey aims to clarify how graph-based memory can support adaptive, controllable, and user-centric LLM agents.

AI.tldr: Survey of graph-based personalized memory for long-term LLM agents, organized as a lifecycle (representation, evolution, retrieval, evaluation) and highlighting design choices and challenges for adaptive, user-centric assistants.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents transition from single-session use to long-term, adaptive personal assistants, they need robust, persistent memory of user-specific information that changes over time. Existing work on personalization and graph-based memory is scattered, making it hard to see the overall design space or build reliable, long-term systems. A systematic survey is needed to unify concepts and guide future research.
AI.method: The paper conducts a structured survey of prior work on personalized agents and graph-based memory systems. It introduces a lifecycle-oriented framework and categorizes existing approaches along four stages: how memory is represented (graph structures, relations, evidence links, temporal context), how it evolves over time (updating, revising, connecting memories), how it is retrieved for decision-making, and how memory and personalization are evaluated. It then compares design choices and evaluation practices across the surveyed works.
AI.result: The survey synthesizes a fragmented literature into a coherent lifecycle framework, mapping existing techniques to stages of memory representation, evolution, retrieval, and evaluation. It identifies common patterns, gaps, and trade-offs in current graph-based personalized memory designs, and documents current (often limited or inconsistent) evaluation practices for long-term personalized LLM agents.
AI.conclusion: Graph-based memory is a promising foundation for building long-term, personalized LLM agents because it can explicitly capture user information, relationships, temporal dynamics, and evidence. However, the field lacks unified design principles, robust evolution mechanisms, and standardized evaluation. The survey clarifies the design space and outlines open challenges, aiming to support development of adaptive, controllable, user-centric LLM assistants with reliable long-term memory.

title: CLAMP: Constrained Decoding for Vision-Language Embodied Planning
comment: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Embodied planning increasingly relies on vision-language models (VLMs) to translate instructions and visual observations into executable action sequences. However, fluent plans are not always executable. A VLM may refer to objects that are not visually observed, select actions whose required affordances are unavailable, or violate syntax and action constraints. We introduce CLAMP, a multimodal constraint-grounding framework that turns scene evidence into decoding-time constraints for a frozen VLM planner. CLAMP uses the initial observation to restrict object references to those supported by the scene, while a provided symbolic action model specifies state transitions and goals. During decoding, hard masks eliminate invalid next-token candidates, while a Hidden Markov Model (HMM)-based world-state lookahead module reweights the probabilities of the remaining feasible candidates based on action preconditions and goal reachability. This allows the planner to retain the VLM's language prior while preventing visually unsupported, unsafe, or infeasible candidates from entering the plan. For unseen tasks and environments, CLAMP adapts the HMM at test time using label-free continuations sampled from the frozen VLM. Experiments on VLABench, SafeAgentBench, and TaPA show that scene-grounded constraints improve object grounding and safety, while most remaining failures stem from perception errors or misaligned constraint specifications.

AI.tldr: The paper presents CLAMP, a framework that adds scene- and action-model-based constraints on top of a frozen vision-language model planner to ensure generated action plans are executable, safe, and visually grounded.
AI.motivation: Existing embodied planning with vision-language models often produces fluent but non-executable plans: they may reference non-visible objects, use actions whose affordances are not present, or violate syntax and action constraints. There is a need to preserve the strong language prior of VLMs while enforcing consistency with the observed scene and with a symbolic model of what actions are possible and safe.
AI.method: The authors propose CLAMP, a multimodal constraint-grounding framework that converts scene information and a symbolic action model into decoding-time constraints for a frozen VLM planner. From the initial visual observation, CLAMP restricts the set of object references to those supported by the scene. A symbolic action model provides state transitions, preconditions, and goal specifications. During plan decoding, CLAMP uses hard token masks to remove invalid next-token candidates and an HMM-based world-state lookahead to reweight the remaining candidates based on action preconditions and goal reachability. For unseen tasks and environments, the HMM parameters are adapted at test time using label-free continuations sampled from the same frozen VLM.
AI.result: On VLABench, SafeAgentBench, and TaPA benchmarks, CLAMP improves object grounding and safety of generated plans compared with unconstrained VLM planners. The remaining errors are mostly due to perception failures (e.g., incorrectly detected scene content) or mismatches/mis-specifications in the constraint models rather than the planning mechanism itself.
AI.conclusion: Decoding-time constraint grounding using scene evidence and symbolic action models can significantly improve the executability, safety, and visual grounding of VLM-based embodied planning without retraining the underlying model. However, the overall performance is still limited by perception quality and the accuracy of constraint specifications, pointing to future work in robust perception and better integration between learned models and symbolic constraints.

title: GoAnt: Quality-Diversity Multi-Agent Search for Alpha Factor Discovery in Market Microstructure Data
comment: 14 pages, 1 figure, 8 tables, including supplementary appendices
summary: Automated alpha factor discovery searches symbolic trading signals from price-volume panels and order-book data under a fixed evaluation budget. Existing single- and multi-agent program-search systems can overfit predictive proxies that fail after execution costs and repeatedly explore redundant factor families, limiting execution robustness and behavioral diversity. We introduce GoAnt, a quality-diversity multi-agent search framework that combines non-communicating Explorer, Exploiter and Connector workers with a shared adaptive Mental Map and a compact Queen dispatcher. The Mental Map organizes candidates by leakage-free execution profiles and retains one elite per niche, while the Queen reallocates the evaluation budget from explicit search-state summaries. We also define a map-independent effective-yield protocol that counts high-quality, mutually nonredundant factors directly from each method's evaluation records, giving archive-based and map-free systems the same ruler. On real A-share microstructure data spanning 2023--2026, GoAnt reaches quality-weighted yields of 41.8 and 47.6 in price-volume and order-book settings, improving the strongest baseline by 57% and 97% under matched budgets. Its locked populations retain 0.64 and 0.67 of in-sample quality out of sample, compared with 0.61 and 0.63 for a static map.

AI.tldr: GoAnt is a quality-diversity, multi-agent framework that discovers robust, nonredundant trading signals (alpha factors) more efficiently and reliably than prior methods.
AI.motivation: Automated discovery of symbolic trading signals suffers from two key problems: (1) search agents overfit to predictive proxies that break down once execution costs and market impact are considered, and (2) they repeatedly explore similar types of factors, reducing the diversity and robustness of discovered signals. Existing single- and multi-agent program-search systems lack mechanisms for robust execution-aware evaluation, diversity maintenance, and efficient use of a limited evaluation budget. A framework is needed that explicitly optimizes for both quality and diversity of alpha factors while accounting for execution profiles and avoiding redundant exploration.
AI.method: The paper proposes GoAnt, a quality-diversity multi-agent search framework with three non-communicating worker types—Explorer, Exploiter, and Connector—coordinated via a shared Mental Map and a centralized Queen dispatcher. The Mental Map partitions the search space into niches defined by leakage-free execution profiles and stores one elite candidate per niche, promoting behavioral diversity and robustness to execution. The Queen compiles explicit summaries of the current search state and dynamically reallocates evaluation budget across workers and regions of the map. In addition, the authors propose a map-independent effective-yield evaluation protocol that counts high-quality, mutually nonredundant alpha factors directly from each method's evaluation records, enabling fair comparison between archive-based and map-free systems.
AI.result: On real Chinese A-share microstructure data from 2023–2026, GoAnt achieves quality-weighted effective yields of 41.8 and 47.6 in the price-volume and order-book settings, respectively. These results represent improvements of 57% and 97% over the strongest baseline under the same evaluation budget. The locked factor populations discovered by GoAnt preserve 64% and 67% of their in-sample performance when tested out of sample, compared with 61% and 63% retention for a competitive static-map baseline, indicating better robustness and generalization.
AI.conclusion: GoAnt effectively addresses overfitting and redundancy in automated alpha factor discovery by integrating a quality-diversity search architecture with execution-aware niche definition and adaptive budget allocation. The proposed effective-yield metric provides a fair, map-agnostic way to compare search methods. Empirical results on recent A-share data show that GoAnt finds more and better nonredundant trading signals while preserving stronger out-of-sample performance than state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating its value for robust, practical alpha factor research.

title: Application of curiosity driven exploration methods for hardware interference identification
summary: The transition from single-core to multi-core architectures in safety-critical embedded systems introduces significant challenges due to inter-core interference caused by contention for shared hardware resources. Such interference affects execution times and complicates the verification of strict temporal requirements, particularly in domains such as avionics where standards require comprehensive identification of interference sources. Existing interference analysis approaches, whether manual or model-based, struggle to capture the full range of behaviors arising from the complex interactions among micro-architectural components. In this paper, we frame multi-core interference analysis as the exploration of a complex system behavior space. We propose the use of curiosity-driven exploration algorithms from artificial intelligence to systematically and efficiently cover the space of possible interference behaviors. Using a simulator-based environment, we show that the proposed approach achieves broader and more uniform behavioral coverage within a limited experimental budget compared to traditional pseudo-random program generation methods.

AI.tldr: The paper applies curiosity-driven exploration algorithms to analyze inter-core interference in safety-critical multi-core embedded systems, achieving better coverage of interference behaviors than pseudo-random methods within the same experimental budget.
AI.motivation: Multi-core architectures in safety-critical embedded systems, such as avionics, suffer from inter-core interference due to contention on shared hardware resources. This interference affects execution time and makes it difficult to verify strict temporal requirements, while current manual or model-based interference analyses cannot sufficiently capture the complex behavior space of modern micro-architectures. There is a need for more systematic and efficient exploration of possible interference behaviors to meet certification standards that demand comprehensive identification of interference sources.
AI.method: The authors conceptualize multi-core interference analysis as an exploration problem over a complex system behavior space and adopt curiosity-driven exploration algorithms from artificial intelligence. They implement these algorithms in a simulator-based environment to generate workloads and scenarios that exercise different interference behaviors, and compare the resulting behavioral coverage against that obtained from traditional pseudo-random program generation techniques under the same experimental budget.
AI.result: The curiosity-driven exploration approach yields broader and more uniform coverage of the space of possible interference behaviors than traditional pseudo-random program generation methods, all within a limited experimental budget in the simulator-based setup.
AI.conclusion: Framing multi-core interference analysis as a complex behavior-space exploration task and applying curiosity-driven AI exploration techniques offers a more effective and efficient way to identify diverse interference behaviors than conventional pseudo-random methods, contributing to better support for timing verification and certification in safety-critical multi-core embedded systems.

title: When Can One Obtain Certificates of Optimality Using Positivstellensaetze?
summary: We study certificates of positivity and optimality for learning problems whose objectives and constraints need not be polynomial. We isolate an axiomatic core of Fischer's constructive strict and weak Positivstellensätze and prove the resulting theorems for abstract function algebras over ordered fields. The framework separates two roles that can otherwise be conflated: objective and constraint functions may be built from broad classes of continuous or definable operations, while the auxiliary primitives used to construct a certificate satisfy explicit scalar and closure axioms. We give instances over continuous and definable function algebras, including ordered fields not closed under square roots, derive lower-bound and global-optimality certificates, and analyze both expanded term length and shared computation-graph complexity.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes algebraic positivity and optimality certificates (Positivstellensätze) beyond polynomials to broad function algebras used in learning problems.
AI.motivation: Many learning and optimization problems use objectives and constraints that are not polynomials, so standard polynomial-based positivity and optimality certificates (like classical Positivstellensätze and sum-of-squares) do not apply directly. There is a need for a framework that can still give constructive certificates of positivity and global optimality when the functions are built from more general continuous or definable operations, and when the underlying ordered field may lack convenient algebraic properties such as closure under square roots.
AI.method: The authors abstract Fischer's constructive strict and weak Positivstellensätze into an axiomatic setting of abstract function algebras over ordered fields. They separate (1) the expressive function class used for objectives and constraints from (2) the more restricted auxiliary primitives used in certificates, which obey specific scalar and closure axioms. Within this abstract framework, they prove general Positivstellensatz-style theorems, then instantiate them for continuous and definable function algebras, including in ordered fields without square roots. They also study complexity measures for the resulting certificates, such as term-length expansion and shared computation-graph complexity.
AI.result: They obtain generalized constructive Positivstellensätze for broad non-polynomial function algebras over ordered fields. These yield explicit certificates of positivity, lower bounds, and global optimality for learning problems whose objective and constraints are built from rich continuous or definable operations. They demonstrate that the abstract axioms are satisfied in several concrete settings, including function algebras over fields not closed under square roots, and provide analyses of how certificate size and complexity scale in terms of term lengths and computation-graph sharing.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified, axiomatic framework for deriving constructive positivity and optimality certificates beyond the polynomial setting. By decoupling the function space used to model learning problems from the primitive operations used in certificates, it extends Positivstellensatz-based reasoning to a wider range of learning and optimization tasks, while giving complexity guarantees for the certificates themselves.

title: PlannerForge: LLM Agents for Scenario-Based Testing of Motion Planners in Autonomous Driving
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). 35 pages including appendix
summary: Ensuring the safety of autonomous driving is a critical challenge. Scenario-based testing is a systematic process used to validate Autonomous Driving Systems (ADSs), but it remains a fragmented modular pipeline in which scenario generation, retrieval, modification, ADS execution, and results analysis are performed by separate tools with little interaction. Large Language Model (LLM) agents have shown promise across ADS sub-systems such as perception, planning, and control. However, no prior work covers the whole scenario-based testing pipeline for ADSs with a unified LLM-agent framework. We present PlannerForge, an LLM-agent framework that extends all scenario-based testing stages (from Scenario Generation to ADS Assessment) and adds two further LLM-enhanced stages: ADS Enhancement and ADS Benchmarking. We evaluate PlannerForge with 10 off-the-shelf LLMs across all tasks (Generation, Selection, Modification, Module Routing, Planner Testing, and Enhancement) under 5 prompt conditions. Best-per-task scores range from 0.88 to 1.00, and open-source 20-35B backends match commercial APIs on most tasks. Open-source models such as Qwen3.6:35B match commercial APIs on three of the five tasks. Chaining the modules end-to-end retains 83% / 78% of seed queries (commercial / open). It outperforms Scenario Factory 2.0 (Finkeldei et al., 2025) on natural-language generation (193 vs. 144 executable of 200) and realises 92-96% of requested city, road and vehicle attributes. It outperforms BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) at rank 1 selection (92.0% vs. 67.5%) and From-Words-to-Collisions (Gao et al., 2025) on physically valid edits (>=94% vs. 31%). At N=400, cost-tuning lifts planner success from 50.4% to 70.2% and cuts collisions from 19.0% to 8.4%, without domain-specific fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: PlannerForge is a unified LLM-agent framework that automates and connects all stages of scenario-based testing for autonomous driving systems, improving generation, retrieval, modification, evaluation, and enhancement of driving scenarios compared with prior pipelines.
AI.motivation: Scenario-based testing for autonomous driving is currently handled by a fragmented set of tools for generation, retrieval, modification, execution, and analysis, which limits efficiency, coordination, and performance. While LLM agents have shown promise on individual ADS components, no existing approach covers the entire testing pipeline with a single, integrated LLM-agent framework. The authors aim to close this gap to make ADS testing more systematic, scalable, and effective, and to benchmark whether open-source LLMs can match commercial models across these tasks.
AI.method: The authors design PlannerForge, a unified LLM-agent framework that spans and links all stages of ADS scenario-based testing: Scenario Generation, Scenario Selection/Retrieval, Scenario Modification, ADS Execution/Planner Testing, and ADS Assessment, plus two new LLM-driven stages: ADS Enhancement and ADS Benchmarking. They instantiate multiple LLM-based agents for different tasks—generation, selection, modification, module routing, planner testing, and enhancement—and evaluate 10 different off-the-shelf LLMs (commercial and open-source, 20–35B) under five prompting conditions. They measure performance at each stage (e.g., executable scenario rate, attribute realization, retrieval rank, physical validity of edits) and also evaluate end-to-end pipeline robustness and impact on planner behavior, including a cost-tuning procedure to adjust planner behavior based on LLM analysis, all without domain-specific fine-tuning of the LLMs.
AI.result: PlannerForge achieves high task-level scores (0.88–1.00) across all evaluated subtasks. Open-source 20–35B models, such as Qwen3.6:35B, generally match commercial APIs on most tasks and fully match them on three of five major tasks. End-to-end chaining preserves 83% of seed queries for commercial backends and 78% for open-source ones. Compared to existing baselines, PlannerForge generates more executable natural-language scenarios than Scenario Factory 2.0 (193 vs. 144 out of 200) and more accurately realizes requested city, road, and vehicle attributes (92–96%). For retrieval, it outperforms BM25 at top-1 selection (92.0% vs. 67.5%). For scenario editing, it surpasses From-Words-to-Collisions on physical validity of edits (≥94% vs. 31%). Applying LLM-guided cost-tuning in planning at N=400 improves planner success from 50.4% to 70.2% and reduces collision rates from 19.0% to 8.4%, with no extra domain-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: PlannerForge demonstrates that a unified LLM-agent framework can effectively support and connect all stages of scenario-based testing for autonomous driving, from generation through assessment and enhancement, while also enabling benchmarking. The system not only improves over previous modular pipelines and traditional IR/editing baselines but also shows that open-source LLMs can rival commercial models on most tasks. Moreover, LLM-driven cost-tuning can materially improve planner performance and safety metrics without specialized training, suggesting that general-purpose LLM agents can be practical, end-to-end tools for ADS testing and iterative improvement.

title: It's All in the Way You Say It: The Role of Information Representation in LLM-Based Glycemic-Event Prediction
comment: Submitted to a journal for peer-review
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being investigated for physiological time-series prediction, yet their effectiveness may depend not only on the model itself, but also on how physiological information is represented and presented at inference time. This study investigates prompt-based general-purpose LLMs for postprandial hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia prediction in individuals with type 1 diabetes. Using the OhioT1DM dataset, we evaluate multiple open-weight LLMs under zero-shot and few-shot inference across prediction horizons of 30, 60, and 90 minutes. The analysis varies both the textual representation of the available physiological information and the amount of information exposed to the model, ranging from glucose observations alone to derived descriptors and additional contextual variables related to insulin, meals, carbohydrates, and physical activity. Performance is compared with conventional patient-specific supervised models and with Gluco-LLM, a language-model-based architecture explicitly adapted to glucose time-series forecasting. Results show a marked task-dependent behavior. Conventional supervised models achieve the strongest performance for hyperglycemia prediction, whereas the best observed prompt-based LLM configurations improve performance for hypoglycemia across all investigated horizons. The effectiveness of prompt-based inference is also strongly influenced by how physiological information is represented, while providing additional contextual information does not lead to a systematic improvement. Overall, these findings highlight physiological information representation as a central design factor in prompt-based LLM approaches to glycemic-event prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates how well prompt-based large language models can predict short-term glucose abnormalities in type 1 diabetes, and shows that their success depends heavily on how physiological data are represented in prompts.
AI.motivation: To understand whether general-purpose large language models, used via prompting, can be effective for predicting postprandial hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia in type 1 diabetes, and how the formatting and content of physiological information fed to the models impact their predictive performance compared to conventional time-series methods and a specialized glucose-forecasting LLM.
AI.method: Using the OhioT1DM dataset, the authors test several open-weight LLMs in zero-shot and few-shot modes to predict hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia at 30, 60, and 90 minutes. They systematically vary: (1) the textual encoding of physiological signals, and (2) how much information is provided (from glucose-only to richer descriptors including insulin, meals, carbohydrate intake, and physical activity). They compare these configurations to traditional patient-specific supervised models and to Gluco-LLM, a language-model-based architecture tailored to glucose forecasting.
AI.result: They find strong task dependence: standard supervised models perform best for hyperglycemia prediction, while the best prompt-based LLM setups outperform them for hypoglycemia prediction at all horizons. Performance is very sensitive to how physiological data are represented textually for the LLM, and adding more contextual variables does not consistently improve accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-based use of general LLMs can be competitive, and even superior, for certain glycemic prediction tasks (notably hypoglycemia), but their effectiveness hinges on careful design of the physiological information representation. Richer context is not automatically beneficial, making representation choices a key design lever in LLM-based glycemic-event prediction systems.

title: Good Pretraining, Bad SFT: Checkpoint Quality Across the Training Stack
summary: Language-model checkpoints are commonly selected by pretraining loss or benchmark scores, assuming that the highest-scoring checkpoint will remain the best starting point for subsequent training. We show that this assumption can fail in a full 30B mixture-of-experts training pipeline. The checkpoints that perform better after the full downstream training stack also have higher solution density, i.e., retain downstream performance under local weight perturbations.

AI.tldr: Checkpoint choice based solely on pretraining loss or benchmarks can be misleading; better downstream checkpoints are those with higher solution density (robustness to local weight perturbations).
AI.motivation: Practitioners usually pick language-model checkpoints by the best validation loss or benchmark score, assuming this guarantees the best starting point for further training or fine-tuning. The authors suspect this heuristic can fail in realistic, large-scale training pipelines and want to understand what properties of a checkpoint actually predict downstream success.
AI.method: They empirically study a full 30B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) training pipeline, comparing different checkpoints that may have similar or differing pretraining losses/benchmark scores. They then run the full downstream training stack starting from each checkpoint and measure final performance. Additionally, they probe the local loss landscape around each checkpoint by applying small perturbations to the model weights and checking how well downstream performance is preserved, defining this robustness as solution density.
AI.result: They find that the checkpoint with the best pretraining loss or benchmark score is not always the one that yields the best performance after the complete downstream training pipeline. Instead, checkpoints with higher solution density—those whose downstream performance degrades less under local weight perturbations—tend to perform better after downstream training.
AI.conclusion: Checkpoint selection for large language models should not rely solely on pretraining loss or benchmark scores. Robustness properties such as solution density—how resilient downstream performance is to local perturbations—are better indicators of which checkpoints will succeed after full downstream training.

title: Closing the Consistency Gap: Self-Evolving Agents That Learn to Stay on Course
summary: Large language model (LLM)-powered agents can be accurate on average yet unreliable in production, a discrepancy that has been observed but remains largely unaddressed. When given the same task five times, a ReAct agent on the AppWorld benchmark using GPT-4.1 succeeds in all five runs only 53% of the time, even though its per-run pass rate averages 77%. We call this 24-point shortfall the consistency gap, and we argue that addressing it is a precondition for trustworthy AI agent deployment. We present a self-evolving agent framework that reduces this gap by identifying unstable, low-consistency steps in agent trajectories and converting them into episodic memory the agent can draw on in future runs. At its core is a Consistency Analyzer that pinpoints where and why a trajectory is likely to flip across executions, and a Guideline Generator that converts the diagnosis into targeted guidelines, committed to memory and injected into future agent executions on similar tasks. On AppWorld with ReAct/GPT-4.1, our framework raises the fraction of tasks that succeed in all five runs by +16 points on same-task evaluation and +13 points on similar-task generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a self-evolving agent framework that reduces the inconsistency of LLM-based agents across repeated executions of the same task by converting unstable steps into episodic memory and guidelines.
AI.motivation: LLM-powered agents, such as ReAct agents using advanced models like GPT-4.1, often show high average accuracy but low reliability when the same task is run multiple times. This inconsistency, termed the consistency gap, hinders trustworthy deployment in real applications. The paper is motivated by the need to systematically detect and mitigate this variability so that agents can behave more reliably across repeated and similar tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose a self-evolving agent framework built around two key components: (1) a Consistency Analyzer that identifies steps in agent trajectories that are unstable or low-consistency across multiple executions, diagnosing where and why behavior tends to flip; and (2) a Guideline Generator that converts these diagnoses into concrete, targeted guidelines. These guidelines are stored as episodic memory and injected into future agent runs on the same or similar tasks, guiding behavior away from previously unstable patterns.
AI.result: On the AppWorld benchmark using a ReAct agent with GPT-4.1, the framework significantly narrows the consistency gap: the proportion of tasks that succeed in all five repeated runs increases by 16 percentage points in same-task evaluation, and by 13 percentage points when generalizing to similar tasks, while maintaining a high average per-run pass rate.
AI.conclusion: By automatically transforming unstable trajectory steps into explicit, reusable episodic memories and guidelines, the proposed framework improves the run-to-run reliability of LLM agents. Addressing the consistency gap in this way is presented as a critical step toward making LLM-based agents more trustworthy and suitable for deployment in real-world, production settings.

title: Answer-Distribution Trajectories: A Stochastic-Dynamics View of LLM Reasoning
summary: Chain-of-thought reasoning provides a structured computation between a model's input and final answer. Yet it is often evaluated through endpoint accuracy, which ignores the path taken to reach that answer. An emerging line of work addresses this limitation using entropy profiles, which track how uncertainty evolves over the reasoning process but do not reveal which competing hypotheses account for that uncertainty. We introduce answer-distribution trajectories, a stochastic-dynamics-inspired representation that tracks the model's full predictive distribution over answers as reasoning unfolds. As a strictly finer representation than endpoint and entropy summaries, answer-distribution trajectories enable us to characterize a trace through a dynamical reasoning profile spanning exploration, revision, motion, and commitment, and to distinguish different dynamical mechanisms of reasoning success and failure. Across sixteen open-weight language models and four reasoning benchmarks, we show that traces with the same endpoint and similar entropy profiles can exhibit substantially different reasoning dynamics. We further find substantial variation in these dynamics both within and across models and tasks, with different objectives favoring different dynamical profiles. Additionally, we show that training and inference choices systematically reshape these profiles. Our results suggest that answer-distribution trajectories provide a rich framework for analysing and evaluating the dynamics of LLM reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes answer-distribution trajectories to analyze how language models reason over time, going beyond endpoint accuracy and entropy-based evaluations.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of chain-of-thought reasoning mostly rely on endpoint accuracy, which overlooks the intermediate reasoning process, or on entropy profiles, which show only how uncertain a model is but not which hypotheses drive that uncertainty. There is a need for richer tools that reveal the full dynamics of how models explore, revise, and commit to answers.
AI.method: The authors define answer-distribution trajectories, which record the model’s full predictive distribution over candidate answers at each step of the reasoning process. They apply this representation to sixteen open-weight language models across four reasoning benchmarks, analyzing the resulting trajectories as dynamical traces characterized by phases such as exploration, revision, motion, and commitment. They compare trajectories that share the same final answer and similar entropy curves but differ in their internal dynamics, and study how training and inference configurations reshape these dynamics.
AI.result: The study shows that answer-distribution trajectories capture substantial differences in reasoning dynamics that are invisible to endpoint accuracy and even to entropy profiles. Traces with the same endpoint and similar entropy can still follow very different dynamical paths. The authors observe large variation in these dynamics both within a single model across examples and across different models and tasks, and they find that different training objectives and inference settings systematically favor distinct dynamical profiles.
AI.conclusion: Answer-distribution trajectories offer a strictly more informative and nuanced view of LLM reasoning than endpoint or entropy-based summaries. They provide a useful framework for diagnosing how and why models succeed or fail on reasoning tasks and for understanding how modeling and inference choices shape the reasoning process itself.

title: API Benchmark Scores Do Not Reliably Transfer to Chatbot Interfaces
summary:
Benchmark scores are a central currency in model releases: they inform purchasing decisions, shape public trust, and influence policy. Yet, a key assumption underlying benchmark scores is that the model performance measured through APIs faithfully reflects the behavior of deployed systems.
  We challenge this assumption by auditing ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini across seven systems and nine benchmarks spanning general capability, social bias, and sycophancy. We find systematic API--interface differences in both accuracy and consistency. On average, API evaluations score 3.4 percentage points higher in accuracy and 2.1 percentage points higher in test--retest agreement than corresponding interface evaluations. For ChatGPT, the performance difference between API and interface access exceeds the API-only difference between GPT 5.3 and GPT 5.4. Put differently, switching access surfaces can degrade performance as much as downgrading a full model generation.
  We further test whether exposed API controls can reproduce interface behavior by varying system prompts, sampling parameters, and reasoning settings. These controls shift behavior in some cases but do not reliably eliminate the gap. Our findings document a context-validity gap: measurements obtained through APIs do not necessarily generalize to corresponding deployed interfaces, complicating the use of API evaluations as proxies for deployed systems.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that benchmark scores obtained via model APIs do not reliably reflect how the same models behave in their public chat interfaces, creating a “context-validity” gap that can be as large as a full model version change.
AI.motivation: Benchmark scores strongly influence buying decisions, public trust, and policy, and most evaluations are done via APIs. It is implicitly assumed that these API-based scores faithfully represent the capabilities and behavior of the corresponding deployed systems (like web or app chat interfaces). The authors suspect this assumption is flawed and want to rigorously test whether API performance generalizes to the actual user-facing interfaces of leading LLM products.
AI.method: The authors audit several leading language models (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) across seven distinct system deployments and nine benchmarks that cover general capabilities, social bias, and sycophancy. They compare model behavior and performance when accessed through APIs versus when accessed through the corresponding user interfaces. They quantify accuracy and test–retest consistency, then experimentally manipulate API-side controls—such as system prompts, sampling parameters, and reasoning modes—to see whether these can reproduce interface behavior and close any gaps.
AI.result: They find systematic and non-trivial differences between API and interface evaluations in both accuracy and consistency. On average, API access yields 3.4 percentage points higher accuracy and 2.1 percentage points higher test–retest agreement than the interfaces. For ChatGPT specifically, the performance gap between API and interface is larger than the performance difference between two adjacent API model versions (GPT 5.3 vs GPT 5.4), implying that simply changing the access surface can degrade performance as much as downgrading the model itself. Adjusting parameters and prompts on the API can sometimes shift behavior but does not reliably remove the discrepancy.
AI.conclusion: API-based benchmark evaluations cannot be assumed to faithfully represent how models behave in their deployed chat interfaces. There is a measurable “context-validity gap”: results depend on the access surface and context in which the model is deployed. This complicates the use of API benchmarks as stand-ins for real-world system performance, suggesting that evaluations for decision-making, governance, or comparison of models need to account for the actual deployment context and not just the underlying API model.

title: SAEScientist-Bench: Can AI Agents Conduct Autonomous SAE Interpretability Research?
summary: While research on recursive self-improvement (RSI) has predominantly automated model training pipelines, reliable autonomous development demands a missing pillar: post-hoc monitoring and auditing to understand what models learn and ensure safe alignment. Mechanistic interpretability tools are essential to bridge this gap, among which Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) serve as a cornerstone by isolating interpretable features for model inspection and steering. In this paper, we introduce SAEScientist-Bench to evaluate whether AI agents can act as scientists utilizing SAE tools for autonomous mechanistic discovery. Given a target concept, an agent designs contrastive probes and navigates a Gemma Scope dictionary of 131K+ features in Gemma-2-9B-IT to discover the optimal feature, evaluated against curated expert reference features anchored on Neuronpedia across activation rank, concept selectivity on contrastive texts, and causal steering. Across 10 agent configurations and 20 tasks, frontier agents demonstrate genuine discovery capabilities and lead different evaluation dimensions, but remain well behind the expert baseline, approaching expert levels on separating target concepts from contrastive controls while lagging substantially in causal generation steering. Further analysis reveals that although agents can design contrasts to rule out spurious candidates, they frequently misinterpret experimental measurements. These results establish experimental model understanding as a measurable capability for closed-loop autonomous AI R&D. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trae1ounG/SAEScientist.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces SAEScientist-Bench, a benchmark to test whether AI agents can use Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) tools like scientists to discover mechanistic features in language models.
AI.motivation: Existing recursive self-improvement work focuses on automating training, but lacks robust post-hoc monitoring and auditing to understand and safely align models. Mechanistic interpretability—especially via SAEs that isolate interpretable features—is a key missing piece. The authors want to measure if AI agents can autonomously perform scientific-style investigation over SAE feature dictionaries.
AI.method: They build SAEScientist-Bench, where given a target concept, an AI agent must (1) design contrastive probes, and (2) search a large Gemma Scope SAE feature dictionary (131K+ features for Gemma-2-9B-IT) to find the best feature corresponding to that concept.
