Performance is evaluated against expert-curated reference features from Neuronpedia along three axes: activation rank, concept selectivity on contrastive texts, and causal steering (how well intervening on the feature steers model generations). They test 10 different agent configurations on 20 tasks, and analyze their strategies and failure modes.
AI.result: Frontier agents can perform genuine feature discovery and achieve competitive scores on some metrics, each leading on different evaluation dimensions. However, they still trail the expert baseline overall: they get close to experts on discriminating target concepts from contrastive controls but perform much worse on causal generation steering. The analysis shows agents are able to design reasonable contrastive probes and eliminate spurious candidates, but they often misinterpret experimental measurements, which limits their effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: SAEScientist-Bench demonstrates that experimental model understanding can be operationalized and quantitatively evaluated as a capability in AI agents. Current agents show promising but incomplete competence at autonomous mechanistic discovery with SAEs, particularly struggling with correctly interpreting causal interventions. The benchmark provides a foundation for future work on closed-loop, agentic AI R&D for safer and more interpretable systems.

title: SkillAdam: Stable and Efficient Skill Evolution for Agents
summary: Agent skills provide a lightweight way to equip frozen language-model agents with domain knowledge and procedural guidance, yet obtaining high-quality skills remains costly and difficult to scale. Expert-written skills require substantial human effort. Recent skill self-evolution methods automate an iterative loop that uses execution feedback to revise skills, but their heuristic update strategies often yield unstable optimization and low iteration efficiency. We identify two challenges in realizing stable and efficient skill self-evolution. Direction Stability requires effective corrections to accumulate rather than be overwritten by iteration-local feedback. Update Adaptivity requires the scope of each revision to reflect the consistency of recent case-level improvements. We introduce SkillAdam, an Adam-inspired framework for optimizing discrete and non-differentiable skill documents. As a functional analogue of Adam's first moment, an optimization memory records identified problems and the outcomes of prior solution attempts to stabilize the update direction. As a functional analogue of Adam's second moment, a volatility-driven edit budget tracks the history-weighted variation of recent case-level improvements and adaptively controls the update magnitude. Across seven benchmarks that span short- and long-horizon tasks, SkillAdam achieves state-of-the-art performance with more stable optimization dynamics. It also obtains stronger skills with substantially fewer optimization iterations and lower cost than prior methods. Code repository: https://github.com/ruc-datalab/SkillAdam

AI.tldr: SkillAdam is an Adam-inspired optimization framework to automatically evolve and improve agent skills for frozen language-model agents, achieving more stable, efficient, and cost-effective skill optimization than prior methods across diverse benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Equipping frozen language-model agents with high-quality domain-specific skills is important but costly: expert-written skills require heavy human labor, and existing automatic skill self-evolution approaches rely on heuristic update strategies that are unstable and iteration-inefficient. The authors aim to address two key challenges—Direction Stability (ensuring corrections accumulate rather than being overwritten) and Update Adaptivity (matching revision scope to the reliability of recent improvements).
AI.method: The authors introduce SkillAdam, a framework that treats skill documents as discrete, non-differentiable objects and optimizes them via an Adam-inspired procedure. It maintains an optimization memory that tracks identified problems and outcomes of previous solution attempts, serving as a functional analogue of Adam's first moment to stabilize the update direction. It also employs a volatility-driven edit budget as a functional analogue of Adam's second moment: this budget monitors a history-weighted measure of variation in recent case-level performance improvements and adaptively scales the magnitude of edits (revisions) to the skills. This yields a more principled, optimizer-like process for iteratively revising skills based on execution feedback.
AI.result: On seven benchmarks covering both short- and long-horizon tasks, SkillAdam achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to prior skill self-evolution methods. It shows more stable optimization dynamics, requiring fewer optimization iterations and incurring lower computational and monetary cost, while producing stronger (more effective) skills.
AI.conclusion: SkillAdam demonstrates that ideas from gradient-based optimizers like Adam can be abstracted into a functional framework for optimizing discrete skill documents for language-model agents. By explicitly modeling direction stability via an optimization memory and update adaptivity via a volatility-driven edit budget, the method stabilizes and accelerates skill self-evolution, improving performance and efficiency over heuristic baselines. The work suggests a promising path toward scalable, low-cost automatic acquisition and refinement of agent skills for frozen language models.

title: ExecCritic: Learn to Test, Test to Improve for Coding Agents
summary: Execution feedback can guide coding agents toward correct repository repairs, but only when the tests capture the behavior requested by the issue. Agent-generated tests can encode incomplete or incorrect behavioral targets; when the same trajectory writes both the patch and the test, their errors can agree and create false confidence. We introduce ExecCritic, combining a test--verify--revise scaffold with a role-specific reinforcement learning recipe for training agents within it. The scaffold separates test construction from source-code repair: a Test agent independently generates repository-native tests, a fail-closed harness qualifies and freezes them, and a Repair agent revises source code from their execution feedback without changing the tests. Both roles use Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B as the backbone and are trained separately. In Learn to Test, the Test agent learns to produce behaviorally valid tests that distinguish correct from incorrect patches. In Test to Improve, the Repair agent learns both direct task resolution and feedback-guided revision. On SWE-bench Verified, test quality determines whether feedback helps: holding the base Repair agent fixed, tests from the base Test agent reduce resolved rate from a no-test baseline of 61.2% to 57.3%, whereas tests from GPT-5.6-sol raise it to 65.3%. Role-specific post-training raises the Qwen Test agent's Base-to-Gold success from 22.2% to 62.2%; composing the two post-trained Qwen agents reaches 72.6%, an 11.4-point gain over the original no-test baseline without stronger-model or Oracle feedback at evaluation time. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/execcritic.

AI.tldr: ExecCritic introduces a two-agent, test–verify–revise framework where independently trained Test and Repair agents leverage execution feedback to improve repository repair, achieving substantial gains on SWE-bench Verified without using stronger models or oracle feedback at evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing coding agents benefit from execution feedback only when tests accurately encode the intended behavior. When agents generate both patches and tests in a single trajectory, shared errors can lead to misleading agreement between faulty tests and faulty patches, causing false confidence and limiting reliability. There is a need to decouple test generation from code repair and to systematically train agents to use tests as trustworthy behavioral specifications.
AI.method: ExecCritic defines a scaffold that separates roles and training for testing and repair. A Test agent first generates repository-native tests, which are then filtered and frozen by a fail-closed harness. A separate Repair agent receives only execution feedback from these fixed tests and revises source code but cannot change the tests. Both agents share the Qwen-3.5-35B-A3B backbone and are post-trained independently with a role-specific reinforcement learning recipe: Learn to Test trains the Test agent to produce behaviorally valid, discriminative tests; Test to Improve trains the Repair agent for both direct task solving and feedback-guided iterative repair, all within the test–verify–revise loop.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Verified, the authors find that test quality is pivotal: with a fixed base Repair agent, tests from a base Test agent actually harm performance, dropping resolution from 61.2% (no tests) to 57.3%, while higher-quality tests from GPT-5.6-sol increase it to 65.3%. Role-specific post-training dramatically improves the Qwen Test agent’s Base-to-Gold success from 22.2% to 62.2%. When both post-trained Qwen Test and Repair agents are composed within ExecCritic, the system attains a 72.6% resolved rate, representing an 11.4-point improvement over the original no-test baseline without relying on stronger models or oracle test feedback at evaluation time.
AI.conclusion: Separating test generation from code repair and applying role-specific reinforcement learning within a test–verify–revise scaffold makes execution feedback reliably useful for repository repair. High-quality, independently generated tests are crucial: they transform feedback from a potential liability into a strong signal for improvement. ExecCritic shows that carefully trained Test and Repair agents built on the same backbone model can substantially outperform a no-test baseline on SWE-bench Verified without resorting to more powerful models or oracle supervision, underscoring the value of structured roles and training for feedback-driven coding agents.

title: A Data-Driven Framework for Identifying and Prioritizing RPA Opportunities in Healthcare Processes
summary: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is widely used to reduce administrative burden in United States hospitals, yet an estimated 30-50% of RPA initiatives underperform because processes are selected informally, without a repeatable method to catalogue candidates, prioritize them, match each to an automation tier -- a Python bot, an open-source orchestrator such as n8n, or an enterprise platform such as UiPath -- and forecast financial return before committing resources. We propose a four-module, data-driven framework unifying these decisions: a Process Taxonomy of twenty recurring hospital processes across five value streams; a Prioritization module deriving an Automation Suitability Index from an Analytic Hierarchy Process matrix with an explicit consistency check; a Tool-Tier Selection module recommending the least-cost technology sufficient for a process complexity, integration, and compliance profile; and a Return-on-Investment module quantifying labor savings, error-cost avoidance, payback, and net present value. Applied to a synthetic portfolio spanning all twenty processes, plus a reference data-flow architecture linking it to hospital EHR/payer/ERP systems: 12 of 20 clear the prioritization threshold; the ranking is robust to +/-20% weight perturbation (Spearman correlation 0.83, top-5 set preserved 97.7%, 2,000 Monte Carlo trials); an Automation Risk Index flags four qualifying processes as Critical risk; a budget-constrained portfolio optimization shows diminishing marginal NPV as spend scales from $400K to $1.03M; and a second Monte Carlo analysis shows portfolio NPV stays positive at its 5th percentile. The framework is a conceptual synthesis of the literature rather than an instrument calibrated on primary hospital data; we discuss HIPAA governance and a research agenda for empirical validation. A supplementary Python implementation accompanies the paper.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a structured, data-driven framework to systematically select, prioritize, technology-match, and financially evaluate RPA opportunities in U.S. hospitals.
AI.motivation: Many RPA projects in U.S. hospitals underperform because candidate processes are chosen informally, without a repeatable, quantitative way to catalog processes, assess their automation suitability, select the appropriate automation technology tier, and forecast financial returns and risks before investing.
AI.method: The authors design a four-module framework: (1) a Process Taxonomy of 20 common hospital processes across 5 value streams; (2) a Prioritization module that computes an Automation Suitability Index using Analytic Hierarchy Process with consistency checks; (3) a Tool-Tier Selection module that recommends Python scripts, open-source orchestrators, or enterprise RPA platforms based on process complexity, integration, and compliance attributes; and (4) an ROI module that estimates labor savings, error-cost avoidance, payback period, and NPV. They test it on a synthetic portfolio, use Monte Carlo simulations for robustness and risk, incorporate an Automation Risk Index, and explore budget-constrained portfolio optimization. A Python implementation is provided.
AI.result: On the synthetic portfolio, 12 of 20 processes exceed the prioritization threshold, rankings remain robust to ±20% weight changes (Spearman 0.83, top-5 preserved in 97.7% of 2,000 Monte Carlo runs), four prioritized processes are flagged as Critical risk, and portfolio optimization reveals diminishing marginal NPV as budget rises from $400K to $1.03M. Monte Carlo analysis shows the overall portfolio NPV remains positive at its 5th percentile.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a unified, quantitative way to choose and design hospital RPA initiatives, integrating process taxonomy, prioritization, technology selection, and financial/risk evaluation. It is currently a conceptual synthesis validated only on synthetic data; the authors highlight the need for empirical calibration using real hospital data, under appropriate HIPAA governance, and provide a Python implementation to support future research and practice.

title: Procedural Graphs: Self-Evolving Execution Structures for LLM Agents
comment: 36 pages including references and appendices, 6 figures, 11 tables
summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as agents that plan over long horizons and act through external tools. Most agents select actions through unconstrained generation over an accumulating history, leaving implicit the procedural knowledge of what to do, in what order, and under which conditions. As trajectories lengthen, agents can lose track of their objectives, invoke tools out of order, and repeat unproductive actions. We introduce the Procedural Graph: just as a knowledge graph organizes factual knowledge into (entity, relation, entity) triplets for what-is questions, a Procedural Graph organizes procedural knowledge into (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets for what-to-do questions. At each decision step, the framework localizes the agent's active node, and a guidance model translates the surrounding subgraph into step-level situational guidance that biases the solver's next action without dictating it. The graph is self-evolving: an LLM refiner contrasts failed trajectories with successful ones and edits the graph's topology and attributes, committing edits that preserve or improve held-out validation performance while retaining rejected ones to discourage repetition. Starting from a minimal skeleton, the loop builds graphs that match or surpass hand-designed ones. It can also repair a flawed expert prior. Across multiple datasets, task types, and LLMs, the Procedural Graph delivers consistent gains over memory-based baselines, and self-evolution further improves performance without manual engineering.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Procedural Graphs, a structure for encoding and evolving procedural knowledge to guide long-horizon LLM agents, improving their reliability and performance over memory-only approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents that act over long horizons using tools often generate actions in an unconstrained, purely sequential manner. As tasks and trajectories become longer and more complex, such agents lose track of goals, call tools in the wrong order, and repeat ineffective actions because there is no explicit, structured representation of procedural knowledge (what to do, in which order, under which conditions). The authors aim to provide a framework that makes this procedural knowledge explicit, structured, and improvable over time so agents can act more coherently and efficiently.
AI.method: The authors propose the Procedural Graph, an analogue to a knowledge graph but for procedures rather than facts. Nodes correspond to procedures, and edges encode relations between procedures, forming (procedure, relation, procedure) triplets. During inference, the agent localizes its current position (active node) in the graph, and a guidance model converts the surrounding subgraph into step-level situational guidance that biases—but does not strictly determine—the next action of the LLM-based solver. The graph is updated through a self-evolving loop: an LLM refiner compares failed trajectories with successful ones, proposes edits to the graph’s topology and attributes, and these edits are validated on held-out data. Edits that improve or maintain performance are committed, while rejected edits are stored to discourage repeating past mistakes. The system can start from a minimal skeleton or from an imperfect expert-designed graph and refine it.
AI.result: The Procedural Graph framework yields consistent performance improvements over memory-based agent baselines across multiple datasets, task types, and base LLMs. The self-evolution mechanism further boosts performance beyond the static versions of the graphs. Automatically learned graphs starting from minimal structure reach or exceed the quality and effectiveness of hand-designed procedural graphs and can also correct or enhance flawed expert priors.
AI.conclusion: Encoding procedural knowledge as a self-evolving graph and using it to provide structured situational guidance significantly improves the reliability and effectiveness of long-horizon LLM agents. The Procedural Graph framework not only outperforms memory-only baselines but can autonomously grow from simple initial structures or refine imperfect expert-designed graphs, reducing the need for manual engineering and enabling scalable, data-driven improvement of agent behavior.

title: Deposon: An Auditable, Conservation-Guaranteed, Game-Theoretically Tested Scattering Layer over LLM Reasoning Paths
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures. Author affiliation: School of Chemistry and Life Resources, Renmin University of China. Code: https://github.com/zeroandcat/Deposon
summary: Multi-step LLM reasoning lacks a machine-recheckable ledger: discarded reasoning paths leave no auditable record. We propose the Deposon scattering layer, which binds each node of an LLM-generated concept-decomposition graph to a two-parameter Deposon state; paths undergo three-channel scattering -- transmission, reflection, irreversible dissipation -- obeying T+R+A=1 for arbitrary parameters, with a maximum per-path energy-audit deviation of 2.2E-16 (machine epsilon). We report all three evidence tiers honestly. On synthetic trap benchmarks the path-filtering gain is closed (pre-registered): unified reaches 100% versus a decoy-capture baseline at 7%/10%. On real benchmarks the layer is indistinguishable from a trivial six-keyword rule filter (GSM8K 0.87 >= 0.85, McNemar p=0.5; StrategyQA 0.899 = 0.899); no difference is detected here, so we sharpen the claim to "the differential value lies solely in machine verifiability." Fusion yields a second negative result: convex combinations with a semantic prior never improve (physics 0.484 -> 0.452), and the apparent lambda=2 gain is an anti-field artifact; any fusion gain must be nonlinear. Modeling the reverse dynamics as a potential game on the graph, we evidence an auditable scalar's monotonicity and near-gradientness and quantify the empirical coordination ratio (ECR). The three formalized dynamical-equivalence propositions (P1a/P1b/T-P1c) are falsified under the pre-registered kill protocol, and the potential-game claim is downgraded to approximate (cyclic-graph median residual 0.669): only consistency-level evidence survives at the dynamical level. Code: github.com/zeroandcat/Deposon.

AI.tldr: They introduce a bookkeeping layer for multi-step LLM reasoning that makes every explored reasoning path auditable with machine-precision energy accounting, and show it behaves like a simple keyword filter on real tasks while adding verifiable structure.
AI.motivation: Current multi-step LLM reasoning explores and discards many candidate reasoning paths, but there is no precise, machine-checkable record of which paths were considered, how they were weighted, or why some were discarded. This creates auditability, reproducibility, and verification problems, especially when one wants guarantees about how evidence was handled or wishes to re-check the reasoning ex post. The authors want a principled, physics-inspired mechanism that (1) tracks how “evidence” flows through a reasoning graph, (2) preserves an exact conservation law that can be machine-verified, and (3) exposes all discarded paths so downstream systems or auditors can inspect them. They also want to test whether such a structured, auditable layer provides any practical performance benefit over trivial heuristics on both synthetic and real benchmarks.
AI.method: They define a “Deposon scattering layer” inserted over the graph of concepts or reasoning steps produced by an LLM. Each node in the decomposition graph is associated with a two-parameter “Deposon state,” and each path segment is treated as a scattering event with three channels: transmission (T), reflection (R), and irreversible dissipation/absorption (A), constrained by T + R + A = 1. They implement this as a per-path energy accounting scheme where numerical conservation is enforced to machine precision (deviation around 2.2E-16). The layer records all paths and their associated Deposon states so that all three evidence tiers—transmitted, reflected, and absorbed—are explicitly logged. They run synthetic trap benchmarks where decoy paths are planted to test whether this scattering-based filtering can avoid traps, and compare it with a baseline that captures many decoys. They then evaluate on real benchmarks (GSM8K, StrategyQA) and statistically compare performance to that of a trivial six-keyword rule-based filter using McNemar tests. Additionally, they study “fusion” where Deposon scores are combined convexly with a semantic prior, and they model the reverse flow on the graph as a potential game to analyze whether there exists an underlying scalar potential function with monotone, near-gradient dynamics. They formalize three propositions (P1a/P1b/T-P1c) about dynamical equivalence and test them under a pre-registered kill protocol.
AI.result: The Deposon layer achieves machine-precision energy accounting: per-path deviations from T+R+A=1 are at the level of floating-point machine epsilon (around 2.2E-16), so the energy-audit constraint is effectively exact. On synthetic trap benchmarks, where decoys are intentionally inserted, the Deposon-based unified method reaches 100% path-filtering success, while a decoy-capture baseline only achieves 7–10%, confirming the closed, pre-registered gain in that controlled setting. However, on real-world reasoning benchmarks like GSM8K and StrategyQA, the Deposon scattering layer performs indistinguishably from a trivial rule-based baseline (e.g., GSM8K accuracy 0.87 vs. 0.85 with McNemar p = 0.5, StrategyQA 0.899 vs. 0.899). The authors therefore restrict their claim: the layer’s advantage is not in accuracy but in providing machine verifiability of the reasoning ledger. Fusion experiments, where Deposon scores are linearly combined with a semantic prior, show no genuine benefit; performance can even degrade (e.g., physics benchmark from 0.484 to 0.452), and a previously observed gain at lambda = 2 is identified as an “anti-field artifact,” implying that any true benefit from fusion would have to be nonlinear. In the dynamical analysis, they model reverse dynamics as a potential game and exhibit an auditable scalar with monotone and near-gradient behavior, and they compute an empirical coordination ratio (ECR). Nonetheless, their three formal propositions about strict dynamical equivalence (P1a/P1b/T-P1c) are falsified under a pre-registered kill protocol, and the potential-game characterization is downgraded to approximate, with a median residual of 0.669 on cyclic graphs.
AI.conclusion: The Deposon scattering layer provides a rigorous, machine-auditable ledger over LLM reasoning paths, achieving near-perfect numerical conservation and making all evidence channels—transmitted, reflected, and dissipated—explicitly verifiable. On synthetic trap benchmarks this structure allows perfect decoy rejection, but on real-world tasks it behaves similarly to a simple keyword filter, offering no measurable accuracy gains. Linear fusion with semantic priors fails to improve performance and can mislead through artifacts, suggesting that any useful combination must be nonlinear. The potential-game view of the reverse dynamics only holds approximately; strong equivalence propositions are empirically falsified, leaving only consistency-level support for the dynamical interpretation. Overall, the main contribution is not improved benchmark scores but a formal, checkable framework for tracking and auditing multi-step LLM reasoning, with open questions about how to translate this auditability into concrete performance or reliability gains.

title: Time-Varying Data as Sheaves: an Invitation to Narratives
summary: Modern science and engineering increasingly rely on time-varying data, yet the mathematical tools used to model temporal phenomena are often developed within separate disciplines, obscuring common principles and limiting the transfer of ideas across fields. This chapter presents the theory of narratives, an abstract framework for time-varying objects of any mathematical kind that supports both theoretical investigations and applications. To illustrate this perspective, the chapter develops three vignettes, each illustrating a different research direction. The first addresses a general concern: What information loss can occur when switching between different representations of temporal data? The second concerns structural and algorithmic approaches: How can we systematically decompose time-varying data into simple pieces and obtain invariants describing its structural complexity? The third is an application to control theory: How can we model multi-agent systems with switching communication topologies? More important than any individual vignette, the central message of this invitation is that a suitable abstract perspective can organize and guide research across remarkably diverse mathematical and scientific domains.

AI.tldr: Introduces an abstract, unified framework (“theory of narratives”) for modeling any kind of time-varying mathematical object, showing how it clarifies information loss, structural complexity, and control applications for multi-agent systems.
AI.motivation: Time-varying data is ubiquitous in science and engineering, but different fields use isolated, discipline-specific mathematical tools, which hinders recognition of shared structure and cross-fertilization of ideas. A unifying abstract framework could reveal common principles, enable transfer of methods, and guide research across domains.
AI.method: Define and develop an abstract framework called the theory of narratives for representing time-varying mathematical objects in a common language. Use three detailed vignettes as case studies: (1) analyze information loss when converting between different temporal representations; (2) develop structural and algorithmic tools to decompose temporal data into simple components and extract invariants of structural complexity; (3) build narrative-based models for multi-agent control systems with switching communication topologies.
AI.result: The narrative framework is shown to be expressive enough to encompass disparate temporal phenomena and representations, while supporting rigorous questions about information loss, structural decomposition, and invariants. The three vignettes demonstrate that the same abstract viewpoint yields insights into representation theory of temporal data, algorithmic structure extraction, and modeling challenges in control theory for multi-agent systems.
AI.conclusion: An appropriately abstract perspective—the theory of narratives—can unify the study of time-varying objects across different areas of mathematics and science. By focusing on common structural features rather than discipline-specific formalisms, it can organize existing results, suggest new questions, and guide applications ranging from data representation to algorithms and control of complex systems.

title: Everything in Moderation: Per-Domain Coverage Optima and Alignment-Resistant Domain Gaps in Multi-Domain Mid-Training
summary: Mid-training, the stage between pre-training and alignment, is where a model's per-domain data composition is typically set by data availability rather than principled design. We ask what that decision buys, and whether a later alignment pass can undo it. In a controlled logical-reasoning setting (Qwen3-8B-Base, with a 4B replication; five semantically rule-disjoint KOR-Bench domains) we train 30 allocations spanning the five-domain simplex, 24 sweep configurations plus six withheld from the fit, at five seeds each. Three findings emerge. First, every domain has an interior coverage optimum: the moderate band ($10\%$-$40\%$) is best for all five domains, and a calibrated permutation test for quadratic interiority gives $P\approx0.010$; the fitted mid-training-only curves, with 8B peaks between $9.9\%$ and $35.1\%$, reproduce for curve shape but not peak location. Second, the gaps survive a fixed-budget alignment pass: compensatory SFT raises 116/120 cells (mean $+4.32\%$) yet bridges $0/240$ pairs at a $5\%$ threshold and $30/240$ at a $10\%$ ratio, an equal-budget uniform control behaves almost identically, and a permutation null would bridge $13.8\pm3.3$ and $77.9\pm8.5$ pairs ($P<0.001$). Third, zero coverage collapses mid-training-only accuracy, though a FineWeb-Edu-only control shows the collapse is commingled with generic drift. An exploratory $θ^*$ allocation attains the largest full-pipeline gain ($+4.36\%$ vs. $+0.80\%$/$+0.64\%$\,pp) but is marginal under Welch test.

AI.tldr: Study on how mid-training data allocation across domains affects final logical reasoning performance and whether alignment can fix suboptimal allocations.
AI.motivation: To understand whether the composition of domain-specific data during mid-training is critical for final model performance, and if later alignment (SFT) can compensate for poor domain coverage choices.
AI.method: Use Qwen3-8B-Base and a 4B replication, with five disjoint logical reasoning domains from KOR-Bench. Train 30 different data allocation schemes over the 5-domain simplex, each with five random seeds. Fit performance curves vs. domain coverage and perform statistical tests. Then apply a fixed-budget SFT alignment pass (including a uniform-control condition) to see if it can close performance gaps from mid-training. Analyze a FineWeb-Edu-only control and an exploratory optimized allocation θ*.
AI.result: (1) Each domain has an interior optimal coverage between ~10–40% of training data; too little or too much domain data hurts performance. (2) Performance gaps arising from different mid-training allocations largely persist after alignment; SFT improves scores but does not equalize allocations, with far fewer bridged pairs than expected under a null. (3) Zero domain coverage severely drops accuracy, partly confounded with generic model drift; an exploratory optimized allocation θ* gives the largest gain but is only marginally significant by Welch’s test.
AI.conclusion: Mid-training domain allocation matters in a nontrivial way: there is an optimal intermediate coverage per domain, and misallocations cannot be fully fixed by later alignment. Completely omitting a domain is especially harmful. Carefully designed mid-training allocation can yield modest but real improvements, beyond what alignment alone can recover.

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Approximate Value Iteration in Self-Play
summary: Combining search with function approximation has driven major advances in game-playing programs, making self-play algorithms more competitive than ever. Still, the computational overhead of the most popular methods, based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), can be substantial. In this work, we investigate whether simpler methods remain competitive in non-trivial, moderately sized games such as Connect Four, Hex(7x7) and synthetic games. We train a minimal self-play implementation of Approximate Value Iteration (AVI) and use ground-truth oracles for exact evaluation. Contrary to expectations, our results demonstrate the surprising effectiveness of AVI: it learns more accurate value functions than those learned by AlphaZero, while its one-step-lookahead greedy policies remain competitive with MCTS-based policies at substantially lower training and inference costs. Preliminary experiments on Othello and Go(9x9) show that AVI trains stably on larger games and learns effective value functions. These findings suggest that the success of MCTS-based methods may have eclipsed simpler approaches that have become increasingly practical with modern deep-learning tools.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a simple self-play Approximate Value Iteration (AVI) algorithm can rival or outperform AlphaZero-style MCTS-based methods in several board games, with much lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Modern game-playing AIs (e.g., AlphaZero) typically combine deep neural networks with Monte Carlo Tree Search, achieving strong performance but at high computational and implementation cost. It is unclear whether such complex search is strictly necessary, or if simpler value-based methods can perform competitively in non-trivial games when paired with modern function approximation and self-play. The authors aim to reassess and quantify the competitiveness of simpler methods like AVI in this context.
AI.method: The authors implement a minimal self-play Approximate Value Iteration (AVI) algorithm that uses function approximation to learn value functions from self-play data. They evaluate AVI in several moderately complex games (Connect Four, Hex 7x7, and synthetic games), using ground-truth value oracles for exact state evaluation to measure the accuracy of learned value functions. They compare AVI’s learned values and the strength of its one-step-lookahead greedy policies against AlphaZero-style agents using MCTS, analyzing training stability, sample efficiency, and computational costs. They also run preliminary experiments on larger games like Othello and 9x9 Go to test scalability and stability.
AI.result: AVI learns value functions that are more accurate than those learned by AlphaZero in the tested games. The policies derived from AVI via simple one-step greedy lookahead are competitive in playing strength with policies that rely on computationally expensive MCTS. Moreover, AVI achieves this at substantially lower training and inference cost. Preliminary results on Othello and 9x9 Go indicate that AVI scales to larger games while maintaining stable training and effective value learning.
AI.conclusion: Simple self-play Approximate Value Iteration, when combined with modern function approximation, can be surprisingly competitive with or even superior to MCTS-based methods like AlphaZero in terms of value accuracy, playing strength, and computational efficiency. This suggests that the field may have overemphasized complex MCTS-based approaches, overlooking the practical potential of simpler algorithms that are easier and cheaper to deploy with contemporary deep-learning tools.

title: MeClear: Cooperative Game-Theoretic Attribution and Risk-Aware Memory Clearance for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Long horizon Large Language Model (LLM) agents rely on external memory systems to preserve user preferences and task knowledge across extended interactions. Conventional retrieval mechanisms optimize semantic compatibility rather than downstream utility, frequently introducing outdated, misleading, or conflicting evidence into the active context. We present MeClear, a task conditioned memory clearance framework that identifies memories featuring negative downstream utility through cooperative attribution and selectively suppresses them from agent execution. MeClear combines Leave One Out screening with sampled cooperative Shapley attribution to distribute utility across interacting evidence, effectively resolving redundant conflict masking where single removal evaluations fail. Utilizing attribution rankings, MeClear executes a query scoped minimal clearance strategy over a nested filtration, verifying task recovery on the cleared context without permanently altering the persistent memory bank. Comprehensive experimental evaluations across ten long dialogue memory pools demonstrate that MeClear achieves a target recall of 85.9% and an overall task recovery rate of 82.3%, representing a 25.5 percentage point improvement over Leave One Out (LOO) baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MeClear, a framework to selectively clear harmful or low-utility memories for long-horizon LLM agents, improving task performance without permanently deleting data.
AI.motivation: Long-term LLM agents must store user-specific and task-specific information in external memory, but current memory retrieval methods focus on semantic similarity rather than whether recalled memories actually help the current task. This often pulls in outdated, misleading, or conflicting memories that degrade performance. There is a need for a principled way to detect and suppress such negatively useful memories at query time.
AI.method: The authors propose MeClear, a task-conditioned memory clearance framework. For a given task and its retrieved memories, MeClear estimates each memory’s downstream utility via two components: (1) Leave-One-Out (LOO) screening, which measures the impact on task performance when a single memory is removed; and (2) sampled cooperative Shapley attribution, which allocates utility across interacting pieces of evidence, addressing cases where harmful effects are masked when only one memory at a time is removed. Using the resulting utility-based ranking over memories, MeClear performs a query-scoped, minimal clearance over a nested filtration of candidate subsets—iteratively suppressing the lowest-utility items and checking whether task performance recovers—without modifying the persistent memory store itself.
AI.result: Across ten long-dialogue memory benchmarks, MeClear reaches a target recall of 85.9% (successfully preserving necessary memories) and an overall task recovery rate of 82.3% when starting from corrupted or noisy contexts. This reflects a 25.5 percentage point improvement in recovery over standard LOO-based baselines, indicating that cooperative attribution and minimal clearance substantially enhance robustness to bad memories.
AI.conclusion: Utility-aware, cooperative-attribution-based memory clearance significantly improves long-horizon LLM agent performance in the presence of noisy, outdated, or conflicting memories. By operating query-locally and non-destructively on the context, MeClear enables agents to recover from harmful memory retrieval without permanently altering the memory bank, suggesting a practical path toward more reliable, persistent LLM systems.

title: A Generalization of Amari's Bayesian Duality
summary: Amari's contributions to information geometry and machine learning are well known. Here, we revisit Amari's work on Bayesian duality which has not received as much attention. We connect Amari's Bayesian duality to a convex duality of Bayes' rule. Using this connection, we present a generalization of Amari's Bayesian duality and discuss its relevance for modern artificial intelligence.

AI.tldr: The paper revisits and generalizes Amari’s Bayesian duality by linking it to a convex duality formulation of Bayes’ rule, and discusses its implications for modern AI.
AI.motivation: Amari’s work on information geometry and machine learning is influential, but his notion of Bayesian duality has been relatively underexplored. The authors want to clarify and extend this concept and show its deeper mathematical structure and relevance, especially in the context of current AI and machine learning methods.
AI.method: They reinterpret Amari’s Bayesian duality in terms of convex duality applied to Bayes’ rule, likely casting posterior inference as an optimization problem with a convex objective and its dual. Using this perspective, they propose a more general form of Bayesian duality that subsumes Amari’s original construction.
AI.result: They establish a formal connection between Amari’s Bayesian duality and a convex dual representation of Bayes’ rule. On top of that, they derive a generalized Bayesian duality framework that extends Amari’s original result.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian duality can be understood more broadly through convex duality, which not only recovers Amari’s original ideas but also extends them. This generalized view is argued to be relevant and potentially useful for modern AI, where convex analysis and variational formulations of Bayesian inference are central tools.

title: Co-Evolving Harnesses and Models: On-Policy Correction Helps Weaker Models Catch Up Where Imitation Fails
summary: Agent harnesses (the system prompt, tool set, execution hooks, and context-management scaffolding around a model) are a critical determinant of agentic task success. Automated harness evolution can enable smaller models to perform well on domain-specific tasks at a fraction of frontier-model cost. Since both the harness and model weights shape behavior, we ask how harness evolution and lightweight fine-tuning should be combined. Across seven enterprise agent tasks, we first evolve a harness with the weaker model, then find that a stronger expert often uses it more effectively, suggesting expert supervision could close the remaining gap. However, training the weaker model on the expert's complete trajectories under the evolved harness backfires: performance regresses on all seven tasks by 4 to 30 points across Qwen3-Coder and Gemma 4, even though the same procedure helps under the unevolved harness. Our analysis shows that imitation transfers knowledge and increases scaffold usage, but disrupts model-harness fit: the weaker model adopts the expert's planning strategy without the competence to execute it and no longer matches the harness evolved around its native planning style. We therefore develop an on-policy expert-correction pipeline, automated by a meta-level MLE agent, that localizes the failing turn in the weaker model's own rollout and asks the expert to rewrite only that turn. This preserves the model's planning style and combines the gains of harness evolution and model adaptation. Our results identify and resolve a source of contention between harness and weight updates, yielding a compatibility-preserving recipe for economical co-evolution on domain-specific enterprise tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to jointly optimize agent harnesses (prompts, tools, scaffolding) and model fine-tuning for enterprise tasks, finding naive imitation can hurt and proposing an expert-correction pipeline that preserves compatibility between harness and model.
AI.motivation: Agent performance depends strongly on the surrounding harness, not only on model weights. Smaller domain-tuned systems could rival frontier models if we can automatically evolve both the harness and the model. However, it is unclear how to combine harness evolution with lightweight fine-tuning without the two interfering, especially when using stronger experts to supervise weaker models.
AI.method: Across seven enterprise agent tasks, the authors first use a weaker model to evolve an effective agent harness. They then analyze how a stronger expert model performs under this evolved harness and try to transfer the expert’s behavior to the weaker model via imitation learning on full trajectories. Observing failures, they diagnose the mismatch between the evolved harness and the modified planning style of the fine-tuned weaker model. To fix this, they design an on-policy expert-correction pipeline, orchestrated by a meta-level MLE agent, which identifies failing turns within the weaker model’s own rollouts and asks the expert only to rewrite those specific turns for supervised updates.
AI.result: Direct imitation of expert full trajectories under the evolved harness significantly degrades performance of weaker models (4–30 point drops on all seven tasks) even though the same imitation procedure is beneficial when the harness is not evolved. Analysis shows this training increases use of the scaffolding but breaks the fit between the weaker model’s capabilities and the harness’s assumptions. In contrast, the proposed on-policy expert-correction pipeline successfully combines the benefits of harness evolution and model adaptation, avoiding the performance regressions.
AI.conclusion: Harness evolution and model fine-tuning can conflict: copying an expert’s global planning style can misalign a weaker model with a harness that was evolved around its original behavior. By instead applying localized expert corrections within the weaker model’s own trajectories, it is possible to co-evolve harness and model in a compatibility-preserving way. This yields a practical recipe for getting strong, cost-effective performance from smaller models on domain-specific enterprise agent tasks.
